findings.title: Hind limb set ~15 cm too far forward: acetabulum under the croup peak, horse stands camped under behind
findings.observed: Standing: point of buttock x=-0.858, hip joint -0.515 (directly under the croup peak at -0.525 and 34 cm ahead of the buttock), hock joint -0.614, point of hock ~-0.70, heel ~-0.59, hind toe -0.491. The buttock plumb line falls 16 cm behind the point of hock (17 cm behind the back of the fetlock, ~27 cm behind the heel, 37 cm behind the toe). Fore toe to hind toe is only 1.12 m (0.69 x WH). The quarters overhang the hind legs, which come out of the middle of the rump, and no point of hip shows on the surface.
findings.expected: Side view: a vertical from the tuber ischii touches the point of hock, runs down the back of the cannon and meets the ground 7.5-10 cm behind the heel (Stashak); a limb in front of it is 'standing under behind'. The acetabulum is ~20 cm cranial to the tuber ischii (TB pelvis point of hip to buttock 52.9 cm), with the tuber sacrale and points of hip 25-30 cm cranial to the acetabulum. The model's stifle 110 deg / hock 146 deg already match TB values; moving the hip back ~14 cm with these angles puts the point of hock within 1-2 cm of the plumb line.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to show the claim gets real horses wrong and could not. The core real-horse claim holds.

1) Plumb line. The rule that a vertical from the tuber ischii touches the point of hock, runs down the back of the cannon and lands about 7.5-10 cm (3-4 in) behind the heel is the standard side-view rule in Adams & Stashak's conformation chapter. A limb set forward of it is the recognised fault 'camped under / standing under behind'. I found nothing that makes standing under a Thoroughbred trait. If Thoroughbreds lean either way it is the opposite one: common conformation summaries list TBs among breeds prone to being 'camped out behind' (Wikipedia, Equine conformation, which cites no source for this line). Sickle hocks would keep the point of hock on the line and only slope the cannon forward. Here the point of hock itself is about 16 cm forward (model: buttock x=-0.858, hock joint -0.614, point of hock about -0.70, heel about -0.59, toe -0.491). The heel is about 27 cm ahead of the line against an ideal of 7.5-10 cm, so it is 17-20 cm out. That is far beyond the few centimetres of normal variation in a sound TB. The 00-stand 'hindleg, right side' tile shows the rump hanging well behind the hock.

2) Pelvis and hip joint. I checked Mostafa & Elemmawy 2020 (PMC7316700, 17 sound jumping TBs). They report pelvis 52.9±1.5 cm, thigh 49.8±1.5, back 93.1±1.7, stifle 113.5±2.7°, tarsal 148.9±1.2°. The model's 110°/146° are within about 3° of those, so the claim that its angles 'already match TB values' holds. In equine anatomy (Budras; Sisson/Getty) the acetabulum sits caudoventral to the ilium, roughly 55-65% of the pelvis length back from the tuber coxae. Conformation guides put the hip joint about a third of the way from the point of buttock to the point of hip. With a 52.9 cm pelvis tilted about 25-30°, that leaves about 18-22 cm horizontally from the acetabulum to the tuber ischii and about 25-30 cm from the tuber coxae to the acetabulum. The model has 34.3 cm hip to buttock, with the hip joint directly under the croup peak (−0.515 vs −0.525). That cannot be right on a real horse, because the croup's high point (tuber sacrale) lies well cranial to the hip joint. A geometry check: moving all hind points 14 cm caudally puts the point of hock about 1.8 cm in front of the buttock vertical, as the finding says.

3) Missing point of hip. Fit TBs show the tuber coxae clearly, so its absence from the model's surface is a real defect.

Minor overstatements and caveats (not enough to rate it 'partly'):
(a) The '25-30 cm' fits the points of hip (tubera coxae). The tuber sacrale sits somewhat caudal to them, so the croup's high point is more like 20-25 cm cranial to the acetabulum.
(b) The '~20 cm' from acetabulum to tuber ischii is my estimate from pelvis length and tilt, not a direct measurement. Mostafa measured from photographs, gives no anatomical landmarks and no height at the withers, and studied a small Egyptian group of jumping TBs.
(c) The 'fore toe to hind toe 1.12 m = 0.69 x WH' comparison has no reference. A plumb-line estimate for a TB standing square gives about 0.8 x WH (about 1.3 m), so the direction is right but the norm is not cited.
(d) Measured from its own hip joint, the model's limb is roughly right: a real hind toe stands about under the hip joint. The error is where the acetabulum sits in the pelvis and trunk, not the limb's angles. The finding's own reasoning already says this. Since body length (point of shoulder to buttock about 1.67 m, about 1.03 x WH) is normal for a TB, moving the hip and limb back fits real proportions better than trimming the rear.

Severity: a 15-20 cm placement error is the main side-view conformation fault, and it shows in every gait's profile, so 'high' is justified.
references: Baxter GM (ed) 2011, Adams and Stashak's Lameness in Horses, 6th ed, ch. 2 Conformation and Movement (tuber ischii plumb line touching point of hock, landing 7.5-10 cm behind heel; 'camped under / standing under behind')

I tried to refute this and could not. Every number in the finding reproduces.

Code (index.html:537): HIND = {hip [-0.52,1.18], st [-0.36,0.92], ho [-0.62,0.56], co [-0.56,0.092], pastern 30 deg}. The TRUNK rear rows (:491-495) put the highest croup row at x=-0.52 (top 1.605) and end the body at x=-0.86. GAITS.stand.hind.xc is -0.56. The other gaits' hind xc values (-0.45 to -0.58) are all centred under that forward hip joint.

Measurements (node, static.standing):
- Hip joint is at -0.515: 1.0 cm in front of the croup peak (-0.525) and 34.3 cm in front of the point of buttock (-0.858, y 1.27).
- Joint angles: stifle 110.0 deg, hock 145.8 deg. The cannon is nearly vertical (2.6 deg, fetlock 1.6 cm behind the hock).
- Lengths: femur 0.306 m, tibia 0.444 m, cannon 0.347 m.
- Fore toe to hind toe is 1.120 m (0.687 x WH).

Surface landmarks, worked out from the limb() and ringAt() sections:
- Point of hock: the hock-block ring is at t=-0.02 with back 0.085, giving x ~ -0.705 at y ~ 0.567.
- Back of the fetlock ~ -0.689.
- Heel: sole.x - bd = -0.56 + 0.069 - 0.058 - 0.038 = -0.587.
- Toe -0.491.

So a plumb line from the buttock lands 15-16 cm behind the point of hock, 17 cm behind the fetlock, 27 cm behind the heel and 37 cm behind the toe, exactly as stated. I found no lateral point-of-hip geometry anywhere: no coxa or haunch bump, and TRUNK has none.

Images: in the 00-stand 'right side', 'left side' and 'hindleg, right side' tiles (cropped and enlarged), the quarters clearly overhang the gaskin and hock. The thigh comes out of the underside of the middle of the rump. The 01-walk tiles show the same overhang.

It is not limited to the standing pose. The rigid hips bone keeps hip-to-buttock at 0.34-0.35 m in every gait. At lift-off the hind toe is only 12 cm (walk), 10 cm (trot) and 14 cm (canter) behind the buttock, and in the gallop it is still 4 cm in front of it. In Muybridge's gallop plates the hind hoof leaves the ground well behind the quarters.

Reference values:
- Stashak (Baxter 2011, ch. 2): a vertical from the tuber ischii should touch the point of hock, follow the back of the cannon and land about 7.5-10 cm behind the heel. A limb in front of that line is 'standing under'.
- Pelvis: the acetabulum sits about 1/3 of the pelvis length cranial to the tuber ischii, roughly 18-22 cm horizontally, and about 25-30 cm caudal to the tuber sacrale (Budras). The model's 34 cm hip-to-buttock and 1 cm hip-to-croup-peak are therefore each off by about 12-16 cm or more.
- The short femur (0.31 m against a real ~0.40-0.45 m) is further evidence: moving the hip back and up would lengthen it.

What I could not refute, with three refinements:
1. By joint angles the limb is not 'camped under': the cannon is vertical and the hock angle is normal. The fault is where the limb sits relative to the quarters, and that counts as standing under only by the plumb-line definition.
2. The lumbosacral pivot of the hips bone is at x=-0.30, so the hip joint is 21.5 cm behind it. Real values are about 25-30 cm. Part of the 15 cm error is therefore the croup peak and buttock sitting too far back, not only the limb sitting too far forward. That favours the finding's own 'split the difference' option over a pure 14 cm limb shift.
3. Body length is fine: 0.81 - (-0.858) = 1.67 m, about 1.02 x WH, which is normal for a Thoroughbred. So any rear trim should be modest, or paired with lengthening the front end.

The arithmetic is also right: shifting the whole limb 14 cm back puts the point of hock at about -0.845, 1.3 cm from the plumb line.

Severity stays high. It is the main side-view hindquarter silhouette, it shows in every pose, and it is a textbook conformation landmark.
model.correction:
Reproduced as stated. Two refinements:
1. The limb's own angles are normal (stifle 110 deg, hock 146 deg, cannon within 3 deg of vertical). The defect is the hip joint and limb sitting about 14-16 cm too far forward relative to the quarters' surface landmarks (buttock and croup peak). That reads as 'standing under' only by the Stashak plumb-line test, not by limb angulation.
2. Relative to the rig's own lumbosacral pivot (hips bone at x=-0.30), the hip joint is only about 5-8 cm too far forward, and the buttock or rear overhang is about 6-10 cm too far back. A combined fix is the better fit: move the limb back about 7-10 cm and trim the rear 5-7 cm. Total body length (1.67 m, about 1.02 x WH) is already correct.
The same hip-to-buttock offset also cuts hind retraction in every gait: at lift-off the toe is only 10-14 cm behind the buttock in walk, trot and canter, and still 4 cm in front of it in the gallop.
references: Baxter GM (ed) 2011 Adams and Stashak's Lameness in Horses, 6th ed., ch. 2 Conformation (hindlimb side-view plumb line from the tuber ischii: touches the point of hock, follows the back of the cannon, meets the ground about 7.5-10 cm behind the heel)

truth.reasoning:
I checked the measurements first. In measurements.json static.standing RH the hip is at (-0.515, 1.171), the stifle at (-0.348, 0.915) and the hock at (-0.614, 0.56). That gives a femur of 0.306 m, a tibia of 0.444 m (ratio 0.69) and a hind cannon of 0.347 m. The femur sits 33 deg forward of vertical and the tibia 37 deg back, so the stifle is 110 deg and the hock 146 deg. The elbow is at 0.96 m. All of the finding's numbers reproduce. In the '00-stand hindleg, right side' tile the thigh is stubby and the gaskin runs long.

What holds up against real horses:
- A joint-centre femur:tibia ratio of 0.69 is outside normal Thoroughbred variation. Conformation guidance says the femur and tibia should be about the same length (Wikipedia, Equine conformation).
- The claim's own surface-landmark source, Senna et al. 2015 (jumping Thoroughbreds), gives thigh 49.66 and gaskin 53.09 cm, a ratio of 0.94. The model's tibia:cannon is 1.28.
- So the femur is too short and the tibia too long. The direction and the medium severity both stand.
- The quoted standing angles are correct: Senna gives stifle 114.9 and hock 148.6 deg, and Ahmad et al. 2025 give 128.6 and 160.4 deg.

What is overstated:
1. **Expected ratio.** "The femur is at least as long as the tibia, ~1.0-1.1" does not follow from the evidence. The Kiesewalter / von den Driesch & Boessneck factors work on greatest bone lengths. In the horse, femoral greatest length includes the greater trochanter, which rises above the femoral head, and the condylar radius. Joint-centre femur length is therefore about 6-9 cm shorter than femoral greatest length. Joint-centre tibia length is about 2-4 cm longer than tibial greatest length, because the stifle axis lies in the femoral condyles above the tibial plateau. At 163 cm this gives a joint-centre femur of about 0.37-0.41 m, a tibia of about 0.38-0.42 m, and a ratio of about 0.9-1.0. The claim's own Senna figure (0.94) contradicts 1.0-1.1. The 0.40/0.36 "horse-proportional leg model" comes from a robotics paper and is weak evidence.
2. **"High stifle" and the stifle-height target.** The 0.84-0.87 m target is probably too low. With a tarsocrural axis at about 0.55-0.56 m (the model's 0.56 is right), a tibia of about 0.39-0.41 m, and the tibia 20-31 deg from vertical (hock 149-160 deg), the real stifle axis sits at about 0.89-0.93 m. That is in the flank fold, roughly 3-10 cm below the elbow. The model's 0.915 m and 4.5 cm gap are plausible.
3. **Where the femur is short.** Fix A's 0.856 m stifle with a 0.37 m tibia would leave the stifle on the low side. The femur deficit sits mainly at the top: the hip joint is about 0.36 m from the point of buttock (-0.858, 1.27). The real acetabulum lies about 0.20-0.25 m cranial to the tuber ischii, given a pelvis of about 51 cm (Senna) with the ischium making up its caudal ~40%. That makes the hip joint about 10 cm too far forward. Lengthening the femur by moving the hip back and/or up, while keeping the stifle near 0.89-0.92 m and shortening the tibia mainly by moving the hock or stifle horizontally, matches real anatomy better than lowering the stifle to 0.84 m.

Caveat: web search was unavailable (budget exhausted), so the joint-centre numbers are my estimates from greatest-length factors plus typical articular geometry. They are not a measured joint-centre dataset.
truth.correction:
The core problem is confirmed: femur:tibia 0.69 is well outside real Thoroughbred proportions, with the femur too short and the tibia/gaskin too long. Two parts of the expected values need correcting.
1. **Ratio.** The real joint-centre femur:tibia is about 0.9-1.0 ("about the same length"; Senna surface thigh:gaskin is 0.94), not "at least 1.0-1.1". Kiesewalter greatest lengths overstate the femur because they include the greater trochanter. Target a femur of about 0.37-0.41 m and a tibia of about 0.38-0.42 m.
2. **Stifle height.** The stifle is not clearly too high. A real stifle axis at 163 cm sits at about 0.89-0.93 m, roughly 3-10 cm below the elbow, so the model's 0.915 m is plausible and the 0.84-0.87 m target is too low.

The short femur comes mainly from a hip joint set about 10 cm too far cranial: it is about 0.36 m from the point of buttock, against a real ~0.20-0.25 m. The preferred fix is to move HIND.hip back and up (toward about x -0.62..-0.66, y 1.18-1.22) and trim the tibia by moving the stifle or hock horizontally, rather than lowering the stifle to 0.84-0.86 m.

truth.reasoning:
The model observation checks out. In measurements.json, the hind toes sit at z ±0.172-0.177 in every gait (centre-to-centre 0.349-0.351 m) and the fore toes at 0.328-0.332 m. That holds at walk (1.44 m/s) and also in the race gallop (16.8 m/s). Hip, stifle, hock and toe share one z, and index.html offsets the femur mesh 0.02 m inward (`inward = V(0,0,-side*0.02)`). The rear tiles in 00-stand and 05-race show this.

The real-horse claim is right in direction but overstated or unsupported in its details:

1. **Outward rotation is supported.** Hind limbs being slightly rotated out is normal or near-universal. Holmström et al. 1990 (EVJ 22:186, 356 Swedish Warmbloods) found 80% had outwardly rotated hind limbs, mostly mild. Bradley (Univ. Missouri Ext. G2843) writes "Almost all horses display cow hocks to a degree". Griffin (Univ. Kentucky, horses.extension.org) says toes slightly out are "perfectly acceptable" because they let the stifle clear the rib cage. The plumb line from the point of buttock bisecting the hock, cannon and foot is the standard ideal (G2843; Adams and Stashak). The model lacks the stifle set out and the slight toe-out.

2. **"Parallel posts" is not wrong in itself.** The same guides say the cannons stand vertical and parallel when seen from behind. "Hocks a little closer" is a common, tolerated deviation, not the ideal: in the ideal, the hocks lie on the plumb line. So the fault is the missing frontal-plane shape above the hock (stifle out, gaskin tapering in) and the missing slight toe-out. Parallel lower legs are correct.

3. **The numbers are unsourced.** Nothing cited supports "tuber ischii ~10-12 cm off the midline, so feet ~20-26 cm apart". Matsuura et al. 2024 (PMC10955269) is a 3D-scanning study of body measurements: croup width 50.6 cm, chest width 38.6 cm in 7 Thoroughbreds and 2 crossbreds. It has no data on limb alignment or foot spacing, so the citation is misattributed. Sisson (1914) gives pelvic inlet and ischial-spine widths of about 15-24 cm but no width between the tubera ischii. Clayton, Buchholz and Nauwelaerts 2013 (Vet J 198:e65) measured base-of-support width at 0.22-0.45 m across 24 horses of 117-666 kg. It is unclear whether that is hoof centres or outer walls. Either way, a 0.33-0.35 m stance for a 475 kg horse is plausibly within normal variation, or at most slightly wide; it is not clearly wrong. Stance width also varies with how the horse stands.

4. **Narrowing with speed: plausible, but no horse data.** The claim that hooves move toward the midline as speed rises fits general quadruped locomotion and is visible in head-on racing footage. The finding cites no study of horse track width against speed, though, and I found none in PubMed or Europe PMC. Weishaupt 2010 and Gmel 2024 describe spatial parameters versus speed, but their abstracts report no lateral width. The suggested values (race half-width 0.05) are guesses.

   At walk and trot, normal horses should not converge toward the midline. "Plaiting" (feet landing on the midline) is a gait fault linked to deviated limbs (Akbari Shahkhosravi et al. 2021, J Biomech 128:110715). Any narrowing at those gaits should therefore stay modest. The clearly unrealistic part is the unchanged 35 cm track at a 16.8 m/s gallop.
truth.correction:
The problem is the hind limb's shape and its behaviour at speed, not the 35 cm standing width as such.

- **Standing:** real Thoroughbreds have the stifle set out, the gaskin tapering toward the hock, cannons roughly vertical and parallel, and the toes turned slightly out. Slight cow-hocks are common and accepted, but the ideal is a plumb line from the point of buttock bisecting hock, cannon and foot.
- **Foot spacing:** no source supports "feet 20-26 cm apart" or "tuber ischii 10-12 cm off the midline". Measured base-of-support widths of 0.22-0.45 m across horses from 117 to 666 kg (Clayton et al. 2013) leave a 0.33-0.35 m stance for a 475 kg horse within plausible normal range, or only slightly wide.
- **Speed:** track width should narrow mainly at canter and gallop, with gallop hoofprints near the line of travel. It should not narrow much at walk or trot, where landing on the midline (plaiting) is a fault. The per-gait numbers in the fix options have no horse data behind them.
- **Reference:** drop Matsuura 2024 as support; it contains no limb-alignment data. Cite Holmström 1990 (80% of 356 Warmbloods had outwardly rotated hind limbs), Univ. Missouri Ext. G2843 and Adams and Stashak for the plumb-line ideal.

Images: I cropped and enlarged the rear tiles of 00 (stand), 01 (walk) and 05 (race). From the hock down, the hind legs are vertical parallel columns at the outer corners of the quarters. The hock centres span about 65% of the rump width. In the race rear tiles the legs do not converge.

Caveats that reduce the finding slightly without refuting it:
1. The mesh outline is not perfectly parallel above the hock. The gaskin rings taper symmetrically about z = 0.175: half-width 0.088 at the stifle and 0.048 at the hock. So the outer outline narrows from about 0.26 at the stifle to about 0.22 at the hock, and the inner outline widens from about 0.09 to 0.13. The silhouette narrows about 8 cm from stifle to hock. The bone axis stays vertical.
2. The 2 cm inward femur offset mainly closes the gap between the inner thighs (inner edges about 9 cm apart). That is anatomically reasonable. It is not evidence against stifle-out. The outer stifle outline comes mostly from the top of the tibia mesh.
3. The "20-26 cm" target rests on an assumed tuber ischii offset of 10-12 cm. A more conservative real value is about 25-30 cm centre to centre, so the model is about 5-10 cm too wide, not 10-15.
   - The model's own trunk supports the point either way. Its half-width is 0.25 at the hip, matching the 50.6 cm croup width in Matsuura 2024. Near the point of buttock (x = -0.80 to -0.86) it is only 0.19 to 0.11. So the hooves at 0.175 sit outside the model's own buttock plumb line.

truth.reasoning:
The main claim holds. Two details are wrong or overstated.

What I checked in the model (my own node script over measurements.json, using the stifle–hock–fetlock angle measured in the sagittal plane):
- Race: RH k=6 reaches 192 deg and LH k=9 reaches 193 deg on the dorsal side, so the cannon is bent back past the line of the gaskin.
- Race RH k=7-9: hock 179-180 deg while the stifle is 128-129 deg, with the toe already off the ground (0.08-0.13 m). LH k=10-12 does the same (hock 179-180 deg, stifle 133-134 deg).
- Canter LH k=21-24: hock 179-180 deg.
- Tile 05-race g=2/8 shows the trailing hind leg as a straight rod.
- Code: race hind has hockPush: 40*DEG.

Real horses:
1. **The hock never reaches 180 deg.** Standing hock angles in normal horses sit well below straight:
   - jumping Thoroughbreds 148.9 deg (J Equine Sci 2020, PMC7316700)
   - French trotters 142 deg
   - Swedish Warmbloods and Morna horses about 160 deg (Ahmad 2025)
   - Gnagey et al. (2006) call a standing angle "large" above 165.5 deg.

   In motion the tarsus flexes during the impact phase and extends in late stance (Gnagey 2006). Walking ROM is only about 36-38 deg (Egenvall 2023), and Hoyt 2002 reports tarsal ROM growing with speed at the trot. A dorsal angle of 192 deg cannot happen without tarsocrural luxation.
2. **The reciprocal apparatus couples stifle and hock.** van Weeren 1990/1992 found the coupling tight in vivo (peroneus tertius strain under 3%) once skin artefacts were corrected. Back 1995 showed stifle, hock and fetlock flex and extend together in swing. Reeves & Trotter 1991 diagnosed loss of the reciprocal apparatus when "the hock could be flexed or extended without influencing the position of the stifle joint", and list peroneus tertius disruption among the causes. The claimed clinical sign is correct.
3. **The hock holds at 180 deg into early swing.** That is also wrong: in real horses the hock starts flexing together with the stifle right at lift-off.

What needs correcting:
- **"Stifle flexed 128-129 deg" is mislabelled.** In this landmark convention (hip joint–stifle–hock) a standing Thoroughbred's stifle is about 113.5 deg, and the model's standing stifle is 110 deg. So 128 deg is more open than at rest, not flexed. The real defect is that the two joints are out of step:
  - at race k=7-9 the stifle is about 18 deg more open than at rest but the hock is about 34 deg more open;
  - at race RH k=30-31 it is reversed: stifle 168 deg (very open), hock 154 deg.
- **The walk example is not a lock-out.** The jump from 150 to 162 deg at lift-off is one frame of late-stance push-off, about 16 deg above the model's standing angle. That is plausible to slightly high, not a defect of the same kind.
- **The resting range is narrower than real variation.** "Rest 148-160 deg" should be roughly 142-168 deg. The model's 146 deg standing angle is normal for a Thoroughbred.
- **The gallop push-off figure is not sourced.** The web-search budget ran out mid-check and later database searches found no published maximum tarsal angle for a racehorse at gallop. The ~160-170 deg peak is a sensible estimate and should scale with each horse's standing angle (perhaps about 175 deg in a post-legged horse), but it is still never 180 deg.

A cap of about 168-170 deg in the IK, and keeping stifle and hock moving together, are justified.
truth.correction:
Keep the finding at high severity, with these changes:
- Restate the defect as the stifle and hock being out of step: at race push-off and early swing the hock reaches or passes 180 deg (192-193 deg) while the stifle is only 18-29 deg more open than at rest (128-139 deg, against 110 deg standing in the model and about 113.5 deg in Thoroughbreds). It is not hock extension "while the stifle is flexed". The reverse happens at race RH k=30-31 (stifle 168 deg, hock 154 deg).
- Drop the walk 150->162 deg example; that is normal late-stance extension.
- Widen the normal standing hock range to about 142-168 deg (Thoroughbred mean 148.9 deg, Gnagey "large" above 165.5 deg).
- Present the gallop push-off peak of about 160-170 deg as an estimate tied to the horse's standing angle, not a published value. The hard limit is that the hock never reaches 180 deg and is never bent back past it.

truth.reasoning:
The defect in the model is real. Joint angles computed from measurements.json for RH (hip-stifle-hock and stifle-hock-fetlock) reproduce the finding. In race stance (k=0-6) the stifle goes 137 -> 90 -> 139 while the hock goes 154 -> 142 and then to 175-180. Before touchdown (k=28-31) the stifle opens 97 -> 127 -> 168 -> 168 while the hock stays at 154. In trot stance the stifle drops from 142 to about 105 while the hock moves 150 -> 142 -> 150. In walk swing the stifle reaches 79 while the hock is at 115-140. The code explains it: footPath returns a scheduled hock flex (hockSag*load - push, index.html:1397), and solve2 then puts all the change in hip-to-target distance into the femur/stifle.

The real-horse "expected" statement is right in direction but overstated in two places.

What holds up:
(1) The reciprocal apparatus (fibularis/peroneus tertius cranially, SDFT caudally) couples stifle and tarsus. After skin-displacement correction, in-vivo coupling matches in-vitro data, and peroneus tertius strain stays under 3% at walk and trot (van Weeren 1990, 1992). Peroneus tertius rupture lets the hock extend while the stifle flexes (Welsh 2021).
(2) Coupling is tight in swing. Back 1995 found synchronous stifle-tarsus-fetlock flexion and extension in swing; Hodson 2001 found stifle and tarsal flexion cycles "well coordinated during the swing phase". The model's stifle snapping 127 -> 168 before touchdown with the hock fixed, and the walk-swing mismatch, are therefore genuine anatomical errors.
(3) In stance, the stifle, tarsus and coffin joints all flex while the fetlock extends, for shock absorption (Back 1995 at trot; Hodson 2001 at walk).
(4) Walk tarsal ROM of about 37-39 deg is confirmed: 37.4-38.6 deg (Egenvall 2023, walking on circles) and 38.0 ± 3.6 deg (Douglas 2026). The stifle figure of 39-43 deg could not be checked from the abstracts.
(5) The tarsus does produce positive work. At walk it assists the hip in energy generation in stance and swing (Clayton 2001). At trot it behaves elastically, absorbing energy and then returning about the same amount (Dutto 2006).

What is overstated:
(a) "Close to 1:1 in stance" is not right. The 1:1-like coupling is a swing-phase property. In stance the stifle moves little: Dutto 2006 says the stifle (knee) "had little movement during the middle of stance when the flexion moment was greatest". At walk the two joints even move in opposite directions in mid/late stance: "the tarsal joint extended slowly, while the stifle began to flex" (Hodson 2001). In real stance yield, the tarsus (and fetlock) take more than the stifle. This makes the model's inversion (stifle -78 deg vs hock -12 deg) even worse than the finding says. It also means fix option 1 should not force a 0.8-1.0 hock:stifle ratio in stance: stance should let the hock yield more than the stifle.
(b) The fetlock is the main hindlimb shock absorber, not the tarsus. The tarsus is secondary.
(c) Tarsal "positive work late in trot stance" is elastic recoil with near-zero net work, and it decreases with speed (Dutto 2006). It is not net push-off generation. Net propulsion comes mainly from the hip.

The proposed hockSag targets (trot about 18 deg, gallop about 25 deg, race about 30 deg) could not be verified against published gallop data.

The fault is large and visible in every gait, so severity stays high.
truth.correction:
Real Thoroughbreds have a reciprocal apparatus (peroneus tertius plus SDFT) that couples stifle and tarsus. The coupling is tight in swing: the two joints flex and extend together at similar amounts, and walk ROM is about 38 deg for each. So the model's late-swing stifle snap with the hock fixed, and its walk-swing mismatch, are genuine errors.

The coupling is NOT about 1:1 in stance. Both joints flex a little at impact, but the stifle then moves little through mid-stance (Dutto 2006). At walk the tarsus extends while the stifle starts to flex in mid/late stance (Hodson 2001). In real stance the tarsus and fetlock yield more than the stifle, which is the reverse of the model's stifle -78 deg vs hock -12 deg.

The fetlock, not the tarsus, is the main shock absorber. At trot the tarsus works elastically, absorbing then returning energy with roughly zero net work. Net positive work comes mainly from the hip.

Recommended fix: keep near-1:1 coupling in swing. In stance, let the hock (and fetlock) take the yield, with the stifle changing only a few degrees. Do not force a fixed 0.8-1.0 hock:stifle ratio in stance.

model.reasoning:
I couldn't refute this. The code works the way the finding says, and the numbers reproduce almost exactly.

**Code.** The finding cites index.html:1436-1440, but the hind IK is now at index.html:1472-1485, and the stance flex term is at 1394-1397.
- In stance, footPath returns `flex = P.hockSag*load - push` (line 1397).
- solveLeg sets `eta = L.hockRest + G.hind.hockOpen + f.flex` (line 1474).
- It then runs solve2 from the hip with a second "bone" of fixed length `hypot(ex,ey)`, from stifle to fetlock (lines 1475-1476).
- So the hock angle follows a fixed schedule. Every change in hip-to-fetlock distance, from fetlock sag, body drop or reaching, goes into the femur/stifle angle. Nothing in the code couples the two joints.
- hockSag is 6/8/10/10/12° for walk/trot/canter/gallop/race (lines 205-241). That matches the finding.

**Re-measurement.** I measured both hind legs from measurements.json with node: sagittal hip-stifle-hock and stifle-hock-fetlock angles, standing at 110° and 146°.

Stance yield from touchdown to the minimum:

| Gait | Stifle | Hock |
|---|---|---|
| walk | 125→108 (−17) | 150→144 (−6) |
| trot | 142→105 (−37) | 150→142 (−8) |
| canter | 136→97 (−38) | 151→141 (−10) |
| gallop | 133→99 (−35) | 152→142 (−10) |
| race | 137→90 (−47) | 154→142 (−12) |

- The stifle takes 3 to 4 times the hock's yield. The finding's −32 for trot and −26 for gallop slightly understate it.
- In gallop late stance (k=8-11) the stifle keeps flexing (105→99) while the hock extends (146→152). The two joints move in opposite directions.

Touchdown snap in the race gait:
- From k=28 to k=31 the stifle opens 97→127→168→168 while the hock stays at 153.6-153.8.
- It then folds 168→137→103 at k=0-1, about 65° in 27 ms.
- The same thing happens on a smaller scale in trot (k=28-31: stifle 95→147, hock 145→150, then 142→127 after touchdown) and in gallop. So the snap is not limited to the race gait.

Regression of hock on stifle over the whole stride:
- Slope 0.54 / 0.70 / 0.66-0.74 / 0.69-0.71 / 0.75-0.79 for walk/trot/canter/gallop/race, with r 0.69-0.91. This matches the finding's 0.54-0.79.
- Shifting by 1-2 samples raises r to 0.85-0.95. So in swing the joints are partly out of phase: the hock reaches its deepest flexion about 3 samples (about 9% of the stride) before the stifle (trot hock min k21 vs stifle min k24; walk k8 vs k11).

**Nuances, which don't overturn the finding.**
1. In the walk, the overall ranges of motion are realistic and close to 1:1: stifle 79-130 (51°) and hock 115-162 (47°). Egenvall et al. 2023 report about 39-43° and 37-39°. So the walk problem is the phase lag plus the stance split, not the size of the motion. The finding's walk example (stifle 79° with hock 131-140°) is a snapshot of that lag.
2. Late in race stance both joints do extend (stifle 90→139, hock 142→175). But the hock overshoots to 192-193°, which is a separate finding on hockPush hyperextension.
3. The stifle and hock sit inside the trunk skin and are small in the 4x3 tiles. In 05-race g=0-1/8 and 02-trot g=0-1/8 the effect is hard to see by eye. The numbers prove it, though: in stance the gaskin rotates while the hock angle barely changes.

**Real horses.**
- Back et al. 1995 (Equine Vet J 27:39-45) describe stance flexion of the stifle, tarsal and coffin joints for shock absorption. They show synchronous flexion and extension of these joints in swing, through the reciprocal apparatus coupling stifle and tarsus.
- Dutto et al. 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:3990-3999) found the distal hindlimb joints, including the tarsus, behave elastically in stance: energy absorption followed by energy return.
- The model has a near-rigid hock and puts the yield in the stifle, which contradicts both.
- I could not check the cited Douglas et al. 2026 (Animals 16(13):1938) reference; it has no Europe PMC hit.

**Severity.** It affects every moving gait and comes from how the IK is built. It also causes the touchdown snap and the hock hyperextension (a separate finding). High stays.

truth.reasoning:
The main real-horse claim holds up. A Thoroughbred's femur never comes close to horizontal in any gait. At full protraction the stifle comes forward under the flank at about the belly line, well below the hip joint (Muybridge gallop plates). Hip flexion/extension range at the walk and trot is small:
- Egenvall, Clayton & Byström 2023 (PeerJ 11:e16373, PMC10625764), walking on circles: 16.8-20.7 deg (hip = stifle / hip-joint / tuber coxae marker angle). Stifle range in the same study is 39-43 deg.
- Shen et al. 2026 (Vet Sci, PMC13119970), straight-line gaits: walk 23.9-26.1 deg, slow trot 26.6-27.5 deg, fast trot 28.6-30.4 deg.

My recomputation from measurements.json (RH, hip->stifle angle relative to the buttock->croup line) confirms the model is far outside this:
- Femur range relative to the pelvis line: walk 69 deg, trot 75 deg.
- World femur angle: walk 0 to 67 deg, with the stifle at 1.04 m against a hip at about 1.2 m.
- Race: the femur reaches 89 deg and the stifle (1.09 m) is level with the hip (1.08 m).
- Minimum stifle angle: race 26-29 deg, gallop 50-52 deg.
For walk and trot the defect and the "expected" values are right.

Several parts are overstated or wrong and need correcting:

(1) "3-5x too large" only holds at the walk. Against 17-26 deg the walk range is about 2.6-4x, and the trot (75 vs about 27-30 deg) is about 2.5x. For gallop and race the finding's own pelvis-relative numbers do not reproduce. It says 76 and 116 deg; I get 50-54 deg (gallop) and 76 deg (race). 116 looks like the femur's world range plus the pelvis tilt range added together, when the two actually move together. A gallop hip range of about 50 deg is not obviously excessive, because canter/gallop add lumbosacral/pelvic flexion. Murray et al. 2019 (J Equine Vet Sci 81:102795) use "femur angle to vertical", hip flexion and lumbosacral flexion as the protraction measures in galloping racehorses. In the fast gaits the real fault is where the swing is centred and how far forward it goes: the femur spends late swing pinned at 82-89 deg world, forced by the short 0.306 m femur (A-HIND-02) and the clamp. The raw size of the swing is not the main problem there.

(2) "Reach comes from coupled stifle/hock flexion" gets the mechanism backwards. Hodson, Clayton & Lanovaz 2001 (Equine Vet J 33:38-43): "flexion and extension of the hip were responsible for protraction and retraction of the entire limb". The stifle and hock, working together, "raise the distal limb as it was protracted". Back et al. 1995 (Equine Vet J 27:39-45) describe the hind limb swinging like a pendulum about the hip. So the hip, plus pelvic/lumbosacral flexion at canter/gallop, supplies the reach; the stifle/hock fold supplies clearance. The fix option "let the stifle/hock fold bring the hoof forward" is therefore biomechanically wrong. The better fix is a shorter, correctly placed hip arc (lengthen the femur, cap world protraction at roughly 55-65 deg at gallop), with stifle/hock re-extending in late swing.

(3) The "stifle bottoms at 80-100 deg" figure has no citation. It is plausible but approximate. Standing stifle is about 114-129 deg (figures quoted in the critic findings from Ahmad et al. 2025), and stifle/hock ranges are 40-65 deg at walk to fast trot (Egenvall; Shen). That puts the swing minimum at about 85-100 deg in trot and perhaps 75-90 deg at gallop. The model's 26-30 deg (race) and 50-55 deg (gallop/canter) are impossible either way.

(4) The walk reference (17-21 deg) comes from circle walking with skin markers. About 20-26 deg is a fairer straight-line value.

The visible defect (the stifle rising toward hip height, so the leg seems to come out of mid-belly in every gait, worst at walk and race) is real, so severity stays high.

truth.reasoning:
The finding's description of what real horses do is mostly right. The one weak spot is the hard limit of "at most ~5-10 deg terminal retraction": no source backs that number, and it is probably too tight for canter and gallop.

1. Hip extends through stance (holds). Dutto et al. 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:3990, horses trotting at 2.5-5 m/s): "the hip did positive work during the stride, generating energy almost throughout stance". The hip extensor moment is positive in stance, so positive power means the hip is extending. At canter the gluteal muscles drive hip extension during stance (St George et al. 2023). At walk the hip is the main joint generating energy (Clayton et al. 2001). Nothing I found shows real horses flexing the hip 8-12 deg after contact. The model does: measured hip angle (croup-hip-stifle) drops 134->128.5 deg at trot (about 6), 135->125 at canter (about 11), 135.5->129 at gallop (about 7) and 134->119 at race (about 15). Femur angle from vertical rises 7, 10, 4.5 and 13 deg. So the flaw is real, though the stated "8-12 deg at trot, canter and race" is slightly off: trot is lower, race is higher, and gallop has it too.

2. Stifle and hock already flexed at contact and yielding together (holds). Back et al. 1995 (Equine Vet J 27:39) describe "stance flexion of the stifle, tarsal and coffin joints" for shock absorption, with the reciprocal apparatus coupling stifle and hock. Hodson et al. 2001 found the same at walk. One caveat: the coupling is tight mainly in swing. In stance Dutto saw little stifle movement at midstance, and Hodson saw the hock extend while the stifle flexed. "Yield together" is a fair simplification for early stance only. The model is far outside this. In race the stifle opens to 168 deg just before contact, with the toe still 4-6 cm up. At contact it is 137 deg, and it reaches 90 deg two frames (0.027 s) later. Stifle range is 69-147 deg at trot and 29-168 deg at race. For comparison, real stifle range at walk is about 39-43 deg and hip range about 17-21 deg (Egenvall et al. 2023, PeerJ).

3. Smooth swing with protraction starting at lift-off (holds roughly). Back et al. 1995 describe hind-limb motion as pendular about the hip socket (acetabulum).

4. Terminal retraction "at most ~5-10 deg" (overstated as a fixed cap). Real horses do retract the limb late in swing, and actively. At canter, the peak angular speeds of hind-limb retraction and hip extension fall in late swing, faster in the trailing hind (St George et al. 2023). Back et al. 1997 show the leading hip more flexed at peak flexion than at impact. I found no published degree value. Late-swing retraction is likely larger at gallop and race speed than at trot, so 5-10 deg is a plausible target for trot, not a proven ceiling for all gaits.

The fault in the model stands anyway. It retracts about 30-50 deg at every gait: femur angle 75.6->43 at trot, 78.7->44.5 at canter, 82.5->48.6 at gallop, 88.9->40 at race. That retraction comes right after the femur has been held at its clamp limit (hip angle stuck at about 104 deg for k=20-27 in race). In race, 46 deg of it happens in about 0.027 s. No real retraction looks like that.

Re-measured numbers (central differences over 32 samples): race femur peak about 1720 deg/s, stifle about 2620 deg/s; gallop 730 and 1190 deg/s. The finding's figures (2044/3051 and 801/1273) are a little higher but the same order. The code evidence checks out: FEMUR_RANGE = [0, 76 deg] with a hard clamp() in swing. Medium severity is right: race is the most visible case, but the clamp-then-retract pattern shows up at every gait.
truth.correction: Keep the core of the expected behaviour: the hip extends through stance (Dutto 2006: positive hip power almost throughout stance at trot); the stifle and hock are partly flexed at contact and flex further in early stance (Back 1995; Hodson 2001); and swing is smooth and pendular. Change the terminal-retraction limit. Real horses do retract the limb late in swing, and at canter and gallop this is an active, speed-dependent move (St George 2023: peak hip-extension and limb-retraction speeds in late swing). It should be described as a gradual reversal over roughly the last 20-30% of swing, plausibly more than 5-10 deg at gallop, but never a jump from a dwell at the limit. The model's 30-50 deg at every gait, including 46 deg in about 0.03 s at race, is still clearly wrong. Measurement corrections: early-stance hip flexion is about 6 deg at trot, 11 at canter, 7 at gallop and 15 at race, so gallop is affected too. The 168 deg stifle occurs just before touchdown (137 deg at contact), then drops to 90 deg within 0.027 s.

- Collapse: stifle 168 (k=31), 137 at touchdown (k=0), then 103 and 90 (k=1-2).
- Peak angular speeds: femur 2047 deg/s and stifle 3051 deg/s in race; 800 and 1272 deg/s in gallop.
- LH does the same (peaks 1791 and 2856 deg/s).

Is it really the clamp? Yes. I subtracted the hips-bone rotation that BODY.race applies (spine.rotation.z = 2.5 deg x cyc(g,1,0.8) plus hips.rotation.z = 2 deg + 9 deg x cyc(g,1,0.9)) to get the femur angle relative to the pelvis. It is exactly 0.0 deg at k=7-9 and exactly 76.0 deg at k=20-27. Those are the two ends of FEMUR_RANGE = [0, 76 deg] (index.html:1432), applied by the hard clamp in swing at index.html:1478-1485. The "86-89 deg" in the finding is that 76 deg limit plus 10-13 deg of pelvis rotation.

About 25% of the stride is spent on the upper limit. The clamp lets go only once the IK target, carried by the swingX retract overshoot, pulls back. The toe reaches 0.837 m ahead of the hip at k=30, then lands at 0.717 m. That forces the near-straight leg (stifle 168 deg) and the 46 deg femur drop within about 27 ms. Relative to the pelvis, the femur then flexes again in early stance: race +15 deg on RH and +13 deg on LH. So the femur goes protract to the limit, retract 30 deg, re-protract, then retract again: it is not monotonic.

Real horses do this much more slowly. Smooth protraction of about 70 deg over a swing of about 0.33 s peaks near 330 deg/s. The model is roughly 6 times faster, and also faster than peak hip and knee speeds measured in elite human sprinters. Back et al. (1995) and Dutto et al. (2006) describe the hip extending through stance (doing positive work), with the stifle and hock flexing only moderately and together in early stance. They do not describe a stifle swinging 168 to 90 deg across contact.

Corrections that do not change the verdict:
1. The line numbers are stale by about 37 lines. The clamp is at index.html:1478-1485 (not 1442-1447). swingX is defined at 395-398 and used at 1406 (not 1369).
2. Measured against the pelvis, the early-swing "dwell" is a hard pin at 0 deg only for k=7-9 (about 0.04 s), followed by a slow rise from 6.5 to 22 deg (k=10-15). The -7 deg in world includes about -7 deg of pelvis rotation.
3. At the touchdown sample itself the stifle is already moderately flexed (137 deg RH, 132 deg LH). The 168 deg peak is 1-2 samples before contact. The fault is the snap and the 47 deg collapse after it, not the angle at contact.
4. Early-stance hip flexion is smaller in the slower gaits: trot 5.8 deg, canter 10.7 (RH) and 3.8 (LH), gallop 6.9 and 2.0, race 14.9 and 12.7. The claimed "8-12 deg at trot" is too high; race is larger than claimed.

The 05-race tiles agree with this: RH trails and folds high behind at g=2/8-3/8 and reaches far forward under the belly at g=7/8. But they are 4 samples apart, so they cannot show the 2-sample snap; the evidence for it is the measured data.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the claim and couldn't. In a real horse the point of hock sits well above the hock joint and well behind it, and this holds for all horses, not just one breed.

1) Where the point of hock is. The tuber calcanei (the top of the heel bone) is the point of hock. It sticks up and back from the tarsus, and the common calcanean tendon attaches to it, with the superficial digital flexor tendon capping it over a bursa (Dyce, Sack & Wensing; König & Liebich). Lewczuk et al. 2025 measured lateromedial X-rays of 198 sport horses averaging 165 cm. From the top of the tuber to the tarsometatarsal joint was 17.71 ± 0.83 cm. The calcaneus itself (measurement G) was 11.8 cm. The central and third tarsal bones together were about 3.1 cm, and the distal tibia was 7.8 cm deep front to back. The tarsometatarsal joint sits about 7–8 cm below the centre of the talus trochlea, which is the centre the hock rotates about. So the bony top of the tuber is about 9–10 cm above that centre, and the skin point is about 10–11 cm above it once the SDFT cap and skin are added. That fits the claimed 8–12 cm. Bone sizes from archaeology agree: a horse of about 134 cm had a calcaneus 105 mm long and a talus 54 mm long (Gudea 2022). Scaled to 163 cm that is about 127 mm and 66 mm.

2) How far behind. The distal tibia is 7.8 cm deep, so its back surface is about 3.9 cm behind the joint centre. The calcaneal tuber and the SDFT cap stick out several centimetres past that. That puts the skin point about 8–10 cm behind the joint centre, so the claimed offset is plausible. The model's back extent of 0.085 m is the right depth; it is just at the wrong height.

3) It moves with the cannon. The calcaneus is a tarsal bone. The intertarsal and tarsometatarsal joints barely move, so the tuber swings with the tarsus and cannon around the tarsocrural joint. The fix of building it into the cannon mesh is therefore anatomically correct.

4) Tendon line and hollow. The common calcanean tendon is made of the gastrocnemius tendon, the SDFT, and the tarsal tendons of biceps femoris and semitendinosus. It runs as a separate cord from the distal gaskin muscles down to the point of hock. In front of it is the depression above the hock where thoroughpin and the plantar pouches of bog spavin show (Adams & Stashak's Lameness). Conformation guides ask for a clean, well-defined point of hock and a clear tendon line. This is normal anatomy for every horse, not a quirk of some breeds.

5) The model really does lack this. In index.html:1188 the cannon's widest back extent (0.085) is at t=-0.02, only 7 mm above the hock pivot (y=0.56). At t=-0.12 (4 cm up) it is down to 0.05. At :1187 the tibia narrows to 0.06 at t=0.8 (8.9 cm up) and 0.045 at the hock. The result is a bump at joint level with a hollow above it, which is the reverse of a real hock. The 00-stand 'hindleg, right side' close-up shows this.

One small correction to the numbers: the absolute height of '~0.62–0.66 m' is a little high for a real 163 cm Thoroughbred. Summing the bones gives a fetlock centre at about 0.15–0.17 m, plus a 0.27 m MtIII, plus 17 cm up to the tuber. That puts the bony tuber at about 0.59–0.61 m and the skin point at about 0.60–0.63 m. In the model, though, the hock pivot is already at 0.56 m (high because the fetlock is at 0.213 m), and the cannon length of 0.347 m is realistic. So the right target there is the hock pivot plus about 9–11 cm, roughly 0.65–0.67 m. The fix should be driven by the 'above the joint' offset, not the absolute range.

The real standing hock angle of a Thoroughbred is about 157° (Mizuno 2025). The model's is about 146°, a separate small difference that doesn't affect this finding. Medium severity is right: the point of hock and the tendon line are a defining part of the hind-leg silhouette in side view at every gait.

The model data checks out. At index.html:1225 (now line 1225, not 1188) the hind cannon sections are [0.25,0.031,0.043,0.036], [0.63,0.03,0.043,0.035] and [0.85,0.03,0.043,0.034]. On the PROF.limb octagon that gives a section about 7.0-7.2 cm wide by 7.3-7.4 cm deep, with a perimeter of about 22 cm (computed). The fore cannon at line 1209 is just as round (7.0 x 7.1 cm).

The main real-horse claim holds: the mid-cannon region of a horse is narrower side to side than front to back. Anatomically, the dorsoplantar depth is the bone (about 3.2 cm) plus the suspensory ligament, the DDFT, the SDFT and skin, which comes to roughly 6.5-7.5 cm. The lateromedial width is the bone (about 3.3-3.5 cm) plus the plantarly placed splint bones and skin, about 4.5-5.5 cm. The model's 7 cm width is therefore too wide by about 1.5-2 cm. Measured circumference agrees: Shojaei et al. (2026, Iranian Arab horses) give a metatarsus circumference of 19.75 ± 0.89 cm and a metacarpus circumference of 18.27 cm. A 475 kg Thoroughbred would plausibly have about 20-21 cm behind, so the model's ~22 cm round section is slightly heavy. The proposed flatter section (5.4 x 7.2-7.6 cm) gives 19.5-20.1 cm, which is closer to real.

The claim does need several corrections:
(1) Calling the hind cannon "flat" mixes up the region with the bone. The equine third metatarsal itself is nearly round. Sisson (1914, Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, p.124): "The shaft is more cylindrical, and is almost circular on cross-section, except in its distal part." The proximal end is also "much wider from before backward" than the metacarpal. By contrast, MC3 is "semicylindrical" with a wide groove behind it for the suspensory ligament. The flat look of the hind cannon comes entirely from the column of plantar soft tissue and the plantar splints (Mt IV is "relatively massive"). So the flattening is real but less marked behind than in front. The classic horseman's "flat bone" ideal is mainly a forelimb description.
(2) The figures 5-5.5 cm and 6.5-7 cm are anatomical estimates that no cited measurement study supports. For the larger hind cannon, a depth of about 7-7.5 cm is equally defensible. The finding's own fix (back extent 0.045-0.048) gives a 7.5-7.8 cm depth, which contradicts its stated "6.5-7 cm" expectation. It also does not keep the circumference: 22 cm becomes about 20 cm, which is actually the more realistic value.
(3) "No distinct plantar tendon edge" is overstated. The back extent is a constant 0.043 from t=0.25 to t=0.85, so the side-view plantar outline is already straight, which is what a correct hind cannon shows. Only the lateral compression, and perhaps a subtle groove between the bone/suspensory and the flexor tendons, is missing.
(4) This is not breed-specific: all horses have a laterally compressed cannon region, and fine-boned Thoroughbreds show it clearly. Severity low is appropriate for a stylised model. The fore cannon has the same issue and, given MC3's oval section, arguably more so.

The model's 7.0-7.2 cm width is therefore too wide, while its depth (7.3-7.4 cm) and straight plantar line are already about right. The hind cannon BONE (MT III) itself is nearly circular in section (Sisson: 'almost circular on cross-section'), so the flattening is less marked than in the forelimb and comes from the plantar tendon/ligament column and the plantar splint bones, not from a flat bone. Suggested fix: half-width about 0.026-0.028 m (sections at t=0.25-0.85), keep the front at about 0.030 and the back at about 0.042-0.045. This gives a perimeter of about 19.5-20 cm, slightly less than now, which is realistic. Apply the same treatment to the fore cannon (line 1209), where the real flattening is stronger.

truth.reasoning:
I could not refute the main real-horse claims. Four specifics need correcting or narrowing.

What holds up:
(1) A standing horse has a continuous caudal outline from the point of buttock (tuber ischii) down the back of the thigh and gaskin to the point of hock. The point of hock sits on, or near, a plumb line dropped from the point of buttock. This is the standard conformation test: Adams & Stashak ch. on conformation, and Wikipedia's Equine conformation page judges camped-out/under against "the plumb line dropped from point of buttock".
(2) The hamstrings move with the limb. Semitendinosus and biceps femoris insert on the crus and, through the tarsal (calcaneal) tendon, on the tuber calcanei (Budras; Dyce, Sack & Wensing). Muybridge's gallop plates show the caudal thigh outline changing shape between protraction and retraction. A rump that stays a fixed ball while the leg swings under it is wrong.
(3) The underline rises from the girth to the flank. The visible belly ends at the fold of the flank (plica lateris), which runs from the cranial stifle to the abdominal wall. Wikipedia's Horse anatomy page defines the flank as "behind the rib cage and in front of the stifle joint". From the side, no belly wall shows behind the stifle.
(4) Seen from behind, each ham is a separate rounded mass. Wikipedia's Equine conformation page: "The back of the thighs or the 'hams' should be thick enough that they touch each other until they split", with full inner thighs giving a "square or oblong look" from the rear. A large gap between the thighs ("split up behind", or cat-hammed thin thighs) is a recognised fault.

My check of the model agrees with the observation. At y=0.83 the tibia axis is at x≈-0.41, so the back of the gaskin is around -0.52 to -0.56. The trunk's corner at (-0.68, 0.85) therefore makes the claimed forward undercut. The point of hock (about -0.70) also sits ~16 cm in front of the model's buttock plumb line (-0.858).

Corrections:
(a) Terminology: "second thigh" is the horseman's name for the gaskin (crus, between stifle and hock; Dictionary.com, Wikipedia Gaskin). It is not the name for the hamstring group, which forms the "hams" or buttock and the back of the thigh. The hamstrings do continue into the back of the gaskin, so the anatomy is right but the label is wrong.
(b) "Widest at the stifles" and "meeting nearly down to the gaskins" are halter and stock-horse (Quarter Horse) ideals. Applied as fixed rules to a racing Thoroughbred they are overstated. Lean Thoroughbreds in training are often about as wide at the points of hip as at the stifles, and their hams commonly part higher. That is normal breed variation, not a fault. A safer target: the hams touch from below the perineum to roughly stifle height, give or take, then part in an inverted U well above the hocks. In this model that means a split at about 0.92-1.05 m. The current flat block runs down to 0.85 m, so the junction is too low and flat-bottomed. I could not fetch a source for the stock-horse origin of "widest at stifles" (web search budget exhausted), so that part comes from judging convention, not a citation.
(c) "No belly wall behind the stifle" is true only of the side-view silhouette. Anatomically, the ventral abdominal wall continues along the midline, between the thighs, back to the prepubic tendon on the pubic pecten (Dyce, Sack & Wensing). That is roughly at the vertical of the hip joint, which in model terms is ~15 cm behind the stifle. The wall climbs steeply there to about pubis height (~1.05-1.1 m), and the thighs hide it.
(d) Two observations describe a real horse correctly.
- From behind, a real horse also has an open gap between the gaskins and hocks, running up to where the hams split. "Legs hanging as separate columns with a gap up to the trunk" is right in kind. The faults are where the gap starts and the flat-bottomed shape, plus gaskins that are too thin.
- In a real horse the femur is also wrapped inside the hindquarter muscle mass. The leg first separates visibly from the body at the stifle, at the front, and at the gaskin, behind. So "the femur mesh lies inside the trunk" is not itself a defect. The defect is that this mass is static trunk geometry rather than thigh muscle that moves with the femur.

The side-view undercut, the missing flank fold and the motionless rump are large silhouette errors in every view and gait, so severity stays high. Fix targets should use Thoroughbred proportions, not stock-horse ideals of maximal inner-thigh mass.

(b) "Widest at the stifles" and "meeting nearly down to the gaskins" are stock-horse halter ideals. The model side of the finding checks out. Re-deriving PROF.trunk and the TRUNK rows (index.html:412, 507-512, 729-745) gives a half-width of 0.107 m at y 1.567 for x=-0.52, about 36 cm full width at y 1.45, and about 40.5 cm at y 1.415. At x=-0.36 (the loin, roughly where the points of hip sit) the width at y 1.45 is about 35 cm. The rear loft closes to one cap at (-0.91, 1.27). measurements.json agrees: croup peak 1.593, hip joints at y 1.17 with z +/-0.175. The `quarters` build factor scales the whole width, so the A-frame shape stays.

The central real-horse claim also holds. In mostly-Thoroughbred horses the tubera coxae are about 50+ cm apart, at least as wide as the hip joints and clearly wider than the chest. Matsuura 2021 defines "waist" as between the tubera coxae, "croup" as between the hip joints and "chest" as between the outer humeri. Matsuura 2024 measured those as 52.2 +/- 1.0, 50.6 +/- 0.5 and 38.6 +/- 0.7 cm. The gluteus medius forms a broad croup, and a moderately conditioned horse has a level back (Henneke BCS 5), not a 58-degree roof. A real horse at point-of-hip level is 14-16 cm wider than the model's ~35-36 cm, so the main defect is real.

Several parts of the "expected" description are overstated or wrong for real Thoroughbreds:
(1) "Square from behind" is too strict. Conformation references call a "square to slightly pear shaped rump" desirable. They also list narrow hips as common in Thoroughbreds and helpful for speed. So the model's widest point at the thigh/stifle (~53 cm) is not a fault in itself. The fault is only the narrow upper 15 cm (croup and loin). The hip points should be about as wide as the thighs, not wider: hips that stick out past the thighs in a flat "T" are a fault in their own right.
(2) "Rafter-hipped" is the wrong label. In horse conformation, rafter hips means wide, flat, T-shaped hips with prominent points, the opposite of what the model shows. Better terms are narrow-hipped or A-frame / peaked croup.
(3) The 52.2/50.6 cm figures come from 9 riding horses (7 TB, 2 crossbreds), mean age 14 years, 542 kg, 159.9 cm tall. They are not 475 kg race-fit horses, so scaling them to "~53 cm" is slightly high; 48-52 cm is a safer target. The 43.8 cm chest figure comes from a different study (Uenal 2025, TB 43.75 +/- 1.22 cm) with different landmarks. Matsuura's own chest width is 38.6 cm. The conclusion (hips wider than chest) still holds.
(4) "Points of hip as angular corners" is overstated. On the Henneke scale, hook bones "appear rounded, but are still easily discernible" at BCS 3 (thin) and are "not discernible" at BCS 4, and racing Thoroughbreds are typically around BCS 4-5. They should be soft, rounded broadenings set forward of and beside the croup peak, roughly over the lumbosacral joint, not sharp corners.
(5) "Two points of buttock" is wrong as stated. Henneke says pin bones (tubera ischii) are "not distinguishable" from BCS 3 up. In horses the vertebral heads of the semitendinosus and semimembranosus cover the tubera ischii. What shows from behind is two full, rounded hams that touch at the midline under the anus and part lower down: a shallow crease, not two points either side of a groove.
(6) A slight peak along the back is within normal variation for a lean racehorse: Henneke BCS 4 is described as "Negative crease (peaked appearance) along back". A mild median ridge is fine; the model's 23 cm width 5 cm below the top and 58-degree sides are not.

Severity is lowered to medium. The side silhouette (the main view) and the thigh width are close to a real horse. The error is limited to the upper croup and loin and shows only in rear, top and three-quarter views, where at race-camera scale it reads as egg- or pear-shaped rather than grossly wrong.
truth.correction: A Thoroughbred's rump from behind should be square to slightly pear-shaped, widest at or below the hip joints and thighs (as in the model, ~50-53 cm). At the points of hip, about 10-15 cm below the croup peak and slightly in front of it, the width should be about the same, roughly 48-52 cm for a 475 kg racehorse. The model has ~35-36 cm there. The croup and loin top should be broad and gently rounded (gluteus medius over longissimus); a slight median ridge is normal for a lean racehorse (BCS 4) but not a 58-degree roof. Points of hip should be soft, rounded prominences, not angular corners (Henneke: discernible only at BCS 3 or below). There are no visible "points of buttock": the tubera ischii are covered by the vertebral heads of the hamstrings, so the rear shows two full rounded hams meeting at a shallow midline crease under the anus. "Rafter-hipped" is the wrong label, because in horses it means wide, flat, T-shaped hips; the defect is narrow-hipped / A-frame croup. Fix by widening the upper 15 cm of the croup and loin rows (wu ~0.95-1.0 and a flatter ridge vertex), not by adding hip points wider than the thighs. The 43.8 cm chest figure is from Uenal 2025 (other landmarks), not Matsuura 2024 (38.6 cm between the outer humeri).

Real-horse truth:
1. **Withers are the height reference and a distinct ridge.** The withers is the dorsal ridge formed by the long thoracic spinous processes: about T3 to T9 in the classic texts, and T3 to T11 in some summaries. The longest spines are about T3 to T5/T6 (Getty/Sisson & Grossman; Budras). The finding's "highest about T4-T6" is within the textbook range. The withers is the standard point for measuring height, and conformation references call well-defined, high withers typical of light riding breeds such as the Thoroughbred. Low "mutton" withers are treated as a fault.
2. **The crest ties in in front of and below the summit.** The funicular part of the nuchal ligament runs from the poll to the tips of the cranial withers spines and continues as the supraspinous ligament (Dyce, Sack & Wensing). So the neck's dorsal line meets the withers on its cranial slope. The summit stands at or above that line, never under the neck. A model whose neck surface sits about 3.5 cm above the summit, at the summit's own x, has no real-horse counterpart in a lean TB.
3. **The back drop holds.** Matsuura et al. 2024 report withers 159.9 ± 2.6 cm and back 150.8 ± 2.6 cm. Caveat: these are 9 riding horses (7 TB and 2 crossbreds including Haflinger crosses), mean age 14, mean 542 kg, not racing TBs. The roughly 9 cm drop is a fair order of magnitude, and the model's 9.5 cm matches.
4. **At racing speed the withers is even more obvious.** The head and neck are extended and lowered, so the withers is plainly the highest point of the topline and the jockey crouches just behind it.

Caveats that do not overturn the finding but should guide the fix:
- **The "dip" is not a target.** A visible dip in front of the withers goes with swan or ewe necks. It is common in Thoroughbreds but counted as a conformation weakness. In a well-muscled neck the crest blends smoothly into the cranial slope of the withers. The fix should make the summit stand proud of the crest; it should not carve a notch.
- **"Local high point" depends on posture.** With the head raised, the crest rises again in front of the withers. Strictly, the withers is then a clear break of slope plus a ridge, not the maximum of the whole topline. With the head lowered (grazing, gallop) it is the true high point.
- **The mane is not wrong at the summit.** On a real horse the mane runs back onto the cranial slope of the withers, often to about the summit. So the first mane blade sitting near the summit is not wrong in itself. The problem is the neck volume covering the summit. If the neck root moves forward, the mane's end should follow it to about the front of the withers, not be cut well short.

I checked the numbers again. The TRUNK loft (index.html:507-525) with PROF.trunk gives ring perimeters of 1.952 m at x=0.34, 1.950 m at 0.18 and 1.902 m at 0.00. Chest depth from the withers (1.622) to girthLow (0.826) is 0.796 m. The barrel is 0.56 m wide.

(a) Matsuura et al. 2024 (J Equine Sci 35(1), PMC10955269) measured 7 Thoroughbreds and 2 crossbreds, all riding horses averaging 14 years old. Means: 159.9 cm at the withers, girth 191.0 cm, body length 175.6 cm, chest depth 76.6 cm, 541.8 kg. Their girth/height ratio is 1.195, which is exactly the model's (1.95/1.63). So the model has the barrel of a mature riding Thoroughbred that would scale to about 560-575 kg at 163 cm, not a 475 kg racehorse.
(b) Secretariat at three was 168 cm, girth 193 cm, body length 177 cm and 513-524 kg. Scaled to 163 cm that is girth 187 cm, body length 172 cm and about 474 kg.

So the core claim holds. A 475 kg, 163 cm racing Thoroughbred has a heart girth of about 1.85-1.88 m, and 1.95 m is about 4% too much girth, or about 8-9% too much implied mass.

What needs correcting:
1. The formula BW = HG² × BL / 11880 is Carroll & Huntington (1988). Wagner & Tyler (2011) only compared it with other methods. Neither formula fits lean racing Thoroughbreds well. On Secretariat, C&H predicts 555 kg and W&T about 580 kg, against a real 513-524 kg. So the finding's "530-565 kg" overstates the excess. It is better argued from measured girth/height ratios.
2. A 163 cm Thoroughbred is longer than 163-166 cm: about 170-179 cm from point of shoulder to point of buttock (ratios 1.05-1.10 in the sources above).
3. The 1.945 m ring at x=-0.52 is the hindquarter at hip-joint level and includes the thighs. Matching the heart girth there proves nothing.
4. The tuck-up part is overstated. The underline is not "almost flat": it already rises 6.4 cm from the girth (0.826) to x=-0.19 (0.89). In real horses the deepest point is just behind the elbow (Matsuura) and the belly rises gently toward the stifle fold. Conformation guides want the depth from the lowest point of the back to the bottom of the belly to be about the same as the girth depth. A sharp tuck-up ("tucked up / herring-gutted / wasp-waisted") is a fault, and in a racehorse it is a sign of being run up light.

So raising the bottoms at x=0 by 4-6 cm would overdo it. Any extra rise should be concentrated caudally, from about x=-0.15 to the stifle fold near x=-0.36, by roughly 3-5 cm, with x=0 raised 1-2 cm at most.

The dip back to 0.845 at x=-0.52 is behind the stifle (x=-0.36), so it is thigh, not belly. That is a separate silhouette issue (no belly wall behind the stifle fold), not a missing tuck-up.

The 0.56 m barrel width is plausible but on the wide side. It is more than the model's own 0.50 m hips, while in Thoroughbreds the barrel is roughly as wide as the points of hip (Matsuura: 52 cm, about 53 cm scaled to 163 cm). A 5% cut is reasonable.

The code already has conf.tuckUp (0..1, default 0; index.html:683, 735), so fix B mostly exists. It would only need a racing-fit default, not a new parameter.

Severity stays low. A 195 cm girth at 163 cm is within normal Thoroughbred variation for a heavier horse of about 520-540 kg. It is only a mismatch with the stated 475 kg reference.

The barrel is too big for the stated 475 kg / 163 cm racehorse, but by less than the formula estimate suggests. Secretariat scaled to 163 cm gives about 187 cm girth at about 474 kg, so the target heart girth is about 1.85-1.88 m (2-4% slimmer in depth plus width), not "1.84-1.86 from C&H". C&H and W&T overestimate lean racing Thoroughbreds by 6-12%. A 163 cm Thoroughbred's body length is about 170-179 cm. The formula is Carroll & Huntington 1988, not Wagner & Tyler.

The underline already rises about 6 cm from the girth. A fit Thoroughbred's belly rises only gently, and a pronounced tuck-up (herring-gutted/wasp-waisted) is a conformation fault. Add only about 3-5 cm more rise, concentrated from about x=-0.15 to the stifle fold (x≈-0.36), and keep x=0 within 1-2 cm. The low outline at x=-0.52 is thigh behind the stifle, not belly. truth.reasoning:
I could not refute the core real-horse facts, but two details need correcting.

What holds:
- **Resting rate.** Merck Veterinary Manual gives 10-14 breaths/min at rest, and clinical texts give 8-16, so the claimed range is normal. The model's graze cycle (about 4 s, roughly 15/min) is at the high edge of that range.
- **One breath per stride at canter and gallop in Thoroughbreds.** Young et al. 1992 (J Exp Biol 166:19-31, Thoroughbreds on a treadmill at 9-11 m/s) found "exactly one breath per stride". Butler et al. 1993 (J Exp Biol 179:159-180) found breathing rate "locked in a 1:1 fashion to stride frequency" at canter and gallop. Lafortuna et al. 1996 (J Physiol 492:587-596) found 1:1 coupling in 10 of 10 canter trials.
- **The per-stride volume change is real and fairly large.** Padilla et al. 2004 measured a tidal volume of about 12.6 L at about 114 breaths/min at the gallop. That much air has to show up as change in body-wall volume. Over a mid-barrel section of about 190-270 L, it works out to roughly 1-1.6% change in each of height and width. So the proposed +/-1-2% is physically about right at the gallop, toward the high end. At rest, tidal volume is about 5-6 L, so it should be roughly +/-0.5%.
- **The code description is accurate.** No BODY function has a barrel channel, and graze has the 0.004 x cyc spine bob at line 1647. One small omission: buildBreath (about line 2966) already emits nostril breath puffs, 1:1 with the stride at canter and gallop. They only appear in locations where loc.breath is set, which is the Hidaka winter scene. So the spine bob is not the only breathing cue, and the barrel motion could be timed off the same breath clock.

What is overstated:
- **"Visible flank and ribcage motion" at rest.** Koterba et al. 1988 (J Appl Physiol 64:337-346) show that a resting horse breathes mainly with the diaphragm and abdominal muscles. Expiration has two phases, the second driven by the abdominal muscles. So what you see at rest is the flank and belly wall moving, with little ribcage expansion.
- **"The flank and abdomen pulse once per stride" at race speed.** The timing is right. Attenburrow & Goss 1994 place expiration in the stance of the trailing forelimb. But the outside movement is only a few millimetres of girth, and it is hidden by the trunk's pitching and back flexion. The flank heaving that people actually notice in racehorses comes after the race, while the horse is still blowing hard.
- **How the coupling works.** Young et al. 1992 found that the visceral piston and the forelimb impact compressing the chest do NOT drive it, and that back flexion probably helps.
- **Other gaits.** At the trot the coupling varies (1:1 in only 5 of 14 trials in Lafortuna 1996), and the walk is not coupled. Non-Thoroughbred gaited breeds can run 3:2 at a submaximal gallop (Criollo horses, Massie et al. 2025).

Implications for the fix: weight the motion toward the ventral flank and belly behind the ribs rather than scaling the whole ribcage evenly. Put the low point (end of expiration) in forelimb stance. Use about +/-0.5% at rest and about +/-1% at gallop. Optionally, a post-race "blowing" state would be the most visible version of this behaviour. Severity "low" is appropriate.
truth.correction:
The real-horse claim is right that horses breathe about 8-16 times/min at rest (Merck: 10-14) and once per stride at canter and gallop (Young 1992; Butler 1993; Lafortuna 1996: 10 of 10 canter trials). Two corrections are needed:
(1) At rest the visible motion is mostly the flank and belly wall, driven by the diaphragm and abdominal muscles with a two-phase expiration (Koterba 1988). The ribcage expands very little.
(2) At gallop the tidal volume of about 12-13 L is real, with expiration during forelimb stance (Attenburrow & Goss 1994). But it shows on the outside as only a few millimetres of girth, masked by trunk pitch. The obvious flank heaving in racehorses happens after the race, during recovery breathing.

Coupling at the trot varies and the walk is uncoupled. Young 1992 found that the visceral piston and forelimb chest compression do not drive the coupling; back flexion probably contributes.

Suggested fix settings: about +/-0.5% at rest and about +/-1% at gallop, concentrated on the flank and belly, timed so the low point falls in forelimb stance. In cold-weather locations the code already has 1:1 nostril breath puffs whose timing the fix can reuse.

So the loin and flank bend a little each stride: the croup-to-girthLow distance changes by 15 mm at race and 6.8 mm at gallop. truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse claim and could not. The main point is standard equine anatomy. The horse has no clavicle, so the forelimb joins the trunk only by muscle (a synsarcosis). The cranial thorax is narrow from side to side, and the scapula lies flat on its wall. Each dorsal border and its scapular cartilage sits beside the withers spines, a few cm from the midline, while the shoulder joints sit much further out. Seen from the front, the two blades therefore converge towards the top. Rough numbers: the TB scapula plus cartilage is about 0.40-0.45 m long, the dorsal border is about 0.05-0.07 m from the midline and the joint about 0.17 m. That makes the blade plane lean about 15 deg from vertical, not 0 deg. In a fit Thoroughbred the outline of the blade can show under thin skin, but it never stands centimetres proud of the withers and neck base as a flat fin.

I checked the code side as well:
- FORE.z = 0.165 is used for both sc and sh (index.html:536), so the blade is vertical.
- The blade's top section half-width is 0.022-0.036 (:1201), so the top spans z of about 0.13-0.20.
- Working through PROF.trunk with the TRUNK row at x=0.46 (w 0.24, wu 0.42) gives a trunk half-width of only about 0.085-0.11 at y 1.50-1.54.
- So the top of the blade sticks out about 3-10 cm, which matches the finding. The 'head, front' and 'front' tiles of 00-stand.jpeg show the two slabs beside the neck.

Small corrections that do not change the verdict:
1. The 1-4 cm skin-displacement figure is right, but it comes from van Weeren, van den Bogert & Barneveld 1990, Equine Vet J Suppl 9:110-118 (the walk study, four Dutch Warmbloods). The cited pages 101-109 are their trot study, where mean displacements ranged from 8 mm to 142 mm. The distal scapula also had the smallest displacement of all sites in the walk study, so it shows that skin there follows the bone. It says nothing about the dorsal border.
2. 'Shoulder joints ~0.35-0.45 m apart' runs high for joint centres. Ünal et al. 2025 report a mean TB chest width of 47.3 cm (withers height 158 cm). That is most likely the surface width at the points of the shoulder; the paper's landmark definitions could not be extracted. That puts joint centres at about 0.33-0.38 m apart, so the model's 0.33 m is plausible and the problem is only that the blade is vertical.
3. 'Thoracic sling' usually means the serratus ventralis plus the pectorals. The trapezius and rhomboideus anchor the dorsal border and cartilage rather than carrying the trunk. All of them are part of the synsarcosis, so the claim's point still stands.
4. The cited Payne, Veenman & Wilson 2004 (J Anat 205:479-490) is correct and backs the serratus ventralis thoracis as the force-bearing sling muscle.

One caveat for whoever picks a fix: do not 'fix' this by cutting scapSwing. Real scapular rotation is large. Biplanar fluoroscopy in a pony (Wagner et al. 2026) measured 27.6 deg range of motion at the walk and 23.3 deg at the trot. Back et al. 1995 found that scapular rotation is pendular and synchronous with the forward-and-back motion of the distal limb. A 36 deg total range (+/-18 deg) in the race gait is therefore plausible. The scapula also turns about a moving centre of rotation inside the blade, not about its dorsal tip. The real dorsal border moves caudally as the limb comes forward, whereas the model pivots on sc, so its top stays fixed. Fixes that tilt the top inward or skin the shoulder fit real anatomy; widening the withers (option 4) does not.

Severity stays high. It is a large, constant error in a defining TB region, shows up in every front and 3/4 view and in every gait, and no amount of normal Thoroughbred variation covers it.
