I tried to refute this and couldn't. The problem shows up in the code, in the measurements and in the pictures.

CODE (index.html)
- Line 584: FORE = { z: 0.165, sc: [0.5, 1.5], sh: [0.72, 1.22], ... }. Line 1193 builds both sc and sh with the same z (P(xy) = V(x, y, z)), so the scapula bone runs from one point to another at the same z. That means the blade stands vertical.
- Line 1201: the blade is limb(sc, sh, [[-0.06, .05, .06, .022], [0.3, .12, .11, .036], [0.8, .1, .09, .04], [1.06, .06, .06, .034]]). It is centred on z = ±0.165 and is 2.2–4 cm thick on each side of that line.
- Lines 1442–1451: the only sideways rotation is scap.rotation.x = atan2(-dz, drop). It only abducts the leg enough to keep the hoof in its track. scap.rotation.z = scapSwing·cos(πw) is a swing about sc, and scapSwing is 18° in the race gait (line 216). There is no rest-pose lean toward the midline anywhere.
- TRUNK rows 0.46 and 0.58 have width factors at the top of 0.42 and 0.5. NECK row 0 has w = 0.19 with wUp = 0.5·w. So the body narrows to about 0.10–0.13 m half-width exactly where the top of the blade sits.

MEASUREMENTS (measurements.json; 5 gaits × 32 phases, both forelegs)
- The top of the scapula sits 16.1–16.8 cm out from the withers midline and 12–13 cm below the top of the withers.
- Lean: shoulder z minus scapTop z stays within ±5 mm in every sample, so the blade is vertical at all times.

PROTRUSION (my own check)
I rebuilt the rest-pose trunk and neck lofts in node, using the defaults: neckLen 1.1, no jitter. Then I ray-cast the body's half-width at each vertex of the scapula and arm shells.
- Body half-width at sc (0.5, 1.5) is 0.127 m.
- The blade's top ring is at z 0.143–0.187. Its outer face stands 7.0–7.2 cm outside the body. Its inner face is also 2.8–3.8 cm outside, so the top of the plate is completely detached, with a real gap between it and the neck/withers.
- At t = 0.3 the outer face is 4.3 cm proud. At t = 0.8 the front edge is 7.1 cm proud.
- I mapped the posed joints back into the chest frame. In every phase of walk, gallop and race, 75% of the vertices in the blade's upper 30% are outside the body. The critic's finer mesh test gave 77–88%, which is consistent.
- At protraction (gallop g ≈ 0.19–0.31, race g ≈ 0–0.31) the shoulder joint moves to x ≈ 0.76–0.79, y ≈ 1.26–1.30. That is in front of and beside the narrow base of the neck, and the blade's front edge then stands 13–16 cm clear.

SHEETS
- In 00-stand ('front', 'head, front') and 05-race ('front g=0', 'front g=1/2'), you can see two flat-topped vertical slabs on either side of the neck, with shadowed gaps between them and the neck.
- The 3/4 views show a ridge above the shoulder.

REAL ANATOMY
In a real horse the front of the ribcage is narrow from side to side. The scapulae lie flat against it, held by the thoracic sling. Their scapular cartilages rise to beside the withers spines (T3–T6), close to the midline, so each blade slopes outward and down toward the point of shoulder (Budras; Dyce, Sack & Wensing; Sisson & Grossman/Getty). A vertical blade 16.5 cm off the midline, standing clear of the withers, is wrong.

ONE QUALIFICATION (arm shell)
The arm numbers reproduce. At rest the arm is 3–5 cm proud at mid-shaft and about 9–12 cm at its ends; at race protraction the coarse probe reads 20+ cm because the shell sits in front of the trunk's outline. But in a real horse the arm and triceps do form the widest part of the forehand, outside the ribcage. Being outside a ribcage-only loft is therefore partly correct anatomy. The real fault in the arm is that at full scapSwing the point of shoulder slides forward past the trunk's front end (x ≈ 0.81) with nothing covering it, where a real horse has the brachiocephalicus and skin.

SEVERITY
I'm keeping it high. These are fixed constants, so every horse in every gait has the problem, and the slabs are among the most visible defects in any head-on or 3/4 camera. Straight side views hide it.
model.correction: The core claim stands exactly as written. I measured a vertical blade (lean under 5 mm), top 16–17 cm out from the midline; its top ring is 7 cm proud on the outside and fully detached from the body (inner face 3–4 cm outside); the upper blade is about 75% outside in every phase. Two small corrections: (1) mid-blade protrusion is about 4–7 cm, not a uniform 6 cm, and the 12–16 cm figures happen only at protraction, when the front edge moves in front of the narrow neck base. (2) An arm shell outside the trunk loft is partly expected, because the triceps and point of shoulder really are the widest part of a horse's forehand. The arm-shell fault is really the uncovered point of shoulder sliding past the chest front at scapSwing 18°, not its width.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the model numbers and they are accurate. In measurements.json (static.standing RF), scapTop is (0.498, 1.500), the shoulder joint (0.720, 1.222), the elbow (0.482, 0.960) and the withers (0.457, 1.622). That gives a scapula of 0.356 m, a humerus of 0.354 m (ratio ~1.0), and a blade top 12.2 cm below and 4.1 cm in front of the withers. The scapula mesh only extends from t=-0.06 to 1.06 (index.html:1201), so the visible blade ends about 10.5 cm below the withers.

The core real-horse claim holds: a horse's scapula is clearly longer than its humerus.
- Belyaev et al. 2025 (J Anat, Table 2) give Equidae scapula length 26.3%, humerus 21.3% and antebrachium 26.3% of trunk length. That is a scapula/humerus ratio of 1.23 on bone greatest lengths, and the authors note the humerus is the shortest forelimb segment in equids.
- One adult horse scapula measured 410 mm from the cranial edge of the glenoid to the dorsal border, without cartilage (3D Print Med 2019).
- Greatest length overstates the joint-to-joint humerus by several cm (the greater tubercle sits above the head; the condyles extend below the elbow axis). The scapular cartilage then adds a few cm to the blade. So for a 163 cm TB, scapula plus cartilage of ~0.42-0.48 m against a joint-to-joint humerus of ~0.28-0.31 m (~1.4-1.6x) is a sound expectation.
- Kiesewalter's withers-height factor (as I recall it, humerus lateral length x 4.87) gives a lateral length of ~33.5 cm at 163 cm, so joint-to-joint ~0.28-0.30 m.
- The model's 1:1 ratio is therefore wrong in both directions: the shoulder is ~15-25% short and the humerus ~15-20% long.

Four parts of the finding are overstated or argued badly:

1. **The Senna surface lens is not robust.** Senna et al. 2015 (51 jumping TBs: shoulder 69±5, arm 34±2.9, forearm 46±2.4 cm) do not define their landmarks. A study that does define them (Iranian Arabs, Open Vet J 2026) found scapula (shoulder joint via the scapular spine to the withers) 40.8±2.5 cm and arm (greater tubercle to olecranon) 41.2±2.5 cm. That is about 1:1 by surface measure. Surface ratios depend on how each study defines its landmarks, so "arm/shoulder 49.7%" and "shoulder ~25% short" cannot rest on Senna. The step "the arm matches" is also flawed. A point-of-shoulder-to-point-of-elbow surface length is longer than the joint-to-joint humerus. Matching 34 cm with a 0.354 m joint-to-joint humerus therefore means the model's arm is too long, not correct. The same applies to the forearm: Senna's 46 cm is a surface length and should not be compared with joint-to-joint values. The bone-based ~0.40-0.43 m from elbow axis to carpus centre is the better target, which leaves the model's 0.46 mildly long.

2. **"Dorsal border close to the withers" is overstated.** The top of the withers is the tips of the T3-T6 spinous processes, plus skin and soft tissue. In a high-withered TB these stick up above the scapular cartilage, so a gap of several cm is normal. Taking a blade of ~0.45 m at the ~58° shoulder-to-ground slope reported for racehorses (Ahmad et al. 2025: 58.4±2.0°) from a joint at ~1.17 m puts the top at ~1.53-1.56 m, i.e. ~7-10 cm below 1.63. The model's 12 cm gap is only ~2-5 cm too low. The 4 cm forward offset is not a defect, since the cartilage spans the withers front to back. Fix option 1's target of scapula top y=1.58 is slightly high; ~1.53-1.56 is more realistic.

3. **"Flat arm" is not a defect.** In the model, the 99° shoulder angle is the scapula slope (51.4°) plus the humerus slope (47.7°). Real surface data (shoulder-to-ground ~58°, shoulder joint 88-99° per Ahmad 2025 and Senna 2015) imply the humerus line is 30-41° below horizontal. Real arms are as flat or flatter than the model's, so only the arm's length is wrong, not its slope.

4. **Point of shoulder ~1.17 m.** I found no reference to confirm this figure; it is plausible but should not be cited as established.

Severity stays medium. This is a real proportion error in the shoulder line and arm lever, which also feeds the arm-swing problem in A-FORE-03. But the withers-gap part is smaller than the finding states.
truth.correction:
Accurate version: in real horses the scapula is clearly longer than the humerus. Bone greatest lengths in Equidae are scapula 26.3% vs humerus 21.3% of trunk length (ratio ~1.23); one adult horse scapula is 41 cm without cartilage. With the cartilage added and the humerus measured joint to joint, the ratio is ~1.4-1.6 (≈0.42-0.48 m vs ≈0.28-0.31 m at 163 cm). The model's 1:1 is wrong: the scapula is ~15-25% short and the humerus ~15-20% long, not "matching".

Three corrections:
- **Surface lengths are not evidence here.** Do not use Senna's surface lengths for ratios. Their landmarks are undefined, and a study that does define them (Iranian Arabs) gives scapula 40.8 cm vs arm 41.2 cm (~1:1). The arm and forearm comparisons with Senna mix surface and joint-to-joint lengths. On bones, the forearm (elbow axis to carpus centre) should be ~0.40-0.43 m, so the model's 0.46 is mildly long.
- **A gap below the withers is normal.** The top of the scapular cartilage normally lies several cm below the withers, because the T3-T6 spinous processes stick up above it. A realistic blade top for a 163 cm TB is ~1.53-1.56 m (7-10 cm below), so the model's 12 cm gap is only ~2-5 cm too low. The 4 cm forward offset is not a defect, and fix option 1's y=1.58 is slightly high.
- **The arm's slope is fine.** The humerus inclination (~48° below horizontal) is within or steeper than real surface data (30-41°). Only the arm's length is the problem.

Code: index.html:552 is FORE = {sc [0.5,1.5], sh [0.72,1.22], el [0.48,0.96], kn [0.48,0.5]}. These are fixed constants. FORE.sc/sh/el/kn are read only at :1193 and :1371, so no conformation or build parameter changes them for any horse. The scapula mesh (:1201) is lofted from sc to sh. The humerus mesh (:1205) runs from sh to el. L.len.arm (:1214) feeds the IK at :1457/:1467.

Re-measured with node from measurements.json static.standing RF:
- Scapula (scapTop to shoulder) is 0.356 m at 51.4 deg from horizontal.
- Humerus is 0.354 m at 47.7 deg. Ratio 0.99.
- Forearm 0.460 m (1.30 x humerus), cannon 0.291 m, pastern 0.140 m.
- scapTop is 12.2 cm below the withers (1.622 m) and 4.1 cm in front of them.
- The shoulder joint is at 1.222 m, which is 75.3% of withers height.
- Shoulder angle (scapTop-shoulder-elbow) is 99.1 deg; elbow angle 137.6 deg.
- I estimated the point of shoulder as the front of the arm mesh at t=-0.14. That puts it at about (0.80, 1.22), and withers to point of shoulder comes to 0.528 m, matching the critic's 0.53.

Against real horses:
- Senna et al. 2015 (jumping Thoroughbreds) measured on the surface: point of withers to point of shoulder 69±5 cm, arm 34 cm, forearm 46 cm. That gives arm/shoulder 49.7% and forearm/shoulder 66.6%. The model's arm/shoulder is 0.67 and forearm/shoulder is 0.87. Its arm and forearm match Senna, so the shoulder is the short member, about 23% short.
- Kiesewalter's withers-height factors put a 163 cm horse's humerus greatest length at about 0.335 m. Joint centre to joint centre that is roughly 0.27-0.29 m, so the model's 0.354 m humerus is long, not just the scapula short.
- J Anat 2025 (PMC11684385, Table 2) gives Equidae bone-only lengths as % of trunk length: scapula L' 26.3% vs humerus 21.3% (ratio 1.23). Those are measured to joint surfaces and exclude the scapular cartilage. Adding the cartilage and measuring between joint centres raises the real ratio to about 1.4-1.7, against 0.99 in the model.

Nuances that do not overturn the finding:
1. The 12 cm gap is to the scapula pivot. The blade mesh starts at t=-0.06 with a 3 cm cap, so its visible tip is at about (0.466, 1.540). That is only 8-10 cm below the withers, and the visible blade is 0.407 m from tip to shoulder joint (1.15 x the humerus). That is still clearly short.
2. The model's 99 deg shoulder angle uses the scapula pivot. Measured as withers-shoulder-elbow, the way Senna's surface landmarks likely were, it is 104 deg. So the angles match Senna only nominally.

Problem confirmed at medium severity. The fix also involves the long humerus (about 20-30% too long), not only lengthening the scapula, as the critic's first fix option already proposes.

Two further checks:
- The 4x enlarged 00-stand right-side tile shows a high point of shoulder. The blade facets stop well below the withers, which is consistent with the numbers.
- Neither cited Uenal 2025 nor Ahmad 2025 (Morna racehorses) reports limb segment lengths. Uenal compares tape with smartphone measurements of withers and shoulder height, body length and chest depth. Ahmad reports only joint angles. Neither adds support for the length claims.

findings.title: Fore swing folds through the elbow: humerus parked near horizontal, elbow closes to 31-58 deg, elbow and hoof enter the barrel (hackney-like action)
findings.observed: In mid/late swing the humerus sits at -72..-79 deg from vertical (ARM_RANGE floor -76 deg; 6-8 of 32 samples in gallop/race) and the elbow interior angle closes to 31-38 deg race, 39-48 gallop, 58 canter, 73 trot (rest 137.6). The elbow rises 13/17/18/20 cm (trot/canter/gallop/race) above the chest's lower lateral surface; against the posed loft it ends 4.0/6.9/6.9/7.4/7.4 cm inside the chest wall (walk..race), and the point of shoulder dips into the breast. The forearm reaches forward (+60-70 deg) before the humerus protracts (g 0.0-0.19, -79->0 deg), and the knee over-folds 93-110 deg vs planned 64-105 once the clamp fallback fires. Race RF toe peaks at 0.95 m at g~0.69 (cannon -139 deg), level with the elbow and 10-17 cm above the belly line, so the hoof passes inside the barrel. Cause: the fetlock target holds full lift (0.63-0.65 m) from ~25-55% of swing, too close to the shoulder.
findings.expected: The humerus is bound to the chest by pectorals and triceps: the elbow stays low against the thorax with the olecranon visible all stride, and protracts with the forearm. The carpus does the folding; elbow working range ~90-150 deg (walk peak flexion late in swing, 84% of stride). In Muybridge's gallop plates the forearm is near vertical at peak carpal flexion with the hoof tucked under the elbow, below the belly line. TB action is long and low.

fixOptions.approach: Peak the fetlock early (~0.25-0.35 of swing) under/behind the elbow, start 'fall' ~0.4, keep shoulder-to-fetlock >= ~0.75 m, lower lift per gait (race 0.44->~0.30).

fixOptions.label: Tighten arm limits
fixOptions.approach: ARM_RANGE floor ~-55..-60 deg, elbow interior floor ~75-80 deg, applied in stance too; excess goes to the carpus via the existing fallback.
fixOptions.risk: When limits bind the hoof misses its target and can jump; best with the path reshape.

fixOptions.label: Scripted humerus / joint-angle swing
fixOptions.approach: Drive the humerus (or all fore joints) from per-gait angle curves (Back 1995, Hodson 2000, Muybridge); IK only in stance and the last ~15% of swing. Makes knee action a running-style parameter.
fixOptions.risk: Blending at lift-off/touchdown; angle data for 5 gaits; largest solveLeg rewrite.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse side of the claim and could not. A few details are overstated, but the core holds.

**The model numbers check out.** I re-ran the angles from measurements.json (RF, 32 samples per gait):
- The humerus starts at -42 deg from vertical at rest. In the race it sits at -75 to -79 deg from u=0.51 to 0.73, and in the gallop at -72 to -76 deg.
- The elbow interior angle falls to 36-45 deg (race) and 45-54 deg (gallop).
- The shoulder joint closes to 57-66 deg, against 99 at rest.
- In that phase the forearm points +57 to +65 deg forward, roughly horizontal out of the chest. Race tiles g=0/8 and 7/8 show this.
- The race toe peaks at 0.95 m (elbow 0.94 m, girth floor 0.79 m).

**Real-horse checks:**
1. **The humerus drives protraction, and the distal limb does the lifting.** Hodson, Clayton and Lanovaz 2000 (EVJ 32:287, abstract verified): "brachial rotation was responsible for protraction and retraction of the limb as a whole, while rotations of the scapula and antebrachium elevated the distal limb during breakover and early swing." So a humerus parked about 11-18 deg below horizontal through mid and late swing, protracting only after the forearm has reached forward, is the opposite of real coordination.
2. **Elbow timing.** The same abstract says the swing flexion peaks come at 76% of the stride for the carpus and 84% for the elbow. So the "84%" is correct. At the walk, though, swing starts at about 62-65% of the stride, so 84% is mid-swing (about 55% of the way through the swing), not late. The carpus peaks first, as claimed.
3. **Elbow range.** "About 90-150 deg" comes from walk and trot data (Back et al. 1995, EVJ 27:31, warmbloods at 4 m/s). I found no hard gallop numbers, and at racing speed the elbow probably flexes somewhat further. A floor of about 75-80 deg, as in the fix options, is safer than 90. Even so, no equine locomotion data come anywhere near 31-45 deg. At that angle the forearm would lie along the humerus, and the olecranon and triceps mass prevent it.
4. **Muybridge gallop plates.** They show peak carpal flexion with the forearm near vertical and the hoof folded behind the forearm, under the elbow or girth. That matches real Thoroughbred low action.
5. **One overstatement.** A forefoot reaching elbow height is not anatomically impossible; very high-action horses can strike the elbow. It is simply not Thoroughbred action. The foot passing inside the barrel is impossible in any horse, because the limb lies outside the thorax.

**Note on the model's cause chain.** At the race toe peak (u≈0.42) the humerus is -57 deg and the elbow 141 deg, both normal, and the forearm is near vertical, as in Muybridge. That hoof-in-belly frame comes from the carpus folding to 58 deg interior, the cannon tipping to -139 deg (49 deg above horizontal, pointing back) and the high fetlock target. Humerus parking does not cause it. The parked humerus and elbow fold come later in the swing (u 0.48-0.73). The fixes should treat these as two problems: lower the lift and the carpus/fetlock fold for the toe height, and limit or script the humerus for the arm.

The claim survives with these minor corrections, and its high severity is justified: the frames are clearly visible in the trot through race sheets.

model.reasoning:
I tried to refute this finding and could not. The numbers reproduce from measurements.json, the code works the way the finding says, and the sheets show the problem. I measured with node scripts in my temp folder and changed no repository files.

**Code.** The finding's line numbers point about 37 lines too early. The cited code is at these lines:
- `ARM_RANGE = [-76°, +2°]` is at index.html:1431. It only binds when `f.u >= G.duty`, so it applies in swing and never in stance.
- The fore solve2 uses bend -1 (:1457). The clamp fallback (:1463-1469) re-solves the forearm and cannon with the humerus pinned at -76° (chest frame), so the knee takes the extra fold.
- footPath (:1407-1408) holds the full fore lift between `rise` and `fall`. Race uses lift 0.44, rise 0.25, fall 0.55 (:216). Gallop uses 0.42, 0.3, 0.5 (:206).

**Re-measured (world frame unless noted).**
- **Humerus in swing at -72° or flatter:** 7-8 of 32 samples in the gallop and 8-9 in the race. Race RF k0 and k25-31 sit at -75° to -79°, only 11-15° below horizontal.
- **Smallest elbow interior angle** (rest 138°):
  - race 31° (LF) and 36° (RF)
  - gallop 39° (LF) and 45° (RF)
  - canter 58° (LF) and 68° (RF)
  - trot 73°
  - walk 92°
- **Elbow position.** I mapped each sample into the chest frame using a rigid fit to scapTop and brisket, then compared it with the TRUNK loft.
  - At rest the elbow centre is 1.9 cm outside the chest wall.
  - It rises 12 cm (trot), 13-18 cm (canter), 19 cm (gallop) and 21-22 cm (race) above its rest height.
  - It ends 4.1 / 6.9 / 6.9 / 7.3 / 7.4 cm inside the chest wall (walk to race), matching the finding's 4.0 / 6.9 / 6.9 / 7.4 / 7.4.
- **Forearm reaches before the humerus protracts.** Race RF k0-6: the forearm is at +57° to +47° while the humerus goes from -79° to 0°. Race LF k1-2: forearm +70°.
- **Knee over-fold.** Race RF k26-29 measures 110 / 106 / 100 / 93° against a planned 104 / 92 / 77 / 63°.
- **Race RF k22 (g = 0.69):** toe at 0.95 m, elbow at 0.94 m, cannon -139°. The toe is 14 cm above the trunk bottom at its x (LF: 12 cm).
- **Cause.** The fetlock sits at 0.63-0.65 m through mid-swing. The shortest shoulder-to-fetlock distance in swing is 0.50-0.54 m (race), 0.56-0.61 m (gallop), 0.70-0.75 m (canter) and 0.78 m (trot), against 1.04 m at rest. That forces the bend -1 solve to fold the elbow.

**Sheets.** In 05-race g=0/8 and 7/8, and 04-gallop g=0/8 and 7/8, the near forearm sticks out of mid-chest at about horizontal with the cannon hanging down. No elbow or olecranon is visible: the hackney-like look is real. In 03-canter the effect is mild.

**Real horses.** The model's rest joint angles are Thoroughbred-like (shoulder 99°, elbow 138°; Senna et al. 2015). An elbow at 31-45° and a near-horizontal humerus are far outside published equine elbow ranges: Back et al. 1995 for the trot and Hodson et al. 2000 for the walk give roughly 90-150°. The 90-150° figure is from memory: my web search budget was used up, so I could not re-check the exact values. In Muybridge's gallop series the elbow stays at the floor of the chest.

**Small corrections (none of them overturn the finding):**
- In the race the deepest elbow sits in late stance (RF k14, LF k17, humerus -80° because the clamp is off in stance), at 7.4 / 6.9 cm. The worst swing values are 7.3 / 6.7 cm.
- The hoof is only partly in the barrel, and only in the race. The RF toe centreline is 4.4 cm inside the side wall at k22 (LF 2.9 cm at k25). The hoof is about 5.7 cm half-width, so roughly half of it is buried. Gallop and canter toes stay at least 13 cm below the belly.
- The point of shoulder is 1.9 cm under the surface at rest and 5-5.6 cm under it at the gallop and race. That 3-4 cm "dip" is minor.
- The running-style `kneeAction` setting (up to 1.4x fore lift, :261) would make this worse for horses tuned with high knee action.
model.correction:

truth.reasoning:
I recomputed the elbow angles from measurements.json using the angle between the shoulder→elbow and elbow→knee lines in the sagittal plane, the same convention vet kinematics uses (cranial angle). Standing, the model reads 138°, close to the real 140-145°, so the convention matches.

Model numbers:
- Race: elbow is 133° at the end of stance, then 177/172/164° at RF k16-18 and 178/173/165° at LF k19-21, right after the toe leaves the ground.
- Canter: LF peaks at 174°.

The core real-horse claim holds. Peak elbow extension in normal gaits, measured with skin markers, is:
- walk 156.6 ± 3.1°
- trot 155.5 ± 3.1°
- canter, leading fore 156.5 ± 3.8°
- canter, trailing fore 159.9 ± 2.1°

These come from Back & Clayton, Equine Locomotion 2nd ed. 2013, as tabulated in Sensors 2023;23:8832. Mean plus 2 SD tops out at about 164°. Extension is checked by the anconeal process seating in the olecranon fossa, helped by the off-centre collateral ligaments and the biceps/lacertus fibrosus. So 170-178° is impossible for a real horse.

Elbow timing is also right as claimed. The elbow is most extended in late stance; the canter EMG/kinematics study (Animals 2023, PMID 37889657) reports the trailing-fore elbow more extended in late stance. It starts flexing around breakover and lift-off, reaching peak flexion early-to-mid swing (Back et al. 1995 EVJ 27:31-38). The model does the opposite: it jumps 44° toward straight right after lift-off. That is a real and serious error.

What is overstated or wrong in the finding's real-horse framing:

1. **The ceiling should be about 160°, not "150-160".** Normal horses reach 160 ± 2° (trailing canter fore). A hard cap of about 155°, as in fix option 2, would cut off normal motion; about 160-162° is better. The 164-165° frames (RF k18, LF k21) are at the edge of normal. Only the 170-178° frames are clearly impossible.

2. **"Leg locks straight before touchdown" is a misdescription.** In a real horse the limb below the elbow is meant to be straight at touchdown: the carpus is fully extended (about 180°) and the elbow is near its maximum (about 145-155°), as Muybridge's gallop plates show. In the model's late swing and touchdown (race RF k6-9, LF k9-12) the carpus is 179-180°, which is normal. The elbow is only 128-139°, which is less extended than a real horse, not "a straight pole".

3. **The humerus claim is overstated at racing speed.** At maximum protraction the humerus comes close to vertical in a real horse. Peak shoulder-joint extension is about 119-126° (Back & Clayton), and the scapula rotates forward on top of that. The model's late-swing pose has the humerus vertical, the shoulder angle at 125° and the scapula rotated 16° forward of standing. All of that is at the edge of real values, not clearly wrong. Vertical is the limit; past vertical is not real.

The real anatomical fault in late swing (05-race g=2/8: the leg seems to grow out of the chest front) is a different one. The shoulder joint itself is carried forward to the trunk front: x = 0.79-0.80 against a trunk front of 0.81, up from 0.72 standing, because the scapula rotates about its top. The elbow under it therefore ends up at the breast. In a real horse the elbow stays behind the point of shoulder and inside the trunk outline at about sternum level. This is a scapula pivot and shoulder placement problem (fix option 3 territory), not elbow over-extension.

**Side observation, out of scope.** The model also over-flexes the elbow in mid swing:
- race minimum 31-36°
- gallop minimum 39-45°
- canter LF minimum 58°

Real maximum flexion is 88.8-104.8° at walk, trot and canter, and 58 ± 3° even in swimming, the most flexed activity measured. This deserves its own finding.

Severity stays high: the early-swing near-straight elbow is physically impossible and happens in the main race gait. Scratch scripts are in C:\Users\Aaron\AppData\Local\Temp\a-fore-04\ (an.js, epmc.js, ft.js); nothing in the repository was touched.
truth.correction:
Elbow peak extension in real horses is about 155-160° (walk 156.6 ± 3.1, trot 155.5 ± 3.1, canter leading 156.5 ± 3.8, trailing 159.9 ± 2.1; Back & Clayton 2013). About 164° is the outer edge of normal; 170-180° never happens. Any cap should be about 160-162°, not 155°.

The elbow is most extended in late stance and starts flexing at or just before lift-off. The model's jump from 133° to 177-178° just after lift-off is the real error.

At touchdown a real forelimb is meant to be straight below the elbow (carpus about 180°), with the elbow at about 145-155°. The model's touchdown elbow (128-139°) is under-extended, not "locked straight".

At racing speed the humerus can approach vertical at maximum protraction (shoulder joint up to about 125° plus scapular rotation), so a humerus pinned near vertical is borderline, not wrong. What is unreal in 05-race g=2/8 is the elbow reaching the front of the chest. That happens because the model's shoulder joint is carried to the trunk front (x 0.79-0.80 against 0.81) by a scapula that rotates about its top. In a real horse the elbow stays behind the point of shoulder, inside the trunk outline.

Separate unflagged error: the model's mid-swing elbow flexion (31-45° in race and gallop) is far beyond the real maximum of about 89-105°.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the real-horse claims against the primary abstracts and checked the model against measurements.json. Fetlock dorsal angle here means the cannon-to-pastern angle, with 180 = straight.

What holds up:
(1) McGuigan & Wilson 2003 (JEB 206:1325), abstract read directly. The distal spring (elbow to foot) changes length by 127 mm (106-128) at the gallop. The proximal spring (scapula to elbow) changes by 12 mm (9-15). Limb force is linear in MCP angle, and neither gait nor digital-flexor activation changes that much. So the elbow and shoulder should not be what shortens the leg. In the model's race gait they shorten it by ~15 cm, which is wrong.
(2) Witte, Hirst & Wilson 2006 (JEB 209:4389). Peak force at 17 m/s is 24.7 N/kg in the forelimbs (range 22.6-26.0) and 15.3 N/kg in the hindlimbs. The 16.8 N/kg at 9 m/s is not in the abstract. It does agree with a duty-factor estimate from the 131 ms stance at 9 m/s.
(3) Ratzlaff et al. 1993 (Acta Anat 146:200), abstract read directly. At gallop hoof contact the fetlock is at 199-206 deg and the carpus at 181-182. Peak heel force falls at or near maximum fetlock extension.
(4) Butcher & Ashley-Ross 2002 measured fetlock dorsiflexion at mid-stance in Thoroughbreds galloping at about 14 m/s. Symons et al. 2014 found marked hind fetlock hyperextension at 12-17 m/s.
(5) The model confirms the problem (measurements.json, fore fetlock dorsal angle, standing 213):
- contact: 173-189, i.e. flexed or straight, vs 199-206 real
- peak, walk: 224
- peak, trot: 223
- peak, canter: 224 non-lead / 228 lead
- peak, gallop: 214-217, only 1-4 deg above standing
- peak, race: 228-230

Real standing is about 218 (Chateau et al. 2001 give 38.4±8.7 deg of MCP extension under neutral loading). So at gallop and race the gap is tens of degrees.

What is overstated or needs correcting:
(a) "In any gait" does not apply to the walk. Peak fore force at the walk is about 0.6 BW, against about 0.28 BW per forelimb standing. My rough calibration is about 3.5-4 deg per N/kg; this is my own inference, fitted between the ~200-206 contact angle and the ~218 standing angle. On that basis the walk should be about 11-13 deg above standing, and the model gives +11 deg with a 1.5 cm drop. The walk is fine. A walk sag of 14-20 above rest could overshoot. The real shortfall is in the trot (needs about +25-30), canter and gallop (about +40-50, pastern near horizontal), and race.
(b) "The non-lead fore sinks more" is true at the canter and slower gallop. McGuigan & Wilson predicted 15.2 vs 12.8 N/kg for non-lead vs lead at 12 m/s. Witte et al. 2004 underline the different jobs of the lead and non-lead limbs at canter and report that the load difference shrinks with speed. Witte 2006 found no significant lead/non-lead difference in any measured variable at 9-17 m/s. So the race gait should be close to symmetric. (The model's canter has it backwards: lead 228, non-lead 224.)
(c) The 127 mm is the whole elbow-to-foot spring, measured from the unloaded limb at about 12 m/s on a treadmill. Measured from standing, the fetlock drop should be about 9-11 cm, not 12.7. The linear law cannot be extended to 24.7 N/kg, because the pastern would go past horizontal. Real extension levels off near ergot-to-ground, so race should be only slightly deeper than gallop.
(d) Hind peak force at 17 m/s is only 62% of fore. Even so, hind fetlock hyperextension at gallop is well documented (Symons 2014), so hind sag at 70-80% of fore is reasonable.

Severity stays high, because gallop and race are this project's main gaits.

The fetlock really is the main limb spring. Its extension is linear in load: distal spring 127 mm vs proximal 12 mm at gallop. It is already extended about 20-25 deg past straight at contact (199-206). So the finding holds for trot, canter, gallop and race. It does not hold for the walk: a real walk extends the fetlock only about 10-15 deg past standing, and the model's +11 deg (224 vs 213) is fine there. Corrected targets, as extension above standing (about 213-218):
- walk: about +10-15
- trot: about +25-30
- canter / gallop: about +40-50, pastern near horizontal
- race: only slightly more than gallop (the linear law levels off near ergot-to-ground)

Peak extension should come near mid-stance (about 40-50% of stance). Lead/non-lead difference: put the extra sink in the non-lead fore at the canter and slower gallop (about 15% more force at 12 m/s). It shrinks with speed and is not significant at 9-17 m/s (Witte 2006), so keep the race gait close to symmetric. Measured from standing, the target drop is about 9-11 cm, not 12.7. Hind at about 70-80% of fore is reasonable: hind force is 62% of fore at 17 m/s, but hind fetlocks hyperextend strongly at racing speed.

truth.reasoning:
The finding's description of real horses is mostly right, but it is overstated. It also misquotes its main source and blames every gait for a fault that only some gaits have.

What I checked in the model (measurements.json, my own node scripts):
- The cannon numbers in the finding are correct. Cannon touchdown and lift-off: walk +27.9/-10.3, trot +30.2/about -8, canter about +32/-15 to -20, gallop +35.5/+1.8 to +5, race +38.6/-25.1 degrees. The cannon is vertical at 56%, 64%, 56-62% and 59-61% of stance, and never in the gallop.
- I also measured the whole-limb axis. Real-horse studies define it as tuber spinae scapulae to coffin joint (Hobbs & Clayton 2019); I estimated the tuber at 45% of the way from scapTop to the shoulder. On that axis the picture changes:
  - Walk: +21.5 to -16.0 degrees, vertical at 55% of stance, mean +2.4.
  - Canter: +25 to -18, vertical at 53-54%, mean +2.7.
  - Race: +29 to -26/-28, vertical at 51%, mean about +0.7. This one is balanced.
  - Trot: +25 to -14, vertical at 58%, mean +5.1.
  - Gallop (6.2 m/s): +24 to -8, vertical at 70%, mean +7 to +8.5. This is the clear outlier.

What real horses do:
1. Walk (Hodson et al. 2000, abstract): "The metacarpus was vertical at 28% stride. This was considerably earlier than the change from a braking to a propulsive longitudinal force (34% stride), which coincided with maximal extension of the fetlock joint." The forelimb is on the ground for about 60-65% of the stride (the model uses 0.60), so these are about 44-47% and 54-57% of stance. The finding's ~45% figure is right. Its phrase "braking->propulsion soon after" is wrong: Hodson calls the gap considerable. A real walking forelimb brakes for more than half of its stance. The model's whole limb passes vertical at 55%, right at Hodson's force transition. So at the walk the problem is the cannon tilting forward relative to the rest of the leg (about 4-5 degrees), not a stance shifted forward. That is about 6% of the stride, or roughly 9 cm.
2. Trot (Hobbs, Bertram & Clayton 2016, 3.3 m/s): mean forelimb angle is -1.3 to +2.3 degrees, so the stance is roughly balanced about vertical. The model's +5 degree forward mean is beyond that range, so the trot claim holds. Forelimb pro-retraction range at the trot is 33-40 degrees (Hobbs & Clayton 2019); the model's 39 degrees is fine, it is just shifted forward.
3. Gallop. I measured Muybridge's "Sallie Gardner" sequence (1878, frames 0.686 m and about 1/25 s apart, roughly 16-17 m/s). The trailing fore touches down at about +30 degrees (limb) and +33 degrees (cannon). It is near vertical one frame later, about 40-45% into a stance of 2.3-2.5 frame intervals. It is still planted at about -20 degrees. The leading fore is about vertical in the first frame after touchdown and still planted at a cannon angle of about -24 (limb about -27) degrees, with the hoof well behind the elbow. So the claim that the forelimb leaves "well behind vertical" holds for the gallop. The model's 6.2 m/s gallop, which lifts off with the cannon still forward of vertical and the limb at only -8 degrees, is clearly wrong.
4. Race: the model's whole limb (+29/-26) matches Muybridge closely. The stance is not shifted. Only the cannon reaches vertical late (about 60% of stance against about 40-45%), which again is cannon and carpus posture.

Caveats:
- Some forward bias is normal. Forelimbs are net braking at the trot, and at the walk they brake for more than half of stance (Hodson), so a lean of a degree or two forward is not a fault.
- Fix option 1 is sound for the gallop (xc 0.76 to about 0.62-0.64, which gives about 6 degrees more retraction) and the trot (0.68 to about 0.62). For the walk and canter, lowering xc to 0.58 would push the whole limb into retraction against Hodson's force timing. The cannon timing there should be fixed through cannon, carpus and fetlock posture instead.
- The trot study does not name its limb markers; I assumed the tuber-to-coffin definition used by the same group in Hobbs & Clayton 2019.

  - Trot: the mean limb angle over stance is about +5 degrees forward. Real horses at the trot average -1.3 to +2.3 degrees, which is roughly balanced (Hobbs et al. 2016).

- Hodson's braking-to-propulsion change comes "considerably" later than the vertical cannon, not "soon after": 34% of stride, about 54-57% of stance. A slight forward bias of the forelimb is normal, so the expected stance is about balanced with a small forward lean, not centred on the vertical cannon.

  - Walk and canter: leave fore.xc near its current value and fix the cannon tilt through carpus and fetlock posture. Moving them to 0.58 would over-retract the leg.

Using a proxy point one third of the way down from scapTop to the shoulder joint, the model's whole-limb angle is:

|---|---|---|---|
| walk | +22.2 | -14.6 | +3.4 |
| trot | +25.6 | -12.6 | +6.2 |

The model-side observation holds. In measurements.json the fore toe, knee and fetlock z stay at ±0.163–0.167 m in every gait, from walk (1.4 m/s) to race (16.8 m/s). The fetlock never leaves ±0.165. Vertical limb planes are correct for the standing pose, since ideal conformation has a plumb line from the point of the shoulder bisecting the whole limb. At speed they are not.

The real-horse direction of the claim survives. A galloping or racing Thoroughbred has phases where one forelimb is the only support. A hoof 16 cm outside the centre of mass at that moment would create a large roll moment, so the forefeet converge toward the midline as speed rises. Head-on racing footage shows this. I could not refute it on real-horse grounds.

The quantitative support the claim cites is overstated or misread, though.

1) Parkes et al. 2020 did not measure hoof placement, track width or adduction toward the midline. They measured a 2D lean against vertical, from proximal forearm to distal cannon, filmed by cameras on the outside rail of an anticlockwise oval. Positive meant a lean toward the inside of the bend.
   - On the "straight", both forelimbs leaned the same way: inside fore 14.3±11.2°, outside fore 4.5±9.3° (Table 2).
   - The authors explain this as pooled strides leaving or anticipating the curve, plus long-axis moments (Chateau 2013). They do not attribute it to midline convergence.
   - A symmetric "toward-midline" component can only be inferred: (14.3−4.5)/2 ≈ 5°, with a standard deviation of about 10°.
   - So "1–10° whole-limb frontal inclination on the straight (Parkes 2020)" is my reading of their data, not a reported result. Their reported straight-line means are 4.5° and 14.3° and include body lean.
   - Their +1.5° per m/s speed effect is a lean effect that mixes in curve running. It is not clean evidence of narrowing with speed on a straight.

2) Parkes found no significant effect of the lead leg on inclination (p=0.57 whole limb, p=0.45 cannon). Fix option 2's "slightly more on the lead leg" has no support.

3) Displacement. About 5° of tilt over the elbow-to-ground height (0.96 m) or shoulder height (1.22 m) moves each hoof about 8–11 cm inward. That takes the model's 33 cm fore track to roughly 11–17 cm between hoof centres at race speed. "Nearly in one track" is fair; literal single-tracking or crossing is not supported. The upper end of the claim's 3–25 cm range needs about 10° of true adduction, and no source here shows that.

4) The "progressively with speed" part is unsupported below the canter. At the walk and trot the horse is never on one forelimb alone; the trot is carried on diagonal pairs, so it does not need a narrow base. Front views of trotting Thoroughbreds show near-vertical forelimbs with at most slight inward placement. The suggested trot track fraction of 0.6 is a guess. About 0.85–0.9 is more defensible, with most of the narrowing at the canter, gallop and race gaits.

5) Self Davies et al. 2019 measured side-to-side ground forces in galloping ridden Thoroughbreds. They found these forces too variable to analyse and reported no foot-placement data. No force-plate study I could reach gives a number for track width.

truth.reasoning:
Most of the anatomy in the claim is right, but the main conclusion about motion is overstated.

What holds up:
(1) A real horse's scapula does not pivot about its dorsal border. Biplanar fluoroscopy (XROMM) of an equid shows it rotating about an instantaneous centre of rotation that moves during the stride, not a fixed pin (Wagner et al. 2026). Musculoskeletal horse models put the scapulothoracic hinge at the level of the scapular spine, about 1/4 of the way down the blade (van Bijlert et al. 2024). That is consistent with "upper part / around the tuber".
(2) Because the centre is below the dorsal border, the dorsal border moves caudally while the glenoid moves cranially. The withers is the most mobile part of the back: about ±18 mm vertical at walk and ±30 mm at trot, attributed to scapular elevation and rotation (Smirnova et al. 2024).
(3) Horses have no clavicle, and the limb is slung by a muscular synsarcosis. Some scapulothoracic translation is therefore expected, though it has never been quantified in horses (van Bijlert et al. 2024 says so explicitly), so it cannot be specified in cm.
The model's data confirm the observation: scapTop stays within about 1 cm of the withers in every gait.

What is wrong or overstated:
(a) "The shoulder joint travels mainly fore-aft" does not follow from moving the pivot. A rigid rotation moves the glenoid perpendicular to the pivot-to-glenoid line, i.e. roughly across the blade. With a blade sloped 50-65 deg to horizontal (the model's is 51.4 deg), protraction necessarily moves the shoulder joint forward and up, about 0.6-1 cm up per cm forward, wherever the pivot is. Moving the pivot 1/4-1/3 down only shrinks the excursion by about 25-33% at the same angle; it does not change its direction. Real horses do raise the point of shoulder at full reach.
(b) Rough real-horse estimate: radius from rotation centre to glenoid about 0.27-0.31 m (a 0.36-0.42 m blade with the centre 1/4-1/3 down). An 18 deg protraction from neutral then gives a chord of about 8.5-9.7 cm, i.e. about +7 cm forward and +5-6 cm up. The model gives +8.4 / +8.7 cm with a 0.356 m radius. So the true excess is roughly 3 cm of rise and a dorsal border that does not move back, not a rise that should be near zero.
(c) The swing angles are not too large; at walk and trot they are too small. Fluoroscopy measured scapular range of motion of 27.6 deg at walk and 23.3 deg at trot in a pony (Wagner et al. 2026). The model's measured range of motion (blade relative to the trunk) is 13.6 deg walk, 15.6 trot, 21.5 canter, 24.2 gallop and 39.5 race. The ±18 deg race swing is plausible for a racing gallop; walk and trot under-rotate by about half compared with the pony data.

Net: the real-horse premise (pivot below the dorsal border, dorsal border moves caudally, possible thoracic slide) is correct. The implied outcome (shoulder joint moving mainly fore-aft, little rise) is overstated. The rise is intrinsic to rotating a sloped scapula and would only be reduced by about a third by moving the pivot.
truth.correction: Real equine scapulae rotate about a moving instantaneous centre below the dorsal border (about 1/4-1/3 down, near the level of the spine/tuber), so the dorsal border moves caudally and somewhat vertically as the glenoid protracts. They may also translate on the thorax (no clavicle), but that translation has never been measured in horses. Even so, the shoulder joint rises during protraction: for a 50-65 deg blade slope it moves forward-and-up, about 0.6-1 cm up per cm forward. Moving the pivot ~1/4-1/3 down only scales the excursion (about 25-33% less at the same angle). Expected real values at full race protraction (+18 deg) are about +7 cm forward and +5-6 cm up, versus the model's +8.4 / +8.7 cm. The defect is about 3 cm too much rise plus a dorsal border that never moves, not a rise that should be absent. Scapular range of motion should not be reduced: real values are about 23-28 deg at walk and trot (pony XROMM), larger than the model's 14-16 deg.

Rotating it by +18 deg in the chest frame puts the shoulder joint at (0.796, 1.302). That is +7.6 cm forward and +8.2 cm up, not the claimed +8.4/+8.7 (0.804, 1.309). In world space at the LF max (k=12) it is +7.2/+7.8. Dog models place the scapulothoracic pivot partway down the blade: Andrada/Fischer assume it at 2/3 of the dorsal-to-ventral marker distance. Lawson & Marlin 2010 measured up to 80 mm of craniocaudal sliding. So in a real horse the dorsal border moves back as the distal end swings forward, and some of the reach comes from sliding rather than rotation. Because the model uses the whole 0.356 m blade as the radius, the joint moves about 1.5-3x further per degree than with a lower pivot.

Moving the pivot down (fix option 1) only shrinks the movement, to about 2/3 or 1/3 of its current size; the joint still rises as it goes forward. Only the translation option (fix 2) makes the path "mainly fore-aft". Real horses also slide dorsoventrally (Lawson & Marlin 2010; Hodson et al. 2000 say scapular rotation helps lift the distal limb in early swing), so a few cm of vertical shoulder travel is realistic.
2. The swing angle itself is not too big. Fluoroscopy gives a scapular ROM of 27.6 deg at walk and 23.3 deg at trot, while the model uses only 14 deg and 16 deg.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute both real-horse claims and could not.

1) Carpal overextension in stance. The line attributed to Back 1995 is close to verbatim. The abstract of Back W et al. 1995, "How the horse moves: 1. Significance of graphical representations of equine forelimb kinematics" (Equine Vet J 27(1):31-38), says: "The carpal joint rapidly snaps into overextension at the beginning of the stance phase to enable the forelimb to work as a propulsive strut." That study used 24 Warmbloods trotting on a treadmill, so on its own it could be called breed- and gait-specific. Burn, Portus and Brockington 2006 (Vet J 171:169-171) closes that gap for Thoroughbreds. In five Thoroughbreds on a treadmill at 1.8-10 m/s, the carpus has a passive extension limit near 180 deg but hyperextends during stance, and peak hyperextension rises linearly with speed (more steeply on a +7.5% incline). A carpus held at exactly 0 deg (-0.2..+0.3 deg) through every stance, at every gait, therefore misdescribes a real Thoroughbred. The 3-5 deg overextension in the fix is a sensible size for trot. Because the effect grows with speed, gallop and race should get more, not one constant.

2) Accessory carpal bone (ACB) bump. CT morphometry of 12 equine forelimbs (Gernhardt et al. 2026, Animals 16:1132) gives an ACB dorsopalmar width of 3.91 +/- 0.37 cm proximally and 4.39 +/- 0.31 cm distally, and a proximodistal length of 4.28 +/- 0.32 cm. Its dorsal edge articulates with the caudal radius and the ulnar carpal bone, so most of that depth sticks out behind the carpal column. Standard anatomy (Sisson and Grossman/Getty) describes it as the palpable prominence behind the knee, forming the lateral wall of the carpal canal. Conformation guides treat a "flat" back to the knee or one "tied in below the knee" as faults. A flush back of the knee is therefore not within normal Thoroughbred variation.

Minor nuances, none of which overturn the finding:
- Net projection behind the carpal bones is probably about 2.5-4 cm, so the stated "~3-4 cm" sits at the upper end.
- The ACB sits palmarolateral, not on the midline. It shows clearly in a lateral profile, but the bump should be biased to the lateral side.
- Hyperextension is driven by load, so it builds to its peak at midstance (peak vertical force) rather than only "at the start".

The low severity is appropriate.

truth.reasoning:
The finding has two halves. The first, that the forehand is a bit wide, holds but is overstated. The second, that the forefeet are too far apart, does not hold for real horses.

1) Chest width. The 38.6 cm figure is real. Matsuura 2024 (PMC10955269) reports 38.6 +/- 0.7 SE cm by hand and 39.9 cm by 3D scan, at 159.9 cm withers. Matsuura 2021 (PMC8437753) defines the measurement as "distance in the front side between the outer sides of the right and left humeri", taken with calipers. Two caveats:
- The sample is 9 riding horses (7 TB, 2 crossbreds) averaging 542 kg, not racing TBs.
- It sits at the narrow end of the literature. Iranian Turkoman horses, measured on the same landmark, give 38.93 +/- 2.08 cm at 157.1 cm (PMC6306294), which is 40.4 cm scaled to 163 cm. Ünal et al. 2025 (Arch Anim Breed 68:253, PMC13275030) measured 24 Thoroughbreds at 43.75 +/- 1.22 cm at 157.9 cm, which is 45.2 cm scaled to 163 cm. Their Arabians were about as wide in absolute terms (43.29 cm), but those were shorter horses (151.8 cm).

So the real range at 163 cm is about 39-45 cm, not a single 39-40 cm target.

The claim also compares the wrong landmark. 48.6 cm is the model's width at mid-arm: humerus section w=0.078 at t=0.6, about 16 cm below the point of shoulder. At the point of shoulder itself (sh, t=0) the arm's half-width works out to about 0.065, so the outer surface is at z ≈ 0.165 + 0.065 = 0.23. That gives about 46 cm across. Against 39-45 cm, the model is roughly 2-17% too wide (about 5-7 cm against the caliper-on-humerus datasets), not 25%. The front trunk rows (46 cm at x 0.46-0.58, y 1.2) do add to the width. In the front views, however, the silhouette is mostly the 56 cm barrel behind the chest. The forehand itself does not read as box-like.

2) Foot spacing. "About one hoof-width apart (10-14 cm clear)" is a rule of thumb from lay guides, not a measured norm. The textbook standard (Stashak, Adams' Lameness ch.1) is that a vertical line dropped from the point of the shoulder should bisect the forearm, knee, cannon, fetlock and hoof. If the outer points of the shoulders are 39-45 cm apart, the limb axes should be roughly 30-36 cm apart. The model's 33 cm between hoof centres falls inside that, and it matches its own shoulder joints at z = ±0.165.

Clayton et al. 2013 (Vet J 198 Suppl 1:e65) measured stance (base of support) widths of 0.22-0.45 m in 24 horses weighing 117-666 kg. The abstract does not say whether that is between hoof centres or outer edges, but 33 cm is within the measured range for a 475 kg horse.

The 22 cm gap looks large partly because the model's fore hooves are only 11.2 cm wide at the sole (HOOF_SHAPE bot w 0.056). A TB forefoot is typically about 12-13 cm, which would give roughly 20 cm clear.

3) The proposed fix would make things worse. FORE.z 0.14 gives 28 cm centres, which puts the forelimbs inside the model's own points of shoulder. By the plumb-line rule that is base-narrow, a conformation fault that Stashak links to winging and interference.

Some of the real-horse description holds up. One part doesn't, and that part is what drives the measured defect and Fix A.

What holds:
(1) In a Thoroughbred seen from the side, the point of shoulder is normally the most cranial point of the trunk. A breastbone that sticks out in front is described as a fault ('pigeon breast').
(2) The deepest part of the trunk is the girth, just behind the elbow. Wikipedia's equine anatomy page puts the girth 'right behind the elbow… where the barrel is at its greatest diameter'. Matsuura et al. 2024 give a chest depth of 76.6 cm at 159.9 cm withers, which scales to a floor at about 0.845 m for 163 cm. The model already does this: girthLow is 0.826 at x 0.18-0.34, below the brisket at 0.898.

What fails: 'the breast meets the forearm at about elbow height', and with it the finding's '6 cm below the elbow = defect'.
- A rounded pectoral mass in front of the top of the forearm is normal anatomy, not a 'pot'. The descending pectoral (from the manubrium to the humeral crest) is the visible 'breast' bulge.
- The transverse pectoral runs from the ventral sternum to the medial forearm fascia (Budras), so the chest floor between and in front of the forelegs normally joins the forearm at or a few cm below the elbow joint. In side view that junction sits roughly at girth-line height plus a few cm.
- The real gap is the model's elbow, not its brisket. The elbow joint sits at 0.96 m with a 0.46 m elbow-to-knee forearm. A radius of about 0.35-0.37 m plus the carpus puts a 163 cm TB's elbow joint centre at about 0.90-0.93 m. The proportions critic made the same point ('shorten the forearm ~4 cm by lowering the elbow').
- The trunk floor meets the forearm's front surface (x≈0.575, from the limb table) at 0.899 m, which is realistic in absolute terms: about 5-7 cm above the girth floor.
- Fix A (raise the floor at x 0.58/0.68 to 0.96/1.02) would therefore be anatomically wrong. It would leave the breast floor about 13 cm above the girth line and open a step at the forearm.

The defensible part is smaller:
- The lower breast at x 0.68-0.81 (floor 0.95/1.02/1.10) is fuller and further forward than in a lean TB.
- Senna et al. 2015 give arm 34 cm and shoulder angle 99°, and Ahmad et al. 2025 give a shoulder slope of 58.4°. Together these put the humerus about 41° below horizontal, with the point of shoulder about 26 cm ahead of the elbow landmark. That puts a real breast front about 17-21 cm ahead of the forearm's front edge, against the model's 23.5 cm (front ring) and 28.5 cm (cap).
- So the front ring/cap stand about 4-8 cm proud of a realistic point of shoulder (about 5 cm ahead of the shoulder joint centre at 0.72).
- The model's 47.7° humerus slope is itself within the range of those external measurements, so the arm is not the cause.
truth.correction:
Accurate version: in a Thoroughbred the point of shoulder is the most cranial point, and the girth just behind the elbow is the lowest point of the chest; the model already has the latter. A rounded pectoral 'breast' in front of the top of the forearm is normal. Because the transverse pectoral inserts on the medial forearm fascia, the breast meets the forearm at roughly girth-line height plus a few cm, which in a real 163 cm horse is about elbow-joint height (about 0.90-0.93 m).

The model's brisket height at the forearm (0.898 m) is therefore realistic. The '6 cm below the elbow' comes mainly from the model's elbow being placed about 3-6 cm too high (0.96 m, with a 0.46 m forearm), not from the breast hanging too low.

The real but smaller deviation is the forward projection:
- The lower breast at x 0.68-0.81 is somewhat full.
- The front ring/cap reaches about 23-28 cm ahead of the forearm's front edge, against about 17-21 cm in a real TB. That is about 4-8 cm beyond a realistic point of shoulder.

Better fix: keep the x=0.58 floor near 0.90-0.92, raise the bottoms at x 0.68/0.76/0.81 by about 3-5 cm, pull the front ring and cap back 3-5 cm, and lower the elbow per the forearm-proportion finding. Do not raise the floor to 0.96/1.02.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to show that the expected front view misdescribes real horses, and it does not.

1) The two pectoral masses and the groove between them are textbook surface anatomy. The superficial pectoral muscle is in two parts. Its descending part (m. pectoralis descendens) runs from the manubrium/cariniform cartilage of the sternum to the crest of the humerus and forms the visible prominence on each side of the breast. Its transverse part (pars transversa) runs from the ventral sternum to the fascia on the inner side of the forearm and fills the floor between the forelimbs. The left and right prominences are separated by the median pectoral groove (sulcus pectoralis medianus). The lateral pectoral groove, between the descending pectoral and the brachiocephalicus, holds the cephalic vein. Budras et al., Dyce/Sack/Wensing and König & Liebich all describe these grooves. The horse's breastbone is keel-shaped (ventral crest, cariniform cartilage), but the pectorals bulge on both sides of it, so the surface shows a groove, not a ridge or a flat floor. The model's single low midline vertex makes a downward keel, the opposite of a groove.

2) Forearms coming out of the sides of the pectoral masses: correct. The transverse pectoral wraps onto the inner forearm fascia, so the inner outline of each forearm continues the outline of the pectoral mass. This is the 'inverted V' between the forelegs that conformation guides describe (Thomas 2005, The Horse Conformation Handbook, chest/front view). It is not a 22 cm flat shelf with the legs hung from its corners.

3) Height is about right. In the standing pose the elbow joint is at y=0.96 and the brisket at y=0.90. In a real horse the top of the V is at the chest floor, roughly at the level of the elbow joint and a little below the point of the elbow.

4) Thoroughbred caveats are small and already in the claim. A race-fit Thoroughbred has less pectoral bulk and a narrower chest than stock breeds (the Quarter Horse's heavily muscled 'inverted V'). The groove is shallow and the V narrow, which is exactly what the finding says ('shallow central groove', 'narrow inverted V'). Normal variation changes how strong the effect is, not whether the masses and groove exist.

One small wording fix: from the front, the rounded masses are mostly the descending pectorals. The transverse pectorals show mainly as the floor of the V between the forearms. That does not change the finding.

Severity stays low: this is a front-view detail of the silhouette, not a fault in proportions or movement.

Sources: my web-search budget for the session was already used up, and the pages I tried to fetch were unavailable or said nothing about the pectorals. So point 1 rests on the textbooks above, cited from memory, not checked online.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the claim against the code and against measurements.json. The core of it holds.

What holds:
- hoofGeo (index.html:1158-1164, not 1122-1128 as the finding says) builds every hoof from a level top ring at co.y+0.012 = 0.104 m and a sole ring at y=0.002.
- The fore dorsal wall runs from co.x+0.037 at the top to co.x+0.069 at the ground. That is 3.2 cm forward over 10.2 cm of height, about 72.6 deg, with a wall length of about 10.7 cm.
- measurements.json (static.standing) puts the fore fetlock at (0.484, 0.209) and the coffin at (0.560, 0.092), which gives a 57 deg pastern. The hind pastern is 60 deg. So the HPA is broken forward by about 15-16 deg fore and about 12 deg hind.
- A 72 deg toe is club-foot territory. Mata et al. 2024 (Animals 14:2697) recommend a dorsal hoof wall angle of about 50 deg to keep the HPA aligned. Fore 47-55 and hind a few degrees steeper (about 52-57) are standard farriery ranges, and the finding's ranges are fine.
- A TB fore toe (wall length about 8-9 cm) times sin 50 deg gives a vertical toe height of about 6-7 cm. TB heels are about 3-4 cm. So a uniformly 10.2-10.4 cm capsule with a level coronet is clearly wrong: the toe is about 1.5x too tall and the heel about 2.5-3x too tall.
- A ground surface of 10.0 x 11.2 cm is undersized against the roughly 12-13 cm of a 475 kg TB fore foot.

The finding needs correcting on four points:

(1) The heel direction is backwards. A real heel wall slopes the same way as the toe: the heel buttress at the ground sits in front of (dorsal to) the heel coronet and bulbs. That is why toe and heel angles are compared as near-parallel lines, as in Kane et al. 1998's toe-heel angle difference. In the model (ringAt with U = +X, so "up" is the front and "down" the back extent), the fore heel ground edge is at co.x-0.031 and the heel coronet edge at co.x-0.041. That is the correct direction, just far too upright (about 84 deg). The model is not leaning past vertical. Fix option 1's "heel ground edge behind its coronet" would give an inverted, anatomically wrong heel.

(2) "Coffin joint 2-3 cm below the coronet" is overstated. In normal horses the extensor process of P3 lies only a few mm to about 1 cm below the dorsal coronary band; Cripps & Eustace 1999 call this vertical gap the "founder distance". The DIP centre of rotation, in P2's distal condyle, sits roughly level with the coronet in lateral view. The model's 1.2 cm gap (coffin 0.092, coronet 0.104) is therefore plausible. What is wrong is the absolute height: the coffin should be about 5.5-6.5 cm up, not 9.2 cm. The finding's own fix option 3 (COFFIN_Y about 0.06-0.07 with a 6.5-7.5 cm toe coronet) already implies a gap of about 0-1 cm, not 2-3 cm.

(3) A straight HPA with heels parallel to the toe is the farriery ideal (O'Grady & Poupard 2003), not what typical Thoroughbreds show. Racing TBs commonly have low or underrun heels, with the heel angle below the toe angle and a broken-back HPA. Kane et al. 1998 found that a larger toe-heel angle difference raised suspensory-apparatus failure risk. It is a fine modelling target, but it should be framed as the ideal. The model errs the opposite way from the usual TB fault (upright and broken-forward instead of low and broken-back), which strengthens the finding.

(4) "Ground surface wider than the coronet" is already true of the model. The fore top ring is 8.8 cm wide and the sole 11.2 cm, so only the absolute sole size and the coronet slope need changing. Also, 6.5-7.5 cm reads better as a toe wall length range of about 8-9 cm, or a vertical toe height of about 6-7 cm.

Severity stays medium. The hooves are a small part of the silhouette, but the error is obvious in the side close-ups and contradicts basic conformation.
truth.correction:
The real-horse targets are mostly right, with these changes:
- Wall angle: fore dorsal wall about 50 deg (47-55), hind about 52-57.
- Height and slope: vertical toe height about 6-7 cm (wall length about 8-9 cm), sloping to heels of about 3-4 cm.
- Ground surface: about 12-13 cm on the fore foot, narrower and more pointed behind.
- Heel direction: the heel wall slopes the SAME way as the toe, ideally within about 5 deg of parallel. Its ground edge sits about 2.5-4 cm IN FRONT of the heel coronet. The model's heel has the right direction but is too upright (about 84 deg). Fix option 1's "heel ground edge behind its coronet" should be reversed.
- Coffin joint: it is not 2-3 cm below the coronet. The P3 extensor process is normally within about 1 cm of the dorsal coronet (founder distance, Cripps & Eustace 1999), and the DIP rotation centre is roughly level with the coronet. The model's 1.2 cm gap is fine. The error is the absolute height: coffin at 9.2 cm and coronet at 10.4 cm, against roughly 5.5-6.5 cm and 6-7 cm.
- HPA framing: a straight HPA with parallel heels is the ideal. Typical TB racehorses deviate the other way (low or underrun heels, broken-back HPA), whereas the model is upright and broken forward by about 16 deg fore and 12 deg hind.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse side of this finding and could not.

First I checked the observation against measurements.json with a scratch script in the temp folder; the repository was not touched.
- Race RF toes off at k=15.04. The hoof is rotated 33.9 deg from rest at k=15, then 30.4 at k=16, 24.2 at k=17 and 26.8 at k=18, so it rolls back about 10 deg toward flat before flipping to 49 deg at k=19 and 95 deg at k=20.
- The fetlock bend (pastern relative to cannon) is 32.8 deg standing and peaks at 47.8 deg in stance (k=13). It drops to 23.8 deg at toe-off, then rises again to 45.6 deg at k=16-17 with the hoof in the air. That is about 22 deg of re-extension, above the standing angle and close to the loaded peak.
- Gallop LF toes off at k=24.3. Its hoof goes from 33.4 to 31.4 to 21.6 deg (rolling back about 12 deg), and its fetlock re-extends by about 7 deg.
So the observation is accurate.

Real-horse checks:
1) One flexion cycle in swing with no re-extension. Hodson, Clayton and Lanovaz 2000 (PMID 10952376) state that during swing the joints distal to the shoulder show a single flexion cycle, peaking at 81% of stride at the fetlock and 84% at the coffin. The coffin therefore keeps flexing well into swing; it does not relax at lift-off. The weak point is that this is walk data and the finding applies it to gallop. The extrapolation still holds for two reasons:
   - Fetlock extension beyond the standing angle is driven by load (the fetlock angle tracks limb force; McGuigan and Wilson 2003, J Exp Biol 206:1325). An unloaded fetlock cannot go back toward its stance-peak dorsiflexion in the air.
   - Gallop stance studies (Butcher and Ashley-Ross 2002, J Biomech 35:563; Symons et al. 2014, EVJ 46:227) show dorsiflexion peaking around mid-stance and then reversing through late stance.
2) A continuous roll over the toe. In galloping Thoroughbreds, Horan et al. 2021 (Animals 11:2588) timed breakover as a hoof-wall marker turning steadily through 90 deg from the start of heel lift; it took about 24-32 ms. This is direct gallop evidence of a large, continuous rotation with no rollback. The paper does not say whether the full 90 deg is reached before or after the toe leaves the ground. Either way, 34 deg is small for gallop.
3) Steep rotation at lift-off. Muybridge's plates show the trailing forehoof leaving the ground with the pastern roughly in line with the cannon and the sole facing back. That is qualitative but consistent with the 90 deg rotation above.

Minor corrections, none of which change the verdict:
- Hodson 2000 is a walk paper. Horan 2021 and Thomason and Peterson 2008 are the gallop-specific support.
- Back et al. 1995 (AJVR 56:1522) is about hoof and fetlock motion at impact during the trot, not breakover, so it adds little.
- Thomason and Peterson 2008, as cited by Horan, place gallop breakover at about 85-100% of stance. The code's BREAKOVER_START of 0.62 is therefore too early for gallop and race. This supports the gait-dependent fix: a later and larger roll.

Severity stays low: the artefact lasts about 2 frames (about 27 ms) right after lift-off.
truth.correction: No correction to the real-horse claim. Hodson 2000 is walk data; the gallop support comes from Horan et al. 2021 (a continuous 90 deg hoof rotation through breakover) and from the fact that fetlock extension depends on load (McGuigan and Wilson 2003). Thomason and Peterson 2008 put gallop breakover at about 85-100% of stance, so the code's BREAKOVER_START of 0.62 is also too early for gallop and race.

I tried to refute this and could not. Every number in the finding reproduces, and the defect turns out to be wider than reported.

**Code.** I re-read index.html. The cited line numbers are slightly stale: BREAKOVER is at 195-196, not 193-194, and the other code citations are about 35 lines off.
- Stance (line 1389): `tip = BREAKOVER*smoothstep(0.62,1,sp)`, so the heel is up 34 deg at toe-off.
- Swing (1405): `fade = 1 - smoothstep(0,0.3,s)`. Both `tip` and the pastern offset (`A.pastern - BREAKOVER*fade`) shrink back to flat over the first 30% of swing.
- Curl (1409): `curl = G.curl*smoothstep(0,0.28,s)*...`.
- Pose (1491-1492): `aPas = lerp(f.pastern - pitch, aCan + CURL_PASTERN, curl)` and `aHoof = lerp(-pitch - tip, aPas + CURL_HOOF, curl)`.
- Cause: the lerp is nested. Early in swing `aPas` is still close to the stance pastern (about 0 deg). The hoof's curl target, `aPas + 14 deg`, is therefore toe-forward of the breakover pose (-34 deg). So the hoof is pulled back toward flat while `tip` also fades. The hoof only flips up once the cannon (`aCan`) has swung far back.
- Hand check for race RF at k=16 (s=0.0375): fade 0.957, curl 0.049, aCan -50.6. This gives aPas = -5.1 deg (measured -4.9) and a hoof heel-up of 30.5 deg (measured 30.4).

**Measurements** (node, world coordinates). Hoof rotation is the coffin-to-toe angle measured against standing, which is 37.5 deg ahead of vertical.
- Race RF: coffin-to-toe angle 3.5 / 7.1 / 13.3 / 10.7 / -11.7 deg at k=15-19. That is a heel-up of 33.9 at the last stance sample, then 30.4 / 24.2 / 26.8 / 49.2 in the air. The toe is off the ground from k=16 (toe height 0.056 m).
- Gallop LF: 4.0 / 6.1 / 15.9 at k=24-26 (heel-up 33.4, 31.4, 21.6, 20.6, then 42.5).
- These match the finding exactly.
- The dip is not limited to race and gallop. It happens in every gait and every leg because it is the same code:

| Gait | Dip after lift-off | Time to regain |
|---|---|---|
| Race | 9-10 deg | ~13-67 ms |
| Gallop | 13-15 deg | ~53-66 ms |
| Canter | 10-13 deg | 19-94 ms |
| Trot | 16-17 deg | |
| Walk | 22-30 deg | |

- At the walk the hind hoof never re-rotates: it goes from 34 to about 4 deg and stays nearly flat in the air.

**Fetlock.** Measured as the pastern angle minus the cannon angle (standing = 32.8 deg).
- Race fore: 23.8 at toe-off, then 45.6 / 45.6 at k=16-17, then 35.2 and 13.8.
- So the fetlock does not merely "stay over-extended": it re-extends about 22 deg in the air, because the cannon retracts faster than the pastern curls.
- This re-extension is about 5-7 deg at gallop fore, up to 16 deg at canter LH, and none in the race hind legs.

**Sheets.** The 8-phase tiles in 04-gallop and 05-race are 4 samples apart, so they cannot show a 2-4 sample dip. There is no visual contradiction either way.

**Real horses.** Hodson, Clayton and Lanovaz (2000) at the walk and Back et al. (1995) at the trot report the distal joints flexing continuously from breakover into early swing, not re-extending. Muybridge's plates show the hoof leaving the ground well rotated.

**Severity: low.** At race and gallop speed the dip lasts about 25-55 ms (2-3 frames at 60 fps), so it is barely visible. It is most noticeable at the slow gaits (walk and trot), which the finding did not cite. The fix suggested in the finding (a monotonic handoff from breakover tip into the curl, plus starting fetlock flexion at toe-off) addresses the cause.

truth.reasoning:
The model side checks out. In measurements.json the race RF sole tilt, measured as the coffin-to-toe angle against the standing pose, goes 8.2, 3.9, 0.7, 0.0 deg toe-up over k=5..8. At k=8 the toe is still 5 cm in the air, and at k=9 the hoof lands flat. Canter and gallop show the same pattern: tilt reaches 0.0 one or two samples before toe height reaches 0.002. The cause is in index.html: footPath sets tip=0 at u=0 with the toe pinned (about lines 1384-1393 in the current file, not 1347-1353 as cited), and in the swing the breakover fade (s 0-0.3) and the curl fade (s 0.62-0.96) both reach 0 before touchdown.

The real-horse claim mostly holds for the gallop, but it is overstated in four ways.

(1) The PubMed abstract confirms Ratzlaff 1993 (PMID 8470468): "mean angles of the hoof from the horizontal at the time of heel contact were 6-7 degrees." That figure comes from only 2 horses, measured from slow-motion film on a track straightaway, with forelimb (carpus/fetlock) data. Symons et al. 2014 (EVJ 46:227, 5 Thoroughbreds at 12-17 m/s) independently speaks of hindlimb "heel-strike" followed by a horizontal heel slide. Heel-first contact at racing speed is therefore well supported for both fore and hind limbs.

(2) Including the canter goes beyond the evidence. Ratzlaff covers only the gallop. Flat landing is a common normal variant in sound horses at slower gaits: Mokry et al. 2021 (Vet J 268:105593) found flat landing in 70.8% of trot and 39.6% of walk steps in sound Standardbreds, while heel-first is more typical of Warmbloods. For the canter, Crevier-Denoix et al. 2013 (EVJ Suppl 45:54) report only that the leading forelimb hoof is more toe-up than the trailing one. They give no universal heel-first figure that would make a flat canter landing wrong.

(3) The 28-31 deg value is misread. In Ratzlaff it is the hoof angle from horizontal at peak toe force, during fetlock flexion, with the heel raised (heel-up, not toe-up). It is not a continuous rise from the 6-7 deg toe-up contact angle, and it is not the angle at lift-off. The hoof goes from about 6-7 deg toe-up at contact, to flat in mid-stance, to about 28-31 deg heel-up at peak toe load. The model's BREAKOVER = 34 deg heel-lift at lift-off already fits this.

(4) A real heel strike at gallop comes with forward hoof slip, not a clean pivot. Horan et al. 2024 (PLoS One 19:e0311899) measured about 18-21 ms of slip after impact. Parsons et al. 2011 (EVJ 43:216) measured slip and sink distances at 11-19 m/s. The fix's "rotate about the heel to avoid slip" is a reasonable stylisation, not real-horse truth.

Visibility is very low. With race duty 0.2 and T=0.43 s, stance lasts about 86 ms, so a heel-first window of 10-15% is about 9-13 ms, less than one 60 fps frame. Low severity is right.
truth.correction: For the gallop and race, real Thoroughbreds touch down heel-first with the hoof about 6-7 deg toe-up. The evidence is Ratzlaff 1993 (2 horses, forelimbs) and Symons 2014 (hindlimb "heel-strike" with heel slide at 12-17 m/s). The hoof then slips forward for about 20 ms (Horan 2024) before it goes flat. For the canter there is no firm heel-first norm: a flat landing is a common normal variant at slower gaits (Mokry 2021), so the canter part of the finding should be dropped or made optional. The 28-31 deg in Ratzlaff is the heel-up hoof angle at peak toe force during breakover, not a toe-up angle and not a continuation of the contact tilt. The model's 34 deg heel-lift at lift-off already matches it. The only valid fix target is a slight toe-up (about 5-7 deg) at gallop and race touchdown, rolling flat in the first few percent of stance. It is barely visible: less than one 60 fps frame at race speed.

I reproduced the finding from the code, the measurements and the cited paper.

Code (index.html; the finding's line numbers are a few lines off):
- Stance (1385-1397): tip = BREAKOVER * smoothstep(0.62, 1, sp), so tip is exactly 0 at u=0. plantedFetlock (1351-1355) places the coffin joint by rotating about a pinned toe.
- Swing (1409): curl = G.curl * smoothstep(0, 0.28, s) * (1 - smoothstep(0.62, 0.96, s)), so curl is 0 for s >= 0.96.
- Hoof angle (1492): aHoof = lerp(-pitch - tip, aPas + CURL_HOOF, curl). With curl=0 and tip=0 this is -pitch, a sole level with the ground. The sole is therefore exactly flat for the last 4% of the swing and at contact, in every gait.
- The `fade` term the finding cites (1405) goes to 0 by s=0.3. It plays no part in the landing; the curl fade-out is what flattens the hoof.

Measurements: I measured sole tilt as the angle of the coffin-to-toe vector against its rest direction (0.069, -0.09); positive means toe-up.
- Race RF, k=5-9: 8.2, 3.9, 0.7, 0.0, 0.0 deg. Toe height is 0.050 m at k8 (u=0.98) and 0.002 m at k9 (planted). This matches the critic's numbers exactly.
- Every other leg in race, gallop and canter shows the same pattern: about 6-11 deg toe-up at u≈0.85-0.91, falling to 0.0-0.4 deg by u≈0.97, and 0.0 at touchdown and for the whole early stance.
- Trot behaves the same way: 0.0 at u=0.969 and at contact.
- So the model approaches toe-up and then flattens just before contact. The hoof is flat for about the last 11-14 ms of the swing at 1x speed, and it lands flat. It never lands heel-first.

Reference check: I pulled the Ratzlaff 1993 abstract from PubMed (PMID 8470468). It says: "The mean angles of the hoof from the horizontal at the time of heel contact were 6-7 degrees." It also says peak toe forces occurred at hoof angles of 28-31 deg. The expected behaviour in the finding is therefore sourced correctly.

Small corrections to the finding's wording:
1. The 28-31 deg angle is the hoof angle at peak toe force during breakover, which is heel-up. The 6-7 deg at contact is toe-up. These are opposite directions, so "rising to" is loose. The model's BREAKOVER of 34 deg at lift-off is already consistent with the 28-31 deg figure.
2. The paper studied 2 horses with an instrumented forelimb shoe. Applying it to the hind limbs and to the canter is an extrapolation.
3. While the hoof is flat, pinning the toe and pinning the heel look the same. The visible difference is only the missing heel-first contact and its roll onto a flat sole. That lasts about 10% of the stance, roughly 9 ms in the race gait (stance = 0.2 × 0.43 s). It cannot be resolved in the 05-race and 04-gallop sheet tiles.

Severity stays low. The fix can be simpler than the finding suggests, because the late swing already holds 6-11 deg of toe-up. Moving the curl fade-out's end past touchdown, or adding a small residual toe-up that runs into the first ~10% of the stance with a heel pivot, would cover most of it.
