The model numbers are correct. A node script on measurements.json static.standing gives fore pastern 57.0 deg to the ground with the fetlock at 147.2/147.6 deg, and hind 60.0 deg with the fetlock at 147.3/147.0 deg. The constants are at index.html:552-553, not 536-537 as the finding says. The fetlock is built from them at :1194 and :1217, not :1157.

The real-horse claim holds only for the forelimb. The hind half is wrong.

1) Fore: mildly upright, within normal variation.
- Senna et al. 2015 (n=51 jumping TBs, photos) give a fore fetlock angle of 142.73+/-6 deg. I checked this on scialert.
- With a near-vertical cannon, the pastern-to-ground angle is roughly the fetlock angle minus 90, so about 52-53 deg. The clinically normal subgroup of the same cohort (Mostafa & Elemmawy 2020, J Equine Sci 31:23, n=17) had 141.0 deg, so about 51 deg.
- The model's 147.2 deg is about +0.75 SD from the cohort mean. It is slightly upright for a TB but not a fault. Morna racehorses measured 147.7+/-5.1 deg fore fetlock and 60.8+/-3.5 deg fore pastern (Ahmad 2025).
- Concussion risk in TB racing data points the other way. Kane et al. 1998 found condylar-fracture odds fell 0.26x per 3 deg increase in toe angle. Racehorse hooves skew toward low and broken-back angles (Correa 2026: broken-back HPA in 100% radiographically).
- Sloping the fore pastern a few degrees (to about 36-37 deg from vertical, 53-54 deg to the ground) is a reasonable cosmetic tweak.
- The more visible fault is the 72.6 deg fore hoof wall (A-HOOF-01). Lowering the pastern alone would widen the broken-forward hoof-pastern axis, so the hoof must be fixed first or at the same time.

2) Hind: refuted.
- The finding's own source contradicts it. Senna's hind fetlock of 149.84+/-8 deg works out to about 60 deg to the ground, the same as the model.
- In the same cohort, normal horses had a hind fetlock angle of 152.8 deg (about 62-63 deg pastern). Horses with musculoskeletal disorders had a significantly lower 144.7 deg (P<0.05), meaning more sloping or dropped hind fetlocks.
- The model's 147.3 deg sits between the two groups, on the sloping side of normal.
- Morna racehorses: hind pastern 60.3+/-4.0 deg, hind fetlock 155.5+/-2.7 deg. Ahmad 2025 cites about 157 deg for jumping TBs.
- Clinical guides make the hind pastern and hoof 2-5 deg steeper than the fore, so 60 deg behind is ordinary.
- The '53-57 deg hind' figure is hoof-wall trimming guidance, not proof that 60 deg is a concussion fault.

Correction:
- Keep HIND.pastern at about 30 deg from vertical. A per-horse range of roughly 27-33 deg is fine.
- Drop the 'HIND 32-35 deg' fix.
- Reword the fore point as 'slightly upright vs the TB mean (about 51-53 deg), within 1 SD', a low-priority tweak tied to the hoof-angle fix.
- The conf.pastern customization idea stays valid.

2) Hindlimb (refuted). In the same normal jumping Thoroughbreds the hind fetlock is 152.8 +/- 2.0 deg, and Ahmad et al. cite 157 deg. A normal hind fetlock is therefore more upright than the fore, not less. The model's hind fetlock (147.3 deg) is already about 5-10 deg more flexed (more sloping) than these Thoroughbred values. In Mostafa 2020, the horses with musculoskeletal disorders had a significantly lower hind fetlock angle (144.7 +/- 3.1 deg). The critic's own figure (hind 149.8 deg) also puts the model below the mean, i.e. more sloping. truth.reasoning:
The main point holds. One detail in the "expected" text is wrong, and one figure has no source behind it.

What the code does (checked by hand from the bone positions):
- BODY.graze (index.html:1647-1650) drops the spine 0.12 m, pitches the spine -3 deg and the chest -12 deg about the chest bone at (0.3,1.3).
- The shoulder joint moves from (0.72,1.222) to about (0.689,0.980), a 24 cm drop. The withers mesh point falls about 19 cm (1.622 to ~1.43). The brisket falls from 0.898 to ~0.70. The hip joint falls about 9 cm.
- In the stand gait, knee flex is 0 and the fetlock stays at its square rest spot, (0.484,0.209), from footPath at :1378-1380. So solve2 works with the humerus (0.354 m) and a straight forearm plus cannon (0.751 m). The shoulder-to-fetlock distance shrinks from 1.040 to 0.798 m, and by the law of cosines the elbow closes from 137.6 deg to 84.3 deg.
- The finding's numbers are right.

Real horses:
- No grazing horse sinks its forehand 20+ cm or bends its elbows to about 84 deg with the hoof planted. The trunk hangs between the scapulae in the thoracic sling. Serratus ventralis thoracis is a short-fibred pennate muscle (fascicles 48 +/- 17 mm, at about 45 deg) between thick sheets of aponeurosis: an anti-gravity, elastic support for the trunk (Payne, Veenman & Wilson 2005).
- The forelimb stay apparatus keeps the shoulder, carpus and fetlock extended. The elbow is held by triceps tone.
- Grazing reach comes mainly from lowering the neck.
- The staggered grazing stance is well documented. About 50% of 24 Warmblood foals developed a significant preference to protract the same forelimb while grazing, and long limbs with a small head made this more likely (van Heel et al. 2006). This persisted in 24% of 3-year-olds (van Heel et al. 2010). McGreevy & Rogers (2005) used the forelimb advanced while grazing as their motor-laterality measure in Thoroughbreds. Long-limbed Thoroughbreds are exactly the build that tends to stagger.

What needs correcting in the claim:
- (1) "Poll flexion" is the wrong direction. When grazing, the face hangs near vertical and the throatlatch opens. Relative to the alert stance the atlanto-occipital joint is near neutral or more open, not flexed. The reach comes from lowering the neck at its base (the caudal cervical and cervicothoracic joints). The code already opens the head relative to the neck (head.rotation.z +55 deg, nose-up), so fix option 1's "neck1/neck2/head flexion" should not be read as tucking the nose further.
- (2) "Withers drop only a few cm" is an estimate; I found no study that measures it. Geometry supports a few centimetres: protracting one fore 0.25-0.35 m on a limb about 1.2 m long is roughly 12-16 deg, which costs about 3-5 cm of shoulder height. A relaxed sling may add a little more, so roughly 3-8 cm is defensible, and 19-24 cm is not.
- (3) "Typically" is fair, but a square stance is also normal. Laterality is individual (about half of foals, about a quarter of 3-year-olds), so the stagger should vary per horse rather than be universal.

Model note: neck1 pivots at about 1.44 m, which is higher than a real cervicothoracic junction (about the level of the point of shoulder). That is why the fix risk the finding flags (the muzzle may no longer reach the grass) is real. It is a model problem, not a real-horse one.

Severity: medium is right. Background grazers are always on screen, and the crouch with elbows at about 84 deg is a large, visible error.
truth.correction:
The main defect is real: a grazing horse keeps its forelimbs extended and does not drop the shoulder about 24 cm or bend the elbow to about 84 deg. Three corrections:
- (a) The extra reach comes from lowering the neck at its base (caudal cervical and cervicothoracic joints). The poll is not flexed: with the face near vertical, the head-neck angle opens compared with the alert stance. Any fix should keep or increase the head's nose-up rotation relative to the neck, not tuck the nose.
- (b) "Withers drop a few cm" has no published measurement behind it. By geometry, a staggered stance plus a relaxed thoracic sling gives roughly 3-8 cm, so a spine drop of about 0.03-0.06 m is defensible.
- (c) The staggered stance is common, not universal. About 50% of foals (van Heel 2006) and 24% of 3-year-olds (van Heel 2010) show a consistent preference for which forelimb they put forward, and square grazing also occurs. Stagger side and amount should vary per horse.

I tried to refute this finding and couldn't. The code and my re-computation support every main number.

**Code check (index.html)**
- 1647-1650: BODY.graze sets the spine to rest.y - 0.12 (plus about 4 mm of breathing), spine.rotation.z = -3°, hips 0 and chest.rotation.z = -12°.
- 703: the chest bone pivots at (0.3, 1.3).
- 1194-1197: the scapula is a child of the chest (L.root = chest).
- 244-248 and 1378-1380: the 'stand' gait uses fore xc 0.56 and hind xc -0.56, which equal the rest coffin x. footPath returns the rest fetlock (0.484, 0.209) with flex 0, so the knee stays straight. scapSwing is 0.
- 1463: ARM_RANGE only applies in swing, and stand has u = 0.5 < duty = 1. Nothing stops the humerus from folding.

**Re-computation**
I wrote a 2-D replica of the spine→chest→limb transforms and the solve2 IK in node, in my temp folder.
- The replica reproduces the standing measurements in measurements.json: elbow (0.48, 0.96), knee (0.482, 0.50) and fetlock (0.484, 0.209).
- It also reproduces the code's own comment that the grazing muzzle sits "2-10 cm above the ground". Lip/nose come out at y = 0.05-0.08.

Graze compared with rest:
| Measure | Rest | Graze |
|---|---|---|
| Point of shoulder | (0.72, 1.22) | (0.689, 0.978), a 24.2 cm drop |
| Withers | 1.622 | 1.435, an 18.7 cm drop |
| Brisket | 0.898 | 0.703 |
| Shoulder to fetlock | 1.038 m | 0.796 m |
| Elbow angle | 137° | 84° |
| Humerus | | 84.7° from vertical, about 5° from horizontal |
| Elbow position | | moves 14.4 cm back to (0.336, 0.945), about 24 cm above the local belly line, i.e. buried in the barrel |
| Forearm | | slants 11° forward |
| Scapula | 52° from horizontal | 67° from horizontal |
| Shoulder joint angle | 99° | 72° |
| Hip joint | | drops 9.3 cm, to y = 1.087 |

The topline ends up downhill: withers 1.435 against croup 1.50.

**One detail is wrong**
The finding says the hind leg flexes "hocks and stifles". The hock does not flex. eta = hockRest + hockOpen (0) + flex (0) is fixed, so the hock angle stays at 145.8°. Only the stifle closes, from about 113° to about 89°, as the femur rotates. A stifle that flexes while the hock stays still also breaks the reciprocal apparatus, a separate minor issue.

**Anatomy argument**
This holds up:
- The trunk hangs in a muscular thoracic sling (synsarcosis), and the forelimb stay apparatus keeps the shoulder, elbow and carpus extended at little muscular cost (Budras et al., Anatomy of the Horse).
- A standing elbow of about 137° is normal. A sustained crouch to 84° with a near-horizontal humerus is not how horses graze.
- van Heel et al. 2006 (Equine Vet J 38(7):646-651, checked via PubMed) reports a staggered grazing stance: about 50% of foals systematically protracted the same forelimb while grazing, with long limbs and small heads predisposing to it.
- I couldn't find a published figure for how far the withers drop during grazing (web search was unavailable), so "only a few cm" is reasonable but has no source.

**Fix-risk check**
Option 1's warning about muzzle height is real:
- With a 0.03 m spine drop and a -3° chest pitch at the current neck/head angles, the lip sits about 30 cm off the ground.
- It needs neck1 at about -85° to -90° and head at about 65-68° to come back to 7-10 cm. The elbow then stays at about 116°.
- So the neck must take over the reach, or a staggered stance must add some.

**Why the severity drops to low**
The fault is real and large, but few people will see it:
- Only background 'grazer' extras use this pose: two locations in data/locations.js (lines 30-31 and 942-944), 11-18 m off the track.
- The hero horse never uses it.

truth.reasoning: The model-side defect is real. In index.html:984-986 the eye's innermost vertex is at z = 0.106 - 0.024*0.55 = 0.093. I rebuilt the head surface at x = 0.225, y = 0.02 from HEAD :536-545, PROF.head :398 and ringAt (wUp = w*0.78) and got z of about 0.075-0.086, with jitter and the profile term included. So the whole diamond sits off the face with a 0.7-1.8 cm gap. The 'head, front' tile of 00-stand.jpeg shows this: two detached dark diamonds stuck on the sides of a forehead that narrows upward. Most of the real-horse claims hold up. The equine orbit is complete, closed by the zygomatic process of the frontal bone (supraorbital process). The forehead is broad and flat. The skull is widest at orbit/zygomatic level. A study of 14 Standardbred-type cadaver heads measured with soft tissue intact (Merkies, Paraschou & McGreevy 2020) found zygomatic width 22.6 +/- 1.8 cm and cranial width at the orbital notch / frontonasal line 19.0 +/- 0.8 cm. So a real head at and just above eye level is about 19-22 cm wide, not the model's 16.6 cm, with about 12 cm of flat forehead. The globe size (~4-5 cm) is right: CT gives axial length 5.09, height 5.19 and width 4.28 cm (Díaz-Bertrana et al. 2025). The lateral, slightly rostral orientation is also right. Four parts of the claim are overstated or misdirected. (1) The widest bony point (zygion) is on the zygomatic arch, which runs along the ventral orbital margin and back toward the temporomandibular joint. It sits a little below and behind the centre of the globe, not across the orbits at eye-centre height. The model's maximum is 22.3 cm, about 3.7 cm below and 7.5 cm behind the eye. That matches the real 22.6 cm zygomatic width in both size and rough position, so it is not a defect. What is wrong is how sharply the section narrows at and above the eye. (2) 'Prominent brow ridge and supraorbital fossa' overstates it for a young, fit Thoroughbred. Horses have no primate-style brow ridge, only a moderate supraorbital rim. The supraorbital fossa is filled by a fat pad and becomes a visible hollow mainly in old or thin horses. A 2-5-year-old racehorse should show only a subtle rim and shallow hollow. (3) The horse eye is notably prominent: it is laterally placed and the cornea stands proud of the rim, which is why it is so prone to trauma. 'Bulges only slightly' understates this. The model's eye apex (z 0.119) gives about 23.8 cm across the corneas, which is plausible for a real horse: about 22 cm of zygomatic width plus 1 cm of corneal protrusion per side. The eye's lateral position is therefore about right and the head beneath it is too narrow. Fix option 1 ('move the eye in to z ~0.08-0.085') would give about 19 cm across the eyes, which makes them too close-set. The anatomically right fix is option 2: widen the rows at eye height to about 0.095-0.105 half-width with a flatter, broader roof, add a subtle supraorbital rim, and seat the eye so it is about one-third proud of that surface. (4) Severity: the defect is a small cosmetic one. It shows only in front, 3/4 and close-up views and reads acceptably in the side views the game mostly uses. Medium fits better than high.
truth.correction: Correct claims: the eye floats off the head (gap of about 0.7-1.8 cm), and the head is too narrow at and above eye level. Overstated parts: (a) The widest point of a real skull is the zygomatic arch, slightly below and behind the eye centre, so the model's 22.3 cm maximum below and behind the eye is anatomically fine. The defect is the narrowing above it. (b) A young Thoroughbred has only a subtle supraorbital rim and a fat-filled, shallow supraorbital fossa, not a 'prominent brow ridge'. (c) Real horse eyes are prominent and the cornea stands proud of the rim. The model's across-corneas width (about 23.8 cm) is already realistic, so the fix should widen the head at eye height (option 2) and seat the eye against it. Pulling the eye inward to z 0.08-0.085 (option 1) would make the eyes too close-set.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse part of the claim and couldn't. The core statements hold.

What the model does: index.html:987-989 confirms the nostril is an OctahedronGeometry(0.018) scaled (1.4,0.9,0.5) at (0.6,-0.012,±0.066), using the dark eyeMat on a muzzle already painted pal.muzzle for x>0.55 (:979). Nothing in the rig animates or scales the nostrils. The breath puffs (:2966-2990) do fire once per stride for canter/gallop/race. The 00-stand 'head, right side' and 'head, front' tiles and the 06 'jockey close' tiles show a small dark diamond that can hardly be seen from the front.

What real horses do:
(1) Horses are obligate nasal breathers. The soft palate seals the airway off from the mouth except when swallowing (standard veterinary anatomy).
(2) Breathing locks to the stride. Young et al. 1992 filmed Thoroughbreds cantering at 9 and 11 m/s and found 'exactly one breath per stride'. Bramble & Carrier 1983 report 1:1 phase-locking in galloping quadrupeds. At a race gallop of about 2.2 strides/s this is roughly 130 breaths/min.
(3) The nostrils dilate a lot during exertion. Tucker et al. 2024 sutured cadaver nostrils 'in the open/flared position to replicate the muscular dilation that occurs during exertion'. Holcombe et al. 2002 showed the nasal passage (nasal valve) is a significant inspiratory resistance in exercising horses: nasal strips lowered peak inspiratory tracheal pressure and resistance at 100-120% of maximal heart rate. Nostril size and flare are therefore functionally real, not cosmetic.
(4) EquiFACS (Wathan et al. 2015) does code AD38 'Nostril dilator', which acts on the front (rostral) edge of the nostril. It separates this from AUH13 'nostril lift', which pulls the back (caudal) edge up and out through m. levator anguli oris fascialis (caninus / dilator naris lateralis). da Fé et al. 2025 link AD38 with deep breathing.

Small imprecisions, none of which overturn the finding:
(a) 'Framed by the alar cartilages' is loose. The horse's comma-shaped alar cartilage supports the medial wing and the ventral part of the nostril. The dorsolateral wing, where the alar fold leads into the false nostril, is soft tissue. That soft part is what flares, and it is also what collapses or flutters in alar-fold collapse (Strand et al. 2026). A believable flare widens the opening mainly outward and upward, rather than scaling a rigid rim evenly.
(b) The false nostril (nasal diverticulum) is not a separate opening 'above'. It is a blind skin pouch entered through the dorsal part of the same nostril.
(c) AD38 is only a facial-coding label. The evidence for exercise flare comes from airway physiology (points 3 and 4 above), not from EquiFACS.
(d) Real flare is graded with breathing demand, i.e. with speed. It peaks on inspiration, and the nostrils stay largely open at maximal effort. A slow hack canter flares much less than a race gallop. So the fix's 1.4-1.6 scale should ramp with speed or effort instead of switching on by gait name, with a modest per-breath pulse on top.
(e) The finding gives no real nostril dimensions. The model's full octahedron is about 5.0 x 3.2 cm, of which about 3.9 x 2.5 cm shows. That is plausibly small next to a Thoroughbred's resting nostril, but I found no published measurement to quantify it. The stronger problems are the sideways facing, the near-flush seating, the dark-on-dark colour and the missing flare.

Severity stays medium: this is a secondary facial feature, but a flared nostril at racing speed is a strong visual cue in racing close-ups, and the current nostrils are nearly invisible.

truth.reasoning:
Rest pose: the claim holds. The forelock (NAV: cirrus capitis) grows from the poll and falls forward between the ears onto the forehead (Wikipedia "Forelock"; Budras et al., Anatomy of the Horse, hair of the head). At rest, gravity draws it along the frontal bone toward the eyes. A thick forelock can stand off the face by a centimetre or two where it arcs over the poll. A lock that leaves the forehead at about 18 deg and ends about 5 cm clear of the face is wrong, not normal variation. A fine, often pulled Thoroughbred forelock would stand off even less. The code matches the description: the cone is built along +Y and its mount uses rotation.z = HEAD_TILT - 72 deg = -114 deg, so it points 24 deg below horizontal, while the head axis (HEAD_TILT = -42 deg) slopes about 42 deg down. For a lock of about 0.17 m, sin 18 deg x 0.17 is about 5 cm. The 00-stand "head, right side" tile shows a dark forward spike in front of the ears.

At speed: the claim is overstated. A real forelock does not stay flat at a racing gallop. With about 16 m/s of relative airflow and the head nodding each stride, it lifts off the forehead, flips up and back toward or between the ears, and flutters. It can also bounce or fall to one side, and a browband or hood can hold it down. So "lifts further at speed" is not a defect in itself. The real problem is the direction. In BODY.race (index.html:1558-1561), mn.mesh.rotation.z = amp x (0.42 + 0.14 cyc + 0.05 cyc) with amp 0.5. That is a steady +0.21 rad (about 12 deg) with about ±5 deg of flutter. It swings the lock's tip up toward horizontal while it still points forward, so it reads more like a horn. A real forelock would rotate past vertical and lie back over the poll. Fix option 1 ("Lay it on the face", wave amplitude ~0.15) would correct the rest pose but take away a real effect at speed. A correct fix lays the lock on the face at rest and then lets it stream up and back over the poll, scaled with speed: fix option 2, or option 3 plus a speed-driven backward flip. The "expected" text should read: lies on the forehead at rest; at gallop and race speed it lifts and streams up and back over the poll, or flutters, rather than staying flat.
truth.correction: The rest-pose complaint is right: a real forelock comes from the poll and lies along the forehead toward the eyes, and an 18 deg / 5 cm stand-off is a modelling error. The at-speed complaint is overstated. Real forelocks do lift off the forehead at a gallop, blown up and back by the airflow and head nod. The model is wrong only because its lift (a steady +12 deg rotation.z offset in BODY.race) points the lock forward-up like a horn instead of rotating it back over the poll. The fix should lay the lock on the face at rest and stream it up and back with speed. Simply cutting the wave amplitude to 0.15 is not enough.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. The claim about real horses holds, with two small caveats.

The model, checked first:
- index.html:543-544: the last HEAD rows are [0.58, top 0.035, bot 0.105] and [0.63, 0.02, 0.085]. That makes the x=0.63 ring 10.5 cm deep, centred at y≈-0.033.
- index.html:972: loft(headRings, ..., V(0.66,-0.035)) closes the head with a single apex on that centre line, 3 cm ahead of the last ring. The front of the muzzle is therefore a short cone.
- The underside (bot) falls steadily from 0.235 at x=0.15 to 0.085, with no chin bulge and no groove. The finding's mention of HEAD row 0.58 is correct.
- The bit ring is at x=0.555, y=-0.075 (index.html:1072) on a smooth cheek. No commissure is modelled.
- The 00-stand tile 'head, right side' shows a blunt, slightly pointed dark tip with no split between upper lip and chin.
- measurements.json puts poll to muzzle tip at 0.66 m.

The real-horse claims:
1) A large, mobile upper lip that leads the profile. True. Horses have sensitive, prehensile lips used to pick through forage (Budras, Anatomy of the Horse; the Wikipedia equine anatomy page says the same). The upper lip is longer than the lower and overhangs it.
2) A lower lip and a rounded chin below and slightly behind it, then a chin groove. True. The chin groove is defined as 'the part of the horse's head behind the lower lip and chin, the area that dips down slightly on the lower jaw', which is where a curb chain sits (equine anatomy glossary on Wikipedia; the Bit (horse) page lists the chin groove among the bit's pressure points).
3) Mouth corners where the bit rests. True. The mouthpiece sits in the interdental space (the bars, between the incisors and premolars) and pulls on the lip corners (Pollaris et al. 2025, Animals 15:2648). Bit lesions cluster at the lip corners, the bars of the mandible and the cheek lining next to the upper second premolars, teeth 106/206 (Tuomola et al. 2019 Front Vet Sci 6:206; Tuomola et al. 2021; Björnsdóttir et al. 2014). Those papers confirm the corners sit at the front of the cheek-tooth row.
- I found no published figure for the distance from the front of the lips to the mouth corner. A rough estimate from the skull (lip and incisors about 3-5 cm, plus most of an interdental space of about 8-10 cm) gives roughly 8-12 cm in a 16-hand Thoroughbred, so '~8-10 cm' is plausible but not sourced.
- The model's bit sits 10.5 cm behind the tip, so its position is already about right. What is missing is a visible mouth corner and mouth line, not a misplaced bit.

Caveats (they don't change the verdict):
- 'Squarish' is slightly strong for a Thoroughbred. Conformation guides call for a fine, tapering muzzle. In profile the front is blunt and rounded: a near-vertical upper lip in front, with the lower lip and chin set back. So the fix should not carry the full 10.5 cm depth right to the tip, as fix option 1 ('keeping depth') suggests. Better: a rounded upper-lip front about 6-8 cm tall, with the lower lip and chin stepped back about 1-2 cm.
- Fix option 3 ('open mouth at speed'): horses breathe only through the nose and do not open their mouths to breathe when galloping. A gaping mouth in a race usually comes from rein or bit pressure, so it should not be a default animation.

The finding is cosmetic only and has no effect on movement, so low severity is right.

I tried to refute this finding and couldn't. Every factual claim about the model checks out. One descriptive word, "beak-like", goes too far.

Code (index.html):
- HEAD rows 543-544 are [0.58, top 0.035, bot 0.105, w 0.08] and [0.63, 0.02, 0.085, 0.07]. The last ring is therefore 0.02+0.085 = 10.5 cm deep, and the row before it is 14 cm deep.

- The underside of the head rises steadily toward the tip: -0.12 at x=0.38, -0.11 at 0.5, -0.105 at 0.58, -0.085 at 0.63. Nothing bulges outward where the chin would be, and nothing dips in behind it where the chin groove would be.
- I searched the whole file for jaw, chin, lip, mouth, commissure, curb and whisker. None of these features exist on the head. The only muzzle detail is two octahedron nostrils at x=0.6 (:987-989), plus a muzzle colour applied to every face with x > 0.55 (:979). Nothing paints a mouth line.
- Bit ring (:1072): a torus at head-space (0.555, -0.075, ±0.072). I recomputed the head surface at that spot with the same ring and interpolation maths the code uses. The cheek's half-width there is about 0.049 m, so the ring hangs about 2.3 cm off a continuous cheek and no mouth corner passes through it. Its distance behind the tip (0.66 - 0.555 = 10.5 cm) is a reasonable place for a mouth corner. What's missing is the mouth itself, not a correct position for the ring.
- measurements.json (static.standing): poll [1.213, 1.824], muzzle [1.684, 1.36]. That is 0.661 m from poll to muzzle, matching the cap point at head-space x=0.66. So the "muzzle" landmark is that single cap point.

Images: I cropped and enlarged the 00-stand 'head, right side' and 'head, front' tiles and the 06 'jockey close' tile. In each, the head ends in one dark, rounded, slightly tapered knob. Upper lip, lower lip and chin can't be told apart, there is no mouth slit, and in 06 the bit ring sits on the plain cheek behind the dark muzzle band.

Where the finding is overstated: "beak-like" is too strong. The cap is a 120-degree wedge (its upper face climbs 5.5 cm and its lower face falls 5.0 cm over a 3 cm run). With the head tilted 42 degrees, the front of the muzzle in world space falls 6.1 cm while moving only 1.5 cm back, and the underside runs 5.6 cm back while dropping 1.7 cm. The most forward point is the top front corner of the last ring, roughly where the upper lip would be. So from the side the tip looks blunt and roughly square-ended, not sharp. The real flaw is the missing anatomy (lips, chin bulge, chin groove, mouth corner and mouth line), plus a muzzle that thins from 14 cm to 10.5 cm deep over its last 5 cm. In a real horse that region is filled out by the lips and chin.

Real horses (sources below): the lips are separate, mobile structures with a rounded chin under and behind the lower lip. The bit lies in the gap between the front teeth and the cheek teeth (the "bars"), at the corners of the mouth, a few cm behind where the lips meet. The model has the right location for the bit but not the anatomy around it.

Severity stays low. The flaw only shows in close-ups and doesn't affect proportions or movement. The finding's fix options are sound. "Square the muzzle" also has to account for rowAt (:1008-1012), which reads the end row HN for any x beyond the last row, and the snip and bald face markings that select faces with x > 0.55.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the claim and could not. The main anatomy reference supports almost every point about real horses.

1. Shape. Sisson (1914, The Anatomy of the Domestic Animals, pp. 870-871, the Getty edition's ancestor) describes the auricle as a "funnel-like organ". Its convex surface "is widest in its middle part; its lower part is almost circular in curvature, while above it narrows and flattens." The base of the conchal cartilage "is coiled so as to form a tube… funnel-shaped". The apex "is flattened, pointed, and curved a little forward". Sisson describes the ear with its opening facing outward, so once the ear is pricked forward that curve points medially, which matches "tip turned in". So the ear is narrow at a tubular base, widest in the middle and pointed at the tip, which is the reverse of a cone that is widest at its base.

2. The opening faces forward when the ear is pricked, and the ear rotates. Sisson p. 875: the base of the concha sits in a fat pad, "so that the movements of the external ear resemble those of a ball-and-socket joint… movements about the longitudinal and transverse axes are accompanied by rotation. When the ear is vertical or drawn forward ('pricked up'), the opening is usually directed forward; conversely, when the ears are 'laid back,' the opening faces backward." The base is a rhombus 7.2 cm wide across the head and 4.5 cm front to back, and it narrows in a straight line to the tip: 7.2, 5.4, 3.6, 1.8 and 0 cm at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% of the length. There is no narrow, tube-like base, no widest point in the middle third and no hollow inner face.
- **Mount (996-998).** At rest, with HEAD_TILT = -42 deg, the mount tilts the ear back about 9.5-16 deg and leans it out 16 deg. `conf.ears` scales the length by earSize and the width by sqrt(earSize). `earSet` and `earTilt` only move the mount or add tilt.
- **Animation.** The idle ear code (1663-1669) and the gallop, race and canter ear loops (1524-1526, 1554-1556, 1605-1607) only set `e.mesh.rotation.z` (tilt back) and `rotation.x` (lean out). `earsAtSpeed` (1718) adds to `rotation.z`. Nothing sets `rotation.y`, which is the ear's long axis, so the ear never swivels. The comment at 1663 says "Ears swivel", but the code only tilts and leans.
- **Hood cover (1057).** It is a 5-sided cone added as a child of the ear mesh, as the finding says.
- **Pictures.** I cropped and enlarged 00-stand 'head, front' and 'head, right side'. From the front the ears are wide-based triangles that read as cat ears; from the side they are thin spikes. The 05-race front tiles look the same.

Where the finding's description is wrong:
1. **"One colour except a dark tip": there is no dark tip at all.** `paint()` (471-485) colours each face by the centre point of its triangle. The ear has one height segment, and r186 skips the zero-area triangles at the tip, so each side face is a single triangle from base to tip. Its centre sits at y = 0.05 m, and the base cap is at y = 0. So the `c.y > 0.1 ? pal.points` branch at line 993 is never taken. Every face is coat colour (shade varies by ±2%), and the black ear tips intended for a bay never show. This matches the crops. The problem is slightly worse than stated, and line 993 also contains a dead colour branch.
2. **"Broad faces sideways and a ridge forward" is half right.** There is a blunt 116 deg ridge at the front and sharp 64 deg edges at the sides. But the four faces point mostly forward and backward, not sideways. At rest the front pair points about 35 deg outward and 28 deg inward of straight ahead (normals (0.81, 0.10, 0.57) and (0.81, 0.39, -0.43)). The front-outer face is roughly aimed where a real attentive ear's opening faces. It is just flat or bulging rather than hollow, and it is coat-coloured rather than pale. The wide 7.2 cm dimension runs across the head, so the triangle reads wide from the front and thin from the side.
3. **"A symmetric pyramid could not show a swivel anyway" is overstated.** The rhombus is not round, so turning it about its long axis would change its outline: the front-view width would vary between about 7.6 and 4.6 cm. When the ear tilts back (race pose, idle flick), the faces also turn about 15 deg as a side effect (35 to about 50 deg). That is not a real swivel.

Against a real horse: the outer ear (pinna) is a sheet of auricular cartilage. At its base it is rolled into a narrow funnel (the concha) that sits on the scutiform cartilage. Above that it widens into a lance-shaped ear, widest around the middle, with a pointed tip. Its hollow, haired inner surface faces forward and outward when the horse is alert (Budras et al., *Anatomy of the Horse*; Getty, *Sisson and Grossman*; König & Liebich). EquiFACS codes ear movements separately for each ear: EAD101 ears forward, EAD102 adductor, EAD103 flattener, EAD104 rotator, EAD105 ears down (Wathan et al. 2015). Turning the opening toward a sound (EAD104) is a separate movement from flattening or tilting back, and the model cannot do it. Severity: medium is fair. The ears are small at normal viewing distance, but they read clearly in head close-ups and front views. They are one of the most expressive parts of a horse's head, and the user explicitly asked for ear quirks. truth.reasoning:
Some of the real-horse claims hold up. Others are overstated or turn a design preference into anatomy.

What holds up:
(1) Ears are mobile and move independently. EquiFACS (Wathan et al. 2015) defines EAD101 'ears forward' (swivel rostrally), EAD103 'ear flattener' ('flattened and abducted') and EAD104 'ear rotator' (lateral and caudal). It states that the ears 'can, and often do, move independently'. Two ears locked to one formula at canter, gallop and race, with only a 4-6 deg left-right difference, is therefore unrealistic as a constant state.
(2) Forward ears mark attention to something ahead. In a graded feral-horse posture scale (Animals 2026, PMC13295745), a vigilant horse has its ears pricked forward and an alarmed one points them at the threat. A horse that never brings its ears forward over a whole loop reads as dull or unwell.
(3) A passive ear bounce twice per stride has no basis. Head and neck pitch at the gallop cycles once per stride, and the rig itself drives neck and head with cyc(g,1,...). A small bounce once per stride is better grounded.
(4) The code confirms the slider ranges. Rest tilt is HEAD_TILT+58 deg = 16 deg back on the skull, and earsAtSpeed is +/-0.3 rad. My own estimate from the code, with the head pitch taken from measurements.json, matches the reported ranges: race about -18..-34, earsAtSpeed -1 about -16..0, +1 about -35..-51. So the labels 'pricked forward' and 'pinned flat back' oversell what the slider can reach. That is a fair customization bug, but it is a model-side issue, not a real-horse one.

What is overstated or wrong:
(a) Forward is not the neutral carriage. The neutral ear is upright or turned to the side, and a loose, slightly-back ear is normal for a relaxed, bored or tired horse. Wikipedia's Horse behavior article, citing Scott, says 'ears slightly turned back but in a loose position... simply relaxed'. In the feral-horse scale, drowsy horses have flickering ears and sleeping horses have their ears to the side. Dyson and Pollard 2024 count 'Ears forward or erect or rotated to side, but not behind vertical >=5 s' as the normal state, seen in 77.6% of 805 ridden sport horses. One ear forward and one back toward the person is common in working horses. So the walk tilt of -2..-11 deg, roughly upright to slightly back, is within normal relaxed variation. Only the steady -13..-16 deg at trot and canter, with no forward episodes at all, is marginal. The fix 'neutral +5..+15 deg forward' would make the horse permanently vigilant. A better default is about 0..+10 deg, with periodic forward and one-ear-back episodes and flicks in both directions.
(b) At racing speed the expectation is one-sided. 'Racehorses often gallop with both ears forward or one forward/one back' is true for parts of a race, such as cruising or leading. Ears laid back under full drive are also common. I found no peer-reviewed measurement of ear position during flat races, so neither pattern can be called the norm. A moderately swept-back default of -18..-34 deg at full effort is within real variation and is not an anatomical error. The missing pieces are variety and independence, not the mean angle.
(c) Wathan and McComb 2014 is cited for more than it shows. The study found that horses need a conspecific's head orientation plus its eyes and ears to locate the object it attends to. That supports 'ears point at the focus of attention'. It does not show that attentive horses default to forward carriage, and it says nothing about galloping.
(d) Pinned ears are not a simple backward tilt. EquiFACS EAD103 is 'flattened and abducted': the ears go back AND out, with the opening turned away from the front. A sagittal-only tilt to -80 deg would look wrong. The ~70-90 deg should be measured against the skull or neck line, because world tilt depends on head carriage. Fully pinned ears also signal pain, anger or extreme effort, which suits a slider extreme but not a default.

Net: the anatomy is not wrong. Real horses commonly hold their ears upright to slightly back, and laid back at maximal effort. The valid problems are the lack of variety (never forward, ears in lock-step, flicks only backward), the 2x-per-stride flap, and slider labels that promise more range than the code delivers. Medium is too high for the anatomy itself.
truth.correction: Keep: ears should move independently (EquiFACS), sometimes come forward, flick in both directions, and bounce at most once per stride. The slider labels promise more range than the code delivers. Correct: forward is not the neutral carriage. Real relaxed or working horses hold their ears upright, to the side or loosely slightly back, and one ear back toward a rider is common. Dyson and Pollard 2024 count 'forward or erect or rotated to side' as normal in 77.6% of 805 ridden horses. So walk -2..-11 deg is within normal; the problem is never pricking and lock-step, not the mean angle. At racing speed, ears laid back under drive are as common as pricked ears; I found no measured data for flat races. The -18..-34 deg default is therefore defensible, and the fix should add variety (seeded forward / one-back / laid-back states, independent per ear) rather than move the default forward. Set neutral to about 0..+10 deg, not +5..+15. Model pinned ears as back plus abducted, as in EquiFACS EAD103 'flattened and abducted' (rotate about the long axis and splay out), with the angle measured against the skull or neck line rather than world vertical. Wathan and McComb 2014 supports only 'ears point at the focus of attention', not a forward default or gallop behaviour.

model.reasoning:
I measured this myself. I served the worktree read-only on localhost, loaded the page and used the window.__horse hook to pose the studio-bay horse. For each gait I took the ear-mesh axis (local +Y) in the root frame at 32 phases of one stride and 600 phases of the loop. No repository file was changed.

The core claims hold:
(1) With default settings the ears never tip ahead of vertical. In world terms, forward positive, I got:
  - walk −40..−1° (the idle flick takes them back to −40°; at rest they sit at −12..−1°)
  - trot −42..−13°
  - canter −19..−10°
  - gallop −32..−14°
  - race −36..−18°
The swept-back look does not come from head carriage. The model's race head is more nose-down than at the stand (face line −44..−56° against −42° standing), which on its own would tilt the ears forward. The backward tilt comes from the mount and mesh rotations: HEAD_TILT+58° = 16° back at :997, plus mesh.z +0.12 rad at gallop and +0.32 rad at race (:1525, :1555). The code comment at :1663 says "mostly forward", but the result never gets there.
(2) idleEars (:1667) computes fwd + 0.45·max(0,cos)^3, so the flick only ever goes backward. It is noticeably active for about 1/3 of the time.
(3) At canter, gallop and race both ears use one formula that differs only by a phase term of side × 0.1. The largest left-right gap I measured was 4.1°, 5.7° and 4.2°.
(4) run.earsAtSpeed = −1 at race gives −19..−0.5°, never forward. At gallop it gives −16..+2.5°.

Where the finding is wrong or overstated:
(a) "conf.earTilt −1 gives −11° at walk" is wrong. earTilt −1 shifts the ear about 14° forward (0.25 rad). At walk I measured −25..+14°, so the ear does tip forward whenever it isn't flicking. Trot reaches +1.6°. Combined with earsAtSpeed −1, canter is +10..+19° and race −4..+14°. So a "pricked" setting is reachable, though only modestly and only by stacking two sliders.
(b) "Pinned": earsAtSpeed +1 at race gives −54..−35° in world terms (the critic measured −51..−35°). Measured against the skull, that is about 184° from the forward face line (148.6° + 18.3° + 17.2°), i.e. lying along the head's long axis. That counts as flat against the skull, but it is not pressed down along the crest, which I estimate at roughly 60–90° back in world. The shortfall is about 20–35°, not a complete failure.
(c) "Flaps twice per stride, about 4.6 Hz": the 2× term exists only at gallop (±0.08 rad, ±4.6°, 4.8 Hz) and race (±0.06 rad, ±3.4°, 4.65 Hz). Canter uses 1× (:1606). The visible world-space swing is a 1× motion of about 16–18° driven by head pitch, and the 2× term is a small ripple on top of it.

On the anatomy, the finding is right in substance. An attentive horse's ears point forward, and ear position tracks attention (Wathan & McComb 2014). EquiFACS codes the ears as independently mobile action units: EAD101 ears forward, EAD103 ear flattener, EAD104 ear rotator (Wathan et al. 2015). Neither a forward state nor independent left and right ears at speed exists in the model.

Sheets 00 and 05 agree with the numbers. In the stand close-up the near ear stands up and back. At race the ears lie back toward the mane in every phase.

Severity stays medium: the defect shows on every horse in every gait, and the user explicitly asked for ear customisation.

Confirmed with defaults:

- The idle flick only goes backward.
- At canter, gallop and race the two ears move in lock-step, at most 4–6° apart.
- earsAtSpeed −1 at race only reaches vertical (−19..−0.5°).

Corrections to the finding:
- conf.earTilt −1 does give a forward ear at walk, reaching +14° (range −25..+14°). Stacked with earsAtSpeed −1 it reaches +14..+19° at canter and race. "Pricked" is reachable, but weak and needs two sliders.
- earsAtSpeed +1 (−54..−35° at race) already lies along the skull's long axis, because the race head is carried nose-down at −44..−56°. It is not pressed down along the crest, which would be roughly 60–90° back in world terms, so the gap is about 20–35°, not a failure to pin at all.
- The 2× flap exists only at gallop and race and is a ±3–5° ripple. Canter is 1×, and the visible ear motion is a 1× swing of about 16–18° driven by head pitch.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute this finding on the real-horse side and could not. The model side also checks out.

Model side:
- At index.html:389, cyc(g,k,ph) = cos(2π(k·g − ph)). So the spine term 0.022·cyc(g,2,0.32) at :1572 peaks at g = 0.16/0.66 and bottoms at g = 0.41/0.91.
- measurements.json gaits.trot (32 samples) agrees. The LF and RH toes stay at y ≈ 0.002 from g = 0 to 0.406 and lift by g = 0.438, so the diagonal stance runs about 0 to 0.42.
- Withers peak at 1.619 at g = 0.156, which is 37% of stance. They bottom at 1.571 at g = 0.406, which is 97% of stance, at lift-off.
- Croup goes from 1.586 to 1.564. Poll goes from 1.867 (g 0.156–0.188) to 1.797 (g 0.406–0.438).
- So the code puts its high points where real horses have their low points, and the reverse. The comment at :1568 ("lowest as each diagonal pair takes the weight") contradicts the code.

Real-horse side:
- Rhodin et al. 2022 (Animals 12:3053, PMC9657284) is quoted correctly. For trot, minima fall at 39–46% of fore stance for the head, 39–42% for the withers and 41–45% of hind stance for the pelvis. Maxima fall at 92–97% (head), 91–98% (withers) and 92–110% (pelvis). The authors say the lowest and highest positions are "closely temporally related to midstance and hoof-off".
- Rhodin's sample had no Thoroughbreds (Warmblood, Iberian, Icelandic, in-hand overground). I therefore checked for a breed-specific exception. Pfau et al. 2018 (Equine Vet J 50:117–124, PMC5724686) studied racing Thoroughbreds in training and found the same pattern: head, withers and pelvis minima "at approximately mid stance", maxima "at approximately mid aerial phase", with head-to-withers timing differences of only about 3% of the stride. There is no Thoroughbred exception.
- Trot is the textbook bouncing (spring-mass) gait, with the centre of mass lowest at mid-stance. That rests on Cavagna, Heglund and Taylor 1977 and Farley, Glasheen and McMahon 1993. It is also the head-nod and pelvis signal that lameness systems read (Buchner 1996, Keegan 2007).
- Amplitudes are not the problem here. The model's poll range of about 70 mm sits inside Rhodin's 61–78 mm, so this is purely a timing issue.

Small refinements, none of which change the verdict:
1. Real maxima are near hoof-off. Rhodin places them from the last 15% of stance into early suspension, and Pfau at about mid aerial phase. The finding's "highest in suspension" is a slight simplification, but its own quoted 91–98% numbers are right.
2. Real minima come slightly before mid-stance (about 40–45%), not exactly at 50% as an idealised half-sine force model gives.
3. The model's real stance is about 0–0.42, not 0–0.44. A minimum near g ≈ 0.17–0.20 / 0.67–0.70 and a maximum near g ≈ 0.40–0.46 / 0.90–0.96 would match both papers. The finding's "re-phase" fix (minimum at about g 0.20/0.70) lands in that window.

Severity stays high. Trot is a main gait, and the inversion means the legs are longest while carrying weight, so the horse looks like it is vaulting stiff-legged over its legs, as in a walk, rather than bouncing. Its head nod is also the mirror image of a sound horse's.

- LF and RH toes stay at y = 0.002-0.003 from k=0 to k=13 (g 0-0.406) and lift at k=14 (0.024 / 0.021).
- At k=14 all four hooves are off the ground, so that is the suspension.
- Withers: 1.585 at touchdown, rising to a maximum of 1.619 at k=5 (g 0.156, 39% of stance), then falling to a minimum of 1.571 at k=13 (g 0.406, lift-off) and 1.572 at k=14 (suspension).
- Croup: 1.586 maximum vs 1.564 minimum, at the same phases.
- Poll: 1.867 maximum at g 0.156-0.188 (39-47% of stance) vs 1.797 minimum at g 0.406-0.438.
- The pattern repeats exactly in the second half of the stride.
- LF shoulder-to-toe length keeps shortening until k=10 (g 0.31, 1.183 m), as claimed.

Every number the critic quotes matches. The one small difference is that the poll maximum falls at 39-47% of fore stance, not 36-43%.

Reference: I fetched Rhodin et al. 2022, Animals (PMC9657284). At trot the vertical minima fall at these percentages of fore stance: head 41-46%, withers 39-42%, pelvis 41-45%. The maxima fall at head 92-97%, withers 91-98%, pelvis 92-110% ("minima during the diagonal stance phases and maxima around the time of push-off"). The model's maximum sits where real horses have their minimum (about 39%), and its minimum sits where they have their maximum (about 98-100%). This is a true half-cycle inversion of the trot's spring-mass bounce (Cavagna 1977; Farley 1993). The neck and head terms (phases 0.36-0.42) ride on the same trunk motion, so the head nod is inverted too.

The sheet (02-trot, g = 1/8 and 2/8 vs 3/8) is only weakly readable, because the amplitude is about 5 cm. The numeric evidence is decisive, though.

Refinements to the fix:
1. The simplest fix is to flip the sign: -0.022*cyc(g,2,0.32). That puts the minimum at g 0.16 / 0.66 (39% of stance) and the maximum at 0.41 / 0.91 (about 98%). This matches Rhodin's withers timing more closely than the critic's suggested minimum at 0.20 and maximum at 0.45, because Rhodin's maxima sit at push-off rather than mid-suspension.
2. On IK reach: I estimated the flipped bounce by adding the height change to the measured shoulder/hip positions. Planted legs peak at 97.6-97.9% of full chain length at touchdown, up from 96.3-96.7% now. That leaves a margin of about 2.1%, slightly under the 2.5% the walk comment targets, so it should be re-checked but is not a blocker.
3. The ±0.6° spine pitch and the hips/chest/neck terms at phases 0.30-0.42 should be flipped or shifted the same way.

The amplitude being too small is a separate issue (A-TROT-02).

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the claim and could not. Its core holds: in a sound trotting horse the withers and the tuber sacrale rise and fall together, by about the same amount, and that amount is roughly 6-9 cm for a full-size horse.

What I re-measured from measurements.json (gaits.trot, 32 samples):
- Withers move 48 mm peak to peak, croup 22 mm, poll 70 mm. The spine bone moves 44 mm.
- The tail head moves only 3 mm and the point of buttock 4 mm. So the hindquarters are almost cancelled out, which is worse than the finding says.
- The withers-to-croup line pitches 0.4° to 1.9°, in phase with the vertical bounce. That is what makes the croup travel less than half as far as the withers.
- Code at index.html:1572-1575 matches: translation amplitude 0.022 m (44 mm peak to peak), spine.rotation.z 0.6°, hips.rotation.z 1.5°, all on cos(2*TAU*g) terms.
- A half-sine ground-force model with the gait's own timing (T 0.72 s, duty 0.4, so a 0.288 s stance in a 0.36 s step) gives about 66 mm of centre-of-mass travel. This reproduces the finding's "~6-7 cm" figure.

What real horses do:
- **Buchner 1996** (Dutch Warmbloods, treadmill trot at 3.5 m/s): "The head, withers and tuber sacrale showed a similar sinusoidal pattern in their vertical displacement, velocity and acceleration."
- **Rhodin 2022** (in-hand trot): withers and pelvis "rise and fall synchronously twice per stride", lowest during the diagonal stance phases. Withers vs pelvis range: Warmbloods 92 vs 89 mm, Iberians 66 vs 71 mm, Icelandics 47 vs 56 mm. In no breed is the pelvis range anywhere near half the withers range; in two of the three it is larger.
- The 47 mm low end that the head-neck lens used as "within range" comes from small, gaited Icelandic horses. For a 163 cm Thoroughbred trotting at 3.6 m/s, 48 mm at the withers is too small.
- **Buchner 2000**: at a treadmill trot the centre of mass moves 53 ± 6 mm vertically. That is 27% less than the external trunk markers, which works out to about 73 mm.

Minor corrections, none of which change the verdict:
1. The finding's "~6-7 cm" centre-of-mass figure is a spring-mass estimate. The measured value is 53 ± 6 mm (Buchner 2000). The 6-10 cm range applies to trunk landmarks (about 73 mm on a treadmill, 66-92 mm in hand for Warmbloods and Iberians), not to the centre of mass.
2. The Buchner 1996 abstract supports "similar sinusoids" but gives no amplitudes. The numbers should be cited to Buchner 2000 and Rhodin 2022 instead.
3. Trunk pitch is not zero. Faber 2001 measured 2.8-4.9° of sagittal (flexion-extension) motion per vertebra, T6 to S3, at a 4.0 m/s treadmill trot. The withers still match the sacrum because the two move nearly in phase, not because the trunk is rigid. The model's pitch is small in degrees, but it is locked to the bounce so that it always works against the croup.
4. I found no published absolute vertical ranges for Thoroughbreds at the trot. Pfau 2018 reports only asymmetry measures. Warmbloods, bred for an expressive trot, may sit at the top of the range. A target of about 60-75 mm peak to peak, equal at withers and croup, is a safe choice for a Thoroughbred working trot.

Fix option A (amplitude 0.03-0.035 m, i.e. 60-70 mm peak to peak, with the counter-pitch removed) is consistent with this data. The finding should be paired with A-TROT-01: the model's bounce is about 180° out of phase, with its peak at g≈0.16 (mid-stance) when real horses are lowest at mid-stance.

model.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The problem is real, and at the back end it is worse than the finding says.

Code (index.html:1570-1576, BODY.trot):
- The spine translation is `-0.03 + 0.022*cyc(g,2,0.32)`, so 44 mm peak-to-peak. It peaks at g=0.16/0.66.
- `spine.rotation.z = 0.6°*cyc(g,2,0.3)` peaks at g=0.15, and `hips.rotation.z = 1.5°*cyc(g,2,0.35)` peaks at g=0.175.
- A positive Three.js z-rotation turns +X toward +Y. With the horse facing +X, both rotations put the forehand up and the hindquarters down at the moment the trunk is highest. They therefore cancel part of the translation behind the pivots.
- Hand check: at the croup (x=-0.516; hips pivot at x=-0.30) the cancellation is about 0.516·0.6° + 0.216·1.5° ≈ 5.4 + 5.7 = 11 mm of the 22 mm amplitude, leaving about 22 mm peak-to-peak. At the tail head (x=-0.83) the cancellation is about 8.7 + 13.8 ≈ 22.5 mm, which is almost the whole 22 mm.

Measurements (node, gaits.trot, 32 samples), peak-to-peak:
- withers 48 mm (1.571-1.619 m)
- croup 22 mm (1.564-1.586 m)
- poll 70 mm
- spine bone 44 mm
- hip joints 26 mm
- tail head 3 mm
- point of buttock 4 mm

So every number the finding cites reproduces exactly. The croup moves exactly in phase with the spine (r=0.999), only at reduced amplitude. The croup/withers ratio is 0.46. The withers-croup line pitches only 1.5°. The croup-buttock (pelvis) line pitches 4.1°, and that pelvic pitch is what holds the tail head and buttock almost still vertically.

Duty/suspension claim: a half-sine vertical GRF with the model's own timing (T 0.72 s, duty 0.4, 72 ms suspension, peak about 1.96 BW per diagonal) gives 66.5 mm of centre-of-mass excursion. This confirms the "~6-7 cm" figure.

Real horses: Rhodin et al. 2022 (Animals, PMC9657284), in-hand trot, vertical range of motion:

| Breed group | Head | Withers | Pelvis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warmblood | 78 mm | 92 mm | 89 mm |
| Iberian | 64 mm | 66 mm | 71 mm |
| Icelandic | 61 mm | 47 mm | 56 mm |

In every group the pelvis moves about as far as, or further than, the withers (ratio about 0.97-1.2), not 0.46.

How the finding should be read:
- The withers figure on its own is within real ranges, though it equals the smallest group (Icelandic horses) rather than a 163 cm Thoroughbred, whose closest comparison is the Warmblood group at about 90 mm.
- The clear defect is the hindquarters. The model's pelvic points (3-26 mm) sit far below even the Icelandic pelvis interval (50-62 mm).
- I could not fetch the Buchner 1996 abstract (PubMed returned only a cookie page) to check its exact numbers. Rhodin 2022 alone supports the conclusion.

The 02-trot sheet cannot show a 2 cm difference by eye, so the evidence is the code and the measurements.

Caveats for the fix:
- A separate critic finding says the trot bounce is 180° out of phase (highest at mid-stance). The measurements agree: the withers peak at g=0.156, inside the LF+RH stance (samples 0-13), and bottom out at g=0.41, at lift-off. Raising the amplitude alone would make that inverted bounce more visible, so the two fixes should be done together.
- In Fix A, the pitch terms should be cut to about 0 (or re-phased so they do not oppose the translation). Merely "putting them in phase" would push the croup past the withers.

truth.reasoning:
Part of the claim holds. In a sound horse the hind foot does not touch the same-side forefoot as it lands. When it does, the farrier/lameness literature (Stashak, Adams' Lameness) calls it interference. If the hind toe hits the sole or shoe of the departing forefoot, that is forging. If the fore toe hits the coronet, pastern or cannon of the same-side hind leg, that is scalping or shin-hitting. All of these count as gait faults. The model does interpenetrate: in measurements.json the RF toe is 2.4 cm up at k=30 and 7.3 cm up at k=31 while the RH toe lands under and slightly ahead of it, and the 02-trot g=0/8 tile shows the two feet touching. A default sound Thoroughbred should not do this.

The "expected" description of real horses is overstated, though, and that changes which fix makes sense.

(1) "Within ~70 ms of toe-off the fore hoof is flexed up behind the knee" is not what real trotters do.
- The 70 ms comes from the model's own timing: duty 0.40 x T 0.72 s gives 72 ms of suspension.
- Retired Thoroughbred racehorses trotting under a rider at 2.7-3.9 m/s (Horan et al. 2023) spend 43-46% of each forelimb stride on the ground and take about 0.69 s per stride. That puts same-side hind landing only about 20-50 ms after the forefoot leaves the ground; it reaches about 75 ms only in the fastest, lowest-stance trials.
- Hoof sensors on 12 trotting horses (Gottleib et al. 2025) put the forefoot's early-swing peak height at only 12.9-15.9 cm, in a swing of about 360-385 ms.
- So when the real hind lands, the departing forefoot is only partly lifted: a few cm up to about 10 cm, not folded up behind the knee. Real clearance margins are a few cm. That is exactly why forging is so common in young, green, tired, long-toed or short-backed/long-legged horses.

(2) By that standard the model's forefoot is not slow to pick up. 59 ms after toe-off (k=0) its toe is already 14.4 cm up, the coffin joint 25 cm up, and the toe peaks at about 32 cm around k=3-4. That is already higher than real early-swing hoof heights. The collision comes from where the feet are, not from a slow forefoot:
- the hind lands about 12 cm ahead of the RF toe print (computed from the planted toe positions and 2.6 m/32 ground shift per sample);
- the fore and hind tracks are only 1 cm apart sideways (z 0.167 vs 0.176);
- the hoof shells are wider than the 3.3 cm closest approach.
So the "faster fore pick-up" fix (flick 0.1-0.25, earlier curl, toe >10 cm up within 15% of swing) would push the forelimb further from real hoof heights. Shortening fore stance would also cut stance below the measured 43-46%.

(3) "Into or behind the fore print" is incomplete. In Clayton 1994 the working trot is 3.61 m/s with a 2.73 m stride, and the stride lengthens from collected to extended trot through a growing overreach distance. A hind foot landing ahead of the fore print (overtracking, about 12 cm in the model) is normal at working and medium trot, not something to remove.

(4) Wording: the overlap described (fore pastern/hoof inside the hind cannon/pastern shell) is closer to scalping/shin-hitting than to forging in the strict sense. Both are interference faults.

(5) Widening the tracks a lot ("separate the tracks") is a Standardbred-trotter "passing gait" trait, not typical of Thoroughbreds. Real sideways hoof drift in swing is only about 3-6 cm (Gottleib et al. 2025, Table 4). A modest adjustment is acceptable; a large one is breed-atypical.

(6) Back et al. 1995 (Am J Vet Res) is about hoof landing impact and fetlock motion; it says nothing about forging or fore-hind clearance.

Severity: the clipping is small (1.3-1.6 cm deep, about 2 of 32 samples per half-stride, trot only). It is barely visible side-on, and real horses also clear by only a few cm. I'd rate it low rather than medium.
truth.correction: Correct claim: in a sound Thoroughbred at a working trot, the same-side hind foot lands at or just ahead of the fore print (overtracking is normal; Clayton 1994) without touching the departing forefoot. Contact is an interference fault: forging if the hind toe hits the fore sole/shoe, scalping or shin-hitting if the fore toe hits the hind pastern or cannon. It is not true that the forefoot is "flexed up behind the knee" within about 70 ms. Real fore toe-off comes only about 20-50 ms (up to about 75 ms at the fastest) before same-side hind contact: forelimb stance is 43-46% of a ~0.69 s stride at 2.7-3.9 m/s (Horan et al. 2023). At that moment the forefoot is only partly lifted; its early-swing peak is only about 13-16 cm (Gottleib et al. 2025), so real clearance is a few cm. The model's forefoot already rises faster and higher than that (toe 14 cm up 59 ms after toe-off, peak about 32 cm). The overlap therefore comes from where the feet are: the hind lands about 12 cm ahead of the fore print, the fore and hind tracks are only 1 cm apart sideways, and the hoof shells are wider than the 3.3 cm gap. Fixes should be geometric (slightly less overtrack, a small sideways offset of a few cm, or a local collision guard). A faster or higher fore pick-up, or shortening fore stance below about 43%, would make the motion less realistic. Severity is low rather than medium: about 1.5 cm of clipping over about 2 of 32 samples, trot only.

3. In-page mesh test. I served the page locally (read-only) as the Studio bay horse at the trot (stride 2.597 m). I skinned the merged mesh per bone and ran a ray-parity inside test plus a point-to-triangle depth on the RF/LF cannon, fetlock, pastern and hoof against the RH/LH cannon, fetlock, pastern, hoof and tibia, at 1/128-stride steps.
- The toe positions match measurements.json to the millimetre.
- Right side: contact from g=0.9375 to g=0.0, about 45 ms of every stride. At g=0.9297 the gap is 2.2 cm; at 0.9375 the meshes start to overlap. At 0.953-0.977 the RH hoof and pastern sit 2.5-3.8 cm deep inside the RF hoof (up to 43 vertices). At g=0.0 the RF hoof is still 1.8 cm inside the RH pastern. At 0.0078 there is 0.4 cm clearance.
- Left side: the same at g=0.4375-0.5, up to 93 vertices and 3.7 cm deep.
- Walk, canter, gallop and race have no contact at 64 phases on either side, as the critic said.
- Contact begins when the RF toe is only 1.6-2.4 cm off the ground and the RH toe is 3 cm up. So the landing hind toe runs into the toe and sole of the departing fore hoof, which is exactly forging (Stashak, Adams' Lameness: the hind toe strikes the sole of the ipsilateral forefoot during its breakover or early swing).
- A close-up render at g=31/32 shows the dark RF hoof embedded in the white-socked RH pastern. Tile 02-trot g=0/8 also shows the RF hoof on the RH dorsal wall.

- **Which parts collide.** The finding says the RF pastern/hoof sits inside the RH cannon/tibia shell, 1.3-1.6 cm deep. In this build (Studio bay, no racing plates) the overlap is hoof-into-hoof and hoof-into-pastern, about 2-3.8 cm deep. The RF parts never touch the RH cannon or tibia. truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the claim and could not overturn the core of it. The finding quotes the cited studies correctly, and other studies back it up. The walk half is fully right. The trot half is right in direction, but it overstates how much roll the model is missing and misstates the pattern.

**What the real-horse sources say (Europe PMC abstracts)**
- **Faber 2000, walk (PMID 10772104):** 5 Dutch Warmbloods on a treadmill at 1.6 m/s, markers on pins fixed into the bone.
  - Lateral bending and axial rotation each show 1 peak and 1 trough per stride.
  - Lateral bending reaches 5.6 deg in the cranial thorax and the pelvic region, and stays under 4 deg from T17 to L5.
  - Axial rotation rises from 4 deg at T6 to 13 deg at the tubera coxae.
- **Faber 2001, trot (PMID 11341399):** 4.0 m/s.
  - Flexion-extension and axial rotation show a "double sinusoidal pattern during 1 stride cycle". Lateral bending shows 1 peak and 1 trough.
  - Lateral bending range is 1.9-3.6 deg. Axial rotation range is 4.6-5.8 deg, except T10 (3.1 deg) and T13 (3.3 deg).

**Supporting studies (skin markers)**
- Hardeman 2020, trot on a straight line, sound horses: median pelvic roll range 8.5-9.7 deg, pelvic yaw 4.0-4.3 deg. Whole-back lateral bending is 6.5-7.5 deg. That angle is measured between two back segments, so it is real bending, not just the trunk turning.
- Egenvall 2023, walk on a 9 m circle: pelvic roll about 10 deg, pelvic yaw about 9 deg, thoracolumbar bending 15-16 deg. All three are largest at the walk.
- Egenvall also cites Goff 2010: skin-mounted sensors can double the measured pelvic roll at the trot. So Faber's bone-pin numbers are the conservative baseline, and they already exceed the model.

**The model data**
I checked measurements.json and index.html:1570-1626.
- Withers z minus croup z is at most 1 mm. The trunk shifts sideways as one block, 3.8 cm at the walk and 2.8 cm at the trot.
- The withers-croup line turns through only 0.118 deg.
- The roll implied by the line between the hip joints (0.35 m apart) has a range of 1.97 deg at the walk and 2.63 deg at the trot. It is a single cycle per stride.

**Walk: confirmed, and the gap is large**
- Faber's numbers are total ranges in the lab frame, so the swing each way is half: about ±6.5 deg at the pelvis against the model's ±1 deg.
- With tubera coxae about 0.5 m apart, the left-right height difference swings about ±5.7 cm. At the model's hip joints it would be about ±2 cm, against ±6 mm now. "Several cm" is correct.
- Real horses yaw and bend up to 5.6 deg; the model manages 0.12 deg.

**Trot: needs correction**
1. **The roll gap is overstated.** The model's spine roll range is 2.4 deg, which is close to Faber's mid-thorax values (3.1-3.3 deg at T10/T13). At the withers and pelvis the model is about 2x short (4.6-5.8 deg real), not an order of magnitude. Turning and bending (1.9-3.6 deg real against 0.12 deg) is the real gap.
2. **"Two-cycle sinusoid" must not be built as a plain sine at twice the stride frequency.** A sound, symmetric trot mirrors itself between the two diagonal pairs, so roll half a stride later must be the exact negative: roll(phase + 0.5) = -roll(phase). Faber's "double sinusoid" therefore means two humps per diagonal whose sign flips with the diagonal (a 1st-plus-3rd harmonic shape). A plain double-frequency roll would tilt the pelvis the same way on both diagonals, which reads as asymmetric or lame. The finding's fix option "two-cycle hips roll ±2.5 deg" should be restated accordingly.
3. **One statement is unsupported.** "Withers drift toward the planted fore and sacrum toward the planted hind" is not in either cited abstract. It is plausible, given the one-peak bending pattern, but I could not verify it.

**Caveats that do not refute the finding**
- The studies used Warmbloods on a treadmill (n=5), not Thoroughbreds. No source suggests Thoroughbreds lack this motion.
- Speeds are comparable: the model walks at 1.44 m/s and trots at 3.61 m/s.
- The fix option's direction, "stance hip up at hind mid-stance", fits basic mechanics and rider descriptions, but I did not verify it from a primary source.

**Severity:** medium is fair. Pelvic roll at the walk is a prominent feature of a real horse seen from behind, as in the paddock or post parade. The trot shortfall is moderate.

(1) The roll gap is about 2x, not dramatic: the real pelvis and withers range is 4.6-5.8 deg, T10/T13 3.1-3.3 deg, and the model's 2.4-2.6 deg is already near the mid-thoracic values. The main trot gap is turning and bending: 1.9-3.6 deg real (Faber 2001), 6.5-7.5 deg whole-back bending with skin markers (Hardeman 2020), against 0.12 deg in the model. |---|---|---|

**Literature (abstracts fetched from NCBI)**
- Faber 2000, walk (PMID 10772104): lateral bending up to 5.6° and axial rotation rising from 4° at T6 to 13° at the tubera coxae, both one peak and one trough per stride.
- Faber 2001, trot (PMID 11341399): lateral bending 1.9-3.6° with one peak and one trough; axial rotation 4.6-5.8° (3.1-3.3° at T10/T13) as a "double sinusoidal pattern".
- These are ranges of motion (peak to trough). Compare like with like:
  - Walk pelvis: the model rolls about 2° peak to peak against 13°.
  - Walk T6: about 2° against 4°.
  - Trot: about 2.4-2.6° against 4.6-5.8°.
  - Lateral bending: about 0.1° against 1.9-5.6°.

1. At the walk, Faber reports one cycle of axial rotation per stride. So the model's single-cycle walk roll has the right frequency; only its size is wrong, and it is about the same at the chest and the pelvis instead of growing toward the pelvis.

truth.reasoning:
The code observation is accurate. GAITS.trot (index.html:222-223) sets land LF 0 = RH 0 and RF 0.5 = LH 0.5, with one duty of 0.4 for all four legs. measurements.json gaits.trot.meta matches this: T 0.72 s, 2.6 m stride, 3.61 m/s. So the diagonal partners land and lift together.

The real-horse part of the claim is overstated:
1. The 29.8 ± 7.6 ms figure is real, but it comes from a narrow group. Holmström, Fredricson & Drevemo 1994 (EVJ 26:235-240, PMID 8542845) measured 4 approved Swedish Warmblood stallions with trot gait scores of 8.67/10 or higher. Their mean stride was 794 ms, so 29.8 ms is about 3.75% of the stride, not 4%. The same group found that hind-first contact goes with higher judged gait quality, which makes it a mark of an elite mover, not a rule for all horses.
2. At a working-trot speed close to the model's, normal horses split roughly into thirds. Hobbs, Bertram & Clayton 2016 (PeerJ 4:e2190) tested 17 mixed-breed horses at 3.3 m/s ± 10%. Of 34 diagonals, 12 landed hind-first, 11 synchronous and 11 fore-first; categories were classified per diagonal, and Table 1 gives HF-HF 4, HF-S 4, S-S 2, FF-S 3, FF-FF 4. Hind-first landings became more frequent and longer as speed rose.
3. Weishaupt et al. 2010 (EVJ Suppl 42:530-537) tested 38 Warmbloods on a treadmill at 2.5-5.8 m/s. At a slow trot the forelimbs landed first, and the horses only tended toward hind-first landing as speed increased.
4. Weishaupt et al. 2009 (EVJ, passage study) found that Grand Prix horses landed the diagonal pair "almost simultaneously" at trot. The hind always landed first only in passage, where Clayton & Hobbs 2019 report a mean of about 30 ms (3% of the stride).
5. Clayton & Hobbs 2019 (Animals 9:763 review) confirm that fore-first, synchronous and hind-first landings all occur at about 3.3 m/s.

So a synchronous landing at 3.6 m/s is within normal variation. It is not an anatomical error, and a 30 ms hind lead is the high end, typical of elite Warmbloods and passage. I found no Thoroughbred-specific data on this landing offset. Thoroughbreds are not bred for trot quality, so nothing suggests they lead with the hind more than mixed breeds do.

The second half of the claim holds up better. Clayton & Hobbs 2019 say lift-off is "almost always hind-first", and Weishaupt 2010 found the forelimbs lift after the hindlimbs. So "the fore stays down slightly longer" is well supported, and it is the more consistent real-horse feature.

Fix option 1 (RH 0.97, LH 0.47 with a shared duty) gives about 21.6 ms (3%) of hind-first landing and also hind-first lift-off. That is a reasonable, realistic choice, and arguably better than 30 ms. The effect is about one or two frames at 60 fps, so severity stays low.
truth.correction:
The code observation is correct, but real horses do not reliably land the hind first at a working trot. At about 3.3-3.6 m/s, horses land hind-first, synchronous and fore-first in roughly equal shares (Hobbs et al. 2016: 12/11/11 of 34 diagonals). At slow trot the fore often lands first, and hind-first landing grows with speed (Weishaupt 2010). The +29.8 ± 7.6 ms value (3.75% of a 794 ms stride, not 4%) comes from 4 elite, high-scoring Swedish Warmblood stallions and is a marker of gait quality, similar to passage's ~30 ms. So a synchronous landing is within normal variation.

What is consistent in real horses is hind-first lift-off: the fore stays down slightly longer (Clayton & Hobbs 2019; Weishaupt 2010). If this is changed, use a small hind-first offset of about 0.01-0.03 of the stride (7-22 ms), with the hind also lifting off first. Option 1 (RH 0.97 / LH 0.47) does both. It could also be a per-horse running-style parameter, since the offset varies between individuals. Treat it as optional polish, not a correction of an error.

I tried to refute this and could not. The problem shows up in the code and in the measurements; the sheet does not contradict it.

Code: in index.html at lines 221-223, GAITS.trot has land { LF: 0.0, RH: 0.0, RF: 0.5, LH: 0.5 } and one duty of 0.4. makeGait (267-274) copies land unchanged, because trot has no leads flag, and builds one shared stanceLen from stride * duty. footPath (1376-1385) uses u = wrap01(g - G.land[L.id]) with the single G.duty and G.stanceLen for every limb. So diagonal partners share the same touchdown phase, lift-off phase and stance length. tuneGait (256-263) scales duty for all four limbs at once and never touches land, so no horse's running style (look.run) breaks the symmetry. I searched the .html and .js files for 'dap', 'diagonal' and 'advanced placement'; no per-limb offset or advanced-placement setting exists.

Measurements: I ran node on the 32 trot samples in measurements.json, counting a hoof as planted when its toe is below 0.01 m.
- LF and RH are planted on exactly the same frames, k=0..13 (14 of 32). RF and LH are planted on k=16..29.
- Diagonal partners have the same toe and coffin heights to the millimetre in every stance frame: toe 0.002 m, coffin 0.092 rising to 0.116 m.
- At lift-off (k=14) the toes are at 0.024 and 0.021 m. Just before touchdown (k=31) they are at 0.012 and 0.010 m. Both partners leave and reach the ground on the same frame.
So the model has zero diagonal advanced placement at both touchdown and lift-off.

Sheet: the 02-trot tiles (g=0/8..7/8) show the diagonal pairs moving together. Sampling every 1/8 of a stride (90 ms) is too coarse to show a 30 ms offset either way, so the sheet neither confirms nor clears it.

Real horses: a positive diagonal advanced placement (hind hoof first) is the usual finding at trot. Holmstroem, Fredricson and Drevemo 1994 (Equine Vet J 26:235-240) reported it in Swedish Warmbloods and linked it to good gait quality. Clayton 1997 found it grows with collection. Hobbs, Bertram and Clayton 2016 (PeerJ 4:e2190) found mostly positive values of a few to tens of ms. Forelimb stance is also usually slightly longer than hind stance, so the hind tends to lift off first too. I could not re-check the exact 29.8 +/- 7.6 ms figure because the web search limit was used up; the size and direction match the literature as I know it.

Severity stays low. 30 ms is about 2 frames at 60 fps and about 4% of the 0.72 s stride, so it is a subtle refinement and not a visible fault.

On fix option 1: RH 0.97 and LH 0.47 gives 0.03 x 0.72 s = 22 ms. Because duty is shared, the hind would also lift 22 ms earlier. That matches real horses, where the hind lifts off before the fore, so the one-line fix is accurate.

On fix option 2: the risk is right. footPath, the hoof-print code at line 3007 and the dust code at 3085 all read the global G.duty / G.stanceLen and land.
