truth.reasoning:
The main real-horse claim holds up. If anything, it understates the problem. Two details are wrong: the forearm description and the hind-limb baseline.

What the model does, from measurements.json, trot, LF over 32 phases. The speed is 3.61 m/s. That is exactly the working-trot speed Clayton 1994 measured (EVJ 26:230: working trot 3.61 m/s, stride 2.73 m), so comparing against working-trot data is fair.
- Fore hoof peak: toe 0.322 m, coffin/coronet level 0.427 m, fetlock 0.429 m. The fetlock rests at 0.21 m standing. The swing target is `fy = fy0 + lift`, so the 0.22 lift pushes it to about 0.43 m.
- Hind hoof peak: toe 0.187 m, coffin 0.299 m.
- Carpus: smallest interior angle 93° (87° of flexion), at k=19-21.
- Forearm: largest angle 48.3° from vertical, at k=24 (g≈0.75), when the carpus has already reopened to 124°.

Published hoof heights at a level trot:
- Brown et al. 2015 (EVJ 47:107-112), 8 horses: fore 13.8 ± 3.8 cm, hind 10.8 ± 2.4 cm.
- Gottleib et al. 2025 (Animals 15:2376), 9 Quarter Horses and 3 Thoroughbreds, IMU about 1 cm below the coronet: early-swing fore arc height 12.9-15.9 cm across shoeing and surface conditions.
- Against these, the model's fore toe is about 2.3x the mean (+4.7 SD) and its coronet about 3x. That is not normal variation.
- Brown's horses only reached 30.9 ± 4.9 cm with 11-cm poles in their path and 41.0 ± 3.9 cm with 20-cm poles. The model's default trot therefore lifts the hooves the way a horse trotting over cavaletti does.
- Cano et al. 2001 (Res Vet Sci 71:147) found Andalusians flex the forelimb more than Arabians and Anglo-Arabs, and Anglo-Arabs have a smaller protraction-retraction range. This supports "TB-type = lower action". The "daisy-cutter" ideal for hunter-type Thoroughbreds is a standard conformation and judging description.

What needs correcting:
1. **Forearm and Hackney comparison.** A 48° forearm is not "close to horizontal". In tiles g=1/8 and 5/8 the swinging forearm is only about 30° from vertical. The near-horizontal segment in those tiles is the cannon, folded back about 57° from vertical, with the fetlock about 0.43 m up near knee height. The showy look comes from the raised fetlock and hoof, not from forearm elevation. The Hackney/Saddlebred forearm trait (forearm at or above horizontal) is the wrong comparison. I found no Thoroughbred working-trot forearm value to say whether 48° itself is too high; it does not look like the main fault.
2. **The 15-20 cm figure.** It is somewhat generous. Measured hoof-wall or coronet markers peak at about 10-18 cm, mean about 14 cm. The toe, the hoof's lowest point when it is folded back, sits lower still. The proposed fix target (toe peak 0.18-0.22 m) is therefore still about 1.3-1.6x real.
3. **The hind is too high as well.** The finding treats the hind's 0.19 m toe as the normal baseline. The real hind peak is about 10.8 cm, and the model's hind coronet is about 3x that. The real fore/hind ratio is about 1.3 (13.8/10.8), not 1.7. So the hind lift of 0.18 also needs lowering, not only the fore.
4. **Carpal flexion.** About 85-90° of flexion may be upper-range but plausible. I could not confirm an exact Thoroughbred value. In the model, lift and flexion are coupled: the IK has to fold the carpus to reach a fetlock target near knee height. So the excess cannot be blamed only on the lift parameter. The two have to be reduced together.
5. **Citation.** Back et al. 1995 (AJVR 56:1522-1528) compares impact kinematics of the distal fore and hind limbs. It reports no hoof-flight heights, so it does not support the 15-20 cm figure. Brown 2015 and Gottleib 2025 do.

Severity: I raise it to medium. Fore and hind hoof heights are 2-3x the published means at the matching speed, and the fault shows in every trot frame. It is not a matter of style.
truth.correction:
The real-horse claim is mostly right, with these corrections:
- **Hoof height:** at a 3.6 m/s working trot, hoof-wall/coronet markers peak at about 14 cm on the fore (13.8 ± 3.8; 12.9-15.9) and about 11 cm on the hind (10.8 ± 2.4). The toe sits lower still. "15-20 cm" is slightly high.
- **Hind limb:** the model's hind (toe 0.19 m, coronet 0.30 m) is also about 2-3x real, so the hind lift needs lowering too. The real fore/hind ratio is about 1.3.
- **Forearm:** the model's forearm peaks at 48°, not near-horizontal. In g=1/8 and 5/8 it is about 30°. The segment near horizontal there is the folded cannon, with the fetlock raised to about 0.43 m. The Hackney comparison therefore does not apply; the excess is hoof and fetlock height.
- **Fix:** lower fore lift and flex together (the IK couples them), aiming at a fore coronet peak of about 0.18-0.22 m and toe about 0.12-0.15 m. Lower the hind lift to about 0.08-0.10.
- **Citations:** replace Back 1995 AJVR with Brown et al. 2015 and Gottleib et al. 2025.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the claim about real horses and could not. Both sources say what the finding says they do, and the model data match the "observed" description.

1. Rhodin et al. 2022, Animals 12(21):3053 (PMC9657284), "Timing of Vertical Head, Withers and Pelvis Movements Relative to the Footfalls in Different Equine Gaits and Breeds". It used IMUs on the poll, withers and sacrum of 68 horses: 19 Warmbloods, 23 Iberians and 26 Icelandics. At walk, as a percentage of forelimb stance:
   - Head minimum: 48% (Iberian), 47% (Warmblood), 46% (Icelandic).
   - Head maximum: 88%, 87%, 86%.
   - Withers minimum: 5.3%, 13%, 4.6%.
   - Withers maximum: 42%, 44%, 48%.
   - Text: "For walk, the maxima and minima of the head and sacrum were in phase, while the withers were around 25% out of phase compared with both head and sacrum."
   - Check with their forelimb duty factor of about 0.65: (47 - 9)% of stance x 0.65 is about 25% of the stride. Walk has two vertical oscillations per stride, so 25% of a stride means the head and withers move in opposite directions.

2. Loscher et al. 2016, Proc R Soc B 283:20161908 (PMC5136594). Markers were on the occiput and withers of 8 warmblood horses. Findings:
   - Head and withers: "phase shift of 25.0 ± 2.5% (mean ± 1 s.d.) of the stride cycle duration". Their model's energy-optimal value was 25.25%.
   - "being out-of-phase with the thorax, the head reached its highest position ... during the double support phase". Double support here means both forelimbs on the ground.
   - Amplitudes: head 9.1 ± 3.4 cm, withers 3.2 ± 1.0 cm. The model's 116 mm and 34 mm fit these, so "amplitudes are right" also holds.
   - Loscher argues for an energy-saving mechanism that appears in 19 mammal species. Together with Rhodin's agreement across three very different breeds, including a gaited one, this answers the objection that neither study includes Thoroughbreds. The pattern is not breed-specific and does not fall within normal variation; the model's head is about half an oscillation off.

3. Model check (my own node script on measurements.json for the walk):
   - LF lands at g=0.25 and RF at g=0.75, with duty 0.6.
   - The poll is lowest at g=0.31 and 0.81, which is 10% into fore stance and during fore double support. It is highest at g=0.06 and 0.56, about 52% into fore stance.
   - The withers peak and trough on exactly the same samples, so head and withers move in phase.
   - Rhodin's numbers put the head minimum at about g=0.03 and 0.53, and the maximum at about g=0.27 and 0.77, which is during fore double support. That target is also in phase with the croup, as Rhodin reports. The model is roughly inverted from this target.
   - The model's withers timing (lowest at about 10% of fore stance, highest at about 52%) is close to the real data, so only the head is wrong.
   - The code comment "head nods down each time a forefoot takes the weight / lowest just after each fore touchdown" (index.html:1627-1628) is wrong for real horses. A real horse's head is lowest at mid-stance of a forelimb, during single support. It is highest while both forefeet are down.

4. Minor caveats. These do not change the verdict.
   - Fix option 1 calls "+0.45" a stride fraction. But cyc(g,k,phase) = cos(TAU*(k*g - phase)) (index.html:389), so with k=2 the phase is counted in half-strides. +0.45 therefore shifts the nod by about 0.225 of a stride, which is the right target; only the label is wrong.
   - The poll's height adds the in-phase trunk bob to the neck nod. After the shift, the neck amplitude must be large enough that the poll's net motion really ends up opposite the withers. Fix option 1 already says this.
   - The aside "head pitch in phase with head height (already done)" is not covered by either paper. I did not verify it.

Severity stays medium. The walk head nod is the most visible cue at a walk, and here its timing is about half an oscillation wrong. It does not affect the racing gaits.

2. Measurements (node script, fitting the twice-per-stride component of 32 walk samples). The fore stance runs from 0.25 to 0.85, so LF lands at 0.25 and duty is 0.6.
- **Poll:** amplitude 58 mm (range 1.721-1.837 m, 116 mm, as the finding says). It is highest at g = 0.055 and lowest at sample 10 (g = 0.3125).
- **Withers:** amplitude 17 mm (range 34 mm). It is highest at g = 0.061 and lowest at the same sample 10.
- **Poll vs withers phase:** they are 0.006 of a stride apart, so they move together.
- **Poll as % of fore stance:** highest at about 51%, which is fore single support and hind double support. Lowest at about 9%, which is fore double support (LF lands at 0.25, RF lifts at 0.35).
- **Withers as % of fore stance:** highest at about 51%, lowest at about 10%.
- **Head pitch:** varies by 11.1° (126.4-137.5°), in phase with poll height.
All of the finding's observed numbers check out.

3. Real horses.
- **Rhodin et al. 2022 (Animals 12:3053; I fetched it), walk, as % of fore stance:**
  - Head lowest at 46-48% (±5) and highest at 86-88%.
  - Withers lowest at 4.6-13% and highest at 42-48%.
  - The paper says the withers were "around 25% out of phase" with the head.
- **Loscher et al. 2016 (Proc R Soc B 283:20161908; I fetched it):**
  - Horses: head and withers have "a distinct phase shift of 25.0 ± 2.5% of the stride cycle". Their model's optimum was 25.25%.
  - The head is highest "during the double support phase" of the forelegs.
- Since the head bobs twice per stride, a 25% stride shift means the head and withers move in opposite directions.

Compared with this:
- The model's withers timing is correct (10% and 51% vs 4.6-13% and 42-48%).
- The model's head is close to inverted. It is lowest at about 9% of fore stance where a real head is lowest at about 47%, and highest at about 51% where a real head is highest at about 87%. That puts it 0.21-0.24 of a stride off, roughly half a nod out of phase.

4. Shots. On 01-walk, tiles g=2/8 and g=6/8 (fore touchdowns) show the lowest head carriage and g=0/8 and g=4/8 the highest, in step with the withers.

Small points that don't change the verdict:
- In fix option 1, the "+0.45" shift is in cyc's own units, where one unit is half a stride. It is really about +0.225 of a stride. Its targets are still right: φ 0.1→0.55 puts the poll's highest point at g ≈ 0.275 (real: about 0.27).
- It correctly notes that neck1's amplitude must grow. Today the in-phase trunk bob adds about 17 mm to the poll's 58 mm amplitude, so flipping only the neck phase would cut the nod to roughly 25 mm.

Medium severity stands. The walk is the main gait in the paddock parade, and a head nod that runs in time with the withers instead of against them is a classic tell to anyone who knows horses.

truth.reasoning:
I could not refute the claim about real horses. The evidence shows the real effect is larger than the finding says, so it is wrong in the "understated" direction. The corrections are about magnitude and sources.

What I checked in the model (measurements.json, walk, 32 phases):
- The withers move 34 mm (1.593-1.627 m) and the croup moves 6 mm (1.587-1.593 m).
- Each hip joint moves 11 mm. The pitch of the withers-to-croup line changes by 1.86 deg.
- The model's small croup motion is also out of phase. The croup is highest at g≈0-0.03 and 0.44-0.53, which is at or just after hind touchdown (LH at 0, RH at 0.5). It is lowest at g≈0.19-0.25. Real horses do roughly the opposite (see below).
- The tail head does rise 17 mm, peaking at g≈0.31, so a small hind vault exists behind the croup. The croup landmark sits almost on the pitch pivot and barely moves.
- index.html:1622-1626 matches the description: a 12 mm spine translation is cancelled behind by spine.rotation.z of 0.8 deg and hips.rotation.z of 1.2 deg.

What real horses do:
1. **Timing is confirmed.** Rhodin et al. 2022 (Animals 12:3053) used IMUs on 65 horses (Warmblood, Iberian, Icelandic), with the pelvis sensor between the tubera sacrale.
   - At walk the pelvis peaks at 51-57% of hind stance, i.e. hind mid-stance. That is g≈0.31-0.34 and 0.81-0.84 in this model.
   - The pelvis is lowest at 8-11% of hind stance, during two-hind-leg support.
   - The withers peak at 42-48% of fore stance and are lowest at 4-13%.
   - The withers and pelvis maxima are 26-30% of a stride apart.
   - The walk is the one gait where the pelvis peaks at mid-stance; in the other gaits it peaks near hoof-off. So "each end vaults over its stance pair, twice per stride, a quarter stride apart" holds for horses.
2. **Amplitude is understated.** The croup is not just "comparable" to the withers; it moves about 2x as much. Vertical range at walk in hand:

   | Breed | Withers | Pelvis |
   |---|---|---|
   | Warmblood (165 cm) | 33 mm | 79 mm |
   | Iberian | 27 mm | 68 mm |
   | Icelandic | 36 mm | 66 mm |

   - Buchner et al. 1996 (Dutch Warmbloods, treadmill walk at 1.6 m/s) found tuber sacrale amplitude of 5.7 cm in sound horses, as reported in the 2026 Icelandic-lameness paper, PMC12699130.
   - Icelandic ridden/in-hand data in that paper: withers 25-43 mm, pelvis 62-63 mm.
   - The model's withers value (34 mm) is realistic. Its croup value (6 mm) is about 10x too small.
3. **Back flexion is confirmed, with a caveat.** Faber et al. 2000 (AJVR 61:399-406) measured about 7 deg of flexion-extension for vertebrae caudal to T10, with two flexion/extension cycles per stride. That was 5 Warmbloods on a treadmill at 1.6 m/s with bone-fixed markers.
   - Those are angles at individual vertebrae, not a single whole-back angle, so the model's 1.3 deg is not a strict like-for-like comparison.
   - The direction still holds. With the real amplitudes and phase offset, the withers-to-sacrum line would pitch several degrees, not 1.9 deg.
4. **One source is misapplied.** Griffin, Main and Farley 2004 studied dogs, not horses. Horses fit the two-pendulum model better than dogs: their fore-hind lateral lag is 23-27% of the stride (Rhodin 2022 Table 1), while dogs' is 15%.
5. **Breed coverage.** No Thoroughbred-specific walk data were found. Warmbloods are a reasonable stand-in at a similar size (165 cm vs 163 cm), stride time (1.1-1.3 s) and in-hand speed.

Severity: medium is fine. The 10x amplitude shortfall plus the reversed timing could justify high, but this is the slow gait.
truth.correction:
The claim holds, but the expected behaviour should be corrected in three ways.

- **Amplitude.** Real tuber sacrale vertical motion at walk is about 1.5-2.5x the withers, not merely "comparable": 57-79 mm vs withers 25-43 mm (Buchner 1996; Rhodin 2022).
  - A realistic target for this 163 cm horse is about ±28-38 mm (a 55-75 mm range) at the croup, keeping the withers at about 34 mm.
  - The proposed ±10-15 mm hind vault is too small.
- **Timing.** The croup should peak at hind mid-stance (g≈0.31-0.34 and 0.81-0.84 here) and be lowest just after hind touchdown, during two-hind-leg support (g≈0.05 and 0.55).
  - Its highest point should be 26-30% of a stride from the withers' highest point, i.e. in antiphase at the twice-per-stride frequency.
  - The model's current tiny croup motion is roughly reversed: it is highest near hind touchdown.
- **References.**
  - Use Rhodin et al. 2022 for horses' timing and amplitude. Griffin 2004 is a dog study and supports the two-pendulum concept only.
  - Buchner 1996 supplies the 5.7 cm tuber sacrale figure.
  - Faber 2000's ~7 deg is flexion-extension at individual vertebrae, not the angle of the whole back line.

model.reasoning:
I could not refute this one. The code and the measurements both show it.

**Code (index.html:1622-1625).** The walk body motion has three terms that act on the croup:
- `spine.position.y` moves 12 mm either way, twice per stride, peaking at g=0.05.
- `spine.rotation.z` pitches 0.8 deg about x=0, peaking at g=0.10. At the croup (x=-0.525) that is -0.525*sin(0.8 deg) = 7.3 mm, in the opposite direction.
- `hips.rotation.z` pitches 1.2 deg about the hips bone at x=-0.3 (line 702), peaking at g=0.025. At the croup that is -0.225*sin(1.2 deg) = 4.7 mm, also opposite.

Adding these as phasors (2 per stride) gives a croup amplitude of 3.3 mm peaking at g=0.467. A Fourier fit of the measured croup gives 3.0 mm peaking at g=0.469. The croup sits almost exactly on the pitch node, so its rise and fall cancels out. Nothing else feeds it: `applyRun` (line 1717) only adds a constant `bodyLow` offset.

**Measurements (walk, 32 samples, node).**

| Landmark | Vertical range | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Withers | 34 mm (1.593-1.627) | twice per stride, peak g=0.063/0.563 |
| Croup | 6 mm (1.587-1.593) | low 2nd harmonic, peaks g~0.47/0.97 |
| Each hip joint | 11 mm | k1 3.1 mm, mostly side-to-side roll |
| Mean of both hip joints | 7 mm | — |
| Tail head | 17 mm | peaks g~0.33 |
| Point of buttock | 18 mm | peaks g~0.33 |
| Withers-croup line pitch | 1.86 deg | — |

The withers peak lands at 52% of left-fore stance and the low at 10%. Both match real horses, so the forehand is right.

**Real horses.** Rhodin et al. 2022 (Animals 12:3053, PMC9657284) measured upper-body vertical range of motion at walk in hand:
- Withers: 27-36 mm (Warmblood 33.4 mm), which the model matches.
- Pelvis (sacrum): 66-79 mm (Warmblood 78.8 mm). That is more than twice the withers, not just "comparable". The model's croup has about 8% of the real range. Even the best rear landmark, the tail head at 17 mm, has about a quarter.
- Pelvis timing: highest at 51-57% of hind stance, lowest at 8-11%. Withers-to-pelvis maxima are 26-30% of a stride apart.

With this model's footfalls (left hind lands at 0, duty 0.6), the pelvis should peak at g~0.31-0.34 and 0.81-0.84 and be lowest at g~0.05-0.07 and 0.55-0.57. The model's croup instead peaks near hind touchdown (g~0.47/0.97), close to where a real pelvis is lowest. Only the rearmost points (tail head, buttock) rise in the right phase, and only by about 8 mm either way, from the trunk tipping.

**Partly inaccurate details in the finding (the conclusion still stands):**
- Buchner 1996 did include walk (1.6 m/s, tuber sacrale tracked), but its abstract gives no amplitudes. Rhodin 2022 is the better numeric source.
- Griffin 2004 studied dogs, not horses. Its two-pendulum model still applies: the fore and hind ends cancel each other when the fore limb lags the hind by 25% of the stride, which is horse walk timing (lateral dissociation about 25% in Rhodin 2022).
- Faber 2000's ~7 deg is the flexion-extension range of single vertebrae (T10 and further back), not the angle of the withers-croup line. The model's 1.3-1.9 deg is therefore not directly comparable, though it does point the same way.
- The 11 mm per hip joint is mostly roll; the mean of the two hips moves 7 mm.
- The proposed fix of 10-15 mm either way at the croup (20-30 mm range) would still fall short of the real 66-79 mm. Something closer to 25-35 mm either way, peaking at g~0.32/0.82, is needed for the hindquarters to visibly rise over the hind legs.

The problem is not visible in the low-resolution tiles of 01-walk.jpeg, but the numbers above show it clearly. Medium severity stands: the walk reads as a nod at the front only, without the fore-and-aft rocking of the trunk.

Only the tail head and buttock (17-18 mm) peak at the right time (g~0.33). Buchner 1996 measured walk but its abstract gives no numbers. Griffin 2004 studied dogs. Faber's 7 deg is the bending range of single vertebrae, not the angle of the withers-croup line. truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse claim and could not.

What the model does. I recomputed this from measurements.json. Walk support works out as: LH+RF diagonal pair at g 0.10-0.25, left lateral pair (LH+LF) at 0.35-0.50, LF+RH diagonal pair at 0.60-0.75, right lateral pair at 0.85-1.00, with three legs down between these. The withers and croup sit at +19 mm (right) for g 0.34-0.38 and are still at +15 mm at g 0.47. So the model's furthest-right point falls inside left-only support, and its furthest-left point (g ~0.86) falls inside right-only support. The finding describes this correctly. The withers ride about 7 mm further out than the spine because the 1 deg roll tilts the back right at g 0.40.

What a real horse does. The trunk's centre of mass (COM) must follow the centre of pressure, the load-weighted average position of the planted hooves. I modelled this as an inverted pendulum in the front-to-back view: z'' = (g/h)(z - COP), with h about 1.05 m and T 1.1 s. I used the model's own timing, hooves 9 cm either side of the midline, and forelimbs taking about 57% of the load; half-sine and M-shaped load curves gave the same answer. The steady periodic solution puts the COM at its furthest left at g = 0.44, about 20 mm out, and furthest right at 0.94. The forcing is one cycle per stride, and the COM swings in phase with the centre of pressure but with a smaller amplitude. This matches the human frontal-plane result: the body swings toward the stance foot while the force from the ground pushes it back toward the middle (MacKinnon and Winter 1993).

The physics behind it does not depend on breed or style. During lateral-pair support the COM is always on the unsupported side of the line joining the two planted hooves. So it must be accelerating away from those legs, which means it is displaced toward them, exactly as the finding states. Faber et al. 2000 confirm that lateral bending and axial rotation of the walking horse's spine each run one cycle per stride. The model's amplitude (±12 mm at the spine, ±19 mm at the withers) is realistic; only the timing is wrong, by about 0.41 of a cycle (~150 deg).

Corrections and caveats for whoever fixes it:
1. Simply negating the term puts the furthest-left point at g 0.35, the very start of left support. -0.012*sin(TAU*(g-0.19)) puts it at 0.44, matching the estimate. Strictly, the withers should follow the forelimb pair (furthest left around g 0.55) and the croup the hind pair (around 0.30). A rigid sideways shift is a fine approximation.
2. Do NOT negate rotation.x without checking. The model's roll tilts the back toward the unsupported, swinging side while the right legs are in the air. That fits riders' common account that the back/hip drops on the side whose hind leg is swinging, and the stance-side tuber coxae (the point of the hip) riding higher. I could not confirm the roll direction in a primary source (web search was unavailable). Dunbar et al. 2008 also report that trunk roll is visually minimal in walking horses, so it matters little either way.
3. Griffin et al. 2004 deals with front-to-back and vertical pendulum mechanics. It is weak support for a side-to-side claim; Faber 2000 and the frontal-plane inverted-pendulum literature are the better citations.

Severity: low rather than medium. The error is about 2 cm, shows only in the front and rear views (barely visible in the 01-walk front/rear tiles), and the fix is a one-line phase change.

model.reasoning:
I could not refute the main claim. The code and the measurements both show it.

Code (index.html:1621-1624, BODY.walk): spine.position.z = 0.012*sin(TAU*(g-0.1)), which is most to the right (+Z) at g=0.35 and most to the left at g=0.85. The footfalls (index.html:238, land LH 0 / LF .25 / RH .5 / RF .75, duty 0.6) put only LH+LF on the ground at g=0.35-0.50 and only RH+RF at g=0.85-1.0. Walk has no `leads` flag, so nothing mirrors this. applyRun (index.html:1709-1720) does not touch position.z, and phaseOffset is not used in the walk spine terms. The comment on line 1621 says the trunk 'sways over whichever side is bearing weight', so the code does the opposite of what its own author intended.

Measurements (node, walk, 32 samples): withers and croup z reach +18 to +19 mm at g=0.313-0.406. The planted toes then are LH+LF+RF, then LH+LF only (mean planted-toe z -0.172 m, the left side). The mirror image is -19 mm at g=0.844-0.906 with RH+RF planted. The spine bone itself swings +/-12 mm, and the girth +/-6 mm because the 1 deg roll pulls the lower trunk the other way. So the trunk is displaced to the right while only the left legs carry it.

Physics check: I used the planted toe positions with an inverted-pendulum lateral force on each stance leg (load split 58% fore / 42% hind, COM height 1.05 m) and solved for the periodic lateral COM motion. The COM comes out leftmost at g=0.44, during left lateral support, and rightmost at g=0.94. The model's trunk is rightmost at 0.34-0.38, so it is close to antiphase (about 0.4-0.45 of a cycle off). The reason is that two left feet can only push the body to the right (medially), so the COM has to be at its leftmost point, toward the supporting legs, in that phase. Human gait works the same way: the COM shifts toward the stance limb. The amplitude (+/-19 mm) is not in dispute.

Where the finding is wrong or overstated:
1. The roll term should not be flipped. rotation.x = +1 deg*sin(TAU*(g-0.15)) peaks at g=0.4. In three.js a positive rotation.x drops the +Z (right) side, so the right side is down while the right legs are both in swing (RH swings 0.1-0.5, RF swings 0.35-0.75). That is the normal swing-side pelvic drop: the human pelvic-obliquity analogue, and the riding rule that the hip drops on the side of the hind leg that is swinging forward. It is also how a trunk carried only on its left feet would sag. Faber et al. 2000 measured pelvic axial rotation at walk with one peak and one trough per stride and a range of up to about 13 deg at the tuber coxae (4 deg at T6). If anything the model's roll range of +/-1 deg is too small, not the wrong sign. Fix option 1 ('negate both sway terms, including rotation.x') would therefore swap one error for another. Only the position.z term should change.
2. The cited visual evidence does not show the problem. The 01-walk front and rear tiles are taken at g=0, 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4, where the sway is in mid-transition (+/-13-14 mm, about 0.8% of withers height), and the effect cannot be seen at that resolution. The peak phases (3/8 and 7/8) are not among the front or rear tiles.
3. Severity: the error is a phase error on a +/-12 mm translation (+/-19 mm at the withers) at a 1.1 s stride. It is barely visible except in head-on or tail-on views, and the fix is a one-character change. Low fits better than medium.

Note for the fix: if position.z is negated and the roll is kept, the withers' lateral path shrinks to about +/-6 mm (the -12 mm translation partly cancels the +7 mm roll at the withers, which sit 0.4 m above the pivot), while the belly's path grows. A real horse rolls the thorax less than the pelvis (Faber: 4 deg vs 13 deg), so if the withers sway looks too small, apply the roll mainly at the hips rather than to the whole spine.
model.correction: The lateral translation is confirmed to be roughly in antiphase. spine.position.z puts the withers and croup about 19 mm to the right while only LH+LF are planted (g 0.34-0.47) and about 19 mm to the left during RH+RF support. An inverted-pendulum estimate from the planted toes puts the COM leftmost at g≈0.44 and rightmost at g≈0.94. The fix is to negate only the position.z term, e.g. z = -0.012*sin(TAU*(g-0.1)), or -0.012*sin(TAU*(g-0.19)) to put the left extreme at about 0.44. The roll term spine.rotation.x is not wrong: at g≈0.4 the right side is down while both right legs are swinging, which is the normal drop of the swing-side hip. Keep its sign, and consider enlarging it at the pelvis (Faber 2000: up to 13 deg of axial rotation at the tuber coxae). The cited 01-walk front and rear tiles (g=0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4) catch the sway mid-transition, about 13 mm, and do not visibly show it. Severity is low rather than medium.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the model numbers against measurements.json and they hold. In walk ground coordinates the LH toe lands at -0.036, the LF at 1.580 and the next LH at 1.549, so the hind lands 3.1 cm behind the fore toe. The right side gives the same result: RH 0.756 against RF 0.788, 3.2 cm behind. The GAITS comment at index.html:235 ("the hind print lands just past the fore print") is wrong for the current numbers.

The real-horse framing is overstated in three ways.

(1) Clayton 1995 is cited correctly (PubMed 7574149 abstract): six elite dressage horses. Collected walk: 1.37 m/s, 157 cm stride, 1,159 ms. Medium walk: 1.73 m/s. Extended walk: 1.82 m/s, 193 cm, 1,064 ms. The longer stride came from more over-tracking, with no change in lateral placement distance. But the same paper shows the model's walk is a real horse's walk. Its 1.44 m/s, 1.585 m and 1.1 s are each within about 5% of Clayton's collected walk. Treadmill studies also use 1.35-2.05 m/s as the normal walk range (Gmel et al. 2022, 2024). So this is a slow, collected-speed walk, not an anatomical error. In such a walk, hind feet landing in or just behind the fore prints is normal. Over-tracking distance rises roughly one-to-one with stride as the walk lengthens (Clayton 1995; Gmel 2024: over-tracking increases with speed in both breeds).

(2) "Does not track up" uses the wrong term. Tracking up means the hind hoof lands in the print of the ipsilateral fore. Over-tracking means it lands beyond. A Thoroughbred's hoof print is roughly 12-14 cm long (my estimate, not from a source). So a toe that lands 3 cm short puts most of the hind hoof inside the fore print. The model tracks up; it just does not over-track.

(3) The "TB on a loose rein over-tracks ~10-25 cm" figure has no source. Clayton's horses were dressage horses, not TBs, and the abstract gives no over-track values. Harris (Horse Gaits, Balance and Movement, 1993, via Wikipedia) supports the direction only: "Ideally" the hind hoof oversteps the fore print, and more overstep gives a smoother walk. FEI dressage definitions (Art. 403, from memory, not checked) say the same: the medium and free walks need the hind feet clearly in front of the fore prints, while the collected walk only "covers less ground". So over-tracking is ideal and common in a good free walk, not a fixed anatomical rule. The 10-25 cm magnitude is a plausible guess, not a measured TB value.

What remains valid: a Thoroughbred walking freely (paddock, post parade) usually walks faster than 1.44 m/s and visibly over-tracks. A free-walk default of about 1.7 m/s with a stride of about 1.8 m, or an over-track/walk-length style parameter, would be more typical. The stale comment should be fixed either way. Severity is low: the model is within normal real-horse variation, and the gap between -3 cm and about +10 cm of over-track is small on screen.
truth.correction: The model's walk matches a real collected walk to within about 5% (Clayton 1995: 1.37 m/s, 157 cm, 1.16 s against the model's 1.44 m/s, 1.585 m, 1.1 s). It does track up: the hind toe lands 3 cm short of the fore toe, so the hind hoof sits mostly inside the fore print. What it lacks is over-tracking. A Thoroughbred's free or medium walk (about 1.6-1.8 m/s, stride about 1.8 m) normally over-tracks, because the extra stride length comes almost entirely from over-track (Clayton 1995; Gmel 2024). The "10-25 cm" figure for Thoroughbreds has no source and should be called an estimate. A better title would be: "Walk is slow and collected; it tracks up but does not over-track like a Thoroughbred's free walk, and the GAITS comment claiming over-track is wrong." Severity is low, not medium.

The code gives the same result. footPath (index.html:1384) puts the toe down at toeDown = xc + stanceLen/2 + HOOF_TOE, with the same HOOF_TOE (0.069) for fore and hind. That makes the overtrack (xc_h - xc_f) + 0.75*stride = -1.22 + 1.189 = -0.031. Even the unrounded 1.6 m stride gives -0.02. So the GAITS comment at line 235 ("hind print lands just past the fore print") is false. Sheet 01-walk shows RH landing at g=4/8 just behind where RF stood.

Gmel et al. 2024 also report that over-tracking distance rises with walk speed across 1.35–2.05 m/s.

So the hind hoof steps mostly into the fore print, which is tracking up. What the model lacks is over-tracking. This is exactly the FEI's collected walk ("hind feet touch the ground behind, or in, the footprints of the forefeet"), not a walk that fails to track up.
2. **The 10–25 cm figure is unsourced.** The critic's figure for a Thoroughbred on a loose rein is not supported by either reference cited. The abstracts I could check give no overtrack distances.
3. **Some roster horses already over-track.** tuneGait applies run.stride to the walk too, through makeGait(state.gait, ..., r.run) at line 3347. That gives about 0 cm over-track at stride 1.03, about +4.5 cm at 1.07 and about +10 cm at 1.1. Several horses in data/quirks.js use stride 1.03–1.1, so the -3 cm only applies to the default and style-neutral horses.

truth.reasoning:
The direction of the claim holds, but its size and two of its supporting arguments are overstated or misattributed.

What holds:
- Clayton 1995 (Europe PMC abstract, PMID 7574149) says: "Only 1 of the 6 horses had a regular 4-beat rhythm of the footfalls, with equal time elapsing between the lateral and diagonal footfalls."
- Real horses walk with a limb phase slightly under 25%. Usherwood & Self Davies 2017 (eLife, Table 1) give a median of 24% (SD 1.1, n=2) for horses and 24% (SD 2.4, n=28) for zebras. Their work-minimisation model predicts phases "at or somewhat below 25%" for duty factors of 0.6-0.75.

What is overstated or wrong:
1. Size of the effect. The typical deviation is about 1% of the stride, roughly 11 ms in this walk's 1.1 s stride. The model's 25% sits within about 1 SD of real horses (zebra SD 2.4%), so it is a valid textbook walk, not a misdescription. The proposed default LF 0.22 overshoots the median. 0.20-0.22 describes a lateral-tending walk, which dressage judges count as a fault and which ambling types show.
2. Population. Clayton's six horses were dressage horses in collected, medium and extended walk, not Thoroughbreds at a free walk. The abstract does not say which way the other five deviated. The finding shows variation from horse to horse, which argues for a per-horse parameter more than for a global shift.
3. Griffin 2004 is a misattributed source. It studied dogs, not horses: limb phase 15%, forelimbs carrying 63% of body mass. truth.correction:
Real horses walk in lateral sequence with a median limb phase of about 24%, not 25%. Usherwood & Self Davies 2017 report 24 ± 1.1% for horses and 24 ± 2.4% for zebras. Individual horses vary: only 1 of the 6 dressage horses in Clayton 1995 had exactly even intervals. The model's exactly even 25% is therefore a slight idealisation, within about 1 SD of real horses and about 11 ms per beat off, not a misdescription.

Corrections to the finding:
- Cite Griffin 2004 for dogs only (limb phase 15%). The twice-per-stride centre-of-mass rise does not depend on limb phase being under 25% in horses, because their forelimb-heavy weight split already produces it. The model already shows it: the withers rise twice per stride by about 3.4 cm.
- Fore stance is only about 1-2% of the stride longer than hind stance in real horses (734 vs 722 ms in Arabians, Starke & Clayton 2015), which is negligible. The more relevant gap is the overall walk duty: about 0.63-0.67 in real horses against 0.6 in the model.

Recommendation:
- If the default changes, use LF 0.24 / RF 0.74 (at most 0.23 / 0.73), not 0.22 / 0.72.
- Prefer the per-horse "walk lateralness" parameter. Values of about 0.21-0.27 cover normal horses; values under about 0.21 belong to lateral-tending or ambling walks, a known dressage fault.

Byström et al. 2025 (Heliyon 11:e41947) call 25% "the ideal" withers-croup timing at the walk; the ridden horses they measured showed 8-17%. Laffi et al. 2025 (J Anat 246:456) found ipsilateral hoof impacts at the walk cluster in a 1:3 rhythmic category, which is about a 25% lateral interval. Clayton 1995 (verified abstract) says only 1 of 6 dressage horses had equal lateral and diagonal intervals, but the abstract does not say which interval was shorter. Real walks scatter around 0.25, often a little lateral. A fixed 0.25 is a reasonable stylised average for one stride shown at the cited frame rate. It is not an anatomical defect.
2. **The COM argument uses a dog study.** Griffin, Main & Farley 2004 measured dogs, not horses (limb phase 0.15, forelimbs carrying 63% of body mass). The model does not need a limb phase below 0.25 to get two rises and falls per stride. BODY.walk (index.html:1619-1631) already prescribes them, independent of footfall timing: spine height uses 0.012·cyc(g,2,0.1), the trunk pitches with cyc(g,2) and the neck and head nod twice per stride. At the walk the hind stance was 2.7% longer on average. That is the opposite of "fore stance usually slightly longer". Either way the difference is about 0.016 of duty (0.600 vs about 0.616). That is half of one 1/32-stride sample and cannot be seen. One shared duty is therefore not a real problem.

What remains: the walk is fixed at an exact, idealised limb phase of 0.25 with no per-horse variation. The model numbers check out. From measurements.json, the walk swing toe Y for LF peaks at 0.151 m at s≈0.30–0.375, then sinks slowly to 0.125 m by s≈0.61 and drops to 0.015 m. LH rises to about 0.11 m at s≈0.30 and stays flat at 0.107–0.111 m until s≈0.61. The cause is the symmetric smoothstep at index.html:1407, with walk lift 0.14 / 0.12, rise 0.3 and fall 0.6. The real-horse side of the finding is only partly right.

What holds up:
(1) Peak height is too high. Zellner, Bockstahler & Peham 2017 measured the fore hoof at walk on a treadmill at 1.5 m/s, close to the model's 1.44 m/s. The highest point of the flight arc was 82.9 ± 6.8 mm, against 111 mm at trot. That is a lateral hoof-wall marker; the toe sits lower than that marker in the flexed early swing, so real toe clearance is probably lower still. The model's walk peaks (15 cm fore, 11 cm hind) are therefore roughly twice reality. The proposed walk lift of about 0.09–0.10 m is reasonable, and the hind could go lower still: at trot, hind peaks were 5.4 ± 1.4 cm in Clayton et al. 2011 and 10.8 ± 2.4 cm in Brown et al. 2015, against 13.8 ± 3.8 cm for the fore. The claim of "a few to about 10 cm at walk" stands.
(2) There is a real early-swing peak tied to distal flexion after breakover. Pagliara et al. 2025, citing Clayton, report two fetlock flexion peaks in swing at both walk and trot, the first coming from elastic recoil of the palmar structures after breakover.

What is wrong or overstated:
(3) For the forelimb, "peaks early, then travels low and descends gently" misdescribes real horses. The fore hoof flight is biphasic. Gottleib et al. 2025 used hoof-mounted IMUs at trot: arc height a (early swing) was 12.9–15.9 cm and arc height b (late swing, "immediately prior to landing") was 11.7–14.4 cm, so the two peaks are nearly equal. After that late peak the hoof drops fairly quickly to contact; the authors attribute this to caudal muscles lowering the limb in late swing. A fore hoof that stays high through mid-to-late swing with only a shallow dip is therefore more realistic than an early peak followed by a long, low glide. The finding contradicts itself here by also saying "fore arc often bimodal".
(4) The defect in the model's fore profile is not the plateau as such. It is the missing late-swing second rise and the slow, smoothstep landing from s=0.6 to 1, plus the excessive height. The "long low glide" description fits the hind limb, which is usually described as single-peaked (Clayton), and only partly fits the fore.
(5) The gait-specific fetched data are mostly from trot. Walk-specific shape data are thin. The walk fetlock double flexion peak supports a two-peaked walk fore arc, but I could not obtain walk hoof-height time series to confirm it.

Consequences for the fixes: the "skewed lift profile" option (early peak, long decay from s≈0.35–0.4) is right for the hind only. Applied to the forelimb, it would remove the real late-swing peak. The data-driven option (two-peaked fore curve with a ≈ b, single-peaked hind, scaled down for walk) is the correct direction.
truth.correction:
Accurate version: at walk, real hoof clearance is low. Fore hoof-marker peak is about 8 cm at 1.5 m/s (Zellner 2017), and the hind is generally lower. The model's 15 cm fore and 11 cm hind toe peaks are too high, so lowering walk lift to about 0.08–0.10 m for the fore and less for the hind is justified. The swing shape differs by limb.
- Hind: one peak in early-to-mid swing, then a low glide and descent. The "early peak and long decay" profile fits here.
- Fore: two peaks. The first comes soon after breakover as the fetlock recoils into flexion. The second, about as high, comes in late swing just before landing (trot: arc a about 13–16 cm, arc b about 12–14 cm; Gottleib 2025). After it, the hoof descends fairly briskly to contact. The fore hoof does not peak early and then glide low with a gentle descent; a sustained, slightly dipped fore arc is close to reality.
What the model's fore curve gets wrong is the excess height, the missing late-swing second rise, and the over-smoothed landing, not the plateau itself. Use the per-limb, data-driven curve (fore two-peaked, hind single-peaked). Do not apply the skewed early-peak/long-decay curve to the forelimbs.

I re-measured with node from measurements.json (gaits.walk.samples, 32 per stride, sorted by u = g - land). Hind toe heights at s = 0.06 to 0.92: 0.013, 0.054, 0.096, 0.111, 0.109, 0.108, 0.108, 0.107, 0.093, 0.066, 0.037, 0.013 m. The hind fetlock is 0.333 m at every sample from s = 0.30 to 0.61. The hind half of the finding matches the data exactly: a flat top about 11 cm high, within 4 mm, over roughly a third to 40% of the swing.

The fore leg is different. Its fetlock is also flat (0.349 m from s = 0.30 to 0.61), but the toe follows 0.015, 0.060, 0.119, 0.151, 0.151, 0.142, 0.132, 0.125, 0.107, 0.079, 0.045, 0.015 m. So the fore toe already peaks early and decays, which is close to the critic's own fix A. What it lacks is the drop to a low glide: it stays at 83% of its peak or more until s ≈ 0.6, and it has no second peak before landing.

The right-side tiles in sheet 01-walk show only 8 discrete phases. They show the swing hoof lifted, but they cannot show the shape of the height curve over time, so they neither confirm nor refute the finding. The data and code are the evidence.

The height is the clearer real-world problem. Brown et al. 2015 (EVJ 47:107-112), measuring sound horses trotting over level ground, report peak hoof heights of 13.8 ± 3.8 cm fore and 10.8 ± 2.4 cm hind. The model's walk peaks (15.1 cm fore, 11.1 cm hind) are at or above those real trot values. A walk should clear less than a trot, so the critic's lower walk lift (about 0.09-0.10 m) is supported.

The 'fore bimodal, hind unimodal' shape is how Clayton describes hoof flight arcs. I could not check that against a numeric walk source here, because my web-search budget was used up.

truth.reasoning:
The timing claim is right. The amplitude claim is overstated and blames the wrong segment.

**Timing (holds)**
- Dunbar et al. 2008 (PMC2768006, Results) gives the canter pattern in words. Protraction (the neck lowering on the trunk while the head extends on the neck) starts late in suspension and runs into forelimb support. Retraction (the reverse) starts at leading-fore touchdown and runs into early suspension.
- I digitised their Fig. 6E/F representative canter cycle (0.55 s, RH touchdown = 0). Their leading fore is down at about 0.42–0.60 of the stride and the horse is airborne from 0.60 to 1.0.
  - Neck-to-trunk angle (ε): most lowered on a plateau at about 0.38–0.55, most raised at about 0.85–0.93.
  - Neck to space: lowest at about 0.47, highest at about 0.09 (a broad high plateau from 0.82 to 0.15).
  - Their Fig. 3C tracings agree: the neck is stretched lowest during the leading-fore stance and carried highest during hind support.
- I computed the model's canter from measurements.json using Dunbar's landmarks (poll in place of ear, muzzle in place of lower lip, tail head in place of dock).
  - Neck to space: maximum at g=0.625, minimum at 0.125.
  - Neck to trunk: most raised at 0.56, most lowered at 0.06.
  - Head to space: most nose-up at 0.47.
  - Poll height: highest at 0.75.
- So the model's neck nod is 0.35–0.5 of a stride out of phase, close to the opposite of the real pattern. In the model's gallop and race the neck is lowest near lead-fore touchdown (0.375 and 0.344), which is the right timing. The model's trunk pitch timing (nose-up at 0.0, nose-down at 0.5) is roughly right, so the problem is in the neck and head, not the trunk.

truth.reasoning:
I checked both cited sources in full text (Dunbar 2008 via PMC2768006, Egenvall 2023 via PMC10698108) and recomputed the model's numbers from measurements.json using the same definitions the papers use.

The cited numbers are quoted correctly. Dunbar 2008 Table 1, canter: trunk pitch 8±1°, withers vertical 18±5 cm, ear 23±5 cm, dock 20±4 cm, lower lip 22±8 cm, head-to-space pitch 10±4°. The horses were a Thoroughbred, a Warmblood and a TB×WB cross, 164.6 cm and 536 kg, cantering loose at 5.82±0.36 m/s. These subjects suit a Thoroughbred model. Egenvall 2023, canter: pelvic pitch ROM 15–16° and thoracolumbar flexion–extension ROM 9°.

Where the finding is overstated:
1) Trunk pitch is not "half". Dunbar's trunk axis runs from the withers (T3 skin tape) to the dock (tail base), not from the croup to the withers. Measured on that axis, the model's canter trunk pitch is 6.9°, against 8±1°. That is about 85% of the mean and about 1 SD low. The 5.7° in the finding comes from a croup–withers line that the paper does not use.
2) Pelvic pitch is about two-thirds of real, not half. The model gives 10.9° against 15–16°. Egenvall's figure also has caveats: horses were lunged unridden on a 9 m circle at only 3.7 m/s, breeds were mixed (several Iberian horses and a pony), and skin markers were used on the lumbosacral joint and tubera coxae. Faber 2001, a straight-line treadmill canter at 7.3 m/s with bone pins, gives a maximal segmental flexion–extension ROM of 15.8±1.3°. That supports a real pelvic pitch of about 15°.
3) Egenvall's 9° thoracolumbar flexion–extension is a bending angle between three markers (withers, T15, lumbosacral joint). It is not trunk pitch, and the finding does not compare it with anything in the model. Faber also reports relative L5–S3 flexion–extension of up to 8.6°. This back bending is real, so it argues against fix option 1's "remove most chest counter-rotation". The chest counter-rotation and hip gather are what produce the model's back flexion. Raising whole-trunk pitch, height and pelvic gather would be better than flattening the back.

Where the finding holds: the vertical excursions really are about half of Dunbar's means and below mean−1SD.
- Withers: 8.3 cm against 18±5 (46%).
- Dock/tail head: 10.9 cm against 20±4 (55%).
- Poll, used as a stand-in for the ear: 11.9 cm against 23±5 (52%).
- Muzzle: 12.5 cm against a lower-lip value of 22±8 (about 1.2 SD low).
- Head pitch (eye to muzzle): 4.3° against 10±4° (about 1.5 SD low).
The model also runs slower than Dunbar's horses (4.92 vs 5.82 m/s), so this comparison is reasonable. Dunbar's data have limits: only n=3, loose horses urged on by handclaps, 2D video at 60 Hz with skin tape, and wide SDs. Even so, the shortfall in vertical excursion is consistent across every landmark. The 03-canter sheet does show only a subdued rocking motion.

Overall, the canter's vertical bounce and head/pelvis pitch are too small. The specific claim that trunk pitch is "half the real range" is wrong once Dunbar's own axis is used. Medium severity stands, because the rocking-horse bounce is the visual signature of the canter.

truth.reasoning:
What the code does is described correctly. index.html:231 has canter land LH 0.27 and RF 0.27. Both limbs share duty 0.38, so both lift at 0.65. measurements.json gaits.canter.meta gives T 0.6 s, stride 2.955 m and 4.92 m/s, so the model is a working canter. At that stride time a phase offset of 0.04 is 24 ms.

The claim about real horses is mostly wrong, and the papers the finding cites contradict it:

1. "Hind generally first" is wrong for the canter. Burns & Clayton 1997, the finding's own reference, studied Olympic dressage horses. In collected canter, 9 of 11 horses put the trailing FORELIMB down before the diagonal leading hindlimb. A hind-first dissociation (mean 0.164 s) appeared only in the canter pirouette, and there it is a fault that makes the gait 4-beat.

2. "Usually slightly dissociated" is overstated at canter speeds. Clayton 1993, the other cited reference, filmed 9 dressage horses and 7 Thoroughbred racehorses at an extended canter of 6.0–7.0 m/s, at 200 Hz. Its abstract says "the time between impacts of the diagonal limb pair was close to zero in both groups, with individual horses showing some variability in the order of placement." For a Thoroughbred at about 5–6.5 m/s, the diagonal landing at the same instant is the group mean, so it is normal variation and not a defect.

3. Lifting at the same instant is also realistic. Takahashi et al. 2023 measured Thoroughbreds cantering on a treadmill at 7 m/s. Trailing-fore stance was 169 ± 10.9 ms and leading-hind stance was 172 ± 6.2 ms. With near-zero landing offset and stance times only about 3 ms apart, the pair lifts off within a few ms of each other.

4. Two parts of the claim hold up:
   - The diagonal does come apart, hind first, as the canter turns into the 4-beat transverse gallop. Robilliard, Pfau & Wilson 2007 describe the running gaits as a kinematic continuum, and in the gallop the lead hind lands before the non-lead fore.
   - The timing is an individual trait that varies by horse (Clayton 1993).

Consequence for the fix: a default of LH 0.25 / RF 0.29 (hind first by 15–25 ms) as the normal canter is not supported for a working canter. The landing offset should default to 0. It can be offered as an optional signed per-horse running-style knob, roughly ±0.02–0.03 phase. Negative (fore first) suits a collected or slow canter. Positive (hind first) can grow with speed toward the gallop setting (LH 0.1 / RF 0.3). This is a customization nicety, not an anatomy error, so severity stays low at most.
truth.correction:
For a Thoroughbred at a working or extended canter, the diagonal pair (leading hind and trailing fore) lands essentially together. The time between impacts is close to zero, and which limb lands first varies from horse to horse (Clayton 1993, including 7 Thoroughbred racehorses at 6.4 m/s). The two limbs' stance times are nearly equal (169 vs 172 ms at 7 m/s; Takahashi et al. 2023), so they also lift off almost together.

In a collected canter the FORE usually lands first: 9 of 11 Olympic dressage horses (Burns & Clayton 1997). Hind-first dissociation belongs to the faulty 4-beat canter pirouette (mean 164 ms) and to the gallop, where it grows with speed.

The model's fused middle beat is therefore within the normal range, and LH = RF at 0.27 is fine as the default. The model does behave as described, but the finding's "expected" is not supported by its own references.

What I reproduced in the model:
- index.html:231 sets canter `land: { RH: 0.0, LH: 0.27, RF: 0.27, LF: 0.5 }`. The comment at line 227 says this is deliberate ("RH -> (LH + RF together) -> LF").
- `duty` is a single number for each gait (0.38). makeGait (lines 267-275) and footPath (line 1383, `u = wrap01(g - G.land[L.id])`) give every leg the same stance length, so legs that land together also lift together. LH and RF therefore both lift at 0.27 + 0.38 = 0.65.
- In measurements.json (gaits.canter, 32 samples), the LH and RF toe heights match at every sample through stance. Both are 0.006 m at g=0.250, 0.002 m from g=0.281 to 0.625, and 0.006 / 0.003 m at g=0.656. Their contact strings are identical (`.......+##############..........`).
- Tiles g=2/8 to 5/8 of 03-canter.jpeg show the pair moving together. At 8 tiles per stride, a 20 ms offset could not be seen there anyway.
- A right lead uses the RIGHT_LEAD swap (line 270), so it is synchronous the same way.
- The fused middle beat is real.

Where the finding goes wrong:
- It says the diagonal is "usually slightly dissociated, hind generally first". The cited papers say otherwise.
- Clayton 1993 (Acta Anat 146:183-187) filmed 7 Thoroughbred racehorses and 9 dressage horses at 200 Hz, at an extended canter of 6.0-7.0 m/s. It reports "The time between impacts of the diagonal limb pair was close to zero in both groups, with individual horses showing some variability in the order of placement."
- So for Thoroughbreds the average diagonal really is synchronous, and the order is not consistently hind first. The model's canter is 4.92 m/s, close to that speed band.
- Burns & Clayton 1997 (Equine Vet J Suppl 23:58-61) studied 11 Olympic dressage horses. In collected canter, 9 of them put the trailing fore down BEFORE the diagonal leading hind. Hind first, with a mean gap of 0.164 s, happened only in canter pirouettes, which become 4-beat.
- So "hind generally first" is not true of the canter in general. It does hold for the move toward the transverse gallop, and the model's gallop already has that (LH 0.10, RF 0.30).

What is left of the finding:
- A synchronous default matches the measured mean, so it is not an anatomical error.
- Making both legs lift at the same instant is the weaker part. It comes from one shared duty for all four legs, not from the landing times. Clayton 1993 reports different stance durations for each limb, but this finding's proposed fix does not touch lift-off.
- The proposed fix has the wrong default. "LH ~0.25, RF ~0.29" would move every horse away from the measured mean, in a direction the dressage data contradicts.

Better fix:
- Keep 0.27 / 0.27 as the default.
- Add a signed per-horse knob in look.run for the diagonal offset, for example ±0.02-0.04 of the stride, which is ±12-24 ms at T = 0.6 s. Either leg could then land first, which matches the "individual variability" Clayton describes.
- Optionally give hind and fore separate duty values so the pair does not lift at the same instant.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. The real-horse claim holds, with a few small caveats.

Observed values, checked in the code and in measurements.json:
- GAITS.gallop is T 0.42 s and 2.6 m, which is 2.38 Hz. Planted toes in the samples scroll at about 5.8-6.2 m/s, matching meta speedMs 6.19.
- Canter is 1.67 Hz, 2.955 m, 4.92 m/s.
- Race is 2.33 Hz, 7.22 m, 16.8 m/s.
- So the gallop's stride is shorter than the canter's, and its cadence is higher than the race's.

Real-horse data. Witte, Hirst & Wilson 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:4389) measured nine elite Thoroughbreds galloping at 9-17 m/s:
- Stride frequency rose from 2.02 to 2.41 strides/s.
- Duty factor was 0.27±0.03 fore and 0.29±0.02 hind at 9 m/s, falling to 0.18 and 0.22 at 17 m/s.
- Fore stance length was 1.18 m at 9 m/s and 1.31 m at 17 m/s.
- The aerial phase was about 135 ms at 9 m/s and 119 ms at 17 m/s, and it did not depend on speed. 135 ms of a 0.495 s stride is 27%, so the "~27% aerial" figure is right.
- Frequency rises only a little across a near-doubling of speed, so a Thoroughbred gains speed mainly by lengthening its stride.
- The model's race gait (2.33 Hz at 16.8 m/s) sits right on Witte's data, about 2.37 Hz by interpolation. That makes the gallop, not the race, the outlier.
- At 6.2 m/s, with cadence only slightly below 9 m/s values, the stride must be about 3.2-3.4 m, longer than a ~3 m canter stride. A 2.6 m stride at 2.38 Hz is racing cadence on a trot-length stride, which no 475 kg horse does.

Heglund, McMahon & Taylor 1974 (Science 186:1112) back up the low-speed value. Their trot-gallop transition frequency scales with body mass; the commonly cited fit is about 269·M^-0.14 strides/min, which I recalled rather than fetched. That gives about 1.9 Hz at 475 kg. Heglund & Taylor 1988 (J Exp Biol 138:301) say stride frequency scales with about the -0.15 power of body mass.

Caveats, none of which changes the verdict:
1. f = 1.58 + 0.049v is only a straight line through Witte's two endpoints. As transcribed, Witte's own fit is quadratic, f = 1.7052 + 0.0305v + 0.0004v².
2. Witte measured 9-17 m/s only, so "1.7-1.9 Hz and ~3.3 m strides at 6 m/s" is an extrapolation. The linear line gives 1.88 Hz and 3.29 m; the quadratic gives 1.90 Hz. Both agree with the Heglund scaling.
3. "A gallop never has a shorter stride than the canter" is worded too absolutely. It is true for the same horse going faster, because cadence stays nearly constant, but the real rule is that stride length must grow with speed.
4. A duty factor of 0.35 is not wrong at 6.2 m/s, because duty rises as speed falls. The 0.27/0.29 values apply only if the gallop is moved up to 9-10 m/s.
5. The model's gallop aerial phase (about 24% from its footfall table) is already realistic.

On the fix options: option 1 (T 0.49 s, stride 4.5-4.8 m, so about 9.2-9.8 m/s, with fore stance about 0.27 × 4.6 ≈ 1.24 m) matches Witte's 1.18 m stance length at 9 m/s.

Severity stays high. The gallop's cadence is about 25% above a real horse's at that speed, and its stride is shorter than the canter's, which shows up clearly in a main gait.

Heglund & Taylor 1988 (J Exp Biol 138:301) independently predict about 1.9 Hz (4.48·M^-0.14) at the trot-gallop transition for a 475 kg animal. truth.reasoning:
I checked the cited sources and they hold up, but the finding treats the race as more wrong than it is and its fix ignores stride period.

Model numbers, recomputed from measurements.json (peak-to-peak vertical travel):
- Canter, 4.92 m/s: spine 7.0 cm, withers 8.3 cm, croup 7.2 cm.
- Gallop, 6.19 m/s, T 0.42 s: spine 8.0 cm, withers 11.7 cm, croup 0.5 cm.
- Race, 16.8 m/s, T 0.43 s: spine 10.0 cm, withers 12.6 cm, croup 3.0 cm.

What real horses do, from the cited sources:
- **Pfau 2006 (full text):** "Dorsoventral displacement decreased substantially from 185 mm (range 170-200 mm) at 7 m/s to 83 mm (range 75-91 mm) at 17 m/s." The minimum dorsoventral acceleration was "about -10 m/s² (1 g) during the aerial phase", independent of speed. So travel really does fall with speed, and flight really is close to free fall.
- **Dunbar 2008, Table 1:** three horses (Thoroughbred, Warmblood, and a cross; 165 cm), overground canter at 5.82 m/s. Withers 18 ± 5 cm, dock 20 ± 4 cm. Model canter withers 8.3 cm and croup 7.2 cm, and gallop croup 0.5 cm, all fall well below the real range.

Where the finding overstates or misleads:
1. **The race is close to correct.** Spine 10 cm against a real 7.5-9.1 cm is only about 1 cm over the top of Pfau's range at 17 m/s. The order across gaits is inverted mainly because canter and gallop are about 2x too flat, not because the race bounces too much.
2. **One cosine per stride is a fair model of the shape.** Pfau describes the dorsoventral curves as "sinusoidal behaviour with one clear maximum and one clear minimum per stride". The "floats through the suspension" point changes almost nothing: the model's canter flight is 38-72 ms, and the gap between -3.8 and -9.8 m/s² over half of that is 1-4 mm.
3. **Pfau's figure is not a true centre of mass.** It comes from a sensor over T4-T6 (the withers), moved to a fixed point 250 mm below and 200 mm behind it. Dunbar's numbers are withers and dock markers, which include trunk pitch. Neither is a pure centre-of-mass trace, so they compare more directly with the model's withers/croup travel than with its spine point.
4. **Travel depends on stride period, which the finding ignores.**
   - Real gallop stride duration is about 495 ms at 9 m/s, falling to about 419 ms at 17 m/s (Witte 2006). So 185 mm at 7 m/s goes with strides of roughly 0.5 s or longer.
   - The model's 6.2 m/s gallop already uses T 0.42 s, the cadence of a 17 m/s horse.
   - A cosine bounce cannot pull the body down faster than gravity at the top. That caps the cosine amplitude at gT²/4π²: 4.4 cm (8.8 cm peak-to-peak) at T 0.42 s, and 9.0 cm (17.9 cm peak-to-peak) at T 0.6 s.
   - So the proposed "~0.09 m gallop" amplitude at T 0.42 s would need about 20 m/s² (2 g) of downward acceleration at the top, which no horse can do. The current race amplitude, 0.05 m at T 0.43 s, already slightly exceeds 1 g.

How the finding should read:
- Canter: real withers/dock travel is about 13-23 cm at about 6 m/s, so the model canter should roughly double, to about 0.07-0.085 m cosine amplitude. That is feasible at T 0.6 s.
- Gallop: matching the real ~15-19 cm needs both a realistic slow-gallop stride (T about 0.5 s or more, longer strides) and a top shaped like a free-fall parabola. Raising the amplitude alone is not physically possible.
- Race: keep about 7.5-9 cm (cosine amplitude about 0.04 m).
- Croup and dock: should travel nearly as much as the withers in canter and gallop (Dunbar: dock 20 cm), not 0.5-3 cm.

An amplitude of 0.09 m would need about 2 g of downward acceleration.

Recommended targets: canter cosine amplitude about 0.07-0.085 m. For the gallop, lengthen T toward 0.5 s and add a free-fall-shaped top before aiming for 15-19 cm. Race amplitude about 0.04 m. Make the dock and croup travel close to the withers.

truth.reasoning:
The finding's real-horse claim holds in part. It is right about the hip but wrong about the stifle.

1. **Hip: confirmed.** Propulsion comes from hip extension, which swings the whole limb back. Dutto et al. 2006 report that the hip "did positive work… generating energy almost throughout stance". Hodson et al. 2001 found that hip flexion and extension "were responsible for protraction and retraction of the entire limb", with "maximal retraction during breakover". So a hind hoof that leaves the ground well behind the hip with the limb angled back is real behaviour.

2. **Stifle: refuted.** The idea that hip, stifle and hock "extend together" in late stance is wrong for the stifle.
   - Dutto 2006: the knee (stifle) "had little movement during the middle of stance", acting to transmit hip power to the ground rather than generate it.
   - Hodson 2001 (walk): "the tarsal joint extended slowly, while the stifle began to flex when the limb was retracted beyond the midstance position".
   - St George et al. 2023 (canter): the trailing hind shows greater hip extension and retraction together with MORE stifle flexion through stance, and peak tarsal extension in late stance.
   - So a stifle that stays flexed or flexes further at lift-off is normal. Fix option 1, driving the stifle toward about 150° in late stance, would make the model less realistic, not more.

3. **Hock: the citation is overstated, and the model already does this.** Dutto puts the tarsus among the distal joints that "behaved elastically", absorbing energy and then returning it. Its net work was small and fell with speed, so it is not a push-off motor. Late-stance tarsal re-extension is real (Back 1995: stance flexion is shock absorption; St George 2023: late-stance tarsal extension). My node analysis of measurements.json shows the model already does it:
   - trot hock 150° at contact, 142° mid-stance, back to 150° at lift-off;
   - gallop hock 152°, then 142°, then 152°.
   - So "no push-off extension" is false for the hock. The model's late-stance pattern (stifle flat or slightly flexing, hock recoiling) is qualitatively what real horses do.

4. **Caudal bias depends on gait and limb.** It is plausible at walk and trot. At canter and gallop, St George 2023 found the leading hind "more protracted and less retracted" than the trailing hind, and fast-gallop hinds land well forward because the lumbosacral joint flexes. A caudal bias is therefore expected for the trailing hind (the RH in this left-lead gallop), not as a general rule.

5. **What is left of the defect.** It is not about stifle or hock push-off. It is limited femoral retraction:
   - Gallop: the femur is still 23-31° forward of vertical at lift-off, about 20-30° of hip extension over stance. Lift-off is at roughly -14 to -17° limb angle (hoof 0.28-0.35 m behind the hip).
   - Trot: the femur reaches about 0° and the limb about -24°.
   - Possibly too, the stance sits a little forward (trot +28°/-24°).
   - I found no hard published numbers for Thoroughbred hind retraction at lift-off, so this residual is moderate at most.

6. **Small evidence error.** In 04-gallop the RH at g=2/8 (k=8) is mid-stance (hoof 0.05 m behind the hip), not lifting. Lift-off is about g=3/8 (k=12).
truth.correction:
Accurate version:
- **What real horses do:** In late stance the hip keeps extending and retracts the whole limb, and lift-off comes at maximal retraction during breakover, well behind the hip (Hodson 2001; Dutto 2006). The tarsus flexes in early stance and recoils elastically to about its contact angle in late stance; it does little net work (Dutto 2006). The stifle does NOT extend with them: it is nearly still in mid-stance and flexes as the limb retracts past midstance (Hodson 2001). Trailing hinds show even more stance stifle flexion (St George 2023).
- **What the model already gets right:** Its hock re-extension (back to 150-152° at lift-off) and its flat or slightly flexing stifle are realistic.
- **The only defensible defect:** Too little hip extension / femoral retraction, so lift-off is only about 14-17° behind vertical at the gallop. Possibly too, the trot/walk stance is a little forward-biased.
- **Fixes:** Retract the femur more in late stance, or shift hind xc back (fix option 2). Do not use fix option 1, the late-stance stifle extension toward about 150°. Treat a caudal stance bias as a walk/trot and trailing-hind expectation, not one for the leading hind in canter or gallop.

truth.reasoning:
I could not refute the core of this finding. Two independent datasets on Thoroughbreds support it, and the paper's numbers are quoted correctly. One part is overstated: the claim that the three lags are each about 70-75 ms is the finding's own inference, and Witte did not measure it.

**What the sources say**
- **Witte, Hirst & Wilson 2006** (J Exp Biol 209:4389; PMID 17050854). They put accelerometers on 9 elite Thoroughbreds galloping at 9-17 m/s.
  - At 17 m/s, fore stance is 76.7±4.6 ms and hind stance 93.6±5.9 ms. Duty factor is 0.18 (fore) and 0.22 (hind).
  - The stride is 415 ms (2.41 strides/s). The aerial phase is 119 ms, against 135 ms at 9 m/s, and the speed effect is not significant. The paper says "the aerial phase remained at approximately 27%" across the whole speed range; 119/415 is 28.7%.
  - Overlap falls from 183 ms at 9 m/s to 35 ms at 17 m/s and "approached zero at maximum speed".
  - The paper defines the aerial phase as lead-fore foot-off to non-lead-hind foot-on, and overlap as the sum of the four stances minus total contact time. These are the same definitions the finding used.
- **Leach, Sprigings & Laverty 1987** (Am J Vet Res 48:880; PMID 3592394) is an independent check under real race conditions: 22 Thoroughbreds filmed at the start of races. Mean stride was 0.405 s; suspension was 0.114 s (28.07%) and the stance part of the stride 0.291 s (72%). This backs the ~27-29% aerial target.

**The model (checked)**
- `measurements.json` gives race speed 16.8 m/s, so 17 m/s data is the right comparison.
- 13 of 32 samples are airborne (aerial phase 0.43, about 185 ms).
- Total overlap is 0.23 of the stride, about 99 ms (2.8× the real 35 ms).
- Lags are RH→LH 39 ms, LH→RF 77 ms, RF→LF 43 ms. The four hooves land within 0.37 of the stride; Witte's numbers put this at about 0.53 (415 − 119 − 77 = 219 ms of lags, plus the lead-fore stance).

**What needs correcting**
- Witte does not report the individual lags. His Fig. 1 only draws the stance bars to scale, so "~70-75 ms each" is an even split of the 219 ms sum, not a measurement.
- The data only set bounds:
  - Sum of the three lags: about 219-230 ms.
  - Total overlap: 35-46 ms. Note 342 ms of summed stance minus 296 ms of contact gives 46 ms.
  - Each lag cannot exceed the stance of the limb before it.
  - Together these put the hind and diagonal lags at about 50-94 ms and the fore lag at about 30-77 ms.
- Leach 1987 found that hind-pair and fore-pair timing differ significantly: hind overlap was longest and fore overlap shortest. So real lags are not exactly equal. Witte's own introduction also says pair limbs land "in couplets" in asymmetrical gaits. In Hildebrand's sense that means a pair lag well below half a stride, not two near-simultaneous doublets.
- The criticism of the model still stands. A 39 ms hind lag with about 90 ms of hind stance gives about 50 ms of hind overlap on its own, which is more than the measured total for the whole stride. The 43 ms fore lag is likewise at the very bottom of the possible range.
- "Nearly even 4-beat drum roll" is therefore a fair approximation, not an established fact. The proposed land table (0 / 0.17 / 0.36 / 0.53, duty 0.2) gives about 27% aerial and about 0.07 stride (~30 ms) of overlap, which fits the data.

**Severity**
High still fits. This is the main racing gait, and a 43% float with paired beats is plainly different from a real horse.
truth.correction: The targets are well supported at about 17 m/s: aerial phase about 27-29% of the stride (Witte 2006: 119 ms of 415 ms; Leach 1987 race starts: 114 ms of 405 ms, 28.07%), total overlap about 35 ms (about 0.08 of the stride), fore stance 77 ms and hind stance 94 ms, and about 219-230 ms from the trailing hind's landing to the lead fore's landing (about 0.53 of the stride). truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse side of this claim and could not. It holds up.

1) The cited numbers are correct. Pfau, Witte & Wilson 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:3742-57, doi 10.1242/jeb.02439) studied 7 Thoroughbreds in training gallops at 7-17 m/s. They used an IMU over the T4-T6 spinous processes (the withers), under the front edge of the saddle. The Results say: "Pitch range increased from 11.2° (range 10.0-12.4°) to 19.0° (range 18.3-19.7°)". Fig. 9 plots this as the displacement range, which is peak to peak. It is the measure least variable between horses ("pitch being most similar between horses").

2) The flight plateau is real. The paper says: "Pitch displacement curves show one unimodal minimum and a characteristic, broad bimodal maximum (approximately 40-60% stride time), which corresponds to a near zero pitch velocity and acceleration. During this time (aerial phase)…". The Discussion adds that angular kinetic energy is "dominated by pitch movements… peaked during the stance phases and was almost zero in the aerial phase". So a pure cosine that keeps rotating through flight is wrong for a real horse. In the model's race gait, flight runs from g=0.57 to 1.0, and pitch climbs about 4.4° and then falls about 1.9° inside that window.

3) It is not breed-specific or within normal variation. Faber et al. 2001 used bone-pinned markers on Warmbloods cantering at 7.3 m/s. Vertebrae reached up to 15.8° flexion-extension range. Movement between neighbouring vertebrae was small, the largest being 8.6° between L5 and S3. So at gallop speeds the thoracolumbar trunk pitches largely as a unit, by 11-19° or more. Belyaev et al. 2023 also describe the equid thoracolumbar spine as very stiff, with mobility concentrated at the lumbosacral joint. That supports the idea that the croup must rise and fall relative to the withers. The model's croup barely moves: 0.5 cm range at gallop, 3.0 cm at race, against 11.7 and 12.6 cm at the withers.

4) I re-measured the model from measurements.json:
- Race (16.8 m/s): withers-to-croup pitch 7.64° peak to peak (-2.36 to +5.28), nose-up maximum at k=27 (g=0.84), croup y 1.496-1.526.
- Gallop (6.19 m/s): 6.98°, croup y 1.567-1.572.
- The code matches: BODY.gallop uses spine.rotation.z = 3°·cyc and chest -2°·gather.
At 16.8 m/s the real target is about 19° of thoracic pitch, against the model's 3° thorax and 7.6° body. Severity high is justified.

Refinements, none of which overturn the finding:
(a) The model's 'gallop' runs at 6.19 m/s, just below Pfau's 7-17 m/s range. A target of about 10-11° is an extrapolation, but Faber's 15.8° at 7.3 m/s canter supports it.
(b) The 0.15-0.3 m relative motion between croup and withers is the reviewer's own inference from treating withers to croup (about 1.03 m in the model) as rigid. It is not a measured number. Lumbar and lumbosacral flexion could reduce the croup's share somewhat.
(c) 'Pivot near the girth' is an inference too. In flight the body rotates about its centre of mass, which lies roughly there. Pfau placed the CoM estimate 250 mm below and 200 mm behind the sensor.
(d) For the fix: Pfau reports that the CoM's vertical displacement falls with speed, from 185 mm at 7 m/s to 83 mm at 17 m/s. Race should therefore gain pitch rotation, not more vertical bob; the model's spine-root range there is already 10 cm. The slow gallop's 8 cm vertical range is, if anything, on the low side.
(e) Pfau's stride starts at left-fore contact, so the 40-60% plateau lines up with the aerial phase, not with a fixed percentage of the model's stride, which starts at RH contact.
references: Pfau T, Witte TH, Wilson AM (2006) Centre of mass movement and mechanical energy fluctuation during gallop locomotion in the Thoroughbred racehorse. J Exp Biol 209:3742-3757, doi:10.1242/jeb.02439 (PMID 16985191): pitch range 11.2 deg (7 m/s) to 19.0 deg (17 m/s); broad bimodal maximum ~40-60% stride with near-zero pitch velocity during the aerial phase; CoM DV displacement 185 mm to 83 mm

Belyaev RI, Kuznetsov AN, Prilepskaya NE (2023) Truly dorsostable runners: vertebral mobility in rhinoceroses, tapirs, and horses. J Anat 242:568-591, doi:10.1111/joa.13799: stiff thoracolumbar spine, mobility concentrated lumbosacrally

truth.reasoning:
The model's numbers are reproduced correctly, but the real-horse claim behind the finding does not hold up.

**Model check** (my node scripts on measurements.json, poll→muzzle as the head line and withers→poll as the neck line):
- Standing: face -44.6°, neck +15°, head-neck 120.5°.
- Race: face -59..-47° (mean -53), neck +2..+15° (mean +8.7), head-neck 113.6-122.8° (mean 118).
- So the poll is not more flexed at race than at rest. The head-neck angle is about the same. The face points further down only because the neck drops.
- With headCarriage -1 (k=1 at race, index.html:1695, 1712-1715), rotating the sampled points gives face mean -60° and head-neck mean 122° (range 118-126). The poll opens by about 4°. The finding's "lowered and curled" is wrong.

**Real-horse evidence against the "expected" behaviour:**
1. **Dunbar et al. 2008, J Exp Biol 211:3889, Table 1.** Three loose-led or free horses (Thoroughbred, Warmblood, cross); head line lower lip to ear, neck line ear to withers.

   | Gait | Speed | Head | Neck | Head-neck |
   |---|---|---|---|---|
   | Walk | 1.1 m/s | -66° | -4° | 121° |
   | Trot | 2.3 m/s | -56° | +11° | 113° |
   | Canter | 5.8 m/s | -55° | +23° | 109° |

   The authors write that the head "ventroflex[es] clockwise on the neck" as gait speeds up. So "horses extend at the poll with speed" is not a general rule. The data also show that a low neck (the walk) goes with a more nose-down face even though the poll is more open. That is the same coupling the model's low carriage produces.
2. **Real horses at racing speed, measured roughly from images in a scratch folder:**
   - Muybridge 1878, Sallie Gardner at a 1:40 mile pace (~16 m/s): face about -28 to -50° through the stride.
   - Muybridge 1887 plate 626, racehorse Annie G.: about -50 to -60°.
   - Danon Platina winning the 2014 Asahi Hai Futurity (Wikimedia Commons, near side-on): face about -54°, head-neck about 105°. That is more flexed than the model's race.

   Real Thoroughbreds at speed span roughly -30 to -60°. The model's -53 mean and 12° nod sit squarely inside that range. The proposed target (face -40..-45°, head-neck 125-135°) is one end of normal variation, not the norm.
3. **Go, Barton & Ohnesorge 2014, BMC Vet Res 10:118.** They measured the nose ridge against the ground, and the nose against the neck-to-withers line, in horses at rest:
   - extended: 51° and 128°
   - neutral: 72° and 110°
   - flexed: 90° and 90°

   Only the flexed position narrowed the pharynx significantly (28 mm vs 51-58 mm). The model's race head (about 53° and 118°) sits between neutral and extended. It is not an airway-compromising flexed posture.
4. **Petsche et al. 1995** is really Equine Vet J 27(S18):18-22, not 27:18-22. Five Standardbreds on a treadmill. It found that "head and neck flexion causes upper airway obstruction" while extension "has little effect". It does not show that racehorses extend at the poll with speed, and it does not make -53° / 118° "flexed".
5. **The comparison baseline is off.** "More flexed than at rest" compares against the model's own standing face of -44.6°. That is already near Go's extended position; a real neutral head is about 72° to the ground and Dunbar's free walk is -66°. Measured against real resting values, the race face is not more flexed.
6. **Oguri Cap.** The sources gathered in research/quirks (ja.wikipedia citing 小栗 1992 and 優駿 2010; trainer Setoguchi; jockey Ando) say:
   - he lowered the neck as if sinking (沈むように首を下げ)
   - he had a low centre of gravity and low neck position (重心と首の位置が低い)
   - he was called "the horse that crawls along the ground" (地を這う)
   - he used his neck a lot (首を良く使う)

   None of them describes the face near horizontal or the nose poked out. "Face nearer horizontal" and the fix target "neck ~0, face ~-35°" are unsourced inferences.

**What is accurate:** the face stays well in front of the vertical (the model already has 37° clearance), and strong poll flexion does raise airway impedance. The only real point is a code/comment mismatch: "a lowered neck pokes the nose out" holds relative to the neck (the poll opens) but not in world space. Opening the poll more for a low-carriage style is a legitimate style choice. It is not an anatomy correction.
truth.correction: Racehorses at speed show a wide range of face angles: about -30 to -60° below horizontal, with head-neck about 105-125°. The model's race head (mean -53°, head-neck 118°) is within that range and is not flexed in Go's or Petsche's sense. Real horses do not reliably extend at the poll as speed rises; Dunbar 2008 shows head-neck closing from walk to canter. The low style goes nose-down rather than stretching out, which matters because the user asked specifically for Oguri Cap's low running style. Mirror effect: hc = +1 gives face -46 with the head-neck angle closed to 114.
