I tried to refute this and could not. The claim about real horses holds, and the numbers cited are correct apart from rounding.

1) Primary source. The Witte, Hirst & Wilson 2006 abstract (J Exp Biol 209:4389-4397, PMID 17050854, read through the Europe PMC API) covers 9 elite Thoroughbreds galloping at 9-17 m/s. It reports:
   - Mean stance: 131 ms (9 m/s) and 77 ms (17 m/s) in the forelimbs; 143 ms and 94 ms in the hindlimbs.
   - Protraction (swing): 364 / 342 ms fore and 355 / 326 ms hind.
   - Duty factors from these: at 17 m/s, fore 77/419 = 0.184 and hind 94/420 = 0.224; at 9 m/s, fore 131/495 = 0.265 and hind 143/498 = 0.287.
   - These match the finding's "0.18 vs 0.22" and "0.27 vs 0.29".
   - Distance the body travels over a planted hoof at 17 m/s: fore 17 x 0.077 = 1.31 m, hind 17 x 0.094 = 1.60 m. The finding says 1.58 m; that is a small rounding slip and does not change the conclusion.
   - Witte found no lead vs non-lead difference within either pair, so splitting only fore vs hind is the right level of detail.

2) Independent corroboration.
   - Parsons, Pfau & Wilson 2008 (J Exp Biol 211:935-944), galloping Thoroughbreds on level ground: hind duty 0.31 at 9.5 m/s and 0.28 at 12.5 m/s. Both are above Witte's fore values at similar speeds.
   - St George et al. 2023 (Animals 13:1755, PMC10252091), canter at 4.4 m/s with a 0.59 s stride: hind stance 0.32 s for both hinds, fore stance 0.29 s (trailing) and 0.27 s (leading). That gives duty of about 0.54 hind vs 0.46-0.49 fore, so "hinds stay down longer" also holds at canter, as the finding implies for the other gaits.
   - The asymmetry is not universal across species (elephants have higher fore duty), but it is consistently reported for horses at canter and gallop.

3) The model matches the "observed" side.
   - index.html builds stanceLen from a single base.duty in makeGait (line ~274) and footPath uses G.duty for every leg (line ~1382).
   - measurements.json gives race at 16.8 m/s, T 0.43 s, duty 0.2: 86 ms and 1.44 m of stance for every leg. Toe-contact sampling gives an identical 0.219 for all four legs.

4) Severity "low" is right.
   - The model's single 86 ms is almost exactly the average of Witte's 77 ms fore and 94 ms hind (85.5 ms). Only the split is missing.
   - That is about +9 ms for the fores and -8 ms for the hinds, roughly 2% of the stride each, or about 0.15 m of stance length.

5) Caveats for the fix (they do not change the verdict on the real-horse claim).
   - The model's "gallop" runs at about 6.2 m/s (2.6 m stride / 0.42 s), below Witte's 9-17 m/s range. The fix option's "9 m/s gallop 0.27/0.29" should not be copied onto it: at 6 m/s real duty factors are higher. Keep the fore < hind direction, offset by roughly 0.02-0.04.
   - Separate issue noticed while checking: the model's canter duty of 0.38 at 4.9 m/s is well below the real 0.46-0.54 at 4.4 m/s (St George 2023).
   - "Sweep further" assumes the hoof stays planted; hind stance about 1.60 m vs fore about 1.31 m at 17 m/s.

truth.reasoning:
The model-side observation holds. From the mount code at index.html:1118 (Euler X 0.95-1.15 rad after Z = atan2(-up.x, up.y) + 62 deg), with the NECK table and bones at rest, I worked out the blade directions. Every blade points almost straight back along the crest, 87-107 deg from straight down. The withers blades lean slightly to the left (z = -0.08) and the poll blades to the right (z = +0.41). The per-gait overrides only add a few hundredths of a radian at the walk (:1633-1634). This matches the 'spiky crest' in 00-stand 'head, right side' and in the 05-race tiles.

Three parts of the real-horse claim hold up:
- A resting, groomed horse's mane lies on one side of the neck. Convention puts it on the right (off) side: Wikipedia 'Mane (horse)' says the mane is 'traditionally… braided on the right side', and this is standard for US show hunters and eventers.
- A mane never sticks straight back along the crest at a walk.
- At race speed a mane lifts and streams back. The figure of about 150 Pa is right: q = 0.5 x 1.225 x 16^2 = 157 Pa. Muybridge's Sallie Gardner ran at a '1:40 gait', a mile in 100 s, about 16.1 m/s.

Three parts are overstated:
1. 'Streams back and up only in airflow, as at racing speed' is wrong. Much of a mane's lift and flap is inertial and locked to the stride, not caused by airflow. In canter and gallop the trunk is in free flight during the suspension phase, so a mane lock weighs nothing relative to the horse and keeps its upward velocity. Under stance loading it is pressed down with more than 1 g. At a working trot (3.5 m/s, q of about 7.5 Pa, so negligible airflow) a withers bounce of about +/-3-4 cm at about 2.6-2.8 Hz gives a peak vertical acceleration of about (2 pi f)^2 A, roughly 1 g. That is why manes visibly bounce at the trot with no meaningful air speed. This is my estimate. Buchner et al. 1996 (EVJ 28:71-76) measured head and withers vertical acceleration at trot but gives no numbers in the abstract. Pfau, Witte & Wilson 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:3742) measured withers kinematics at 7-17 m/s gallop. Airflow also matters well below race speed: q is about 30-40 Pa at canter and 60-120 Pa at a 10-14 m/s gallop. Lift should therefore grow with speed through trot, canter and gallop. It should not be a switch that only applies at race speed.
2. '0-40 deg from down' fits only a mane of normal or long length (the model's 20-30 cm blades). A short pulled mane does not hang limp. Pulled manes are 3-5 in (76-127 mm) per Wikipedia 'Mane (horse)'. I estimated the bending length of a single hair as (E d^2 / 16 rho g)^(1/3), with E about 4 GPa, d about 0.1-0.15 mm and rho about 1300 kg/m3. That gives about 6-8 cm, close to the pulled length. So a pulled mane arcs over the crest and stands partly off the neck, with a root-to-tip chord nearer 30-60 deg from down. A very short mane (cut Fjord manes, regrowth after hogging) stands upright. Wikipedia also notes a Fjord mane 'is cut short to remain upright'. These hair-mechanics figures are my estimate, not a measured value.
3. A mane that parts on both sides is not un-horselike in itself. Untrained or thick manes often split, and grooms braid them to 'train a mane to lie on a single side… if some of the mane has been falling to the other side' (Wikipedia). For a groomed racehorse one side is the norm, but a split or two-sided mane is normal variation. The real defect is that the model's blades do not hang. That is not the same as their falling on both sides.

The fix advice stands with these changes: drive mane lift by speed squared plus an inertial term tied to the trunk's vertical acceleration and the suspension phase, not by airflow alone. Make the length and stiffness of the rest pose depend on mane length: short and pulled stands partly off the neck, long hangs, hogged stands upright. The severity stays medium, because the error shows in every side view but is cosmetic.
truth.correction: Real manes hang under gravity on one side at rest. Groomed horses conventionally carry it on the right (off) side, though natural split manes are normal variation. A mane never sticks straight back along the crest at a walk, as the model's does (87-107 deg from down at rest). Two things should change. First, lift and flutter are not 'only airflow at racing speed'. Inertial loads tied to the stride are about 1 g at the trot, and the mane is weightless during the canter and gallop suspension phase. Airflow is already about 30-120 Pa at canter and gallop. So lift should increase gradually through trot, canter and gallop, roughly as v^2 plus a stride-locked inertial term. Second, '0-40 deg from down' fits only a mane of normal length. A short pulled racing or show mane (76-127 mm) partly stands off the neck, with a chord of about 30-60 deg from down, and a cut or hogged mane stands upright. Both points are my estimates from hair mechanics.

- The mount applies `rotation.set(0.95+0.2*rnd(), 0, atan2(-up.x, up.y) + 62°)`. In three.js 'XYZ' order the Z turn is applied first in the parent frame: it turns the blade from the crest normal 62° toward the tail.
- The X roll (0.95-1.15 rad) only splits whatever is left of the vertical (Y) part into Y and Z.
- The crest normal leans back 33° at the withers (`up` = -0.55, 0.83) and about 0° at the poll. So the Z turn is 96° at the withers (just below horizontal, and the roll pushes it left) and 59-62° at the poll (above horizontal, pushed right).
- Bones have identity rest rotation (`attach`, line 664), so these mount angles are world angles at rest.
- `mergeRigid` (1293-1323) keeps the mount nodes as skinning bones, so the per-gait mesh rotations still apply.
- There is no option for which side the mane lies on, no plaited or hogged mane, and nothing driven by speed or gravity (a grep for plait/braid/roach/hog/maneSide finds nothing).

**Re-measured.** I wrote my own node script (3x3 Euler XYZ matrices, bone chain spine→chest→neck1→neck2). It used the BODY.* rotations copied from lines 1509-1655, 32 phases, and rnd ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}. Angles below are degrees from straight down; side lean is + toward the right (off) side, − toward the left (near) side.

| Pose | From down | Above crest line | Side lean |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rest | 87-107 | 11-30 | withers −5, mid-neck 0, poll +25 to +28 |
| Walk | 86-120 | 8-30 | −9 to +30 |
| Trot | 83-113 | | −14 to +26 |
| Canter | 79-110 | | −23 to +24 |
| Gallop | 77-126 | | −19 to +36 |
| Race | 72-125 | −9 to +22 | −38 to +13 |
| Graze | 62-113 | | +37 to +65 |

- At rest every blade points almost straight back, nearly horizontal: the stiff comb the finding describes.
- Walk (86-120) and race (72-125) are essentially the same envelope. This matches the critic's 87-117 and 74-123.
- In graze the neck blades (i = 2-15) point 101-113° from down, so 11-23° above horizontal, and lean 37-65° to the right. They stick out sideways and upward from the lowered neck instead of hanging.

**Shots.**
- 00-stand: the "head, right side" and "left/right side" tiles show a row of spikes along the crest pointing back and up.
- 01-walk and 05-race: the same spiky crest in all 8 phases, with no visible change between walk and racing speed.

**Small corrections; none of them weakens the finding.**
1. "Mid-neck upright" really means the mid-neck blades have no side lean. They lie flat backward along the neck's midline, not vertically.
2. The parting is uneven. Withers blades lean only about 5° left at rest, while poll blades lean about 25° right. It is more a twist from the midline to the off side than a true split.
3. At racing speed the constant +0.42 rad mesh-Z offset tips the blades down and toward the near side: −12 to −38° at the withers, down to 72° from down (18° below horizontal). So speed changes which side the mane leans to, not how much it lifts. That is the opposite of airflow, which should lift it.
4. Strictly, the overall range is 18° below to 36° above horizontal, not "horizontal to 33° above".

**Real horses.**
- At rest a mane hangs under gravity against one side of the neck. Convention trains it to the off (right) side (Pony Club Manual of Horsemanship). Racehorse manes are usually pulled to about 10-15 cm.
- Only airflow and the bounce of the stride lift it. At 16 m/s the airflow pressure is ½ρv² ≈ 0.5 × 1.225 × 16² ≈ 157 Pa. In Muybridge's 1887 gallop plates the mane rises and falls with each stride.
- None of this shows in the model, so the finding stands as written.

Medium severity fits. It is visible in every side view and every gait, but it is cosmetic and does not affect the motion or the rest of the anatomy.

Check of the code: I re-ran the race tail chain from index.html (tail build at :1124-1144 with tAng += 9 deg, BODY.race tail at :1562-1566, applyRun tailCarriage at :1719, spine and hips rotations at :1547-1551) as a 2-D sum of the rotations. The finding's numbers check out. The dock swings from -10 to +15 deg. The last segment points 21-43 deg below horizontal. Bends between segments are 0-12 deg and always in the same direction (concave down). tailCarriage rotates only segment 0, so the whole chain turns as one rigid piece: at -1 the chord is -18 to -42 deg and the tip -40 to -61 deg; at +1 the chord is -8 to +16 deg. What the finding leaves out is the chord from dock to tip at the default setting: it runs from -1 to -25 deg, so the tail already streams mostly backwards.

Check against real horses. Muybridge is the source the finding cites, so I measured his frames.
(1) "The Horse in Motion", 1878: Sallie Gardner, "running at a 1.40 gait" (a mile in 100 s, about 16 m/s), which is the same speed as the model's race gait. Across 11 frames the tail chord is roughly 5 to 30 deg below horizontal (about -5 deg in frame 9, about -30 deg in frames 5-6). The end of the hair hangs 40-60 deg below horizontal in frames 4-6. The tip rises and falls about 40 cm relative to the dock over one stride. The dock leaves the croup at about 0 to +20 deg. In frames 1 and 9 the tip curls back upward, so the curvature reverses along the tail.
(2) Animal Locomotion plate 626, 1887: Annie G., a Thoroughbred, in real photographs. Her tail is banged (cut square at the end) and in almost every frame it streams nearly straight and level, chord about 0 to -5 deg.

What this means for the claim:
- "Drag streams the hair nearly straight back from a raised dock" describes one end of the normal range (Annie G.), not every racing Thoroughbred. Sallie Gardner, at a measured racing speed, droops as much as the model or more. The model's default chord, distal angle and tip swing (about 49 cm) all fall within what she shows, so "a stiff drooping club" overstates the defect. A large vertical tip swing is real, not a sign that the tail is a rod.
- What holds up:
  - Real tails flex with travelling waves, including reversed curvature where the tip flicks up. The model never does this, because all its bends have the same sign.
  - Tail carriage at speed differs between horses (the two Muybridge horses differ clearly). Clamped or one-sided carriage is also a recognised behavioural sign (Dyson et al. 2018).
  - Only the dock is under the horse's muscle control. The dock is a chain of about 15-21 caudal vertebrae that bends along its length; it is not a hinge at the root. The hair is passive and shaped by drag. So a change in dock angle should not swing the whole hair as a rigid body. The -1 extreme (chord down to -42 deg, tip down to -61 deg) is droopier than either Muybridge horse at speed.
- Fix A as written (0-2 deg droop per segment at race) would turn the tail into a straight rod, which matches only the Annie G. type.
truth.correction:
At racing speed a real tail streams backwards, but how much it droops varies between individuals. A Thoroughbred at a measured 16 m/s (Muybridge's Sallie Gardner, 1878) carries the tail with its chord about 5-30 deg below horizontal. The end of the hair hangs 40-60 deg down in some phases, and the tip rises and falls about 40 cm per stride. Annie G. (plate 626, banged tail) streams nearly level. The model's default race tail (chord -1 to -25 deg, last segment -21 to -43 deg) is therefore within the real range and is not a "drooping club". The real deficits are smaller:
(a) There is no travelling wave with reversed curvature. In real tails the tip flicks up in some phases (Sallie Gardner frames 1 and 9), while the model only ever bends one way, by 0-12 deg per joint.
(b) tailCarriage rotates the whole chain as one rigid piece. Only the dock is muscular, and it bends along its length, while the hair passively re-streams in the airflow. The -1 extreme (chord down to -42 deg, tip down to -61 deg) is droopier than the real horses at speed.
Recommended fix: keep a moderate mean droop at race speed (chord roughly 0 to -20 deg) instead of 0-2 deg per segment. Add more phase lag between segments plus a second-harmonic term so the curvature can reverse near the tip. Have tailCarriage bend the dock segments, while the hair segments partly counter-rotate back toward the streaming line.

- Last segment: 20.9..43.4 deg below horizontal. The critic said 21-44.

Gallop really is 9.0 and walk 10-12 at the base. The model therefore already straightens the tail with speed (walk ~11 -> gallop 9 -> race 6.1 deg/joint). That is a partial form of the critic's own Fix A, which they missed.
2. It is not a "pivoting rod". The per-segment phase lag (0.08/segment) makes a real travelling wave of bending. The joint with the most bend moves down the tail: joint 1 at g=0.14, joint 2 at 0.19, joint 3 at 0.25, joint 4 at 0.31, joint 5 at 0.375. The bend at each joint swings about 0..11.6 deg, not "only 5-12". Muybridge's gallop plates (1878 Sallie Gardner; 1887 Animal Locomotion gallop series) show the same per-stride rise and fall of the tail hair. They do not show a tail held fixed and horizontal. - The tail at speed has a uniform, symmetric curve (same mean bend at every joint) and no spreading of the hair.

truth.reasoning:
The main real-horse claim is correct. In a real horse the thigh is one continuous hindquarter under mobile skin. The flank fold (plica lateris) joins the stifle to the abdominal wall. A thigh that reads as a hard shelf or a separate panel is never correct. The skin-displacement figures are also real (checked against Europe PMC abstracts). At the walk, the total skin displacement over the caudal greater trochanter was 13-17 cm (PMID 9259818). At the trot, the mean Y-displacement there was 142 mm (PMID 9259817). The finding needs four corrections:

(1) Citation and number details. The walk figure comes from Equine Vet J Suppl 9:110-118 (PMID 9259818). The finding cites the trot paper (pp. 101-109, PMID 9259817) twice and never cites the walk paper. 142 mm is the largest mean value, not an "up to" maximum. Both studies used four Dutch Warmbloods at walk and trot only. Neither measured Thoroughbreds or the gallop. The numbers show the skin is highly mobile; they are not a gallop target.

(2) "The croup-to-gaskin outline stays smooth" is overstated. A galloping Thoroughbred's outline is continuous, but it is not featureless. The flank fold creases at full protraction, the groove between biceps femoris and semitendinosus shows, and the hamstrings bulge at push-off. The right expectation is "continuous, with no seam or hard edge, plus soft folds", not "smooth".

(3) Most of the protraction defect comes from a pose no real horse adopts. measurements.json, race, RH, k = 24-28 (g ≈ 0.75-0.88): the femur is 86-89° from vertical, which is 75-78° relative to the hip-to-buttock line. The stifle is at 1.07-1.09 m, level with the hip joint. The femur relative to the pelvis ranges over 69° at walk, 74° at trot and 76° in the race gait. A real hip moves far less. Protraction comes largely from coupled stifle and hock flexion, and at full gallop the stifle stays under the flank, around the belly line (Muybridge 1887 gallop plates). The femur-over-rotation finding elsewhere in this review covers this. Fix the femur range first, and do not tune the skinning to cover an impossible pose.

(4) The extension defect is genuine, but the reason given is partly wrong. At race k = 10-12 (g ≈ 0.31-0.38) the femur is near vertical (about 0° world, 9-12° relative to the pelvis). That is a plausible late-stance or lift-off angle, so the visible hamstring panel there is a real skinning and silhouette fault. However, being "50% outside the trunk" is not itself wrong. In a real horse the thigh and hamstrings form the rear outline, beyond the barrel, from the point of buttock to the gaskin. The defect is the hard edge between the shell and the buttock, not the volume outside the trunk.

The rig facts check out. The femur shell sits rigidly on L.fem (index.html:1223, back half-depth 0.22 m). The trunk skin is weighted only to spine, hips and chest (index.html:748). FEMUR_RANGE is [0, 76°] and is applied only during the swing (index.html:1432, 1479-1484). With (3) taken into account, the remaining real-horse-grounded defect is the extension-phase seam plus a residual flank fold. I lowered the severity from high to medium for that reason.
truth.correction: Real hindquarters are continuous, and the skin over the femur is very mobile. Total skin displacement over the caudal greater trochanter is 13-17 cm at the walk (van Weeren et al. 1990, Equine Vet J Suppl 9:110-118, PMID 9259818). The largest mean displacement at the trot is 142 mm (van Weeren et al. 1990, Suppl 9:101-109, PMID 9259817). Both studies used Dutch Warmbloods, not Thoroughbreds, and neither measured the gallop. The outline is not perfectly smooth: the flank fold creases at protraction, and the hamstring groove and bulge show at extension. What it never shows is a hard seam or a detached panel. The protraction "shelf" happens mainly because the model's femur reaches 86-89° from vertical, 75-78° relative to the pelvis, with the stifle level with the hip joint. No real horse does this; at full gallop the stifle stays under the flank. Fix the femur range first and then judge what protrusion remains. The extension-phase hamstring panel happens at a near-vertical femur, which is a realistic angle, so it is a genuine defect. But the thigh lying outside the barrel is anatomically correct; only the hard edge is wrong.

truth.reasoning:
The mesh defects the finding reports are real. Its claim about how a real neck bends to graze is wrong in the part that drives its first fix.

1) "Neck flexion is spread over the cervical joints" is the reverse of the in-vivo data. Clayton, Kaiser, Lavagnino & Stubbs (2010) tracked 8 horses with the chin between the front fetlocks, which is close to a grazing posture. The largest angle changes were at the cranial and caudal ends of the neck. Each mid-neck joint changed by less than 10°. Their conclusion: "the articulations at the extremities of the cervical vertebral column are primarily responsible for sagittal plane position and orientation of the head and neck." The angle at C1 opened from 86±8° to 132±11°, about +46° at the poll. The thoracic joints also flexed 3–7° per segment.

The model's graze pose has the same pattern:
- chest −12° (forehand and withers flex)
- neck1 −65° at a joint placed at about the cervicothoracic junction (0.56, 1.44), just in front of the scapula
- neck2 −6° in the mid-neck (under the 10° limit)
- head +55° at the poll (matches the +46±11° opening)

So the bone angles are anatomically right. Fix option 1 ("neck1 −35, neck2 −25") would put about 25° into the mid-neck, which contradicts the in-vivo data.

2) The Clayton & Townsend 1989 figure is real but misused. The abstract says dorsoventral motion was greatest at the atlanto-occipital joint (86.4°), which was 32% of the cervical total. That is a range-of-motion result showing the poll is the single most mobile joint in this plane. It does not show that a grazing posture spreads the bend evenly. Calling it "only ~32%" turns the point around.

3) What does hold for real horses:
- Soft tissue spreads the bend at the neck base over the C5–T1 region and the withers (roughly 25–35 cm), so the surface is a smooth arc.
- Skin never passes through itself.
- The mane is rooted in the crest skin and cannot slide 12 cm.
- A local crest strain of about 2× is not realistic. I re-derived it with a quick hand calculation: ring 0 to ring 1 goes from 0.20 m to 0.43 m when neck1 rotates −65°.

The real crest and nuchal ligament do lengthen a lot when the head is lowered, though. The fix should spread that lengthening along the withers-to-mid-neck span, not keep the crest length fixed.

4) The "throat" wording needs correcting. The ventral line that folds at the first two rings is the ventral base of the neck where it meets the breast, not the throatlatch. When grazing the throatlatch opens (C1 angle 86→132°), so its skin stretches rather than wrinkles. A real horse does show a concave crease with skin folds at the ventral neck base, but never a fold-through like the 146° turn.

Corrected statement: the bone pose is realistic. The defect is in the skinning and mesh: too few rings and too narrow a linear-blend window at the neck base, plus mane blades on rigid single-bone mounts. The right fixes are options 2 and 3: add base rings or a neck0 bone with wider blend windows, and skin the mane roots. Option 1 is not. Severity stays medium: the artefact is clearly visible in the idle grazing pose but does not affect any gait.
truth.correction: The skinning artefacts are real: the ventral fold-through at the neck base, the roughly 2× local crest stretch and up to 12 cm of mane slip. However, the expected behaviour should not say grazing flexion is "spread over the cervical joints." In vivo (Clayton et al. 2010, chin-between-fetlocks posture), the head and neck are lowered mainly at the two ends of the neck: the caudal neck and cervicothoracic junction, plus 3–7° of flexion per thoracic segment, and the poll, where the C1 angle opens about +46°. The fix belongs in the mesh (more rings at the base, a wider blend window or a neck0 bone, and skinned mane roots). Moving rotation into neck2, as fix option 1 does, would make the pose less realistic. The crest should also be allowed to lengthen, spread along its span, because the real nuchal ligament and crest stretch when the head is lowered. truth.reasoning:
The main real-horse claim holds up. In the caudal back, flexion and extension are concentrated at the lumbosacral (LS) junction, and the lumbar segments in front of it are the stiffest part of the thoracolumbar spine. Three studies support this:
- Townsend, Leach & Fretz 1983 (in vitro): dorsoventral movement is greatest at the LS joint and at T1-T2, and "the caudal thoracic and the lumbar spine is the least mobile region of the equine back".
- Haussler et al. 2001 (pins at T14-16, L1-3 and L6-S2, at walk, trot and canter): "the largest motion of the 3 instrumented vertebral segments was at the lumbosacral junction", and the canter gave the most segmental motion.
- Faber et al. 2001 (canter): the largest flexion-extension was between the L5 and S3 markers.
The LS joint sits on the midline, roughly on the line through the tubera coxae and just cranial to the tubera sacralia, which form the croup's highest point. So in a real horse the hinge belongs a few cm in front of the croup peak, not in mid-loin.

Three parts of the finding are overstated or need correcting:

(1) The Faber figure is misquoted. Faber et al. 2001 measured 5 Dutch Warmbloods on a treadmill at a 7.3 m/s canter. Maximal flexion-extension ROM was 15.8 ± 1.3°, and the largest value, "up to 8.6°", was between the L5 and S3 markers. That span covers two mobile joints (L5-L6 and L6-S1); S1-S3 is fused sacrum. So 8.6° is the top value for that span, not a per-joint figure, and it comes from warmbloods at a canter, not Thoroughbreds at a racing gallop. The model's race LS swing of -7..+11° (18°; index.html:1549, 2° + 9°·gather) is about twice that value. No bone-pin data exist at racing speed.

(2) The lumbar spine is stiff but it does still bend. Thoracolumbar flexion-extension ROM is about 4° at walk and about 9° at canter (Egenvall et al. 2023, skin markers). A short skin blend with some gentle loin curvature is realistic; a single hard LS crease would not be.

(3) "Mid-loin" is true relative to the croup surface, but not relative to the hip joint. The hips pivot at x=-0.30 is 21.5 cm in front of the model's own hip joint (HIND.hip x=-0.52; measured RH.hip x=-0.515). In a real horse the LS joint, points of hip and tuber sacrale lie about 20-30 cm in front of the acetabulum, so relative to the femur the pivot is roughly where an LS joint belongs. The 22 cm gap comes from misplaced pelvis landmarks: the croup peak (x=-0.52) sits directly over the hip joint, and the hip joint is 34 cm in front of the point of buttock. A Thoroughbred pelvis is about 53 cm from point of hip to point of buttock (Mostafa & Elemmawy 2020, as cited by the companion 'pelvis landmarks are misplaced' finding — I could not check that paper myself). That puts the real LS roughly 40-48 cm in front of the buttock, i.e. x ≈ -0.38..-0.45 in this model. So the pivot is about 8-15 cm too far forward relative to the croup and buttock, around L4-L5 rather than mid-loin, but not relative to the hip joint.

Moving the pivot to (-0.42, 1.45) without re-seating HIND.hip (the companion fix suggests about (-0.64, 1.25)) would leave the LS hinge only about 10 cm in front of the acetabulum, which is anatomically worse. The pivot move should be made together with the pelvis fix, not on its own.

The evidence line numbers are also stale for the current file: hips bone index.html:702; trunk skin keys :748; tack keys :777 and :830; hips.rotation.z in gallop :1517, race :1549, trot :1575, canter :1600, walk :1625.

Severity stays low: this is a skinning/hinge-placement detail, and it is secondary to the pelvis-proportion problem.
truth.correction:
Real horses do concentrate caudal back flexion-extension at the lumbosacral (LS) joint. It sits on the midline about level with the tubera coxae, just cranial to the tubera sacralia (the croup's highest point), and the lumbar segments in front of it are the least mobile part of the back. Corrections:
(a) Faber 2001's "up to 8.6°" is the flexion-extension range between the L5 and S3 markers. That span holds two mobile joints (L5-L6 and L6-S1), so it is not a per-joint value. It was measured in Warmbloods at a 7.3 m/s treadmill canter, where maximal flexion-extension ROM was 15.8°. The model's 18° LS swing in the race gait is about double the largest canter value.
(b) The lumbar spine is not rigid. Total thoracolumbar flexion-extension is about 9° at canter, so some distributed loin curvature next to an LS-dominant hinge is realistic.
(c) The pivot is too far forward relative to the croup peak and point of buttock: a real LS would sit at about x -0.38..-0.45 here, so the error is about 8-15 cm, at roughly L4-L5. Relative to the model's hip joint, though, the pivot (21.5 cm in front of it) is about where a real LS sits, because the croup peak itself wrongly sits directly over the hip joint. Move the hips pivot together with re-seating HIND.hip and the croup peak (companion pelvis-proportions finding), not on its own, and then tighten the skin keys to about [-0.48 hips], [-0.30 spine] at both the trunk keys (:748) and the tack keys (:777).

truth.reasoning:
I could not refute the main point about real horses. A flat jockey since Sloan's "monkey crouch" (1897) stands in very short irons. The irons hang on leathers from the stirrup bars, and the rider's weight goes through them, not through the seat. Pfau et al. 2009 (Science 325:289; abstract checked via Europe PMC) shows that the crouched, standing posture is what lets the jockey isolate himself from the horse's movement. Walker et al. 2016 (J Biomech 49:3368-3374) measured this directly with instrumented stirrups on six jockeys. Peak stirrup forces at the gallop on real horses were more than double those on a simulator. The jockeys' feet moved in phase with the horse, while the pelvis worked as an inverted pendulum, 180° out of phase fore-aft. So the feet belong in irons carried by the horse, and a rider with no leathers and feet beside run-up irons is wrong for a real race seat.

The code agrees with the observation. At index.html:957 the leg points are Hj (0.18, T+0.30, ±0.10), K (0.44, T+0.26, ±0.28), A (0.30, T-0.12, ±0.31) and Toe (0.42, T-0.15, ±0.31), where T = top(0.2) ≈ 1.55 m. At :868 the irons are always the run-up boxes at (0.36, top-0.07, ±(0.62w+0.03)), and no leather geometry exists. TRUNK top at x=0.44 is about 1.62 m, so the knee (y ≈ 1.81) sits about 19 cm above the withers line and 28 cm out to the side. In a real crouch the knee sits at about withers height, against the knee roll and the withers or shoulder. Sheet 06 shows this: the white thigh is level well above the back, and the black boot hangs beside the cloth with no iron under it.

Corrections:
(1) The "~13 cm off the barrel" for the feet overstates the error. A correctly placed foot in an iron still has its ankle or toe centre about 6-8 cm off the hair: half a boot width of about 4-5 cm, plus the iron's side bar, the leather and the cloth. So the feet are only about 5-7 cm too wide. The bigger errors are the knee (about 20 cm too wide and about 15-20 cm too high), the feet sitting too high (only 12-15 cm below the back), and the missing irons and leathers.
(2) Pfau 2009 does not mention foot placement or the knee resting on the flap. Cite Walker 2016 for loaded stirrups and feet moving with the horse. "Ball of the foot" is the usual coaching norm, but riders vary: some ride on the toe only, and US riders often ride "acey-deucey" with the left iron set longer.
(3) In a real race seat the knee and lower leg are not a fixed rest pose. They are the spring that takes up the horse's movement, and their contact with the flap and shoulder changes through the stride. That favours fix option 3 (feet pinned in irons skinned to the trunk, legs solved to the pivot) over option 2's static re-pose.

Severity: this is tack and rider rigging. It does not affect the horse's anatomy or gait, and at race-camera distance it shows mainly as splayed knees and the absence of irons and leathers. It is clearly visible in close and 3/4 views, so medium rather than high.

Three changes are needed. (a) A correctly placed foot in an iron is itself about 6-8 cm off the hair, so the foot error is about 5-7 cm, not 13 cm. The main errors are the knee (z 0.28 and about 19 cm above the withers line, where it should be about 5-8 cm from the withers or shoulder and at about withers height), the feet set too high, and the missing irons and leathers. truth.reasoning:
I couldn't refute the main point. Jockeys do isolate themselves from the horse's motion. Pfau et al. 2009 (Science 325:289) say "jockeys move to isolate themselves from the movement of their mount", and that this "would be difficult or impossible with a seated or upright, straight-legged posture". So a jockey whose seat moves as much as the withers, and whose head moves more, is unrealistic. A full crouch at a walk is also wrong. Horan & Pfau 2025 (PLoS One, PMID 40455846) describe racehorse trot exercise ridden in rising trot or a two-point seat, and the code confirms one pose for every gait (buildJockey at :877-964). Two smaller errors in the model are also supported by the literature. First, the rider should lag the horse slightly rather than move in phase with it. Horan 2021 cites prior work showing "a slight delay" of the jockey's pelvis vertically, and Horan & Pfau 2025 found the delay grows by 2.8-4.5% of the stride when the rider stands in the stirrups. Second, the rider should be steadier fore-aft than vertically. In Horan 2021 the jockey's reduction relative to the horse was "proportionally greatest in the CC-axis" (fore-aft).

The numbers in the "expected" field are misused, though, so the target they suggest is not supported.
(1) Legg et al. 2025's 0.06 m vs 0.12 m are not a per-stride head bob. They are the 3D displacement magnitude (vertical plus side-to-side plus fore-aft), averaged over 200 m sections of each ride. The signal went through a 0.1-1.1 Hz Butterworth filter, and the horse's stride rate (1.96 Hz at exercise, 2.33 Hz in trials) is above that cutoff. The filter therefore strips out most of the stride-rate oscillation, and strips more of it at the faster trial stride rate. The vertical-only medians were 0.13 m (exercise, 8.7 m/s) and 0.06 m (trials, 16.6 m/s). The "falling with speed" slope (-8.3 mm per m/s) is mixed up with this filter effect and with the change from exercise to trial riding. Legg's figure cannot be read as "~6 cm head travel per stride". The paper's qualitative statement, that race-riding jockeys attenuate about half of the horse's oscillation, is usable, but it cites the authors' own 2022 work.
(2) Horan et al. 2021 is the better per-stride reference. It used a 1-15 Hz filter at a 2.06 Hz stride, on retired racehorses ridden by British Racing School jockeys at below race speed. Peak vertical displacement of the horse at the girth was +66/-65 mm, about 13 cm peak to peak. The jockey's sensor (a phone on the kidney belt, near the jockey's centre of mass) gave +39/-46 mm, about 8.5 cm. So the jockey's vertical motion is about 0.65 of the horse's, not "much less". The model's withers at 12.6 cm is realistic. The seat should travel about 8 cm rather than 12.6 cm, and the head at or below that, roughly 6-8 cm if Legg's "half" holds. Fore-aft isolation should be stronger than vertical. The proposed k of about 0.5-0.6 on the vertical bob is a reasonable starting point.
(3) The cited studies say nothing about hand motion. Real jockeys' hands follow the horse's head and neck nod to keep rein contact, and the code already does this. The 19.7 cm vertical and 10.5 cm fore-aft hand travel is not shown to be wrong, and the fix should not freeze the hands along with the torso.

On severity: the error is real and visible, especially the crouch at a walk and the head bobbing more than the withers. But it is a secondary rider and tack issue, not horse anatomy. Against the correct per-stride reference the vertical gap is about 1.5x at the seat and about 2x at the head, smaller than the finding implies. Medium rather than high.
truth.correction:
The qualitative claims hold. Jockeys isolate themselves from the horse's motion (Pfau 2009). Their vertical motion is smaller than the horse's and lags it slightly. They ride upright or in a two-point seat at a walk or trot, and crouch only at speed. The numbers need correcting:
(a) Legg 2025's 0.06 m vs 0.12 m are the 3D displacement magnitude (all three axes), averaged over 200 m sections after a 0.1-1.1 Hz filter. The stride rate (1.96-2.33 Hz) is above that cutoff, so these are not per-stride head bob and do not support "~6 cm head travel" directly. The vertical-only medians were 0.13 m (exercise, 8.7 m/s) and 0.06 m (trials, 16.6 m/s). The speed trend is mixed up with the filter and with the change from exercise to trial riding.
(b) Use Horan 2021 for per-stride targets. Horse at the girth: about 13 cm peak to peak (+66/-65 mm). Jockey near the centre of mass (kidney belt): about 8.5 cm (+39/-46 mm), about 0.65x the horse. The reduction is proportionally greatest fore-aft. So the seat should move about 0.6-0.7x the withers (about 8 cm against 12.6 cm), the head at or below that (about 6-8 cm, Legg's roughly half), with stronger fore-aft damping and a small phase lag.
(c) Hand motion that follows the horse's head nod is realistic. The cited references don't establish that the hand excursion is wrong.

truth.reasoning:
The main real-horse point holds. A rein is a taut strap running from the jockey's hands to the bit ring, and it physically cannot pass through the neck. Tack guidance on the running martingale, which is the only martingale allowed in racing, says the reins "make a straight line from the rider's hand to the bit ring". At race pace the head and neck are stretched forward and the bit sits well below the crest. The jockey's hands, usually bridged, sit over the lower third of the neck. So a straight hand-to-bit line would cut through the upper neck and throatlatch. A real rein therefore lies against, or just above, the upper sides of the neck and the mane. The code matches the observed geometry. Hands are at Hn=(0.83, T+0.23, ±0.08) (index.html:945). Bit and hand markers are joined by a straight strap in a fixed z=±0.08 plane with a built-in 5 cm parabolic sag (index.html:1258-1262). Nothing in the code makes the strap follow the neck surface. The line from about (0.87, 1.78) down to the bit near (1.6, 1.42) passes the throat at about y=1.57 and z=0.08, where a real neck is wider than ±8 cm. So "through the neck" is a genuine impossibility, and the 5 cm sag at race speed is unrealistic for a strap under contact.

Three parts are overstated or wrong.
(1) "Hands hover 6-10 cm off the neck" is not a defect in itself. Jockeys rest the bridge on the neck when cruising or when the horse pulls. In the drive and finish the hands lift and pump along the neck, and hand height varies a lot between jockeys. 6-10 cm above the surface is within normal real-world variation for a hands-and-heels ride. The real fault is that the rein does not follow the neck. The forearm vertices dipping into the neck are a separate model collision, not evidence that the hands are too high. Fix option 2, which clamps the hands onto the crest, is therefore not required for realism.
(2) "Taut with contact at speed" is right as a general rule. In the finish the jockey's hands follow the head nod, so the effective rein length stays roughly constant. Brief slack does occur, so "never slack" would be too strong.
(3) The cited reference does not support the claim. Pfau et al. 2009 (Science 325:289) is about the jockey's crouch: the rider's trunk moves independently of the horse, which smooths the combined centre of mass. It says nothing about rein routing or hand height. Walker et al. 2016 (J Biomech) measured jockey limb and pelvis motion and stirrup forces at gallop, but not hands or reins. My web search budget was used up, so I could not fetch racing-school texts on bridging. The bridge and push description rests on standard flat-racing practice, not on a numeric source.

Severity: the interpenetration is real and shows in every race phase with a jockey, but it is a thin strap on tack, not horse anatomy. Medium stays defensible because the fix is cheap: route each rein through a waypoint on the neck surface and drop the sag at race speed (fix option 1). The hand-gap part should be downgraded to optional or low.
truth.correction: Keep the rein-interpenetration defect. Real reins are near-straight, taut straps from the bit rings to bridged hands over the lower third of the neck. Because the bit sits below the crest, they lie along or just above the upper sides of the neck and throatlatch and never pass through them. A built-in 5 cm sag is wrong at race pace. Drop "hands hover 6-10 cm off the neck" as a defect. Jockeys rest the bridge on the neck when cruising or when the horse pulls, but in the push and finish the hands lift several cm and pump along the neck, and hand height varies by jockey. The forearm clipping into the neck is a separate collision bug. Contact at speed is normal, but brief slack happens, so do not require constant tautness. Replace the Pfau 2009 citation: that paper covers the jockey's crouch and centre-of-mass decoupling, not reins. The running-martingale guidance ("straight line from the rider's hand to the bit ring") is the relevant source.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse half of this finding and couldn't. Each "expected" statement holds for Thoroughbreds. Two refinements are worth knowing.

1) Girth position. Saddle-fitting guidance (USPC and BHS manuals, and fitters generally) puts the girth in the girth groove, the narrowest part of the barrel just behind the elbow, about four fingers to a hand's width (8-10 cm) back. Racing and exercise saddles are girthed in the same groove. That matches the claim.
- Refinement: the guideline is measured from the point of elbow (tuber olecrani), not from the joint axis. The olecranon and triceps sit caudal and proximal to the humeral condyles.
- The model's "elbow" in measurements.json is the joint centre (standing RF elbow x 0.482). The triceps icosahedron at el+(-0.04, 0.06) with x half-extent of about 0.094 reaches back to x of about 0.35 at rest.
- So even standing, the girth band (0.355-0.39) starts roughly where the triceps mass ends, not a hand's width behind it. Moving the girth 4-6 cm caudally (fix option 2) is the more anatomically faithful fix, not just a workaround.

2) Overgirth. A racing overgirth or surcingle is a tight elastic band that "completely encircles the horse around belly and the saddle's seat" (Wikipedia, Girth (tack)). It lies on the saddle seat above and on the girth or skin below the flaps. It is never 4-6 cm proud of the coat. Its whole job is to hold the saddle down, so it is tensioned.
- In the code, the overgirth is shell(0.3, 0.325, 1, 0.056): a uniform 5.6 cm grow all round, placed 3-6 cm behind the girth rather than over it. That can't be right for a tensioned strap.
- Fix option 1, a grow that depends on height (about 1-2.5 cm on the sides and belly, thicker only over the saddle), matches reality.

3) Elbow vs girth. Real horses do retract the elbow toward the girth at late stance. That is why girth galls and chafing behind the elbow are a common racing and riding injury. It is also why "anatomical" girths with elbow relief exist "so the horse is not restricted as his leg moves backward" (Wikipedia, Girth (tack)), and why grooms pull the forelegs forward after girthing to smooth skin wrinkles.
- So "slides close" should read "may touch and push the skin and the girth's front edge at late stance". That is a refinement, not a refutation.
- No real elbow goes 3.8 cm into the girth line. The interpenetration is a model artefact.

4) The model's motion makes it worse. In a trunk frame (withers-croup axis, spine origin), my calculations from measurements.json give:
- In the race gait, the RF elbow joint goes from x 0.292 to 0.810 against a standing 0.474. That is 18 cm behind its rest position and 52 cm of total fore-aft travel.
- The humerus reaches -173 deg, almost horizontal and pointing backwards; standing is -134 deg.
- The elbow joint angle spans 36.5-177.3 deg. Full extension near 177 deg and flexion below 40 deg are outside normal equine elbow motion; the joint never reaches straight. The gallop gait is less extreme (elbow 45-136 deg, elbow x down to 0.324).
- So part of the clash comes from exaggerated late-stance humerus retraction, already raised in A-FORE-03. The rest comes from tack placed too far forward and grown too far out.

Severity stays low. This is cosmetic tack fit with a clear real-horse target, and the rule it judges by is correct.

For each of 32 race phases I tested them for being inside the RF/LF forearm and humerus parts (the arm loft and the triceps icosahedron). The test was ray parity (2 of 3 rays agreeing), and depth was the distance to the nearest triangle of the part.

- Girth: 0.8-2.9 cm.
In a close side shot from slightly below (g=0.25), the black overgirth visibly hangs below the belly line, lower than the cream girth.

2) Elbow travel. In measurements.json, RF.elbow x in the race runs from 0.289 to 0.807, and LF.elbow reaches 0.299. In the live rig the girth band sits at world x 0.34-0.41, and both elbow joints are behind its front edge for about g 0.375-0.97.

3) Interpenetration (Symboli Rudolf, race):
- None at rest and none for g 0-0.34.
- From g 0.375 to 0.875, 1-7 of the 48 distinct girth/overgirth vertices lie inside forearm or humerus parts of either foreleg. The worst phases are g 0.47-0.81 (6-7 vertices).

So "half the racing stride" and "up to ~3.8 cm deep" hold. The critic's count of "30 of 108 vertices" does not match the mesh (the two bands have 48 distinct vertices, 144 corners), but the size of the problem matches.

One correction to the cause and the fix. In the race, RF is planted g 0.27-0.47 and LF g 0.37-0.57. Most of the intersecting phases (g 0.47-0.88) are therefore early swing, not late stance. The elbow stays back because the humerus stays retracted, near-horizontal on the ARM_RANGE floor, through early swing (the A-FORE-03 issue). Fix B should target swing-phase humerus protraction, not "late-stance retraction". Alternatively, move the tack back about 5 cm.

A real girth lies on the skin in the girth groove just behind the olecranon (Sisson and Grossman). The elbow comes close to it: girth pressure peaks behind the elbow, which is why contoured "anatomical" girths exist (Murray et al. 2013). Real geometry cannot pass through it, though.

Severity low is right. At normal race-camera distance it is hard to see, but it shows in close-ups (the overgirth hoop below the belly, and the girth vanishing into the forearm).

Shoulder (S0) to elbow is 0.227 m and elbow to wrist (Hn, which the sleeve comment calls the wrist) is 0.280 m, a ratio of 0.809. Seat to shoulder is 0.427 m. The Winter figures are quoted correctly. They come from Drillis & Contini via Winter Fig. 4.1: thigh 0.245H, leg 0.246H, upper arm 0.186H, forearm 0.146H. The arithmetic for 1.58 m is also right (0.39 / 0.39 / 0.29 / 0.23 m). Sheet 06's close tiles do show a short white-breeched thigh above a long boot.

The core real-human claim holds:
- **Leg:** No norm has a shank 27% longer than the thigh. Winter gives thigh/shank 1.00. Joint-centre data (de Leva 1996, Zatsiorsky-based) gives about 0.97 for males. Bone lengths give femur/tibia of about 1.2 (crural index about 80-85; Trotter & Gleser regressions give a femur of about 47.7 cm and a tibia of about 38 cm at 175 cm).
- **Arm:** No source has a forearm longer than the upper arm. A brachial index of about 75 means the humerus is about 1.3 times the radius.

So the direction of the claim is right. Two parts are overstated:
1. **The arm target uses the wrong landmark.** Winter's 0.186H upper arm runs from the acromion, which sits about 3-5 cm above the glenohumeral joint centre. The model's arm swings from a joint (S0). With joint centres the upper arm is about 0.16-0.17H and the forearm about 0.15-0.155H. My recollection of de Leva's male values is about 282 vs 269 mm, a ratio of about 1.05. Working from bones (humerus 33.5 cm minus its head and the distal part beyond the elbow axis, radius 25 cm plus the joint offsets) gives about 30 vs 27 cm, a ratio of about 1.1. The finding's ratio of 1.27 and its 0.29 m upper arm are therefore about 10% too long for this rig.
2. **The blame falls on the wrong segments.** Stature implied by each segment is inconsistent: thigh gives 1.30 m, upper arm 1.22 m, torso (0.288H) 1.48 m, shank 1.65 m, forearm 1.92 m. At the torso's stature of about 1.49 m:
   - forearm is 0.19H against a norm of about 0.15H, roughly 25% too long, which is the main arm error;
   - shank is 0.27H against about 0.25H, too long;
   - thigh is 0.21H against about 0.24H, too short;
   - upper arm is 0.15H against about 0.165H, only about 10% short.

   The title says "thighs and upper arms too short", but on the arm the bigger fault is the forearm being too long.

The 1.45-1.58 m stature is within the normal range for flat jockeys, so it needs no correction.
truth.correction:
The model's proportions are wrong as the finding says. Thigh/shank is 0.785, below every human norm: Winter about 1.0, de Leva joint-centre data about 0.97 for males, femur/tibia bones about 1.2. Upper arm/forearm is 0.81, but in all data the upper arm is the longer segment. The targets need two corrections:
1. **Arm target.** Winter's 0.186H upper arm is measured from the acromion. For the model's joint-centred shoulder, use an upper arm of about 0.165-0.17H and a forearm of about 0.15H (ratio about 1.05-1.15, not 1.27). At 1.58 m that is about 0.26-0.27 m for the upper arm and about 0.24 m from elbow to wrist, not 0.29 / 0.23 m.
2. **Main error.** Scaled to the stature the torso implies (about 1.48 m), the main errors are an over-long forearm (0.19H vs about 0.15H) and an over-long shank (0.27H vs about 0.25H), together with a short thigh (0.21H vs about 0.24H). The upper arm is only about 10% short. The fix is mostly to shorten the forearm and shank and lengthen the thigh, not to lengthen the upper arm by about 28%.

The body doesn't hang together. Against a 1.58 m rider, the thigh is 18% short, the upper arm 23% short and the shank 4% long. One part of the finding is wrong: the forearm benchmark. The model's forearm tube ends at the fist: the hand blob is centred at Hn + 0.02 and the rein grip is at Hn + 0.04. So 0.28 m is elbow to fist, not elbow to wrist. For a 1.58 m rider, elbow to grip should be about 0.146H plus 0.045H, roughly 0.30 m, so the forearm is already about right. The 1.27 upper-arm/forearm target and the 0.23 m forearm should not be applied: that would leave the hands short of the reins. Like for like, the upper arm should be about the same length as elbow-to-grip, but the model's is 0.72 of it. The fix is to lengthen the upper arm by about 6 cm and the thigh by 5–7 cm, and keep the shank and forearm roughly as they are.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the finding's model numbers and they are correct: poll to muzzle is 0.661 m, poll to withers is 0.783 m, and withers to croup is 0.982 m (measurements.json static.standing). The "real horse" side is where the claim falls apart.

1) The head is not 15-20% too long. That figure comes from comparing two different measurements. Figures 1 and 2 of Ünal et al. 2025 define TB head length (54.79±2.45 cm at 157.92 cm withers height) as the tape distance from the crista occipitalis to the os incisivum. In their front photo that line stops on the face between the nostrils, not at the lip. The model's 0.661 m runs from the head-bone origin, about 8 cm inside the skull, to the end cap of the lips. Measured the same way, the model reads:
- 0.58-0.60 m from the surface poll to nostril level (head space x≈0.58-0.60);
- against 0.566±0.025 m for Ünal scaled to 163 cm. That is +3-6%, about 1 SD, well inside normal TB variation.

Taken to the lip, the classical "geometric length" (Bourgelat, quoted in Goubaux & Barrier: nape to the end of the upper lip) is withers height / 2.5 = 40% WH ≈ 0.65 m. The model's 40.6% sits on that. Ünal plus roughly 7-10 cm of muzzle below the nostrils gives about 39-41% WH. Saint-Bel's 1791 proportions of Eclipse give a shorter TB head (WH = 3 heads, 33%), and Goubaux & Barrier say a saddle horse's head "should be short". So the model's head is at the long, generic-canon end for a TB, not 15-20% oversized.

2) The expected neck:head ratio of 1.6-1.8 is made up. It divides Senna's 100.7±5.6 cm neck by Ünal's short head measure. Senna reports no head length and no withers height, and gives its landmarks only in a figure (it was probably taped along the crest). In Ünal's own data the neck (mandible to scapula) is 55.5 cm, the same as the head. Classical sources for poll to withers: Bourgelat 1.0 head, Vallon 1.2 heads (0.72 m on a 1.60 m horse), Saint-Bel's Eclipse 1.5 heads (0.5 WH ≈ 0.815 m at 163 cm). The model's 0.783 m straight line (1.18 heads, 48% WH) falls inside that range, so the code comment's ~0.76 m target is not "low". Along the crest the model's neck is ≈0.92 m, close to Senna's mean minus 1.4 SD before any height scaling.

3) "Neck shorter than the back" mostly reflects a long back in the model. Ünal's back (withers peak to sacrum) is 81.2 cm at 157.9 cm, about 0.84 m at 163 cm. The model's 0.982 m is about 17% longer than that, and its croup landmark sits directly over the hip joint.

4) "Neck topline about 2x the bottomline" is a conformation-guide ideal, not a measured TB norm. The model's ≈1.3 (0.92 m crest against 0.72 m underside along the stretched rows) is on the low side, but it is a style point.

What holds up: for a refined Thoroughbred, the default head is at the long end of the range and the straight-line neck at the short end. A small trim of about 5% to the head or neck is a defensible refinement, but the anatomy is not wrong.
truth.correction: Compared like for like, the model's head is at most ~3-6% longer than measured Thoroughbreds. From the surface poll to nostril level it is 0.58-0.60 m, against Ünal's 0.566±0.025 m scaled to 163 cm (Ünal stops at the os incisivum between the nostrils, not at the lip). Poll to lip it is 40.6% of withers height, which matches Bourgelat's classical canon (WH = 2.5 heads); Saint-Bel's Eclipse had a shorter TB head (33%). The 0.783 m poll-to-withers line (1.18 heads, 48% WH) sits inside the classical range: 1.0 head (Bourgelat), 1.2 (Vallon), 1.5 (Saint-Bel's Eclipse, ≈0.815 m at 163 cm). The 1.6-1.8 neck:head target came from dividing Senna's crest-taped neck (no landmarks or heights given) by Ünal's short head measure, so it should be dropped. The low neck:back ratio comes mainly from the model's long back: 0.982 m against ≈0.84 m scaled from Ünal's withers-to-sacrum. At most, treat this as an optional low-severity TB refinement: default headSize about 0.95, or NECK_BASE about 1.15. The 15-20% head cut and the 1.2-1.25 neck stretch are not supported.

That canon is an idealised general riding-horse proportion, not TB data. The head does read large in the side tiles. Note that the suggested default of headSize ~0.87 is below the Head slider minimum of 0.88 (CONF_CONTROLS, line 3262). Roster horses also already use head 0.93-1.12.

Ünal's own TB neck is 55.54±2.72 cm, about the same as the head, so the two papers clearly define neck length differently. Senna's markers (A-J) don't include the poll, so the definition can't be checked. Against Senna's back/neck ratio of 0.92, the model's back/neck is 0.982/0.851 = 1.15, which does suggest the neck is short. Part of that may be the model's long back (withers to croup is 60.5% WH). Allowing for the uncertainty, the neck looks roughly 5-15% short, and the low neck:head ratio comes mostly from the long head. The code comment at 547 already acknowledges that the authored neck is short and compensates with NECK_BASE 1.1.

The direction of the claim holds, but the size of the problem and the "long tube" framing are overstated, and the cause is placed in the wrong spot.

1) Is the back long? Yes. I checked the primary source. Ünal et al. 2025 (Arch Anim Breed 68:253-261) Fig. 1 defines back length as "peak of the withers and sacrum" (tape). That is the same pair of landmarks the finding measured (withers to croup peak). Table 2: 24 Thoroughbreds, withers height (WH) 157.92±6.38, back 81.21±1.91 cm (51.4% WH), body (caput humeri to tuber ischii) 156.88 (0.99 WH), rump (tuber coxae to tuber ischii) 44.38 cm. Other Thoroughbred datasets give longer backs:
- Senna et al. 2015 (Asian J Anim Sci 9:208, 51 jumping Thoroughbreds, back = point of withers to point of croup): 92.47±5.66 cm.
- Weller et al. 2006 (EVJ 38:616, National Hunt racehorses, as cited by Senna): 87 cm, about 52-53% of WH for a typical 163-168 cm horse.

The model measures 98.2 cm straight, or about 99.8 cm along the topline (60.6-61.5% WH). That is longer than every dataset, so "long back" stands.

2) The size is overstated. The "~14 cm too long" figure uses the shortest sample: small 158 cm Turkish sport Thoroughbreds with an unusually tight SD of 1.9 cm. Against Senna's Thoroughbreds, which use the same landmarks, the model is only +1.0 SD (+5.7 cm). Against Weller's racehorses it is about +11 cm. A fair figure is 6-12 cm too long, not 14.

3) "The body reads as a long tube" is wrong for overall length. Point of shoulder to buttock is 1.66 m = 1.02 WH, which is normal for a Thoroughbred (Ünal 0.99). The frame already is about as long as tall. Including the end caps, the outline is 1.09 WH. Real breast muscle and hamstrings stick out a few cm past the point of shoulder and point of buttock, so that is not abnormal either.

What is really wrong is how the length is split. The withers sit too far forward:
- The withers peak (x 0.457) is only 2.5 cm behind the elbow and 4 cm ahead of scapTop.
- Withers to point of shoulder is 0.544 m. Senna's shoulder length (point of withers to point of shoulder) is 69±5 cm, so the model is about 3 SD short.
- Back/shoulder ratio is 1.81 in the model against 1.34 in Senna.

In Ünal's Fig. 1 photo (rough pixel scaling), front, back and croup-to-buttock come out at about 0.31 / 0.46 / 0.20 WH. The model is 0.21 / 0.61 / 0.21. So the croup-to-buttock span is fine, and the length missing from the shoulder has been added to the back.

4) Consequence for the fixes. Option 1 (scale mid-trunk stations by 0.88 and move the hind end forward) would cut body length to about 0.95-0.96 WH, short for a Thoroughbred. The correct fix keeps body length the same and moves the withers peak (and the top of the scapula) back about 8-10 cm, which also lengthens and slopes the shoulder. Pair it with the separate fix that moves the hip joint back within the pelvis (A-HIND-01). The "short base of support / overhang" comes from where the legs stand (camped under at both ends: the hind cannon is about 0.23 m ahead of a plumb line from the buttock), not from back length. Option 3 (back length as a conformation parameter) is valid, since long- and short-coupled horses are real variation.

truth.reasoning:
The code observations are accurate. index.html:675 parses conf.head as one scalar, and :772 does head.scale.setScalar(headSize), so the eyes (:984), nostrils (:987-989), ears (mounted on the head, :998-1000) and forelock all scale together. The HEADP profile (:688) moves only the top line. The neck in conf has only neck length (0.85-1.2) and crest (0.6-1.6) (CONF_CONTROLS :3259-3263). There is no jowl, throatlatch, neck-set, eye or nostril control.

Most of the real-horse claim holds:
- Skull shape does differ by breed. Evans & McGreevy 2006 (Anat Histol Embryol 35:221-227, PMID 16836585) measured 9 head dimensions and 6 indices on 30 live horses and found significant skull-morphology differences between Arabians, Thoroughbreds and Standardbreds.
- Skulls also vary a lot within a breed. Ming et al. 2024 (Mamm Biol 104:345, PMID 39070961) report "high intrabreed variation".
- Jowl width between the jaw branches, throatlatch refinement and how high the neck ties in are standard conformation traits (Thomas 2005).
- The project's own researched quirks need exactly these traits but cannot map them (param null in data/quirks.js): Oguri Cap's broad, well-developed jowls (line 178), Sakura Laurel's large nostrils (line 384), and Biwa Hayahide's "big, LONG head" (line 327), which is forced onto the uniform head scale.

Parts that are overstated or wrong for real horses:
1. "Ear size independent of head size" is not how real horses work, and it is not missing from the model. Real ear size varies with head and body size, and when people call a horse's ears "big" or "small" they mean relative to its head. The model already has a separate relative control, conf.ears (0.7-1.4, CONF_CONTROLS :3264), plus earSet and earTilt. It multiplies on top of a head scale that only spans 0.88-1.15, so a big head with ears 0.7 still gets small ears (about 0.8 of standard). The requested small/big-ear quirks are already possible, and multiplying ear size by head size is the biologically sensible default.
2. The real objection to uniform head scaling points the other way from what the finding implies. Heck, Sanchez-Villagra & Stange 2019 (PeerJ 7:e7678, PMID 31576240; 194 skulls from 38 breeds) found that size explains 42% of skull-shape variation. Bigger heads have relatively longer faces, and relatively large orbits occur only at the miniature extreme (adult Falabella). So a bigger head should get longer, not uniformly bigger, and its eyes should grow less than proportionally. Over the 0.88-1.15 range this error is small.
3. The skull-index evidence compares breeds (Arabian vs Thoroughbred vs Standardbred, n=30). Within Thoroughbreds, long-narrow vs short-broad varies over a much narrower range, so a headLength or headWidth control should have modest limits.
4. "Large eyes" is weak as a Thoroughbred trait. Eye-globe size varies little within a breed. The roster's eye quirks are about expression and visible sclera, not size: Mr. C.B.'s "human-like" eyes (line 96), Sweep Tosho's sanpaku (line 691), Dantsu Flame's white-showing eye (line 617). An eye-white or expression option fits the data better than an eye-size slider. Resting nostril size does vary between horses, but at speed every horse flares its nostrils fully, so a nostril-size control matters mainly at the stand and walk.
5. Neck set-on and neck carriage are different things. Mayano Topgun's low neck (line 426) is carriage and is already mapped to run.headCarriage. A neckSet control is valid for conformation but should not be confused with it.

Low severity is right. This is a gap in what can be customised, not an anatomy error.
truth.correction:
The code observations are correct, and Thoroughbreds do differ individually in head length versus width, jowl, throatlatch and neck set-on. The roster quirks show this: Oguri Cap's jowls, Sakura Laurel's nostrils and Biwa Hayahide's long head cannot be expressed today.

Three corrections to the expected behaviour:
(a) Real ear size is not independent of head size. It varies with head size, and "big/small ears" means relative to the head. The model already has that as conf.ears (0.7-1.4), which multiplies on top of the head scale, so the ear-size quirks are already possible and no ear change is needed.
(b) The real-horse problem with uniform head scaling is allometry. Larger heads have relatively longer faces and relatively smaller eyes (Heck et al. 2019, PeerJ 7:e7678: size explains 42% of skull-shape variation). The useful fix is a separate headLength (x) control, perhaps with eye size scaled less than the head, kept within a narrow Thoroughbred range (about ±5-8%). The breed-level skull-index differences (Evans & McGreevy 2006: Arabian vs Thoroughbred vs Standardbred) are larger than any Thoroughbred will show.
(c) "Large eyes" in the quirks means expression or visible sclera, not globe size, so eye-white or expression is a better parameter than eye size. Neck set-on is a different trait from the existing run.headCarriage.

Priority order for fixes: headLength, jowl, throatlatch, neckSet, nostril size.

I re-checked the code and nearly all of the mechanical claims hold up.

- index.html:772 calls `head.scale.setScalar(headSize)`. The eyes and nostrils (983-989), the ear mounts (995-1000, added with `head.add(mount)`), the forelock and all head gear (`toHead`/`attach(head, …)`) are children of that bone, so they all scale uniformly with conf.head.
- index.html:688 (HEADP) moves only the `top` value of each head row. `bot` and `w` are untouched, so the profile changes only the top line.
- Every key read anywhere in index.html is one of: neck, crest, head, profile, ears, earSet, earTilt, chestDepth, chestWidth, barrel, hindquarters, withers, tuckUp, bone, hoof, tailSet. There is no headLength or headWidth, no jowl, eye size or nostril size, no neck set-on and no throatlatch. Eye and nostril sizes are hard-coded octahedra (0.024 and 0.018 at 984 and 987). The neck has only `neck` (0.85-1.2) and `crest` (0.6-1.6) in CONF_CONTROLS (3260-3261). `run.headCarriage` exists, but it controls motion, not conformation.

So the lack of independent head-shape and neck-set controls is confirmed. That matters because skull shape does vary independently between horses: Evans & McGreevy 2006 report different skull indices across breeds.

What is overstated is the ear framing, in two ways.

1. The finding says a big head also gets big ears, and that ear size must be independent of head size before the requested small/big-ear quirks can exist. But an independent ear control already exists. conf.ears (0.7-1.4, 'very small ears <-> very big ears', at 3264) is applied at 998 as `mount.scale.set(sqrt(e), e, sqrt(e))`. conf.earSet and conf.earTilt (lop ears) exist too, and the quirk data already uses them (data/quirks.js:20: ears 1.15, earSet 0.8, earTilt 0.6). The user's ear request is supported now.

2. The coupling is real but small and bounded. The effective ear length is headSize × ears, and head is limited to 0.88-1.15. That is ±12-15%, against the ear control's -30%/+40%. In practice the horses tagged big-headed (data/horses.js:614 head 1.12, :387 1.08; data/quirks.js:189 and :941 1.12, :324 1.15) get ears 8-15% longer than average with no ear evidence behind it. That is a minor side effect, and the fix is one line: divide the mount scale by headSize. Also, real ear length scales somewhat with head size, so full independence is not something anatomy requires. It only matters for data hygiene.

The finding also misses a coupling of its own. Skin weights at 762 hand the top of the neck to bone 5, the head bone (keys [0.62,4] and [0.97,5]). The skeleton is bound at 771 before the head is scaled at 772. So conf.head also enlarges the last neck rings about the poll: the throatlatch thickens with head size instead of being independent. NECK row 5 runs from crest (1.14, 1.885) to throat (1.13, 1.67). At head 1.15 that ring grows about 15% about the poll, so the throat edge drops roughly 3 cm.

Net result: the missing head-shape, eye, nostril, jowl, neck-set and throatlatch controls are confirmed. "Big head means big ears, so independent ear control is needed" is mostly refuted, because ear size already has its own control and the leftover coupling is at most ±15%. Low severity still fits.

truth.reasoning:
The code does what the finding says. In buildBreath (index.html:2969-2993), puff i has age = wrap01(n*p - i/4)/n*loopPeriod, and the visible count is min(4, ceil(life*n/loopPeriod)+1) = 2 for every gait. For canter, gallop and race, life = 0.9*T gives life*n/loopPeriod = 0.9, so two puffs show. That makes two emissions per stride, at g=0 and g=0.25: about 4.65 Hz in the race gait (T=0.43). At walk/trot, life = 1.2 s against a 2.5 s cycle, which gives two puffs 0.625 s apart. The quarter-cycle stagger is clearly a bug: the comment says "a puff at each exhale".

Real-horse claims, checked against the sources:
(1) 1:1 breathing per stride at canter and gallop holds up. Young et al. 1992 (Thoroughbreds on a treadmill at 9 and 11 m/s): "taking exactly one breath per stride". Attenburrow 1982: in phase "only at the canter and gallop". Lafortuna et al. 1996: 1:1 coupling at canter in 10 of 10 trials.
(2) Expiration during forelimb support holds up. I read the Young 1992 full text (a Wayback copy of the JEB PDF): "The period when the forefeet are on the ground corresponds to the period of increasing and maximum expiratory flow" (Fig. 3). Expiration starts slightly before back flexion begins. So it starts at about first-forefoot (trailing-fore) contact, which is G.land 0.27-0.30 in race and gallop. The code's g=0 puff (trailing-hind touchdown) falls while the forefeet are off the ground, which is inspiration. The g=0.25 puff is roughly in phase. Fix B is therefore well supported. Its "moderately certain" hedge can be raised.

Where the claim is overstated:
(a) "At walk/trot breathing is not stride-locked" is too strong for the trot. Bramble & Carrier 1983 report 1:1 coupling at trot in quadrupeds, horses included. Lafortuna 1996 found 1:1 at trot in 5 of 14 trials, and mean breathing frequency was not significantly different from stride frequency at any speed from 1.4 to 6.9 m/s. Art et al. 1990 saw 2:1 coupling in ponies at a fast trot. Cotrel et al. 2006 describe variable coupling in Standardbred trotters. So a trotting horse breathes at roughly the stride rate, loosely locked: about 1.4 Hz, or 80/min, at this working trot (T=0.72 s). The code's 2.5 s cycle (24/min) for the trot is about 3x too slow, and the finding implicitly accepts it.
(b) The walk "double puff" is not pure fantasy. Resting horses have a biphasic expiratory airflow: a passive phase followed by an active abdominal phase, giving two flow peaks (Koterba et al. 1988). Art et al. 1990 also saw expiratory gastric-pressure peaks matching the "first and/or second" expiratory flow peak at walk and trot. A real exhale is still one continuous plume, perhaps with a second surge, not two separate puffs each starting from scratch. "One puff per breath" is the right visual target, but the walk part is a weaker defect than the gallop part.

Severity is lower than claimed. The effect only runs where loc.breath is set, and that is a single location: the Hidaka winter farm (data/locations.js:931). It is a cosmetic particle effect, not body anatomy or motion, and the fix is a one-line S change.
truth.correction: Core claim confirmed. At canter, gallop and race there should be one exhale per stride, starting at about first-forefoot (trailing-fore) contact, G.land ≈0.27-0.30. Young et al. 1992 state that the forefoot-contact period matches rising and peak expiratory flow, so the g=0 puff (hind support, which is inspiration) is out of phase. Two corrections to the expected text. (1) At the trot, breathing is not obligatorily locked to the stride, but it is often coupled (1:1 in 5 of 14 trials, 2:1 at fast trot), and mean breathing frequency roughly equals stride frequency (Lafortuna 1996; Bramble & Carrier 1983; Art 1990). So the trot should use a breath period near the stride period (~0.7 s), not 2.5 s. (2) At walk/rest, equine expiration is biphasic, with two flow peaks in one continuous exhale (Koterba 1988). One puff per breath, optionally with a mild second surge, is right; two discrete fresh puffs are not. Severity is low: it only appears in the one cold location (Hidaka winter farm) and is a cosmetic particle effect.

findings.observed: bulk is computed as sqrt(kg / (475 s^3)), which assumes the cross-section grows as bulk^2. It is applied to the trunk half-width only (w*bulk, line 736). truth.reasoning:
The core real-horse claim holds. If a horse gets heavier while its height and length stay the same, the extra mass has to go into cross-section. Girth then has to grow roughly with the square root of weight, which is the structure of Carroll & Huntington's girth^2 x length / Y formula. Their abstract (PMID 3366105) gives r^2 = 0.90 and an average Y of 11,900.

I rebuilt the trunk loft in a scratch script and got the finding's numbers exactly. At bulk 0.92 / 1 / 1.086 the girth at x = 0.36 is 187.6 / 193.9 / 200.8 cm, the width 47.2 / 51.3 / 55.7 cm, the depth 75.3 / 75.9 / 76.6 cm, and the volume 0.912 / 1.000 / 1.096 of the reference. So the model under-delivers by about half when the height is pinned.

Parts of the finding are overstated or wrong about real horses, and part of its code claim is too broad:

(1) The 400 -> 560 kg at 163 cm example goes beyond real Thoroughbred build. The formula's 205 cm girth at 163 cm is a girth-to-height ratio of 1.26. Real Thoroughbreds are about 1.10-1.17:
- Secretariat: 193 cm girth at 166 cm (NYRA/Gilman measurements)
- Haiseiko: 188 cm at 171 cm
- the yearling: 176.5 cm at 158 cm

Heavy Thoroughbreds are heavy mainly because they are taller and longer. ja.wikipedia gives the standard as 160-170 cm and 450-500 kg. Even so, the shortfall survives at realistic values. Over 440-510 kg at 163 cm the formula wants about 182 -> 196 cm (14 cm), and the model gives 191.0 -> 196.8 cm (6 cm), about 45% of the change.

(2) C&H's Y comes from mixed breeds and overestimates racing Thoroughbreds. C&H themselves found racing Thoroughbreds significantly lighter than non-racing ones of the same height and condition score. Secretariat's measurements (193 cm girth, 177 cm body length) give 555 kg by C&H against a real 513-524 kg, 6-8% high. A racing-Thoroughbred Y of about 12,500-12,700 is needed, so the girth targets are about 3% lower than the finding says. Note too that the model's own reference girth (193.9 cm, about 500 kg by C&H) is already at the top of the finding's quoted range.

(3) "Real TB girths ~176-190 cm" is anchored on a yearling. Mature racehorses run about 180-195 cm (Secretariat 193 cm).

(4) Where the weight goes: depth from withers to sternum is skeletal and barely changes when one horse gains condition. Condition goes to the fat depots scored by Henneke et al. 1983 (crest, withers, behind the shoulder, over the ribs, loin, tailhead) and to gut fill, which shows as belly. So widening the trunk is not wrong in kind, only too small in amount. Extra depth is a difference between horses (frame), not within one horse. A wider forehand stance belongs to chest width as a conformation trait, not to weight as such.

(5) Code scope: the title says weight changes "trunk width only". In fact bulk also thickens the neck (neckBulk, index.html:751) and the upper limbs (kUp/kMid, :1183), and the width factor applies to every trunk ring, quarters included. The half shortfall also happens only when withersCm is set. Only about 10 of about 149 roster horses have it, and data/quirks.js sets none. Without a height, buildFactors lets weight raise the scale as well. Then 400 -> 560 kg gives a volume equivalent of about 414 -> 545 kg (about 82% of the change), with C&H-implied 440 -> 569 kg.

Severity is medium, not high. This is a calibration gap in the Weight slider that shows mainly when the height is also set, not a gross anatomical error.
truth.correction:
Real-horse correction:
- At a fixed frame, girth should grow roughly with the square root of weight, and the model gives about half that response when the withers height is pinned.
- The finding's 173.5-205.3 cm target range at 163 cm is a formula extrapolation outside real Thoroughbred build. Real girth-to-height ratios are about 1.10-1.17, and 560 kg Thoroughbreds are usually 168 cm or taller.
- Over a realistic 440-510 kg at 163 cm, the target is about 182-196 cm and the model gives 191-197 cm.
- C&H's Y = 11,880-11,900 overestimates racing Thoroughbreds by about 6-8% (Secretariat: 193 cm girth, 177 cm length, 513-524 kg). Calibrate with Y of about 12,500-12,700 for Thoroughbreds.
- Mature racehorse girths are about 180-195 cm. The 176.5 cm figure is a yearling's.
- Within one horse, extra condition goes mostly to width and the crest, behind-shoulder, rib, loin and tailhead fat depots, plus gut fill. Chest depth is skeletal. More depth and a wider stance come from frame and conformation differences between horses.

- bulk already thickens the neck (0.8x) and the upper limbs, and widens the quarters too.
- The roughly 50% shortfall applies only when withersCm is set. For most roster horses, weight also raises the scale and about 80% of the change reaches the body.
