truth.reasoning:
Most of the software side checks out against the code, but the real-horse framing goes too far.

What holds (index.html:150-151, 632-637): the height slider runs 150-176 cm, but s is clamped to 0.93-1.07, so the model renders 151.6-174.4 cm. Godolphin's stud-book 14.1½ hh (146 cm) therefore renders at 151.6 cm. When a horse has no withersCm, s = 1 + (kg-475)/2400 (clamped 0.95-1.05), so the Weight slider changes height. Oguri Cap reads 157.9 cm at 400 kg and 168.8 cm at 560 kg. The bulk is sqrt(kg/(475 s^3)) clamped to 0.92-1.1. This gives the stated dead zones (176 cm: ≤~492 kg; 150 cm: ≥~462 kg). A slope of 1%/24 kg works out to M ~ h^5.05. All of this is confirmed.

What is overstated on real-horse grounds:

(1) The dead zones sit at slider corners where no real Thoroughbred is. Martinson et al. 2014 give ideal BW = 2.8·length + 4.2·height − ~600, which is about 7 kg per cm when length tracks height. Isometric scaling from 163 cm/475 kg gives about 8.7 kg/cm. On either rule, a 176 cm Thoroughbred in race condition weighs about 565-600 kg and a 150 cm one about 370-390 kg. A 176 cm horse at 400-490 kg would be emaciated, and a 150 cm horse at 460-560 kg would be obese or of another breed. So the clamp delivers a realistic horse, which is what the "~573 kg" and "~436 kg" C&H readings show. The defect is the readout, not the anatomy.

(2) "M ~ h^3 is the usual first guess" is a geometric-similarity convention, not an empirical way to predict height from race weight. Carroll & Huntington found that weight correlated much less with height (r²=0.62, in a mixed population) than with girth²×length (r²=0.90). Within one breed the height range is narrower, so the correlation is lower still. Height also contributes only weakly once girth and length are known (Martinson exponent 0.599). The best estimate of height from weight therefore shrinks toward the mean, with slope r·σh/σM. Tozaki et al. 2016 (Japanese Thoroughbreds in training) report SEs that imply SDs of about 2.2 cm and 23 kg; adult populations run to about 4 cm and 30 kg. With r between 0.6 and 0.8 the slope is about 0.06-0.10 cm/kg. That brackets the existing rule's 0.068 cm/kg and is flatter than h^3's 0.114 cm/kg. The roster's own height/weight pairs scatter by ±4-5 cm: 500 kg horses at 161 and 166 cm, a 468 kg horse at 167 cm, 430 kg at 160 cm, 540 kg at 170 cm. The RMSE is about 3.4 cm with h^3 and about 3.8 cm with h^5, which is no real difference. The "squeeze" to 158.9-168.8 cm is a defensible expectation, and 414→155.7 / 560→172 cm should not be presented as real-horse truth.

(3) The range is fine as extremes. Breed descriptions give 15.2-17.0 hh (157-173 cm), averaging 16 hh (163 cm). But the roster includes a 146 cm foundation sire, so the slider minimum of 150 cm already excludes a real profile, not only the clamp.

(4) The C&H numbers are in the right ballpark but depend on normalisation. My reconstruction of the TRUNK rings puts the reference model at a girth of about 195 cm and a length of about 162 cm, which is about 518 kg by C&H, not 475. On that basis 176/400 gives about 585-594 kg raw (about 540 normalised), and 150/560 gives about 453-459 kg raw (about 418 normalised).

Severity: the anatomy impact is small, because every rendered combination is a plausible Thoroughbred. What remains is honesty in the UI (the displayed value differs from the rendered one, by 5.6 cm for Godolphin) and the surprise of a weight slider that moves height. The fix to decouple weight from height is sound. Switching the inferred height to the cube root is not better supported by real-horse data than the current rule.
truth.correction:
The code facts are accurate: the clamps don't match the sliders, there are dead weight zones, the weight slider changes height for horses without withersCm, and Godolphin is shown as 146 cm but rendered at 151.6 cm. The real-horse claims need correcting:
(a) The clamp bites only at height/weight combinations no real Thoroughbred has. A 176 cm horse in race condition is about 565-600 kg and a 150 cm one about 370-390 kg (Martinson 2014 ideal-BW slope of about 7 kg/cm; isometric about 8.7 kg/cm). The rendered "~573 kg" and "~436 kg" horses are therefore the realistic ones; only the readout is wrong.
(b) M~h^3 is a scaling convention, not the real-horse way to infer height from weight. Within Thoroughbreds, weight varies mostly with girth and condition (C&H: r² 0.62 for height vs 0.90 for girth²×length). The best estimate of height given weight is compressed toward 163 cm, with a slope of about 0.06-0.10 cm/kg, close to the existing 0.068 cm/kg (1%/24 kg). Real individuals scatter by ±4-5 cm around either rule, so 414→155.7 / 560→172 cm is not "expected" real-horse behaviour.
(c) Thoroughbreds are typically 157-173 cm (15.2-17.0 hh, average 163). 152-178 cm is fine as extremes, but the roster includes a 146 cm foundation sire, so the slider minimum should go down to about 145 cm.
(d) By C&H the reference model itself reads about 518 kg (girth about 195 cm, length about 162 cm), so the quoted C&H figures depend on normalisation.
The recommended fix stays valid: show the rendered height, decouple weight from height, and widen the s clamp and slider so 146 cm is reachable. The cube-root inference has no better real-horse support than the current rule.

Code check (index.html):
- Lines 150-151 give the sliders as 150-176 cm and 400-560 kg (step 2).
- In buildFactors (633-637):

  - With no withersCm, s = clamp(1+(kg-475)/2400, 0.95, 1.05).

- The readout (4051-4053) prints look.size.withersCm ?? round(163*rig.scale) and sets the range input to that value. A range input clamps 146 up to its min of 150.

Re-run in node with the real buildFactors and data/horses.js (scratch script under %TEMP%):
- The roster has 149 horses. 10 have withersCm and 139 do not. All 139 have a weight, from 414 to 560 kg.
- Godolphin Barb has withersCm 146 and typicalKg null. It renders at s=0.93, which is 151.6 cm. The readout says 146 cm and the thumb sits at 150.
- At slider values 150 and 151 the horse renders at 151.6 cm. At 175 and 176 it renders at 174.4 cm.
- At 176 cm, bulk is 0.920 for every weight from 400 to 492 kg; it first rises at 494 (0.921). The threshold is 0.8464 × 581.9 = 492.5 kg.
- At 150 cm, bulk is 1.100 for every weight from 462 to 560 kg; at 460 it is 1.097.
- Oguri Cap (withersCm null):
  - 400 kg gives s 0.9688, 158 cm, bulk 0.962.
  - 560 kg gives s 1.0354, 169 cm, bulk 1.031.
  - So the Weight slider does move the Height readout and the rendered height.
- The local exponent is d ln M / d ln h = 2400/475 × s ≈ 5, so M ~ h^5 holds. That rule maps 414-560 kg to 158.9-168.8 cm.
- With (kg/475)^(1/3), the same weights give 155.7 and 172.2 cm, as the finding says.

Caveats. They change neither the verdict nor the severity:
1. The coupling only lasts until the user touches the Height slider. That writes withersCm into the overrides and pins s.
2. No roster horse hits the bulk clamp at its default weight (0 of 149 clamped). Only Godolphin Barb hits the height clamp. The dead weight ranges show up only when a user sets an extreme height and weight together.
3. The Carroll & Huntington weights (~573 kg and ~436 kg) depend on how the reference model is calibrated.
   - My ellipse-perimeter estimate at the girth row (TRUNK x=0.18: depth 0.715 m, half-width 0.28) gives roughly 540-570 kg for 176 cm/400 kg and 420-450 kg for 150 cm/560 kg.
   - Even the code's own intended mass model, 475 s^3 bulk^2, gives 492 kg at 176 cm/400 kg.
   - So the direction and rough size of the error are right, but the exact values are approximate. Part of the gap comes from bulk mostly scaling width: depth only changes by (bulk-1)×0.12 m, so the girth grows more slowly than the formula assumes.

Extra example: a horse with no weight gets bulk 1. At s=0.93 that is about 382 kg by the code's own model, but the Weight readout shows 475 kg.

Reference ranges: 15-17.2 hh is 152.4-177.8 cm. Carroll & Huntington is BW = girth² × length / 11877 (cm, kg). The user explicitly asked for more customisation, so sliders that misstate what they render matter. Medium is right.

findings.title: Measured roster girth and cannon values are ignored, and the quirk 'bone' setting counts height twice
findings.observed: data/horses.js stores measured girthCm and cannonCm (Haiseiko: 171 cm withers, 188 cm girth, 21.5 cm cannon; Kitasan Black: 170 cm withers, 190 cm girth). index.html never reads girthCm or cannonCm (grep: no match). As rendered: Haiseiko girth 200.5 cm (+12.5) and fore cannon 21.7 x s 1.049 x bone 1.07 = 24.3 cm (+2.8 cm, +13%); Kitasan Black girth 202.3 cm (+12.3) and cannon 23.9 cm. The quirk workflow converts an absolute cannon size to bone (~20 cm = 1.0, 21.5 cm = 1.07). But the model's reference cannon at 163 cm is already 21.7 cm, and it is multiplied again by the height scale s, so tall heavy-boned horses get bone counted twice. Haiseiko is labelled build 'heavy' ('heavy tank: thick neck, deep chest'), yet he gets bulk 0.964, a narrower trunk, neck and upper limbs than the 163/475 reference. His documented short cannons (膝下が短く) and body length shorter than his height (163 vs 171 cm) cannot be expressed.
findings.expected: Measured figures should drive the model directly. A 171 cm/188 cm-girth horse has girth:withers 1.10; Kitasan Black and the 158 cm yearling (176.5/158) are ~1.12. The model reference is 1.19 and Haiseiko renders at 1.17. Haiseiko's cannon should render near 21.5 cm.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the code side and it holds up. My own reconstruction of the trunk loft from TRUNK, PROF.trunk, ringAt and buildFactors gives a reference girth of about 195 cm at 163 cm, a ratio of 1.19-1.20. Haiseiko renders at about 201 cm (bulk 0.964, s 1.049) and Kitasan Black at about 203.5 cm. The fore cannon's narrowest ring is 21.5-21.7 cm at reference, and for Haiseiko it is 24.2 cm (x1.049 x1.07). girthCm and cannonCm are never read.

Real-horse facts that hold up:
1. ja.wikipedia confirms the 21 Dec 1974 measurements: 体長163, 体高171, 尻高169, 胸囲188, 管囲21.5 cm. It also confirms 「膝下が短く」 (short below the knee).
2. The reference girth is too big for a 475 kg Thoroughbred, which strengthens the finding. Carroll & Huntington (BW = girth² x length / 11880) give about 182-185 cm for 475 kg at a body length of 163-170 cm, a ratio of about 1.12-1.14. A 195 cm girth would mean about 520-540 kg. Secretariat, whose girth was famously large, measured 193 cm at 166 cm (ratio 1.16) at about 515 kg. The model's 1.19 at 475 kg is larger than his.
3. Bone should be judged relative to size, so counting height twice is a real error. The conformation rule is 7-8 in of cannon per 1000 lb. Haiseiko's 21.5 cm at 510 kg is 7.5 in/1000 lb, the same as 20 cm at 475 kg. Scaled to height instead, it is about 1.025. Either way, bone 1.07 overstates his relative bone, as the finding says.

Corrections:
(a) "Labelled heavy yet bulk 0.964" is not a real-horse contradiction. ja.wiki says 「体格の大きなハイセイコーの走りは重戦車にたとえられた」: the "heavy tank" image describes the running of a big-framed horse, not stocky proportions. ja.wiki also calls his body 「胴の詰まった体型」 (short-coupled). His measured girth:height ratio of 1.10 and his 510 kg are lean for his height: a 163/475 reference scaled up to 171 cm would weigh about 548 kg. So bulk < 1 agrees with the measurements, and hitting 188 cm would make him slimmer, not bulkier. The finding's own "expected" girth contradicts its complaint.
(b) "Body length shorter than height cannot be expressed" is overstated. The model is already slightly short-coupled: point of shoulder (x 0.72) to point of buttock (x -0.858) is about 158 cm at 163 cm withers, a ratio of 0.97. Scaled up, Haiseiko renders about 166 cm long against a measured 163 cm, only about 1.6% too long. His short cannons are the part that really cannot be expressed.
(c) The comparison ratios are weak support. Efforia's 176.5/158 is a yearling sales-catalogue figure that the data file deliberately leaves out. Kitasan Black's 170/190 was taken at age 2 at the 育成公社, before he raced. Immature horses are not a norm for adults. Mature Thoroughbred ratios run from about 1.10 (Haiseiko) to 1.16 (Secretariat).

The core claim stands (measured values should drive the model; bone should be relative to size; the rendered girth and cannon are too big), but sub-claims (a) and (b) need correcting. Severity: medium. The reference girth error it exposes affects every horse by about 5%, while the per-horse errors (about 6% girth, about 13% cannon) are modest on a stylised model.
truth.correction: The main claim holds: the measured girth and cannon are ignored, and the quirk bone value is absolute while the model then scales it by height. The model's reference girth (about 195 cm, 1.19) is too large for any 475 kg Thoroughbred. Carroll & Huntington predict about 183-185 cm, and Secretariat was 193 cm at 166 cm (1.16). The core of the finding is real. Several supporting claims are overstated or wrong, and the visible effect is small and touches very few horses.

Reproduced:
1. index.html never reads size.girthCm or size.cannonCm (grep finds no match). buildFactors (index.html:633-638) uses only withersCm and typicalKg/weightKg.
2. Only 2 of the 149 roster horses have a measured girth (Haiseiko 188 cm at 171 cm; Kitasan Black 190 cm at 170 cm). Only Haiseiko has a measured cannon (21.5 cm).
3. I rebuilt the trunk loft (TRUNK rows, the bulk/belly terms, the 12-point PROF.trunk polygon) in node. The reference ring at x=0.18 (the girthLow landmark in measurements.json) measures 195.0 cm, a girth:withers ratio of 1.196. Haiseiko gets s=1.0491 and bulk=0.9643 and renders at 201.0 cm (ratio 1.175, +13 cm over his measured girth). Kitasan Black gets s=1.0429 and bulk=1.001 and renders at 203.5 cm (+13.5). The finding's 200.5 and 202.3 are within about 1 cm of these.
4. The fore cannon ring at t=0.55 (0.030/0.041/0.035 on the 8-point limb profile) is 21.66 cm. Multiplied by boneK 1.07 and the root scale 1.049, Haiseiko's cannon renders at 24.31 cm against 21.5 measured (+13%). Kitasan Black renders at 23.95 cm.
5. horse-quirk-research.js:26 maps an absolute cannon to bone with about 20 cm = 1.0 and 21.5 cm = 1.07. The model's bone=1 cannon is 21.66 cm × s, so a measured cannon is skewed twice.

What is overstated or wrong:
(a) Height is not the main cause of the cannon excess. Of the +13%, about 8.3% comes from the baseline mismatch (21.66 vs 20 cm). Only 4.9% comes from the height scale.
(b) The complaint that a 'heavy' horse gets bulk 0.964 and so a 'narrower trunk, neck and upper limbs than the reference' is misleading. Widths are multiplied by s × bulk = 1.011, so in absolute terms Haiseiko is about 1% wider than the reference, not narrower, and his rendered girth (201 cm) exceeds the reference horse's (195 cm). He is narrower only relative to his height. His own measurements point toward a slimmer build, not a heavier one: girth:withers 1.10, and 510 kg at 171 cm is lighter than 475 kg scaled up isometrically (548 kg). So bulk < 1 is the right direction. The 「重戦車」 'heavy tank' label is a press epithet that his measured girth does not support, and the finding's own first fix would make him slimmer still.
(c) The body-length gap is tiny. The model's point of shoulder (x 0.72) to point of buttock (x -0.858) is 157.9 cm at the reference, a length:height ratio of 0.969, so the model is already shorter than it is tall. Haiseiko renders at 165.6 cm against 163 measured: +2.6 cm, or 1.6%. 'Cannot be expressed' is true, since there is no length control in CONF_CONTROLS, but the M-effort length-control fix buys very little.
(d) Fix 2 says it would regenerate 16 bone values. Only Haiseiko's bone (quirks.js:61) comes from a measured cannon. The other 15 come from words like 華奢 (slight, delicate) or 骨量に富み (rich in bone), so a height-relative cannon mapping changes only one value.
(e) The girth excess does not come from ignoring girthCm. It is systematic: the reference ring itself is too big for the 475 kg the model claims. The Carroll & Huntington formula, weight = girth² × length / 11880, gives 195² × 158 / 11880 ≈ 506 kg for the reference ring. 475 kg would need about 189 cm (ratio ≈ 1.16). That means every roster horse renders roughly 3% too big around the girth, not only the 2 with measured data.

Visible impact on the two horses involved: girth is +6–7% (about 2 cm on the half-width) and the cannon is about 3 mm thicker in radius. That is subtle on this flat-shaded model and affects 2 of 149 horses. The data path is still worth fixing and cheap to fix: read girthCm/cannonCm when they exist, and re-centre the reference cannon or the quirk mapping to about 20 cm. As a reference point, a typical Thoroughbred cannon is about 8 in, roughly 20 cm.

Confirmed: girthCm and cannonCm are never read. Haiseiko renders with a 201 cm girth (188 measured) and a 24.3 cm cannon (21.5 measured), and Kitasan Black with a 203.5 cm girth (190 measured).

truth.reasoning:
The direction of the real-horse claim holds, but its size and its reasoning are overstated.

What holds:
- Colts carry more cannon than fillies. Shojaei et al. 2026 is real (PMC13314181, Open Vet J 16(1):646-652): Arab stallions 18.96 cm vs mares 17.74 cm metacarpal circumference, P=0.001, about +7%. In Thoroughbreds, Tozaki et al. 2016 (PMC5048357, 18-month-olds) report colts 19.54 vs fillies 19.18 cm at almost equal weight (448 vs 443 kg), and 19.74 vs 19.24 cm by March. That is +2 to 2.6%.
- Bigger-framed horses tend to have more bone and larger feet.
- The TB cannon range of about 19-21.5 cm is right.

What is overstated:
1. The scaling laws do not apply here. Alexander 1979 (d ~ M^0.36) and McMahon 1975 (elastic similarity) describe scaling between species across orders of magnitude of mass, with length scaling too. They say nothing about how bone varies with body weight inside one breed at a fixed height. Within a breed, much of the weight difference is muscle, fat, gut fill and body depth. Real horses also do not keep bone stress constant. Biewener 1983/1989 showed that mammals keep safety factors mainly through limb posture, not bone allometry. A heavy-bodied horse on light bone ("light of bone", "not enough bone for his size") is a recognised real conformation fault. It is not something anatomy rules out.
2. The within-TB data show a much weaker link. In Tozaki 2016, colts gained 34 kg (+7.6%) and grew 5.4 cm taller from Sep to Mar, yet the cannon grew only 0.20 cm (+1%). Fillies gained 24 kg and their cannon grew 0.06 cm. The bone barely follows weight. The LCORL C/T colts were 17 kg heavier (+3.9%) and 1.6 cm taller, with +0.65 cm (+3.3%) of cannon. That is a skeletal-frame gene effect, not weight alone.
3. The target of 23 cm is outside the breed. Turning the published SEs into SDs (SE x sqrt n) gives a population SD of about 0.5-0.6 cm, roughly 3%. The finding's 20 -> 23 cm (+13-18%) would sit about 5 SD above the TB mean and above its own quoted 19.5-21.5 cm range. Its own example contradicts it: Haiseiko, a big and heavy horse (~510 kg), measured only 21.5 cm.
4. The stress arithmetic uses the wrong area. The measured cannon circumference (管囲) is the girth of the whole region: MC3 plus flexor tendons, suspensory ligament and skin. It is not a bone cross-section. The ~40% stress rise is therefore not a real-horse quantity. In TBs, bone adapts to load mainly by thickening the cortex (dorsal MC3 cortex) rather than the outer girth.
5. Hoof size follows frame and body size between horses, so heavier horses usually do wear bigger plates. But TBs are known for small feet relative to their mass. A horse that gains weight does not grow a larger hoof. A fixed sole area is therefore within real variation, though a mild scale with frame or mass is reasonable.

Corrected expectation at a fixed 163 cm, from 400 to 560 kg: about +4-8% cannon girth (e.g. ~20 -> ~20.8-21.6 cm), an exponent of roughly 0.1-0.25, not 0.35-0.5. Hoof scaling should be similar or smaller. Add a sex term of about +2-3% for colts.

The code observation itself is accurate: boneK and hoofK carry no mass term (index.html:1175-1177, 1209, 1225, 1160). But because the real difference between a light and a heavy TB of the same height is only a few percent, the anatomical error is minor. Severity drops from medium to low.
truth.correction: Heavier and male Thoroughbreds do tend to have somewhat thicker cannons and larger feet, but not by 13-18%. Interspecific allometry (Alexander 1979; McMahon 1975) and a constant-stress assumption do not describe variation within a breed at a fixed height. Within TBs, cannon circumference has a population SD of only about 3% (~0.5-0.6 cm). In Tozaki 2016, colts that gained 34 kg (+7.6%) grew only 0.2 cm (+1%) of cannon, and the sex difference (colts +2-2.6% in TB, stallions +7% in Arabs per Shojaei 2026) exists at equal body weight. A realistic rule at fixed height is about +4-8% cannon girth from 400 to 560 kg (exponent ~0.1-0.25; e.g. 20 -> ~21-21.5 cm, matching Haiseiko's 21.5 cm), not ~23 cm, which is outside the TB range. The measured cannon girth includes tendons and skin, so it cannot be used to compute bone stress. Light bone under a heavy body is a real (faulty) conformation, not an impossibility. Hoof size should scale with frame/mass only mildly, since TBs are known for small feet relative to body mass. Sex and build defaults (fix option 2) are well supported. The mass exponents in fix option 1 (0.35 / 0.3) should be roughly halved.

Re-measurement (scratch node script, same PROF.limb 8-point ring and the same clamps as buildFactors). All of the finding's numbers reproduce:
- The fore mid-cannon ring (t=0.55) has a perimeter of 21.66 cm and an area of 35.3 cm^2. At 163 cm it is 21.7 cm at both 400 and 560 kg.
- Area per 100 kg falls from 8.82 to 6.30 cm^2 between those weights.
- The fore sole is 10.0 x 11.2 cm (79.5 cm^2); the hind sole is 66.8 cm^2.
- At 150 cm the load on the four soles is 1.58 kg/cm^2 at 400 kg and 2.21 at 560 kg.

Where the finding overstates: it holds only when withersCm is set. buildFactors (634-636) handles a weight-only profile differently: s = 1 + (kg-475)/2400, and that scales the whole horse, distal bone and hooves included. That weight-only path covers 139 of the 149 roster horses; only 10 have withersCm. In the customizer it applies until the user moves the Height slider; line 3954 sets typicalKg and leaves withersCm alone.
- On that path the lightest horse (414 kg, Twin Turbo / Vivlos) gets a 21.1 cm cannon and the heaviest (560 kg, Hishi Akebono) gets 22.4 cm. That is +6.2%.
- Sole area grows 12.7% for 35% more weight.
- Across the roster, weight and modelled cannon correlate at r = 0.62, about +1.5 cm per 100 kg.

So for most horses, weight does thicken the bone and enlarge the feet. The exponent is about M^0.2 (d ln s / d ln M = 475/2400), roughly half the M^0.33-0.375 the finding expects. "A 560 kg colt stands on a 400 kg filly's bone" is literally true only at a fixed, explicit height: the 10 height-sourced horses, and the customizer after Height has been touched.

A related problem the finding mentions only in a fix option, and which is arguably the bigger fault: calibration.
- The reference cannon is 21.7 cm at 163 cm / 475 kg. The quirk vocabulary takes 20 cm as bone = 1.0.
- Bone quirks therefore stack on an already thick baseline and on the height scale. Haiseiko (171 cm, bone 1.07, measured 管囲 21.5 cm) renders at about 24.3 cm, 13% over his real measurement. Kitasan Black (170 cm, bone 1.06) renders at about 23.9 cm.

The near-orthographic sheets show only the 163 cm / 475 kg reference horse, so they cannot show a difference between weights. The fix options still make sense, but the mass term should apply only when withersCm is given (or should replace the s-from-kg coupling), so the weight-only path is not double-counted.

findings.title: Stride rate never depends on size, so height sets the speed, and in Field mode the hero's height sets the whole race's pace
findings.observed: makeGait scales stride by s but keeps T, so every horse has the same stride rate. The race gait runs at 1/0.43 = 2.33 Hz at any size, and the hero's speed scales with height (live, Tokyo, W=400 m). A 150 cm hero races at 15.25 m/s (61 strides of 6.56 m in 26.23 s); 163 cm at 16.32 m/s; 176 cm at 17.55 m/s, all at 2.33 Hz. In Field mode every runner's phase follows the shared ground scroll (updateRace: pose(r, (scroll+x)/strideM)), and that scroll moves at the hero's speed. Pick Twin Turbo (158.9 cm) as hero and the field runs at 15.77 m/s; pick Kitasan Black (170 cm) and it runs at 17.05 m/s, +8%. The same-sized opponent (158.9 cm) then strides at 2.33 Hz in one race and 2.51 Hz in the other. Meanwhile the race story assumes RACE.speed = 16 m/s and only its clock is rescaled.
findings.expected: Under dynamic similarity, horses of different sizes move alike at equal Froude number v^2/(g h). Stride rate then scales with h^-0.5 and speed with h^0.5. So 150 vs 176 cm should be ~2.41 vs ~2.25 Hz at ~15.7 vs ~16.9 m/s, half the model's speed spread (Alexander & Jayes 1983). Between species, stride rate at equivalent gait speeds falls ~M^-0.15 (Heglund & Taylor 1988). In racehorses, speed sets cadence. Witte et al. 2006 measured stance plus swing of 131+364 ms at 9 m/s (~2.0 Hz) and 77+342 ms at 17 m/s (~2.4 Hz), so stride rate rises with speed. Horses in one race share the race's pace whichever horse the camera follows. At the same speed a bigger horse takes longer, slower strides (stride ~h^0.7 by Alexander's stride formula).

truth.reasoning:
Two of the finding's real-horse claims hold up, and both are the ones that matter for Field mode. Horses in one race share the race's pace, and at a shared speed a bigger horse covers it with longer, slower strides (Alexander's stride formula gives stride ~h^0.7 at fixed speed). The cited numbers are also right. Witte et al. 2006 (PMID 17050854) report fore stance 131/77 ms and protraction 364/342 ms at 9/17 m/s. That is 495 vs 419 ms per stride, about 2.02 vs 2.39 Hz. Heglund & Taylor 1988 (PMID 3193059) report stride frequency at equivalent speeds scaling with M^-0.15 across species. So, from real-horse truth, the Field-mode result is a valid defect: changing the hero from Twin Turbo to Kitasan Black should not speed up the whole field by 8%, and a same-sized opponent should not change cadence between races.

Several parts are overstated, though.

(1) The expected solo-mode behaviour (equal Froude, speed ~h^0.5, so 15.7 vs 16.9 m/s for 150 vs 176 cm) does not describe Thoroughbreds at racing effort. Alexander & Jayes is a similarity rule for comparing animals at equivalent gaits, and it is reasonable for walk, trot and canter. It does not predict maximum speed. Hirt et al. 2017 (Nat Ecol Evol 1:1116) and Usherwood & Gladman 2020 (Biol Lett 16) find maximum speed is hump-shaped with body mass, flat to falling at horse size. An 8% speed gap from height would be about 190 m over 2400 m, while real race times between horses of very different heights differ by about 1-2%. Small and large horses alike win G1 races. Schrurs et al. 2022 (PMC9741461, 421 Thoroughbreds) found that a shorter or longer stride did not predict race success. Height should mainly change stride length and cadence, not pace.

(2) "Speed sets cadence" is weak at racing speeds. Schrurs et al. note that racehorses raise speed first through stride frequency up to about 45 km/h, then mainly through stride length at 45-65+ km/h. Witte's data agree: across 9-17 m/s, stride length rises about 60% (4.45 to 7.1 m) but frequency only about 18%.

(3) Height is only one factor in cadence, and not the biggest. Schrurs et al. measured peak stride frequency of 2.28-2.46 Hz with SD of about 0.05-0.08 Hz, and peak stride length of 7.3-7.9 m with SD of about 0.2-0.3 m. Sprinters stride about 0.1 Hz faster and about 0.3 m shorter than stayers, and the trait is moderately heritable (h2 about 0.2). That type and individual effect (the pitch vs stride style the user mentions) is as large as the size effect, so it should stay a separate per-horse parameter (run.stride) on top of any size scaling.

(4) Heglund & Taylor's -0.15 exponent comes from 16 species, mouse to 200 kg horse. Applying it inside one breed over a 1.6x mass range is an extrapolation. It does agree roughly with h^-0.5.

(5) The model's actual per-horse values are realistic. 2.33 Hz with strides of 6.56-7.53 m at 15.3-17.6 m/s all fall inside the measured Thoroughbred ranges above. No single horse looks wrong. The error is relational: pace depends on the hero's height, and in solo mode speed scales with h^1, which is too steep. Severity is therefore lower than medium.

Correct fix direction: race pace should be independent of size (RACE.speed, or a per-horse ability term worth about 1-2%). At that pace, stride ~ stride0·s^0.7 (times the run.stride style) and T = stride/v. Equal-Froude scaling should apply only to walk, trot and canter.
truth.correction:
Keep: in a race all horses share the pace, so a horse's height should change its stride length and cadence, not the field's speed. Bigger horses take longer, slower strides (stride ~h^0.7 at fixed speed). The Witte 2006 and Heglund & Taylor 1988 figures are quoted correctly. Correct:
(a) Speed ~h^0.5 (equal Froude) is right for comparing walk, trot and canter at equivalent speeds. It is not a real-horse prediction for racing speed. Within the Thoroughbred breed, racing speed is roughly independent of height (max speed vs mass is flat to falling at horse size: Hirt et al. 2017; Usherwood & Gladman 2020). Race and gallop speed should be size-independent, perhaps with a per-horse ability term of about 1-2%.
(b) At racing speed, cadence changes only weakly with speed. Above about 12.5 m/s speed comes mainly from stride length (Schrurs et al. 2022; Witte 2006: stride length +60% vs frequency +18% across 9-17 m/s).
(c) Individual and type differences in cadence, about ±0.07 Hz SD with sprinters about 0.1 Hz faster than stayers (Schrurs et al. 2022), are as large as the height effect. Model them separately from size.
(d) Every model horse's individual cadence (2.33 Hz) and stride (6.6-7.5 m) is within real Thoroughbred ranges. The defect is the hero-dependent field pace plus solo speed scaling with h^1, so severity is low.

truth.reasoning:
The code observations hold. root.scale.setScalar(scale) is at index.html:653. buildJockey (877-964) builds the rider under that root, from jockeyPivot = joint(spine, …). The cloth span C0=-0.22..C1=0.45 and the irons (BoxGeometry 0.06x0.05) are rest-space values that inherit s. fitDistance multiplies by k = rig.scale at 3164-3168, and setView multiplies the target by k at 3795. So a size change is mostly cancelled on screen. The size factor is clamped to 0.93-1.07 (about 152-174 cm), or to 0.95-1.05 when it is derived from weight, which keeps the effect modest.

What real horses and riders do:
1. Correct: rider, saddle cloth and irons have absolute sizes that do not depend on the mount. The JRA saddle cloth is one standard size: ja.wikipedia "ゼッケン (競馬)" gives a 510 mm x 695 mm trapezoid. This matches the code note and the 67 cm span at s=1. NAR Oi uses cloths that are shorter top to bottom, so the size is fixed per jurisdiction, not worldwide. Racing irons are sized to the jockey's boot, and leather length is set by the rider's leg and seat, not by the horse.
2. Overstated: "jockeys roughly 1.50-1.65 m". Real top riders span about 1.50-1.72 m. Yutaka Take is 171 cm and 50 kg (en.wikipedia). Eiji Nakadate is 152.0 cm and Hiroshi Kitamura 158.0 cm (ja.wikipedia infoboxes). Retired Irish jockeys averaged 1.65 ± 0.03 m (Cullen et al. 2016, J Sci Med Sport).
3. The named examples work against the claim. Kitasan Black's regular rider from 2016 was Yutaka Take, one of the tallest JRA jockeys at 171 cm. Twin Turbo's famous rider was Nakadate at 152 cm. In the iconic photos the rider-to-horse ratio of these two horses is therefore almost the same (about 1.0 vs 0.96). They would not show the "small rider on Kitasan Black, large rider on Twin Turbo" contrast the finding predicts. The contrast appears only with other riders, such as Kitamura on Kitasan Black in 2015 or Take on Twin Turbo in the Teio Sho.
4. "The main visual cue for size in racing photos" is overstated. Height varies by about ±6% among jockeys (152-171 cm), much like Thoroughbreds (about 152-174 cm here). That makes the rider-to-horse ratio a noisy cue. The fixed 51x69.5 cm cloth, rails, posts and other runners are steadier references.
5. Weights: under the JRA rules (ja.wikipedia 負担重量) the weight includes the rider, silks, protector and saddle. It excludes the helmet, whip, number cloth and goggles. Since 2023 the base weights are: older horses 58 kg (fillies and mares 56), 3yo G1 57/55, 2yo 55. The handicap minimum is 49 kg (open races) or 50 kg (other races). The real range is about 49-60 kg, typically 54-58, so "52-58" is a little low and out of date.

Net: the principle is sound, and the camera and cloth parts stand on their own. The expected behaviour needs correcting, though. A single fixed rider of about 1.52 m would make Take on Kitasan Black about 11% too short. The fix should be a counter-scaled rider whose height is a parameter (per-jockey data), not one fixed body.

truth.reasoning:
The code observation is accurate. A grep finds h.sex used only at index.html:3998 through the SEX label map at :3191. BUILD_CONF at :3293 has only rangy, tall, compact and heavy, and confFor at :3296-3297 merges build, quirks and own conf with no sex term. data/horses.js has 112 'male' and 37 'female' entries and no geldings.

The real-horse claim is right that the sexes differ, but it overstates the size of the difference for racing-age Thoroughbreds and rests on citations from other breeds.

1) Weight and size. Thoroughbred dimorphism is real but small. In Kentucky Thoroughbred yearlings (J Equine Vet Sci 2023), colts averaged 461.7 kg vs 446.8 kg for fillies (about 3.3%) and stood 155.3 cm vs 153.7 cm (about 1.6 cm). Japanese studies of young Thoroughbreds in training (J Vet Med Sci 2022, 2024) found colts had higher body weight and fat-free mass and a lower fat percentage than fillies. The roster's 486 vs 466 kg gap (about 4%) matches this, and the model already reflects it through weight and bulk. The 20 kg gap is small next to the 400-550 kg spread between individual Thoroughbreds.

2) The two cited studies are not Thoroughbred evidence. Toishimanov et al. 2026 (Animals) studies Mugalzhar horses, a Kazakh native milk and meat breed (100 mares, 120 adults, 68 foals). Its abstract does not state the "~7.8% heavier" figure, and that number cannot be applied to Thoroughbreds. Shojaei et al. 2026 (Open Vet J) measured 30 adult Iranian Arab horses. It reports significant stallion vs mare differences in scapula length, arm length, forepastern length and metacarpus circumference, but the abstract gives no sizes. Neither study supports the "8%" figure or specific limb factors for Thoroughbreds.

3) Crest, jowl and heavy forehand. These are testosterone-dependent traits of mature entire males, and they develop strongly with age and stud duty. They are weak in 2-3-year-old colts in race training. They are correct for horses shown as mature or at-stud stallions, such as Haiseiko at 650 kg. Applying them to every male, as the proposed crest 1.12 does, would exaggerate racing colts. A small racing-age difference of about 1.03-1.05 in neck width or crest, plus a larger multiplier gated on age 4+ or stud display, would be accurate.

4) "Longer, deeper-flanked barrel" for mares. This is a broodmare ideal and an effect of pregnancy, not a documented norm for racing fillies. Racing fillies are mainly lighter, with less fat-free mass. A wider pelvis in mares is true of the bony pelvic inlet, which is obstetric. External croup and hip width differ only slightly. A finer head and neck in fillies is reasonable.

5) The claim that geldings fall between the sexes is reasonable, but it does not apply here because the roster has no geldings.

Overall, the direction of the claim holds, but the effect sizes and evidence are overstated. Most of the visible Thoroughbred difference (about 3-4% body mass) is already modelled through race weight. What is missing is a subtle neck and forehand difference in racing colts and a strong crest only for mature stallions. Severity should be low, not medium.
truth.correction: The roster's 112 colts and 37 fillies do share one build apart from race weight. The "longer, deeper-flanked barrel" in mares is a broodmare and pregnancy trait, not a racing-filly norm. A suitable fix is small: about +3-5% neck and crest for colts and slightly finer head and neck for fillies. A larger crest should apply only to horses aged 4+ or shown at stud, and explicit quirk values should override these defaults rather than add to them.

The core claim holds up in the code. `sex` appears only twice in index.html: the SEX label map at :3191 and its use in the 'Born' info row at :3998. buildHorse (:641 onward), buildFactors (:633-638), BUILD_CONF (:3293), confFor (:3296-3298) and lookFor (:3306-3322) never read it. Two roster entries with the same size, conf and quirks would build identical meshes whatever their sex. The roster counts are right: 112 male, 37 female, no geldings. Mean race weight is 485.9 kg vs 466.4 kg, and mean bulk 1.0026 vs 0.9958. I re-ran buildFactors in a scratch node script on data/horses.js. That weight gap does reach the mesh at full strength: scale and bulk split it, and volume (s^3 x bulk^2) differs by about 2.3% on each side of the 475 kg reference.

Several supporting statements are wrong or overstated.

(1) "The weight gap is the only difference the model shows" is false for the roster as it stands. BUILD_CONF.heavy gives crest 1.1 and neck 0.98, and the researched data puts 27 males and no females in the 'heavy' build. With confFor applied to every horse, 29 of 112 males get crest above 1 against 1 of 37 females. The mean effective crest is 1.034 for males and 1.007 for females. Hindquarters, head and bone also differ slightly by sex through quirks: stay-gold bone 0.92 with the note 'skeleton like a filly's'; haru-urara bone 0.9. A sex-correlated crest difference therefore already exists, though it comes in through the build labels and per-horse data, not through a sex rule.

(2) "Only 4 of 149 horses get a crest value from quirks" is miscounted. Six horses carry an explicit crest. Three come from data/quirks.js: mejiro-ryan 1.2, forever-young 1.3, and gran-alegria 1.25, who is a filly. Three come from the horse's own conf in horses.js: godolphin-barb 1.45, haiseiko 1.2, hishi-akebono 1.25. On top of these come the 27 heavy-build defaults. Haiseiko's crest comes from his own conf; his quirks entry only adds bone 1.07.

(3) Magnitude. Even where crest is set, it only raises the crest line by 0.07 x (crest - 1) m (:692): 7 mm at 1.1, 14 mm at 1.2, against a mid-neck depth of about 0.4-0.5 m (NECK table :527-534). It never widens the neck. Neck half-width is w0 x neckBulk, with neckBulk = 1 + (bulk - 1) x 0.8 (:751-753). So the visible lack of a 'stallion neck' comes from two things together: no sex rule, and a crest control that has little effect. The second fix option (neck width driven by sex and weight) tackles the more important half.

(4) Realism. The roster is shown at race age with race weights, and the weight gap is already modelled. At 2-4 years, colt-vs-filly differences in shape are subtle compared with mature stallions: the testosterone-driven cresty neck and heavy jowl develop with age and at stud. So a default sex layer would make only a small visible change for most of the roster. The 'stallion' multiplier would only fit stud-age depictions, which the app does not use since it builds from race weights.

I could not check the two 2026 references (Toishimanov et al.; Shojaei et al.) because the web-search budget was used up. They should be treated as unconfirmed.

Net result: the missing sex dimension is real and is a fair customisation gap. But the claim that a colt and a filly look identical except for weight is overstated for the actual roster, the crest counts are wrong, and the visual impact at race age is small. I rate it low-to-medium, nearer low.

findings.title: Roster build labels barely change the body: 'heavy' and 'rangy' differ by about 1% in barrel width, and tall horses get thinned automatically
findings.observed: size.build ('average' 80, 'heavy' 27, 'tall' 15, 'compact' 18, 'rangy' 9) only nudges the neck: rangy neck x1.04, tall x1.03, compact x0.97, heavy neck x0.98 and crest x1.1. It never touches bulk, chest depth, bone, leg length or back length. Across all 149 roster horses bulk ranges only 0.957-1.045 (barrel width 49.1-53.6 cm). Mean bulk by label: heavy 1.013, rangy 1.000, compact 0.983. Because bulk divides weight by 475 s^3, a tall horse at a real race weight automatically comes out narrower. 'Heavy' Haiseiko (171 cm/510 kg) gets bulk 0.964 and Special Week (167 cm/468 kg) 0.957. 'Rangy' and 'tall' horses described as long-legged (Tamamo Cross '脚の長さだけが目立つ', Kitasan Black '背が高く、脚の長い体型') keep the same body depth to leg length as everyone else: withers-to-girth 0.80 m over girth-to-ground 0.83 m at 163 cm.
findings.expected: In conformation terms the build types are shape differences. A 'rangy' or 'leggy' horse has leg length clearly greater than body depth and a longer frame. A 'compact' or 'cobby' horse is short-coupled with a deep body. A 'heavy' horse carries more muscle in the neck, forehand and quarters and has more bone. Tall horses are not uniformly scaled-up small horses.

truth.reasoning:
The code facts check out. BUILD_CONF (index.html:3293) only sets neck and crest. bulk = sqrt(kg/(475*s^3)), clamped (633-637). Over 149 horses bulk runs 0.957-1.045, and the per-label means (heavy 1.013, rangy 1.000, compact 0.983) match the finding. Haiseiko gets 0.964 and Special Week 0.957. Note that Special Week is labelled 'average', not 'heavy', and that quirks.js already adds bone, hindquarters or barrel values for about 16 horses. The textbook definitions in 'expected' are correct in general: rangy/leggy means long-limbed with a shallow body, cobby means short-coupled, deep and short-legged, and shape is a separate axis from size. Several of the real-horse claims are overstated or point the wrong way.

1) The roster labels do not carry the textbook meanings. Of the 18 'compact' horses, almost all are described in their own notes as 小柄/華奢 (small, slight, delicate): Stay Gold ('skeleton like a filly's'), Admire Vega (小ぶりで華奢), Silence Suzuka (華奢で小柄), Rice Shower, Twin Turbo, Phalaenopsis, Haru Urara, Dream Journey, Vivlos, Mr CB, Samson Big and Biko Pegasus. Only Yamanin Zephyr and the Godolphin Barb are truly short-coupled and powerful. Mapping 'compact' to {chestDepth 1.05, barrel 1.04} would make these known slight horses deeper and broader, which contradicts the sources. Most 'heavy' horses are labelled for being 大型馬 (over 500 kg). For Meisho Doto the notes say outright that 'heavy' was inferred from race weights alone. That says nothing about extra muscle or extra bone. Bone thickness is a variance axis separate from overall size: Brooks et al. 2010, 1,215 horses across 65 breeds, found PC1 = overall size (loading positively on every measurement) and PC2 = bone thickness. So 'heavy = more bone' is not a safe default.

2) The Haiseiko example does not show an error. His measured girth of 188 cm at 171 cm gives a girth-to-height ratio of 1.10. Kitasan Black's measured 190 cm at 170 cm gives 1.12. Real measurements therefore support a slimmer barrel for Haiseiko relative to his height than for Kitasan, which is what the model produces (0.964 vs 1.001). What really sets Haiseiko apart is shape: short coupling (body length 163 cm, less than his 171 cm height) and short cannons ('膝下が短く'). That supports the leg-length and body-length gap, not more width. 'A tall horse at the same weight comes out narrower' is correct physics when shape is held fixed. Special Week at 167 cm and 468 kg was a lean horse, so making him slimmer is realistic.

3) Uniform scaling is the right first-order model. In Brooks 2010, PC1 (overall size) is the dominant component, and the roster's 414-560 kg race weights imply only about ±5% linear differences under isometry. A small width spread is therefore partly what the masses predict. Shape departures from scaling are real but second-order, so 'tall horses are not uniformly scaled-up small horses' is overstated as a rule.

4) Much of the 'long-legged' evidence describes foals. Kitasan Black is 'long-legged from birth', Speed Symboli as a foal or yearling, Nishino Flower at one month, Mejiro Bright at birth, Symboli Kris S at three months, Neo Universe as a foal. All foals look leggy. Rogers et al. 2021: at birth a foal is about 60% of mature height, the limbs make up 68% of withers height (falling to 63% by 6 months), and the distal limb bones are already close to adult size. Adult descriptions do support some genuinely leggy, thin-bodied horses: Win Variation (脚長だけど薄手), Katsuragi Ace, Tamamo Cross.

5) An average Thoroughbred already has legs longer than its body is deep. In Matsuura et al. 2024 (7 Thoroughbreds and 2 crossbreds), mean withers height was 159.9 cm and chest depth 76.6 cm: depth about 48% of height, leg about 52%. The model's 0.80/0.83 m is within that range. 'Rangy' is a matter of degree, perhaps depth around 44-46% of height, not legs simply longer than depth.

Net: the gap is real. The model has no leg-length or body-length (coupling) control and no adult leggy/shallow shape, so the finding stays low severity. But the label meanings, the Haiseiko example and the proposed compact/heavy defaults misdescribe the actual horses.
truth.correction: Shape does vary independently of size in real horses, and the model cannot show leg length relative to body depth or body length (coupling). That part stands. However: (a) in this roster 'compact' mostly means 小柄/華奢 (small and slight), and 'heavy' mostly means 大型馬 (over 500 kg, often inferred only from race weight). Neither means cobby/deep or more muscle plus more bone, so the proposed defaults compact→{chestDepth 1.05, barrel 1.04} and heavy→{bone 1.05, chestDepth 1.05} would misrepresent horses such as Rice Shower, Stay Gold, Admire Vega and Meisho Doto. Bone is an independent axis (Brooks 2010 PC2). Rangy→{chestDepth below 1, barrel below 1} does fit the adult sources (Win Variation, Katsuragi Ace, Nishino Flower). (b) Haiseiko's measured girth/height (188/171 = 1.10) is below Kitasan Black's (190/170 = 1.12), so his lower bulk is consistent with real data. His real quirk is short coupling (body length 163 cm against 171 cm height) and short cannons, which argues for body-length and leg-length controls rather than more width. Special Week (labelled average) being slim at 167 cm/468 kg is realistic. (c) Uniform scaling is the correct first-order approximation, since overall size is the dominant variance component and the roster's weight range implies only about ±5% linear change. (d) Many 'long-legged' descriptions are of foals, and foals are universally leggy (limbs 68% of withers height at birth). (e) The average Thoroughbred already has legs longer than its chest is deep (chest depth about 48% of withers height), so 'rangy' is a matter of degree.

- There is no leg-length or body-length control in CONF_CONTROLS (3259-3276). In data/quirks.js the long-legged notes for Tamamo Cross ('脚の長さだけが目立つ') and Kitasan Black ('背が高く、脚の長い体型') both have param:null, so the gap is real.
- measurements.json (static standing pose): withers y 1.622, girthLow y 0.826. That is 0.796 m withers-to-girth over 0.826 m girth-to-ground, as stated. Nothing in either horse's conf moves this: only 1 of 149 horses sets chestDepth.

Overstated or wrong:
1. "Never touches bone", and the named examples keep everyone's body. The label doesn't set bone, but the precedence chain does (build default < quirks < own conf). 40 of 149 horses get shape values from quirks: bone 16, hindquarters 15, barrel 10, chestWidth 7. Haiseiko ends up with {neck 0.98, crest 1.2, bone 1.07}, Kitasan Black with bone 1.06 and Tamamo Cross with bone 0.92. The only thing those three really lack is leg and body length.
2. "Tall horses get thinned automatically" is not a defect in itself. bulk = sqrt(kg / (475 s^3)) normalises by isometric volume. That matches how weight scales in real horses (Carroll & Huntington 1988: body weight ∝ heart girth² × length). Tall horses at proportionate weight are not thinned: Kitasan Black, 170 cm / 540 kg, gets bulk 1.001. Haiseiko's own measurements back his slightly narrower bulk. His recorded girth is 188 cm at 171 cm, a girth/height ratio of 1.099, below Kitasan Black's 190/170 = 1.118 and around the Thoroughbred norm of roughly 1.11-1.13. What made him a 'heavy tank' was a short body (体長 163 cm vs 体高 171 cm, quirks-verified.json:333), heavy bone (21.5 cm cannon) and a thick neck. The fix he needs is a body-length or short-coupling control, not more width. Special Week is labelled 'average', not 'heavy', and 468 kg at 167 cm is simply lean for his height.
3. The barrel widths are slightly off. The widest TRUNK rings (x = 0 and 0.18) have half-width 0.28, which is 56 cm at bulk 1 and scale 1. So the roster spans about 53.6-58.5 cm (times s), not 49.1-53.6. The ±4.5% relative spread and the roughly 1.3% gap between heavy and rangy are right.
4. Side observation: the model's heart girth at the reference size is about 195 cm (perimeter of the 0.18/0.34 rings), against roughly 180-185 cm for a real 163 cm Thoroughbred. The base barrel is already on the stout side.

Net: the build labels are deliberately "gentle" (the horses.js header says so) and do little beyond the neck, and there is no leg-length or body-length control. Both points are confirmed. The "auto-thinning" framing and the Haiseiko example are misdiagnosed. Severity low is appropriate.

findings.title: Chest depth slider lowers only the floor of the chest. The elbow stays put, so a deep chest buries the elbow and a shallow one leaves it hanging below the ribs
findings.observed: chestDepth subtracts (chestD-1)*0.75 from the trunk floor over x 0.2..0.74. FORE.el (y 0.96), the forearm and the withers height do not change. Girth floor (lowest point, x~0.18) below the elbow joint: neutral 13.0 cm; slider min 0.90 gives 5.8 cm; max 1.12 gives 21.9 cm (clamp 0.85/1.15: 2.8/24.2 cm). Rib-wall half-width at elbow height (y 0.96) at x=0.40: 0.157 m neutral, 0.092 at 0.90, 0.203 at 1.12. The humerus inner/outer faces are at z 0.095/0.235, so at 1.12 the arm stands only 3.2 cm proud of the ribs (7.8 cm at neutral) and the elbow is buried. At 0.90 the arm's inner face sits outside the rib wall, and at 0.85 the ribcage does not reach elbow height at x 0.40-0.46 at all. The same window also drops the breast in front of the forearm (floor at x=0.58: 0.90 -> 0.81 m, 15 cm below the elbow and 10 cm ahead of the forearm). Leg (floor to ground) / body depth goes from 1.05 at neutral to 1.25 at 0.90 and 0.84 at 1.12, all from the belly moving. Sheet 11, bottom row: in 'deep chest' the forearm grows out of the barrel; in 'shallow, tucked up' the elbow and arm hang below a shallow trunk.
findings.expected: The elbow joint lies beside the sternum, so the chest floor sits a roughly constant 10-13 cm below the humeroradial joint. Estimate: TB chest depth 76.6 cm at 159.9 cm withers puts the floor at ~83 cm (Matsuura 2024); forearm 45.5 cm + cannon 28.8 cm (Mostafa & Elemmawy 2020) + ~21 cm fetlock height puts the elbow at ~95 cm. truth.reasoning:
The core real-horse claim holds. The horse's elbow sits against the lower side wall of the thorax at about the level of the sternum, held there by the superficial pectorals, which run from the sternum to the humerus and forearm fascia (Budras; Dyce, Sack & Wensing). Comparing depth of body with length of leg is the standard way conformation texts tell a deep-bodied horse from a leggy one (Baxter, Adams & Stashak ch. 2). So a horse of the same height with a deeper body does carry its elbow lower. Matsuura 2024 gives withers height 159.9 cm and chest depth 76.6 cm, which puts the chest floor at about 83 cm and gives a leg-to-body ratio of about 1.09, close to the model's neutral 1.05.

The deep end of the slider is outside what real horses show. A girth floor 22-24 cm below the humeroradial joint means the barrel reaches down to the upper forearm, which no horse has. The breast hanging 15 cm below the elbow and 10 cm in front of the forearm is also wrong: the inverted V of the pectorals meets the forearms at about elbow height. I checked the model numbers in measurements.json and they match: neutral elbow at y 0.96, girthLow at 0.826, so 13.4 cm.

The claim is overstated in four ways.

1. **The 10-13 cm offset is not an anatomical constant, and its derivation is weak.**
   - Matsuura's n=9 riding horses include 2 Haflinger crossbreds (7 TB). The paper does not state the chest-depth landmarks. The SD of about 3.6 cm, taken from SE 1.2, belongs to that mixed group, not to Thoroughbreds.
   - Mostafa & Elemmawy's 45.5 cm forearm is a lateral skin-landmark length; the frontal length is 47.9 cm. The paper gives neither withers height nor chest depth.
   - Adding forearm, cannon and fetlock height ignores carpal overlap and differences in landmark conventions. The estimated elbow-joint height (about 95 cm) is therefore uncertain by about ±5 cm, so a real floor-to-joint offset anywhere from about 5 to 18 cm is defensible.

2. **Real chest depth does not all sit below the elbow.** Depth measured from the withers partly comes from the height of the withers' spinous processes, which does not move the elbow. A deeper heart girth also carries some sternal, pectoral and fat depth below the elbow. Moving the elbow fully with the floor (1:1) is a reasonable approximation. Partial coupling (roughly 60-100% of the floor change), plus a few centimetres of free floor-to-elbow variation, would be closer to real horses.

3. **The shallow end is not unreal because of the vertical offset.** At slider 0.90 the elbow sits about 6 cm above the floor, which is inside real variation. What is wrong there is the model's geometry: the rib wall does not reach elbow height, so the arm stands off the chest. A real elbow lies against the chest wall, and being 'out at the elbow' is a conformation fault.

4. **Severity is lower than claimed.** The neutral horse is correct. The defect only appears at the slider extremes, and is clear mainly at the deep end and in the lateral rib-wall gap. That makes it medium rather than high.
truth.correction: Real horses tie the elbow to the sternum, and a deep-bodied horse at the same height has a lower elbow and a shorter leg below it, so the coupling the finding asks for is right. Two parts of the finding go too far. First, the floor-to-elbow-joint offset is not a fixed 10-13 cm; the cited sources only support roughly 5-18 cm. Second, not all extra chest depth lowers the elbow: some comes from withers height or from sternal and pectoral mass below the elbow. So the elbow should follow most of the floor change (about 60-100%) rather than a strict 1:1. The deep end is clearly unreal (girth floor 22-24 cm below the elbow, breast dropped 15 cm in front of the forearm). At the shallow end the 6 cm offset is acceptable; the fault there is the rib wall not reaching the elbow from the side. The SD reference is weak: Matsuura's n=9 includes 2 Haflinger crossbreds and does not define chest depth.

truth.reasoning:
The real-horse rules about the belly are right. The finding then applies them to the wrong part of the body.

1. What holds. In a fit Thoroughbred the belly is deepest at the girth, or just behind the xiphoid. The standard abdominocentesis site, "the most dependent point of the abdomen", is about 5-10 cm caudal to the xiphoid. From there the belly rises to the fold of the flank (plica lateralis), which runs from the abdominal wall to the stifle. A very steep rise is the herring-gutted / wasp-waisted fault. Tuck-up does not make the belly drop again.

2. The model's belly already obeys this. I re-ran the trunk replica (trunk.cjs) in 4 cm steps from x 0.40 to -0.36:
   - tuckUp 1: rises 0.831 → 0.943.
   - lean (chestDepth 0.9 + tuckUp 1): rises 0.905 → 0.943, with a plateau from -0.20 to -0.36.
   - chestDepth 1.12 + tuckUp 1: rises 0.741 → 0.943. A 20 cm rise is what "deep chest + tucked up" should give at the extremes: a herring-gutted look.
   So in every combination the belly is deepest at the girth and rises to the flank.
   The rows the finding calls the lowest point (x -0.52 to -0.68, at 0.845-0.876) are not belly. They lie between the hip joint (x -0.515) and the point of buttock (-0.858), on the midline between the thighs. That is hindquarter and hamstring mass.

3. The finding's own 'expected' says "behind it the outline is thigh". It should also say what that implies: on a real horse the profile does fall again behind the flank fold. The stifle and the cranial thigh drop below the top of the flank hollow, and the stifle sits at about the belly line. The caudal outline then runs down the hamstrings (semitendinosus, biceps femoris) and the gaskin to the point of hock, about 0.56-0.6 m here. That follows from the conformation plumb line from the point of buttock to the point of hock (Stashak).
   - So the hollow between belly and stifle is real anatomy.
   - At x = -0.68 a real horse's lower outline is much lower than 0.855, not higher.
   - "Lowest point 32 cm behind the stifle, below the girth" is therefore not a real-horse fault.

4. The drop behind the stifle does not come from the sliders. The neutral horse has it too: 0.889 at x -0.20 falls to 0.845 at -0.52. It belongs to the static box-shaped hindquarter, which another critic has already reported ("The belly line stays flat and then drops between the hind legs, leaving a box-corner ledge over the gaskin" in critic-findings-raw.json). The underline sliders are not the cause.

5. "A shallow-chested horse is still deepest at the girth" is overstated.
   - It holds for race-fit Thoroughbreds.
   - An unfit horse, a broodmare or a grass-bellied horse often has a belly level with or below a shallow girth. That is a condition fault, but it is common normal variation.
   - In the model, chestDepth 0.9 alone puts the belly only about 1 cm below the girth at x 0 to -0.2. That is negligible. Its 3 cm drop at -0.36 is at the stifle, where the outline turns into the stifle and flank fold.

6. Both proposed fixes would make the model less like a real horse. Clamping or raising the rows from -0.52 to -0.86 up to the fold height (about 0.94) would lift the crotch and the rear outline. That opens the 'split up behind' gap and removes the second thigh. A real horse fills that region lower, with hamstrings down to the gaskin, not higher.

Severity is low. The belly is anatomically fine in every slider combination tested. The visible defect is the hindquarter box corner, which is a separate finding.

The real-horse description of the belly is right: deepest at the girth or just behind the xiphoid, rising to the fold of the flank at the stifle, with no second belly drop. But the model's belly already does this for every slider combination checked:

truth.reasoning:
The core real-horse claim holds, but the evidence is weaker than stated and the amplitude argument uses the wrong yardstick.

What holds:
- In a Thoroughbred the withers are a summit above both the lowest point of the back and the crest where the neck ties in. They are formed by the long dorsal spinous processes of about T3–T11, and the summit is at about T4–T6 (sources differ by one vertebra).
- The standard "height at withers" is taken at that highest point.
- I checked Matsuura 2024 (PMC10955269, Table 1, full text): withers 159.9 ± 2.6 (SE) cm, back 150.8 ± 2.6 cm, croup 159.2 ± 2.6 cm. The same group's 2021 method (PMC8437753) defines "height at back" as ground to the lowest point of the back. So a drop of about 9 cm from withers to back is a fair figure.
- I verified the model side. The trunk-top bell adds +1.44 cm at x=0.34, +2.5 cm at x=0.40 and +3 cm at x=0.46. NECK_ROWS[0] barely moves under stretch (about 2 mm), so the crest at x=0.46 is about 1.66 m and still above the raised trunk top (1.655 m).
- The model's withers landmark (1.622 m) is about 9 cm above its lowest back (about 1.53 m at x=0). So the model's average drop already matches the real one. The defect is that the summit is hidden under the crest, not that the drop is missing.

What is overstated or needs correcting:
1. "In TBs" is too strong. Matsuura 2024 measured 9 riding and research horses as one group: 7 Thoroughbreds plus 2 Haflinger crosses, aged 4–19 (mean 14.1 years), weighing 542 ± 43 kg. Only group means with SE are reported, with no breed split. These are older riding horses, not 2–5-year-old racehorses. Backs tend to dip more with age, so the 9 cm is an approximate mixed-sample figure, not a Thoroughbred norm.
2. Comparing ±3 cm to "a third of the drop" is a framing error. The roughly 9 cm withers-to-back drop is something every horse has. It is not the spread between low and high withers. Even flat or mutton withers stand above the lowest point of the back, so the slider should not cover the whole drop. No cited source puts a number on the between-horse spread of withers prominence in Thoroughbreds. The proposed ±5 cm therefore has no data behind it, and ±3 cm may well be within normal variation. The real problem is that the bump is invisible because the crest covers it, not that it is too small.
3. Mutton (low, broad, poorly defined) withers are uncommon in Thoroughbreds, a breed known for high, well-defined withers. Wikipedia also links high withers with a narrow chest. A horse with mutton withers has no summit above the neck tie-in; the neck blends into the back. The model's current hidden-summit topline is therefore close to the real "low, flat" end, not wrong for every horse. Only the "high, prominent" end cannot be reached.
4. Withers height and where the neck ties in are related but treated as separate traits in conformation guides. Saying the withers slider "changes where the crest ties in" is reasonable for the high end. It is not a measured relationship.

Net: the topline the finding expects is right for a typical Thoroughbred, and the slider really does fail to make a visible summit. The amplitude argument and the "Thoroughbred" label on the data need the corrections above.
truth.correction:
Real horses do have a withers summit at about T4–T6 that stands above the lowest point of the back. In a typical Thoroughbred with normal or high withers it also stands above the crest where the neck ties in, so "high, prominent" should form a visible peak, and the current slider cannot make one.

Corrections to the finding:
(a) Matsuura 2024 (159.9 vs 150.8 cm) is a mixed group of 9 riding horses (7 Thoroughbreds, 2 Haflinger crosses) with a mean age of 14 and only group means reported. It is an approximate drop for the group, not a Thoroughbred racehorse norm.
(b) The roughly 9 cm withers-to-back drop is the average topline every horse has, and the model already reproduces it (withers landmark 1.622 m vs back about 1.53 m). It is not the spread between flat and high withers, so "±3 cm is a third of the drop" is the wrong comparison. No source supports ±5 cm, and even low or mutton withers stay above the lowest point of the back.
(c) Mutton withers are uncommon in Thoroughbreds and look like the current blended topline with no summit. So the fault is that the high end is unreachable and hidden under the crest, not that the amplitude is too small.
Fix the visibility first: put the summit just behind the crest root and lower or move back NECK_ROWS[0] at the high end. Keep the amplitude near the current few cm unless measured data says otherwise.

model.reasoning:
The core of the finding holds up, but the claim that the slider is "invisible" and that both settings give "the same topline" goes too far.

Code (index.html):
- Line 734 adds withersH*0.03*bell(x,0.46,0.14) to each TRUNK row top. Rows exist only at x = 0.18, 0.34, 0.46 and 0.58, and the loft is linear between rows, so the bell only changes those row values.
- NECK_ROWS (691-695) puts the first crest row at stretch(0.40,1.63) = (0.4017, 1.6313) and the second at (0.5974, 1.7334). The neck's first ring is tilted in the crest–throat plane, so no neck geometry exists behind x = 0.40.

Midline topline, computed with a node script that replicates the TRUNK, NECK, stretch and bell code (jitter ignored):

| Location | withers -1 | withers 0 | withers +1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trunk top at x = 0.46 | 1.595 | 1.625 | 1.655 |
| Neck crest at x = 0.46 | 1.662 | 1.662 | 1.662 |
| Topline at x = 0.34 | 1.581 | 1.595 | 1.609 |
| Topline at x = 0.40 | 1.588 | 1.610 | 1.632 |
| Step at the neck root (crest minus trunk) | 4.3 cm | 2.1 cm | -0.15 cm |

- At x = 0.46 the crest stays above the trunk even at +1. From x = 0.42 forward the topline is identical for all values.
- The critic's +2.5 cm at x = 0.40 is really +2.2 cm in the mesh, because the value is interpolated between the 0.34 and 0.46 rows.
- No value of the slider gives a local maximum between x = 0.2 and 0.6. The topline always rises steadily from the back into the crest. So the claim that it "never forms a summit" is confirmed.
- The standing measurement puts the withers landmark at (0.457, 1.622), on the trunk top hidden under the crest.
- In motion the neck drops at most about 10° relative to the body (race: neck1→poll at 19-26° vs 28.8° standing). Even at +1 that uncovers the bump by only a few millimetres, so the gaits do not change this.

What is overstated:
- The slider is not invisible. Over x ≈ 0.20-0.40, the topline differs by up to 4.4 cm between -1 and +1.
- Most visibly, it changes the step where the neck root meets the back: 4.3 cm at -1, 2.1 cm at 0, nothing at +1.
- I cropped and enlarged the side close tiles of sheet 11 with PIL. The neutral and 'low withers' tiles show a notch where the crest rises off the back. The 'high withers' tile shows a smooth ramp from the back into the crest. So the toplines are not the same.

The real defect is a little different from what the critic says. The slider works, but in the wrong place and in the wrong direction for how it reads. 'High, prominent' removes the only cue that marks the withers (the step at the neck root) and blends the back into the neck. 'Low, flat' deepens that notch. Neither setting ever makes a withers summit.

Notes on the critic's evidence and fixes:
- Reference check: Matsuura 2024 (PMC10955269) does report withers 159.9 cm and back 150.8 cm. These are pooled from 9 riding horses (7 Thoroughbreds and 2 crossbreds), not Thoroughbreds alone.
- The model's default trunk drop from withers row to lowest back is already 9.5 cm (1.625 vs 1.530 at x = 0), so ±3 cm is indeed about a third of it.
- Fix option 1 needs care. Moving the bell centre to x = 0.42 only reweights the rows at 0.34 and 0.46, so on its own it cannot make a peak at 0.42. A summit needs a trunk row near x 0.38-0.42, or the crest root (NECK[0]) lowered and moved forward, as the critic also suggests.

Severity stays medium: a labelled conformation control does not produce the conformation it names.
model.correction: The slider does change the topline, but only behind the neck root. Between -1 and +1 the topline differs by up to 4.4 cm at x = 0.40 (±2.2 cm, not 2.5) and 2.9 cm at x = 0.34. It also changes the step where the crest meets the back: 4.3 cm at -1, 2.1 cm at 0, about 0 at +1. In sheet 11 this shows as a notch in the neutral and low tiles and a smooth ramp in the high tile. So the two toplines are not identical. What is true is that the bell's peak at x = 0.46 stays under the neck crest (1.662 vs at most 1.655), so no setting ever gives a withers summit above both the crest tie-in and the back. 'High, prominent' actually blurs the back into the crest, the opposite of what the label says. The Matsuura 159.9 / 150.8 cm figures are pooled from 9 riding horses (7 Thoroughbreds and 2 crossbreds). A fix needs either an extra trunk row near x 0.38-0.42 or the first crest row (NECK[0]) lowered and moved forward. Moving the bell centre alone is not enough, because the loft is linear between the rows at 0.34 and 0.46.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the code against the finding and it matches. index.html:683 clamps bone to 0.85-1.2, and line 3273 sets the slider to 0.9-1.15. The mid-cannon section is [0.55, 0.03, 0.041, 0.035] on the PROF.limb octagon (line 1209), with the hind cannon at 1225. I recomputed the perimeters: 21.66 cm fore and about 22.0 cm hind at bone 1, 24.9 cm at bone 1.15 and 26.0 cm at 1.2. The fitted ellipse comes to 22.15 cm. The pastern/coronet replica gives the stated overhangs: 0.9 mm at bone 1.15, 3.5 mm at bone 1.15 with hoof 0.9, and 6.8 mm at the clamp extremes.

The real-horse expectation is where the finding goes too far.

1. The data behind "~20 cm, ±2 SD ≈ ±5%" comes from young or mixed horses.
- Tozaki 2016 measured colts aged about 18-24 months, with withers height 159.2 cm and 482.7 kg in March. Colts were 19.54 cm in September and 19.74 cm in March, so they were still growing.
- In that study the LCORL genotype alone shifts colts by about 0.65 cm (C/T 20.1 vs T/T 19.5 cm).
- The derived SD of about 0.5 cm is the within-cohort, within-sex spread of one group of young horses. It is not the spread of the breed.
- Matsuura 2024 (20.6 ± 0.3 SE) measured 9 riding horses, 7 TB and 2 crossbreds, aged 4-19 years and 502-594 kg. They are not "mature TBs" in the racing sense, and the SD from that study is about 0.9 cm.

2. A larger adult sample of a TB-derived light breed gives a wider spread. The Sardinian Anglo-Arab study (Mura et al. 2020, n=6033, all at least 3 years old) found cannon circumference 20.5 ± 1.0 cm overall (CV 4.9%), and males at 162.9 cm withers height 20.9 ± 1.1 cm. Weller 2006 confirms that every circumference measure correlates with withers height. So a mature 163 cm Thoroughbred should be about 20.5-21 cm, with SD about 1-1.2 cm. That puts ±2 SD at about ±10% (roughly 18.7-23 cm), not ±5%.

3. What this means for the model:
- The neutral 21.7 cm is about +0.7 SD. That is normal to slightly heavy-boned, not "off-centre".
- Scaling by 0.93 to reach 20 cm would match a yearling or filly and make the reference horse fine-boned. About 0.95-0.97 (about 20.8 cm) is the right target.
- The slider's low end (19.5 cm) is fine. The clamp's low end (18.4 cm) is borderline at about -2.3 SD.

4. The upper end is a real problem. 24.9 cm is about +3.6 SD for adult males (more than +4 SD only against the young-horse SDs) and is outside the Thoroughbred range. The 26 cm clamp is further out. Only 0.9-1.08 is used by the 16 quirk horses, so no current roster horse reaches it.

5. The coronet point holds. In a sound horse the coronary band is not overhung by the pastern; a bulge above the coronet goes with problems such as high ringbone. However, at the slider's own limits the overhang is only 0.9-3.5 mm, which is barely visible.

6. The finding notes the change is "invisible". That fits real horses: across the breed, ±2 SD is only about ±0.6-0.7 cm of cannon width. This supports the option to read bone at the knee, hock and fetlock rather than mid-cannon.

Taken together, the anatomy defect is real but small, and the reference numbers need correcting. I rate the severity low.
truth.correction:
Correct parts: the slider's top end (bone above about 1.06-1.08, 23+ cm) is outside the Thoroughbred range, and heavy bone with a small foot letting the pastern overhang the coronet is anatomically wrong.

Overstated parts:
- Target for neutral: an adult 163 cm Thoroughbred should be about 20.5-21 cm, not 20 cm. 20 cm is the value for 18-24-month-old colts (Tozaki 2016: 19.74 cm at 159 cm) and fillies (19.24 cm). The current 21.7 cm is about +0.7 SD, normal to slightly heavy.
- Spread: the breed-level SD is about 1.0-1.2 cm (CV about 5%; Sardinian Anglo-Arab adults, n=6033: males 20.9 ± 1.1 cm at 162.9 cm). So ±2 SD is about ±10% (about 18.7-23 cm), not ±5% (19-21.5 cm).
- The ">4 SD" figure: 24.9 cm is about +3.6 SD for adult males. It exceeds 4 SD only against the young-cohort SDs.
- Matsuura 2024 measured mixed riding horses (7 TB, 2 crossbreds, aged 4-19), not a pure mature TB sample.

Suggested fix: scale the sections by about 0.96 (about 20.8 cm at bone 1), or keep the section and narrow the slider to about 0.86-1.06. Tie the coronet width to the pastern width. Put most of the visible "bone" difference into the joints and tendon depth.

truth.reasoning:
The qualitative real-horse point holds up. Heavy quarters on a real horse are muscle (middle gluteal over the croup, and biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus, which in the horse have vertebral heads reaching up toward the tail root, behind the thigh), sitting on a fixed skeleton. So they show as a fuller, rounder croup and caudal-thigh outline and as width through the thighs and stifles. Scaling only half-widths of a box-shaped trunk will not reproduce that. Rib spring showing behind the elbow from the front and from above is standard conformation description. The quantitative support, though, is overstated, and two cues need correcting.

1) The statistics are real, but the finding draws more from them than they support. I checked the source. Matsuura 2024 (PMC10955269) reports mean ± SE, so the SDs in the finding are SE×3: chest 2.1, croup 1.5, waist 3.0, girth 5.4 cm. That arithmetic is right. But the sample is n = 9 riding horses: 7 TB and 2 crossbreds (the 2021 companion paper lists Haflinger crosses), aged 4–19 years, mean 542 kg. That is not a Thoroughbred racehorse population. With n = 9 the 95% CI of an SD runs from about 0.68x to 1.9x the point estimate (chest SD 1.4–4.0 cm, tuber coxae 2.0–5.8 cm). Matsuura 2021 (PMC8437753) confirms the definitions: chest = outer humeri, croup = between the hip joints, waist = between the tubera coxae. These are caliper widths between bony landmarks. Muscle mass, which is what a 'hindquarters' control is meant to vary, hardly changes them, so they do not bound how much the muscled silhouette varies. Tozaki 2016 (PMC5048357) is also mean ± SE. Its SD for chest circumference works out to about 3.1–3.7 cm (SE 0.4–0.5, n = 48–59), but that is a uniform cohort of 18–25-month-olds in training and a circumference, not a width.

2) '±10–15% spans about ±3–4 SD' is not uniform. At 15%, using the finding's own SDs: chest width is about 2.8 SD, tuber coxae 2.6 SD, croup 5 SD. Barrel 1.1 changes girth by only about 1.9 cm (0.35 SD), so that slider is timid in girth terms. At the CI upper bounds, chest and tuber coxae fall to about 1.4 SD.

3) 'More width at the stifles than at the points of hip' is mainly a stock-horse (QH) judging ideal. In racing TBs the stifle width is usually about equal to the width at the points of hip. As a direction of change with heavier quarters it is right. As an absolute target for a TB default it is overstated. Another real rear-view cue is missing: a well-muscled croup is rounded or grooved in cross-section, while a lean one is peaked at the tuber sacrale.

4) The croup summit (tuber sacrale) is bone under thin cover. Muscling rounds the posterior and lateral croup, between the point of hip, the tail head and the buttock. It does not raise croup height. So fix option 1's '+2–3 cm at max' over x −0.36..−0.8 would wrongly raise the croup peak (row −0.52).

5) 'Second thigh' is the gaskin (the region from stifle to hock). The finding's text uses it correctly, but the fix's 'hamstring / second-thigh mass' runs the two terms together. Related raw findings even call the hamstrings 'the second thigh'.

On the model side, the code matches the description: rear = smoothstep(−0.2, −0.55, x) acts on width only, the TRUNK rear rows are unchanged, and kQuarters only thickens the femur and tibia. An enlarged crop of sheet 11 shows 'rear: quarters 1.15' about 10% wider at the rump than neutral, so 'look the same' holds for the top and side views but is overstated for the rear view. Severity stays medium: this is a customisation control that barely reads, which matters given the user's goal, but it does not break the anatomy.

truth.reasoning:
The code observations are accurate. Line 1127 sets the tail root y to 1.5 ± 0.025 and the dock angle to -100 ∓ 14°, with dir = (sin a, -cos a). That makes the dock leave the croup about 4° below horizontal at tailSet = -1, 10° above at 0 and 24° above at +1. The TRUNK croup rows and HIND.hip (-0.52, 1.18) do not depend on tailSet. In the standing pose, croup (-0.525, 1.593), tail head (-0.833, 1.481) and buttock (-0.858, 1.27) give a croup-to-tail-head slope of about 20°.

The real-horse part is where the finding overreaches.

1) The Weller evidence is quoted correctly but applied to the wrong trait. The Weller 2006b abstract defines the coxal angle as "the angle between the ilium and ischium". That is the shape of the os coxae at the acetabulum. It is not the pelvis's inclination to the horizontal, not the croup (sacral) slope, and not tail set.
- The quoted results do check out from the abstracts:
  - Weller 2006a: "biggest relative variation in hoof related measurements and in stifle and coxal angle".
  - Weller 2006b: a larger coxal angle went with better performance and lower pelvic-fracture risk, and it was "the only parameter to have an effect on both risk of injury and performance".
- Their proposed mechanism is muscle alignment with the axis of the pelvis. It has nothing to do with tail carriage.
- Rotating the rear trunk, pelvis and dock as one rigid unit (fix option 1) would leave Weller's coxal angle unchanged. Modelling that angle would mean moving the point of buttock (tuber ischii) relative to the hip joint and the point of hip (tuber coxae).
- The Weller results also need caveats:
  - The cohort was 108 National Hunt (jump) Thoroughbreds, not flat racers.
  - 2006b calls itself preliminary with limited statistical power.
  - 2006a concludes that "variation in conformational parameters was relatively small".
  - The companion reliability paper (Weller 2006, PMID 17228574) found that locating anatomical landmarks caused the biggest measurement variation for proximal parameters. So the large relative variation of the coxal angle is partly measurement noise.

2) "Tail set follows from the croup" is a tendency, not a rule. Standard conformation summaries (Wikipedia, Equine conformation, drawing on texts such as Hedge & Wagoner 2004 and Thomas 2005) say:
- A high tail set is "often, although not always" associated with a flat croup, and has "no direct performance consequence".
- A low set is "only aesthetic concern unless directly caused by pelvic conformation".
- The croup angle and the pelvic ("hip": point of hip to point of buttock) angle "do not necessarily correlate". A horse can have a relatively flat croup and a well-angled pelvis.
- Racehorses do well with pelvic angles of 20–30°.
- "Goose rump" is used for two different things: a steep rump, and a peaked croup with a flat but sloping pelvis that drops to a low tail connection.
