truth.correction:
Real horses often link tail set to croup slope: a flat croup tends to go with a high-set tail and a steep croup with a low-set one. It is only a tendency ("often, although not always"). Croup (sacral) slope and pelvic (point of hip to point of buttock) inclination can vary somewhat independently, and in Thoroughbreds a tail set that differs from what the croup predicts is cosmetic, with no proven performance or injury effect.

Weller's "coxal angle" is the angle between the ilium and ischium, which is the pelvis's own shape. It is not croup or pelvic slope and not tail set. The only performance and pelvic-fracture result in the finding (a larger coxal angle was better) is preliminary: 108 National Hunt Thoroughbreds, limited statistical power, partly confounded by landmark-placement error. It cannot justify a croup-slope or tail-set control.

If a pelvis control is wanted, keep two separate knobs:
- (a) croup/pelvis inclination, which moves the croup rows, the tail root and the acetabulum together;
- (b) a true coxal-angle (pelvic shape) control, which moves the point of buttock relative to the hip joint.

Fix option 2 (coupling the croup end to tailSet) is the right size for a cosmetic issue. Neither should be presented as performance-relevant anatomy.

Checking the real-horse claims against the PubMed abstracts (pulled through E-utilities):
- Holmström 1990 is quoted exactly: 356 horses, 60% bench knees, 50% toe-in forelimbs, 80% outwardly rotated hind limbs. But these are Swedish Warmbloods, not Thoroughbreds, and the abstract says "the majority of these deviations were mild or moderate". For Thoroughbreds, Weller 2006a (PMID 17228575, 108 National Hunt racehorses) found 25% of conformation parameters differed between left and right. It also concluded that Thoroughbreds differ from other breeds in joint angles and deviations, so Warmblood prevalences should not be carried over as Thoroughbred norms.
- The Weller 2006b summary is conflated. Fetlock (MCP) valgus lowered performance. Carpal valgus (and a larger MCP angle) raised the risk of superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT) injury. Tarsal valgus raised the risk of pelvic fracture. The paper is labelled "preliminary", the authors say its statistical power is limited, and it studied jump (National Hunt) racehorses rather than flat Thoroughbreds.
- "Offset knees contributed to fetlock problems" is quoted correctly from Anderson 2004b. But the same paper found carpal valgus protective: higher carpal angles lowered the odds of carpal fracture and effusion. So the finding's one-sided "valgus is bad" message is contradicted within its own sources.
- The flight-path statements (toe-out breaks over the inside toe and wings in; toe-in paddles; base-narrow plaits) are standard textbook teaching (Adams & Stashak). They are qualitative, though, and the quantitative evidence is thin. In Nauwelaerts 2017 (31 sound horses with varying dorsal hoof-wall asymmetry, measured on a pressure mat), the side-to-side (mediolateral) path of the centre of pressure under the hoof differed between each horse's left and right forelimbs. Hoof-wall asymmetry did not predict path asymmetry either way. No reference is given for the proposed 2-5 cm lateral swing excursion; it is a design guess.
- Several of the roster notes describe angular deformities, not rotation. Maruzensky's legs "bent outward below the knee, forming an 'A'" is carpal valgus, and Super Creek's left fore was "crooked". A static toe yaw at the pastern cannot show that. A per-leg frontal-plane angle at the knee or fetlock (valgus/varus) is needed alongside the toe yaw and base width.

Severity: the default straight, parallel legs are the textbook ideal and fall within normal Thoroughbred variation. Mild deviations of a few degrees would barely show on a low-poly model. This is a missing customisation, not an anatomical error. It matters mainly for the named roster horses, which the user explicitly asked to support, so medium fits better than high.
truth.correction:
The model genuinely has no frontal-plane conformation. Frontal-plane deviations are common in real horses and are linked to differences in limb flight and injury. Corrections:
(1) Holmström's 60/50/80% figures are for Swedish Warmbloods, and most of those deviations were mild or moderate. They are not Thoroughbred norms. For Thoroughbreds, Weller 2006a found left/right asymmetry in 25% of measured parameters.
(2) Weller 2006b, a preliminary study of jump racehorses with limited power: fetlock (MCP) valgus lowered performance, carpal valgus raised the risk of superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT) injury, and tarsal valgus raised the risk of pelvic fracture. It did not find that "carpal and fetlock valgus" both lowered performance and raised tendon risk.
(3) Anderson 2004b also found carpal valgus protective against carpal fracture and effusion in 3-year-old Thoroughbreds, so valgus is not simply harmful.
(4) Winging-in, paddling and plaiting are qualitative textbook associations. Their sizes are not well measured, and the proposed 2-5 cm swing arc should be treated as an artistic choice.
(5) Toe yaw plus base width is not enough. Notes like Maruzensky's "A-shaped below the knee" and Super Creek's "crooked" leg describe angular (carpal/fetlock valgus) deviation. That needs a per-leg frontal-plane angle at the knee or fetlock, a lateral offset of the cannon for bench (offset) knees, and inward hocks plus hind toe-out for cow hocks.
(6) Severity should be medium. The default straight legs are the correct ideal, and the gap matters mainly for the named roster quirks.

truth.reasoning:
The code facts hold. FORE.sc [0.5,1.5] and FORE.sh [0.72,1.22] are shared by every rig (index.html:552). In measurements.json the standing RF scapula slope is 51.4 deg and the knee is 179.9 deg. solveLeg sets fore flex = 0 in stance (1397). scapSwing comes only from GAITS (206-247), and tuneGait reads only look.run (257). The quirk notes exist: Saint Lite "upright (steep) shoulder" (data/quirks.js:39), Grass Wonder "very sloping shoulder" (:519), and Godolphin "slightly over at the knees" / "well laid back" (:28-29), all with param:null.

The finding overstates or misattributes several of its real-horse claims:

1. Ahmad 2025 (PMC11768722) measured Morna horses, a Pakistani breed, not Thoroughbreds. The figure, 58.38 ± 2.02 deg shoulder-to-ground at n=50, is right. But an SD of about 2 deg means normal variation is narrow, so the proposed ±8 deg is about ±4 SD and beyond normal TB variation; about ±4-5 deg (±2 SD) covers it. Weller et al. 2006a, a 98-parameter 3D study of 108 Thoroughbred National Hunt racehorses, concluded that "variation in conformational parameters was relatively small", and the largest relative variation was in the hoof, stifle and coxal angle, not the shoulder. The model's defaults already sit at TB norms: scapulohumeral angle 99.1 vs 99.0 ± 0.9 SE, elbow 137.6 vs 139.7 ± 0.8, knee 179.9 vs 178.0 ± 0.5 (Mostafa 2020, normal group).

2. Holmström 1990 is correctly quoted ("élite dressage horses and showjumpers had ... more sloping scapulas"). But it studied Swedish Warmblood dressage and jumping horses, not racehorses.

3. Weller 2006b does not support a sloping-shoulder racing advantage. The variable is the "flexor angle of the shoulder joint", the scapulohumeral joint angle, not the slope of the scapula to the ground. With the humerus fixed, a more sloping scapula makes that joint angle smaller. A larger joint angle comes with a steeper scapula or humerus, the opposite of "sloping is better". The authors also say the study's statistical power is limited.

4. Knee: Mostafa 2020 studied jumping Thoroughbreds aged 5-15, not racehorses. 178.0 ± 0.5 SE with n=17 is an SD of about 2.1, so "178 ± 2" is fine. The absolute value depends on the landmarks used: Ahmad reports 171.5 ± 2.4 for the same angle.

5. Back at the knee (hyperextended carpus) is described imprecisely. It puts tension on the palmar carpal ligaments and compresses the dorsal surfaces of the carpal bones. The injury it is classically linked to is dorsal carpal chip or slab fracture, not palmar loading as such. That link rests mostly on clinical opinion (Adams & Stashak). The objective Thoroughbred racehorse study (Anderson, McIlwraith & Douay 2004, PMID 15581320) found that carpal valgus seen from the front was protective and that offset knees contributed to fetlock problems; its abstract reports no result for sagittal back at the knee. Mild over at the knee is generally rated less serious and is common.

6. "Upright shoulder = shorter, choppier stride and higher knee action; sloping = more reach" is traditional conformation lore. None of the cited studies measured stride or knee action against scapular slope. Motion coupling ("build drives motion") is therefore a stylistic choice and should be a small effect, not presented as established biomechanics.

Net: the gap is real and matches the user's request for quirk customisation. The defaults are correct, real TB variation is only a few degrees, and the cited performance evidence is either for other horses or for a different angle. Severity drops to low.
truth.correction: Shoulder slope and standing knee angle do vary between horses, and an optional per-horse control is a fair customisation gap (three roster notes call for it). But variation within Thoroughbreds is small: Weller 2006a found TB conformation "relatively small" in variation, and Morna horses show an SD of about 2 deg in shoulder angle. Use about ±4-5 deg for the scapula, not ±8. For the knee, use about +3..+6 deg for over at the knee and at most about -3 deg for back at the knee. The current defaults (scapula 51 deg, scapulohumeral 99 deg, knee 180 deg) are already within TB norms. Correct the citations: Ahmad 2025 is Morna horses, Holmström 1990 is warmblood dressage and showjumpers, Mostafa 2020 is jumping TBs. Weller 2006b's "shoulder flexor angle" is the scapulohumeral joint angle, not scapular slope, so it does not show that a sloping shoulder improves racing. Back at the knee strains the palmar carpal ligaments and compresses the dorsal carpal bones (dorsal chip fractures); this is mainly clinical opinion, not proven in the objective TB study (Anderson et al. 2004). The upright-shoulder-means-choppy-stride/high-knee-action link is lore: if build feeds motion, keep the coupling weak and optional.

truth.reasoning:
The core real-horse claims hold up. Thoroughbreds do differ in how leg length compares with body depth, in cannon length ("short below the knee", meaning short cannons with knees and hocks set low), in withers-to-croup height (which is how uphill and downhill are judged) and in left/right symmetry. The model's numbers are also reported correctly: from measurements.json, forearm 0.96-0.50 = 0.46 m, fore cannon 0.50-0.209 = 0.29 m, hind cannon 0.56-0.213 = 0.347 m, withers 1.622 vs croup 1.593 m, girth floor 0.826 m (leg/depth about 1.04). Several supporting references are misquoted or overstated, though, and the real range of variation is smaller than the finding implies.

1) Mostafa & Elemmawy 2020 (PMC7316700). The paper says "All data are presented as mean and standard deviation (SD)", not SE as the finding states. The horses were 17 sound jumping Thoroughbreds at the Armed Forces Equestrian Club (aged 5-15, 450-600 kg), not racehorses. Withers height is not reported, so the lengths cannot be scaled to 163 cm. The lengths are skin-landmark distances (after Anderson et al.). The hind/fore cannon ratio of 37.4/28.8 = 1.30 is well above the usual MT3/MC3 bone ratio, which means the hind-cannon landmark starts above the hock joint centre. So 37.4 cm is not a like-for-like target for a rig built on joint centres.

2) Anderson & McIlwraith 2004 (PMID 15581319). The abstract reports "moderate to strong" relationships between long-bone lengths and withers height; "strongly" is a slight overstatement. The same abstract says distal-limb bone length grows only 5-7% from weanling to age 3, so cannon length is set early and does not grow much.

3) The finding leaves out the most relevant data: Weller et al. 2006 (PMID 17228575, 108 National Hunt Thoroughbreds measured in 3D).
- Variation in conformation was "relatively small".
- Most length measurements correlated with withers height, which the existing uniform scale already covers.
- The largest relative variation was in hoof measurements and in the stifle and coxal angles.
- 25% of parameters differed between left and right.
- No pattern of combined traits was found.

So segment variation that is independent of size is modest. A ±3 cm cannon range (about ±10% of the cannon) is at or beyond the normal Thoroughbred extreme. Real left/right differences show mostly in the hooves (mismatched feet) rather than in cannon length, so a per-leg hoof height or angle setting is a more realistic way to show asymmetry than a per-leg cannon change.

4) Matsuura et al. 2024 (PMC10955269) measured 9 riding horses: 7 Thoroughbreds plus 2 Haflinger crosses, aged 4-19. Heights were 159.9 ± 2.6 vs 159.2 ± 2.6 cm, which is effectively level. That is not a "mature Thoroughbred" sample. The model's withers sit 2.9 cm above the croup, which is within normal range. Young racehorses are often croup-high while they are still growing (Anderson & McIlwraith 2004 found withers and croup heights still increasing to age 2).

5) "Longer legs cover more ground at the same stride rate" is true geometrically, and dynamic similarity puts stride length in proportion to leg length (Alexander & Jayes 1983). At the gallop, however, stride length depends mostly on speed and the airborne phase, so a few centimetres of leg length gives only a small change in stride.

Overall: the customisation gap is real and the user asked for it. The claim that leggy-vs-deep is mainly a split between body depth and leg length is sound. But calling it "high" severity, and quoting real-horse numbers as precise segment targets, overstates how much Thoroughbreds actually vary.
truth.correction: Mostafa 2020 values are mean ± SD as published, not SE. They are skin-landmark lengths from 17 jumping Thoroughbreds with no withers height reported, and the hind cannon (37.4) starts above the hock joint centre, so it is not a direct target for the model's joint-centre 0.347 m. Anderson & McIlwraith report moderate-to-strong (not uniformly strong) correlations between long bones and withers height, and distal-limb bones grow only 5-7% after weaning. Weller et al. 2006 (n=108 racing Thoroughbreds) found conformational variation relatively small, with most lengths scaling with height. A uniform scale therefore covers most real variation. Independent per-segment ranges should be small: roughly ±1-2 cm on the cannon rather than ±3 cm. Leggy vs deep is mainly the split between body depth and leg length, and left/right asymmetry is better shown in the hooves than in the cannon. Matsuura 2024's 159.9 vs 159.2 cm comes from 9 riding horses (7 Thoroughbreds plus 2 Haflinger crosses) and shows mature horses are roughly level; the model's +2.9 cm withers is normal. Longer legs give only a proportional, small gain in stride length at the gallop. Severity: medium.

truth.reasoning:
The code-side gap is real. The only conf keys in index.html are neck, crest, head, profile, ears, earSet, earTilt, chestDepth, chestWidth, barrel, hindquarters, withers, tuckUp, bone, hoof and tailSet. None controls trunk length, and the roster really does contain long-bodied and short-coupled notes with param:null. Several parts of the real-horse framing are wrong or overstated, though.

1) The Matsuura 2024 reference does not describe "mature TBs". It is a 3D-scanner validation study of 9 riding horses: 7 Thoroughbreds plus 2 crossbreds (a Haflinger cross and a Haflinger x Japanese native). Mean age was 14.1 years and mean weight 541.8 kg. The means of 159.9 / 175.6 cm cover all nine horses, and body length was taken the way the Wagner & Tyler weight formula needs it. The resulting 1.10 ratio is high for racing TBs. Stick-measured norms and the classic conformation rule ("body length about equal to height, the horse fits in a square") give about 1.0. Another lens in this same review cites Ünal et al. 2025 for 24 TBs: body length 156.9 +/- 5.9 cm at 157.9 cm withers, a ratio of 0.99. I could not open its tables to confirm.

2) Haiseiko's numbers are correct: 171 cm withers and 163 cm body length, measured 21 Dec 1974 (ja.wikipedia, citing Akagi 1975). His ratio of 0.95 is only about one SD below the ~0.99 norm (an SD of ~6 cm is ~0.04). That makes him compact, not an extreme outlier. Setting it against Matsuura's 1.10 also mixes measurement methods: the Japanese 体長 is a straight measuring-stick distance.

3) "Short-coupled = loin (last rib to point of hip)" is correct English conformation terminology. But the roster sources (胴が詰まった, 胴長, 胴伸びの良い, Haiseiko's 体長) describe the length of the whole trunk. Shoulder slope, the thoracic back and hip length all contribute to point-of-shoulder-to-buttock length. A difference of about 0.95 vs 1.05 is about 16 cm at 163 cm, more than loin variation alone can supply. The control should therefore scale the thoracolumbar trunk (back plus loin, and possibly the croup), not only x -0.5..0.1.

4) The motion claim (short loin = stiffer, quicker strides; long back = more flex, longer looser strides) is mostly conformation-book lore. The only quantitative support I found is Johnston et al. 2002, a study of 20 sound riding horses on a treadmill at walk and trot. There, a long thoracic back gave greater lumbar lateral bending. Longer strides went with more caudal-saddle flexion-extension at the walk, but not at the trot. Nothing was measured at canter or gallop, and nothing on stride frequency. Jeffcott's classic association is about soundness, not stride: short backs with dorsal spinous process impingement, long backs with muscle strain. If coupling feeds motion at all, it should be a small effect, mainly lateral and lumbar bend, and not a stride-length or stride-frequency change. That change would also double-count with the run 'stride' slider.

5) The title's "long-bodied stayers / short-coupled sprinters" is trainer lore. Haiseiko's own trainer, Suzuki Katsutaro, thought his compact body capped him at 1800 m. He then won the 2000 m Satsuki Sho, and Suzuki said the horse had overturned that expectation. So body length should be a visual conformation control, not a proxy for distance aptitude.

Medium severity stands. Body length is a prominent side-silhouette trait, 11 roster notes need it, and the user explicitly asked for this kind of customisation.
truth.correction:
The control gap is real (no conf key changes trunk length). The real-horse framing needs these fixes:
(a) Thoroughbred body length is about equal to withers height, a ratio of ~0.99-1.0. Ünal et al. 2025 report 24 TBs at 156.9 cm body length vs 157.9 cm withers, and "fits in a square" is the conformation norm. The 1.10 figure comes from a mixed 9-horse group of older riding horses (7 TBs and 2 Haflinger crosses, mean 542 kg) in a 3D-scanner validation study (Matsuura 2024), so it is not a TB norm.
(b) Haiseiko's ratio of 0.95 (163/171 cm, stick-measured 体長, Dec 1974) is a compact horse about one SD below the mean, not a striking outlier.
(c) "Short-coupled" strictly means a short loin, but the roster notes (胴詰まり / 胴長) describe whole-trunk length. A ±5% body-length control should therefore scale the thoracolumbar back plus loin (and possibly croup length), not the loin alone.
(d) Effects on motion are weakly supported. Johnston et al. 2002 found only that a longer thoracic back gives more lumbar lateral bending, at walk and trot. Any motion coupling should be a small extra amount of bend and should not change stride length or frequency.
(e) Do not imply that body length sets distance aptitude: Haiseiko's trainer judged him an 1800 m horse from his compact body, and he went on to win the 2000 m Satsuki Sho.

truth.reasoning:
The code description is accurate. index.html:503 sets PASTERN = 0.14. Lines 552-553 set FORE.pastern to 33 deg and HIND.pastern to 30 deg. Lines 1194/1217 build the fetlock from those values, plantedFetlock (1351-1355) and footPath (1379-1403) reuse them, and per-gait sag is 8-17 deg (206-241). HOOF_SHAPE (1158) is fixed. The measurements agree: standing pastern is 33.0 deg fore and 30.0 deg hind from vertical. The four quirk notes are in data/quirks.js with param:null. Japanese Wikipedia also has Tokai Teio's farrier praising his soft pasterns.

The real-horse claims mostly hold up:
- Anderson & McIlwraith 2004a (PMID 15581319): "The front and rear pastern angles were significantly correlated with the angle of the dorsal surface of the front and rear hooves."
- Anderson, McIlwraith & Douay 2004b (PMID 15581320): "Long pasterns increased the odds of a fracture in the front limb."
- Weller et al. 2006b (PMID 17228576): "The risk of suffering from superficial digital flexor tendon injury increased with increasing metacarpophalangeal joint angle."
- Variation between horses is real. Mawdsley 1996 found over 65% of linear traits in Thoroughbreds had CV > 10%. Weller 2006a, however, calls Thoroughbred variation "relatively small", with the biggest variation in hoof measurements.
- The long/sloping vs short/upright contrast is standard conformation teaching: long pasterns absorb impact but strain the tendons and suspensory ligament; upright ones give less shock absorption.

Where the claim overstates or needs correcting:

(1) "The hoof must follow the pastern" is the farriery ideal, not what real Thoroughbreds show. The 2004a result is a correlation, not equality. A broken-back hoof-pastern axis (low or underrun heels) is the norm in racehorses: Correa et al. 2026 found it in 55% of 3-4-year-old Thoroughbreds by photo and 100% by radiograph. Kane 1998 linked the toe-heel angle difference to suspensory failure. Hoof angle is also the most variable trait (Weller 2006a). So the hoof should get its own angle or hoof-pastern-axis offset, defaulting to aligned, rather than being tied to the pastern. Note that the current model is not aligned either. The dorsal wall runs from (co.x+0.037, 0.104) to (co.x+0.069, 0.002), about 73 deg from horizontal, against a 57 deg pastern. That is broken forward by about 16 deg, the opposite of a typical Thoroughbred.

(2) The "springy pastern" idea is mostly expert opinion. No study measures how far the fetlock sinks against pastern length. The give comes from the fetlock's suspensory apparatus (suspensory ligament, SDFT, DDFT). Pastern length and slope only lengthen the lever that ground force acts through at the fetlock. Tissue stiffness varies on its own: Butcher & Ashley-Ross 2002 (PMID 11955495) found faster fetlock dorsiflexion in 2-year-olds, attributed to a less stiff suspensory apparatus. So 'give' should be a separate control, as in fix option 1. Option 2's sag x(1+0.6*(len-1)) coupling is a modelling guess, not an established fact.

(3) The injury papers are risk associations, not motion data. Anderson 2004b studied 3-year-old flat racers with stepwise regression. Weller 2006b studied 108 National Hunt (jumping) horses, and its own abstract says statistical power is limited. Its MCP angle is the standing fetlock angle, not fetlock drop under load. Neither paper supports particular sag sizes.

(4) A multiplier on today's sag would barely show. My script over the measurements found that at race speed the fore pastern only reaches about 50 deg from vertical. The fetlock drops 2.7 cm fore (0.209 to 0.182 m) and 2.2 cm hind. In galloping Thoroughbreds (from memory, not checked this session), the fetlock sinks until the pastern is near horizontal, and the back of the fetlock can hit the track ('running down'). The baseline sag needs fixing before a per-horse give factor is worth having.

Separate fore and hind controls (option 1) are justified: Gold Ship's note is hind-only and Loves Only You's is front-only. The proposed ranges (length x0.85-1.2, angle +/-6 deg) are plausible upper bounds. Severity stays medium: it is a real customization gap for documented roster quirks, not a structural anatomy error.
truth.correction:
Real-horse pastern length and angle do vary, and the cited injury links are quoted correctly. Three corrections:
(a) Pastern and hoof angles are correlated, not equal. The straight hoof-pastern axis is the farriery ideal, while a broken-back axis is typical of racing Thoroughbreds (Correa 2026; Kane 1998), and hoof measures vary most (Weller 2006a). Give the hoof its own angle or axis offset, defaulting to aligned. Note that the current hoof wall (~73 deg) is broken forward against the 57 deg pastern.
(b) The 'springiness' is fetlock-suspensory compliance. Pastern length and slope only lengthen the lever at the fetlock, and tissue stiffness varies independently (e.g. with age). Use a separate fore/hind give factor rather than deriving sag from length; the length-to-sag link is expert opinion, not measured.
(c) Anderson 2004b and Weller 2006b (a small National Hunt sample with limited power, using the standing MCP angle) are injury-risk associations that say nothing about how much the fetlock should sink.
Also: the model's baseline fetlock drop at racing speed (pastern ~50 deg from vertical, fetlock lowered ~2.7 cm) is far below a real gallop, where the pastern nears horizontal. Fix the baseline before adding per-horse multipliers.

truth.reasoning:
The core real-horse premise holds. Standing hock angle and hock height do vary between horses. Sickle-hocked and post-legged ("straight behind") are standard conformation categories with textbook problems: sickle hocks go with curb (plantar ligament strain); straight hocks go with upward fixation of the patella, bog spavin and hind suspensory strain. So a per-horse control is a legitimate gap. But several supporting statements are overstated or misattributed.

1. Mostafa & Elemmawy 2020 (PMC7316700). I read the full text. It says "All data are presented as mean and standard deviation (SD) values". The tarsal angle is 148.9 ± 1.2 (17 sound horses) vs 148.6 ± 0.6 (34 with musculoskeletal disorders), with no significant difference. The finding relabels ±1.2 as an SE with "SD ~5". That reading is plausible, because SD 0.6 is implausibly small, but it is an inference that contradicts the paper's own wording. The same paper also found that hock angle did not separate sound from lame Thoroughbred jumpers, which weakens the injury link.

2. Ahmad 2025 (PMC11768722) studies Morna racehorses, a Pakistani breed (n=50), not Thoroughbreds. Angles were taken by goniometer from joint midpoints, and the paper itself says the Morna values "differ from jumping Thoroughbred and French trotters", for which it cites an ideal of about 142°. Its 160.4 ± 3.89° is not a Thoroughbred norm. Read together, these sources show that published hock-angle "norms" range from about 142° to 165° depending on breed and on which landmarks are used.

3. Holmström et al. 1990 (EVJ 22:186, abstract checked). The elite horses were Swedish Warmblood dressage and show-jumping horses, not Thoroughbred racehorses. The injury link is only a hypothesis in that paper ("It is suggested that ... hocks with small angles are more prone to injury"), not a measured result. Gnagey, Clayton & Lanovaz 2006 (EVJ 38:628) point both ways. Horses with large (straight) standing tarsal angles absorbed less concussion at impact, which may lead to degenerative joint disease, and produced less vertical impulse. Their smaller extensor moment may lower the risk of plantar ligament injury. So "small angles are more injury-prone" should read: both extremes carry different risks.

4. "Reach further under the body in stance" has no quantitative support in these sources. Only "stands with the hind feet forward of the plumb line" is a definition-level fact.

5. The model's default is not abnormal. 145.8° (stifle–hock–fetlock joint centres) is about 3° below Mostafa's Thoroughbred-jumper mean of 148.9°. It would count as "small" on Gnagey's scale (markers over joint centres: small <155.5°, intermediate 155.5–165.5°, large >165.5°), but that scale came from 16 horses of unstated breed. The model's hind cannon is nearly vertical (2.6° off plumb) and the tibia is 36.8° off vertical, so by the cannon/plumb-line criterion the default horse is not sickle-hocked.

6. Weller et al. 2006 (EVJ 38:616), 108 National Hunt Thoroughbreds: "Variation in conformational parameters was relatively small". Within-breed spread is a few degrees, so this is a fine-grained quirk, not a major source of variation between horses.

7. Fix-option arithmetic, checked from the measured joints. Moving the hock ±4 cm in x changes the angle by about ±10.5–11° (135.3° to 156.7°), roughly 2.7° per cm, not ±6–8°. ±2–3 cm gives about ±5–8°, which matches a realistic 2–3 SD Thoroughbred range. ±4 cm should be the caricature limit.

Severity: the default is within normal range, Thoroughbred variation is small, and only two roster notes (Neo Universe, Grass Wonder) would use the control. This is a low-to-moderate customization gap rather than an anatomy defect, so I lowered it to low.

truth.reasoning:
The code facts check out. hoofK is a single value per horse (index.html:684, clamped to 0.85-1.15; the UI slider at 3274 spans 0.9-1.1). HOOF_SHAPE (1158) is a fixed table for fore and hind. hoofGeo(co, pale, fore) at 1159/1179 gets no leg id. HOOF_H and HOOF_TOE (503-504) are constants used by plantedFetlock (1352-1353, 1379). So the model cannot show a mismatched pair, and the gap is real.

Most of the real-horse claim also holds, and Thoroughbred-specific data support it more strongly than the papers the finding cites:
- Chan et al. 2026 (AJVR 87(6)): of 169 retired Hong Kong TB racehorses, 70% had a wider right fore hoof and 65% a wider right hind hoof.
- Tanaka et al. 2009 (J Equine Sci 20:15): club foot in 16% of 1,118 TB foals in Hidaka, Japan's main TB breeding area, with 69% of those grade II or higher.
- Robert et al. 2013 (Vet J 198:e75): 13% club feet at weaning across TB, French Trotter and Selle Français foals.
- Tanaka et al. 2015 (J Equine Sci 26:67): club-foot-associated contracted hooves were smaller and narrower than the healthy contralateral hoof. This supports "upright foot smaller and steeper, partner wider."

Where the claim is overstated or needs correction:
1. Weller 2006 is quoted correctly ("biggest relative variation in hoof related measurements and in stifle and coxal angle"), but hoof measures share that rank with two joint angles. The authors also concluded that variation was "relatively small" overall. The cohort was 108 UK National Hunt (jump) racehorses, not flat racers. Much of the hoof variation comes from trimming and shoeing rather than inherited conformation.
2. van Heel 2006 studied 24 Warmblood foals, not Thoroughbreds. The "about 50%" figure is a grazing limb preference (laterality) that led to uneven feet. It is not a breed prevalence and should not be presented as TB data. The long-limbs/small-head predisposition is likewise Warmblood-only.
3. Common does not mean conspicuous. Mild left-right width asymmetry is close to universal in TBs (Chan 2026), and it is also found in the hind feet (65%), so a fix should not be fore-only. A visibly mismatched or club foot is a minority condition: roughly 13-16% of foals, and fewer that are marked by racing age.
4. Two of the four roster notes do not support the proposed fix. 'Thin hoof walls' (mr-cb, durandal) is a horn-quality trait: wall thickness and brittleness. A size or angle parameter cannot show it on the outside of the hoof, so those notes should stay param:null. Manhattan Cafe's 'flat as a plate' feet are the modellable kind (low wall angle, low heel, wide). They are also the most typical TB fault: Correa et al. 2026 found low heels in 85% and underrun heels in 97% of 59 Brazilian TBs. Only Daiichi Ruby has a true visible mismatch. Her 'adult's fist' right fore against a normal TB fore hoof about 12-13 cm wide gives roughly 0.7-0.8, so the suggested 0.8-1.2 range is reasonable.
5. Related point for the fix. From HOOF_SHAPE and ringAt, the default hoof's dorsal wall rises from toe x=co.x+0.069 at y=0.002 to x=co.x+0.037 at y=0.104. That is about 72-73 degrees from horizontal, and the heel is as tall as the toe (level coronet, about 10 cm). Typical TB fore feet are about 50-55 degrees with heels much lower than the toe (Adams & Stashak). So before any per-leg variation, the shared base shape already reads as upright/boxy. A per-leg {angle, heelHeight, size} parameter should begin from a corrected default. The pastern angle should be tied to the hoof angle; Anderson & McIlwraith 2004 found front and hind pastern angles correlated with dorsal hoof angle at all ages.

Severity: the feature gap is real, but only one roster horse has a visible mismatch and one has flat feet. At normal viewing distance the hoof is a small part of the model, so I rate it low rather than medium.
truth.correction:
A per-leg hoof mismatch cannot be represented, and that is a valid gap. The real-horse evidence needs these corrections:
- Weller 2006 (108 UK National Hunt racehorses): hoof measures share the 'biggest relative variation' with stifle and coxal angles, overall variation was 'relatively small', and much of the hoof variation comes from farriery.
- van Heel 2006 studied 24 Warmblood foals, not TBs. The ~50% is a grazing laterality rate, not a TB prevalence.

truth.reasoning:
Code check: the observation is accurate as far as it goes. tuneGait(b, R) (index.html:256-264) reads only look.run (stride, kneeAction, hindDrive), and makeGait (267-275) passes only `run`. The only look.conf value that affects motion is chestWidth/hindquarters, through rig.legZ (687), which sets track width. Two corrections to the observed text, though. (a) "legZ is the only build-to-motion link" leaves out overall size: makeGait multiplies stride by the horse's scale s (272-273), so a bigger or leggier horse already takes longer strides in metres. (b) The example horse in the finding (upright-shouldered, short-cannoned, toed-out, sloping-shouldered) cannot be built at all. CONF_CONTROLS (3259-3276) has no shoulder-slope, pastern, cannon-length, toe-angle or coupling axis. The conf axes that do exist (neck, crest, head, profile, ears, chest depth/width, barrel, quarters, withers, tuck-up, bone, hoof, tail set) have little or no published kinematic effect in real horses.

Real-horse claim, "conformation shapes movement, so each build axis should carry a default motion change": true in general but overstated, and the cited evidence is weaker and less specific than presented.
1. Holmström 1990 (EVJ 22:186-193, PMID 2361507) studied Swedish Warmbloods (élite dressage horses and showjumpers), not Thoroughbreds. It reports that élite horses had larger hock angles and more sloping scapulas. The authors explain the hock finding through injury risk and the ability to collect. The paper measured no stride or gait variables, so it cannot support "shoulder slope -> scapSwing/lift".
2. Weller 2006b (EVJ 38:622-627, PMID 17228576) studied 108 National Hunt (jump) racehorses. Its outcomes were race performance and injury, not kinematics. It found positive effects of shoulder flexor angle, coxal angle and intermandibular width, and negative effects of girth, hind digit length and fetlock valgus. The authors themselves say statistical power is limited and the results are preliminary. It shows conformation is associated with performance, not how a horse moves.
3. The best large Thoroughbred dataset contradicts strong conformation effects. Love et al. 2006 (EVJ 38:597-603, PMID 17228572) assessed 3916 Thoroughbred yearlings. Turned-out feet were the most common "defect" at 30%. Only weak conformation-performance associations were found, and these were almost entirely explained by sire. Mild toe-out is therefore normal variation in Thoroughbreds. Anderson, McIlwraith and Douay 2004 (EVJ 36:571-575) even found carpal valgus (toe-out at the knee) protective against carpal fracture.
4. Toe-out -> winging in and toe-in -> paddling is standard textbook teaching (Adams & Stashak), but objective support is thin. In 24 Standardbreds, mild toe-in/toe-out made no difference to landing pattern or limb-load asymmetry (Mokry et al. 2021, Vet J 268:105593). Forelimb foot placement was "to a large extent independent of foot conformation" (Wilson et al. 2016, EVJ 48:90-96). At most it is a small, inconsistent swing-arc effect.
5. Where real links have been measured, they are small and depend on context. Back conformation correlates with back motion at walk and trot (Johnston et al. 2002, EVJ Suppl 34:314-318). In 71 Lipizzans, distal limb length correlated with stride and cadence within some work groups, but "no significant associations were found at the whole-cohort level" and some effects reversed between groups (Zupan Šemrov et al. 2025, Front Vet Sci 12:1569067). In racehorses, speed dominates the stride variables: stance fell from about 131 to 77 ms (fore) between 9 and 17 m/s, while the aerial phase did not change with speed (Witte, Hirst & Wilson 2006, J Exp Biol 209:4389-4397).
6. The strongest real build-to-motion link is body size and leg length -> stride length (dynamic similarity, Alexander & Jayes 1983). The model already has it through scale s. Chest width -> track width is also already in the model.
7. "Long, compliant pasterns change fetlock drop" mixes up pastern length with the stiffness of the suspensory apparatus. Fetlock extension under load is governed by the suspensory ligament, SDFT and DDFT. Long pasterns are known clinically for injury risk (Anderson 2004: higher odds of forelimb fracture), not as a measured kinematic driver. The model also has no pastern conf axis.
8. The famous running quirks the finding cites (Oguri Cap's low, stretched head carriage, Almond Eye's reach, the Teio step, Vodka's hind action) are documented as individual traits of each horse. None has been shown to follow from a measurable conformation axis. Keeping them as explicit run sliders, which the user asked for, is closer to reality than deriving them from build.

Net: the gap exists in code, but "each build axis should come with a default motion change" is not supported for Thoroughbreds. Only a few couplings are justified, and both are already present: size/leg length -> stride and chest width -> track. At most, a small optional toe-angle -> swing-arc term or back-length -> lumbosacral term could be added if those axes are ever introduced.
truth.correction: Accurate version: tuneGait/makeGait read only look.run, so the existing conf axes (neck, crest, head, ears, chest, barrel, quarters, withers, bone, hoof, tail set) do not change gait. Two build links already exist: chest width/quarters -> track width (legZ), and overall size (scale s) -> stride length. In real horses, conformation affects movement only modestly and inconsistently. The cited studies measure performance and injury (Weller 2006b: National Hunt jumpers, preliminary) or Warmblood élite status (Holmström 1990), not kinematics. Large Thoroughbred data show weak links explained by sire (Love 2006). Mild toe-out is the most common Thoroughbred trait (30%) and in objective studies does not reliably change landing or foot placement (Mokry 2021; Wilson 2016). Morphology-gait correlations disappear at the cohort level (Zupan Šemrov 2025). So most build axes should NOT drive motion by default. Keep the famous horses' movement quirks as explicit run sliders. Optionally add small couplings only for axes with some support: leg length -> stride (already via scale), toe angle -> a slight swing-arc deviation, and back/coupling length -> lumbosacral/lateral motion (Johnston 2002), and only if those conf axes are ever added. Low priority.

CONF_CONTROLS (3259-3276) covers only neck, crest, head, profile, ears, ear set, ear tilt, chest depth, chest width, barrel, quarters, withers, tuck-up, bone, hooves and tail set. Once they exist and move the joint constants, much of the effect would come through the IK on its own. Wiring the existing mostly mass and shape axes into tuneGait would do little.
(2) legZ is not strictly the only link. conf.neck moves the neck2 and head bone positions through stretch() (704-706), and conf.head scales the head (772). The same BODY neck rotations therefore swing a longer neck and head through a larger arc. The link is passive and minor.

The cited references are real and correctly paginated, but they concern Swedish Warmbloods (Holmström 1990) and National Hunt jumpers (Weller 2006b), not flat Thoroughbreds. They show associations between conformation and performance or soundness more than they give gait parameters. findings.expected: Camped out / camped under, fore and hind, is a recognised standing conformation, judged against plumb lines: from the point of buttock past the point of hock and down the back of the cannon behind, and from the scapula down through the forearm to the hoof in front (Adams & Stashak; Ross & Dyson). Camped-out hinds often go with straight (post-legged) hind limbs; camped-under hinds with sickle hocks.

truth.reasoning:
The code side checks out. GAITS.stand (index.html:247) sets fore.xc 0.56 and hind.xc -0.56. footPath's stand branch (1378-1380) plants every hoof at P.xc with nothing added per horse, and no conf or run field touches xc anywhere. Both notes in data/quirks.js (loves-only-you, titleholder) have param:null, so neither stance is modelled.

Most of the real-horse claim holds up:
- Camped out and camped (standing) under, in front and behind, are standard side-view conformation terms in Stashak / Adams & Stashak, judged against the lateral plumb lines.
- Hind plumb line: a vertical from the tuber ischii touches the point of the hock, runs down the back of the cannon and meets the ground about 7.5-10 cm behind the heel.
- Front plumb line: a vertical from the tuberosity of the scapular spine bisects the forearm, knee, cannon and fetlock and meets the ground just behind the heel. The finding's "down through the forearm to the hoof" is slightly loose here.
- Camped under behind going with sickle hocks is standard. Wikipedia's sickle-hock entry: "the hind leg slants forward, in front of the plumb line".
- A ±8 cm offset is about the size of the normal heel-to-plumb-line gap, so it is a plausible range.

Three corrections:
1. The link between camped-out hinds and post-legged hinds is weak. Wikipedia's entry links camped out behind to "upright rear pasterns" (its exact words), not to post-legged (straight) hinds. Its post-legged entry (open hock and stifle angles, near-vertical tibia) is listed separately with no stated link. Treat any hind-angle coupling as optional, not as something real horses "often" show.
2. The two roster notes describe habitual resting postures, not conformation. A real horse's standing posture is largely behavioural and changes from moment to moment:
   - Idle horses usually rest one hind leg, alternating sides, using the stay apparatus.
   - Grazing horses usually advance one foreleg (van Heel et al. 2006), and this stand gait is the 'graze' body mode.
   - Conformation is judged only after the horse is set up square on level ground.
   - Breed matters: a stretched "parked-out" hind stance is a trained show pose in Saddlebreds, Morgans and Arabians. Thoroughbred conformation photos use an "open" stance with the legs staggered, not a camped one.
   - A persistent rocked-back stance (fores camped out in front, hinds camped under) is the classic sign of laminitis pain, not conformation.
   So a per-horse stance offset is a reasonable cosmetic quirk. It should be labelled as a habitual posture, not a conformation fault, and ideally sit on top of natural weight-shifting.
3. The Titleholder note is ambiguous ("forelegs set forward, leaning forward" / 前方にせり出す). I could not fetch either Sponichi source to check it, so its direction should be confirmed before it is encoded.

truth.correction: Camped out / camped under are recognised conformation terms judged against Stashak's lateral plumb lines, and camped under behind does go with sickle hocks. Two adjustments to the real-horse claim. First, the plumb lines: the front line drops from the tuberosity of the scapular spine and meets the ground just behind the heel; the hind line drops from the tuber ischii, touches the point of the hock, runs down the back of the cannon and lands about 7.5-10 cm behind the heel. In real horses those are largely behavioural and change constantly: resting one hind leg, a grazing stance with one foreleg advanced, trained show stretches in other breeds, and a rocked-back stance as a sign of laminitis pain. So model it as an optional per-horse habitual-stance offset (about ±8 cm) layered over natural weight-shifting, not as fixed conformation. Check the direction of the ambiguous Titleholder note against its source first, and fix the neutral camped-under hind placement before adding offsets.

truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the real-horse side of the finding. Its core holds, but three parts are wrong or overstated.

What holds:
(1) The elbow cannot close to 16 deg, or to 31 deg. Santosuosso et al. 2021 measured the elbow with markers on the greater tubercle, the lateral humeral epicondyle and the ulnar carpal bone. These are the same three points the model's shoulder-elbow-knee angle uses. Under passive mobilization the elbow flexed at most to 58.1 +/- 8.2 deg, and during swimming to 52.8 +/- 7.6 deg. On that convention the model's standing value of 138 deg is realistic. The default race gait already reaches 31 deg (measurements.json: LF 31-36 deg at g=0-0.09; RF 36-45 deg), and kneeAction 1.3 takes it to 16 deg. Both are far past the anatomical limit.
(2) A real hoof never enters the trunk. When the limb is completely folded, the shoe can just reach the elbow; horses get shoe boils (capped elbow) this way, while lying down.
(3) High knee action does raise the forearm forward. Wikipedia describes the Hackney's front legs as having "sharply bent knees that are stretched well forward".

What needs correcting:
(a) "The hoof folds under the forearm ahead of the breast" is wrong for a normal gallop. The carpus reaches peak flexion first, in early swing, while the forearm is still near vertical or behind it; the elbow peaks after it (Santosuosso 2021; Hodson et al. 2000 for the walk). So at maximum fold the hoof sits behind the forearm, under the elbow and girth, close to the chest wall. It is ahead of the chest only at peak forearm elevation in a true high-action gait. The model's worst hoof-in-chest moment is exactly in this early-swing fold. At kneeAction 1 the RF toe peaks at 0.95 m at g=0.69, about 15 cm behind the girth, with the forearm 17 deg behind vertical. At kneeAction 1.3 the finding's LF penetration is at swing fraction s≈0.13. The cause is not a failure to lift the forearm. The model already swings the forearm to 70 deg forward of vertical, and to 85 deg at 1.3, which is probably more than a Thoroughbred does.
(b) "Shoulder flexion ... carries the elbow forward" uses the wrong term. In equine joint conventions the shoulder's flexor side is caudal (St George et al. 2023), so moving the elbow forward is shoulder extension. Hodson 2000 reports that rotation of the humerus does the protraction and the shoulder extends in terminal swing. St George 2023 found that the more-protracted leading forelimb had less shoulder flexion in late swing. The model actually has too much shoulder flexion: in the race swing the scapula-humerus angle drops to 55-64 deg (99 deg standing), the humerus sits 76-80 deg behind vertical, and the elbow rises from 0.96 m to 1.10 m, only about 7 cm below the point of shoulder. A fix written as "more shoulder flexion" would make this worse.
(c) Closing the elbow to raise the forearm is a real mechanism; the model just takes it too far. St George 2023 found that greater protraction comes from greater elbow flexion during swing. Hodson 2000 reports that rotation of the scapula and forearm lifts the lower limb in early swing. So the model is right in kind and wrong only past roughly 55 deg.

Smaller points:
- The carpal minimum of 39.5 deg is within the passive limit of 30.6 +/- 4.9 deg, so the carpus angle itself is not impossible. The elbow and shoulder angles are.
- High knee action is unusual in Thoroughbreds, whose norm is a low "daisy-cutter" action, so kneeAction 1.3 is an extreme for the breed.
- Tokai Teio's source line ("前脚が肩のあたりまで振り上がるほどのフォーム", forelegs swung up to about the shoulder) is hyperbole and may describe a high, straight forward reach rather than a folded knee. His famous high-kneed "Teio step" was a paddock walk, and Japanese Wikipedia says it disappeared at racing speed.
- The hoof is already 9.8 cm inside the chest at kneeAction 1, so the slider makes an existing default defect worse; this overlaps with the earlier elbow finding.

Severity stays high: the hoof is visibly inside the chest, the elbow and shoulder angles are anatomically impossible, and it affects famous roster presets such as Tokai Teio.
truth.correction:
A real horse never puts its hoof inside the trunk. Its elbow (shoulder-elbow-knee angle) closes no further than about 53-58 deg, so the model's 31 deg (default race) and 16 deg (kneeAction 1.3) are impossible. The extra height of a high knee action comes from carrying the elbow forward (humeral protraction, which in equine terms is shoulder EXTENSION) together with elbow flexion that raises the forearm. The finding needs these corrections:
- In a gallop the hoof is most folded in early swing, when the forearm is near vertical or behind it. The hoof then sits behind the forearm, under the elbow and girth, close to the chest wall; at the extreme fold it can reach the elbow. It is ahead of the breast only at peak forearm elevation in a true high-action gait.
- The model's penetration happens in that early-swing fold behind the elbow, not because the forearm fails to lift. The model already lifts the forearm to 70-85 deg forward of vertical.
- The model's shoulder is over-flexed, not under-flexed: scapula-humerus angle 55-64 deg, humerus 76-80 deg behind vertical, elbow raised to 1.10 m. Any fix should open the shoulder and bring the elbow forward and down.
- The carpal minimum of 39.5 deg is within real limits.
- High action is atypical for Thoroughbreds. The Tokai Teio "forelegs to the shoulder" quote is hyperbole and may describe a high, straight reach rather than a folded knee.

model.reasoning:
I reproduced the problem in a headless page (served read-only from a scratch server under %TEMP%). I sampled window.__horse at 64 race phases at Tokyo. For each phase I computed the skinned world vertices of the trunk triangles (dominant bone spine, hindquarters or chest) and ran a vertical line through the toe's actual (x, z) against them.

**Joint angles match the finding exactly.**
- Byerley Turk, kneeAction 1 vs 1.3: fore lift 0.44 -> 0.572 m and flex 125 -> 138.1 deg.
- Forearm max 70.2 -> 85.4 deg; knee interior min 55 -> 39.5 deg.
- Elbow interior min: RF 31.1 -> 15.9 deg, LF 36.7 -> 21.3 deg.
- Tokai Teio's toe peak is 0.947 -> 1.066 m, which matches the finding's 0.95 -> 1.06.

**The toe does end up inside the barrel.**
- Tokai Teio preset (ka 1.3, stride 1.1, hindDrive 0.95), gear off: RF toe at y 1.066 against a barrel underside of 0.901 at the same x and z (g=0.766), so 16.5 cm inside. LF is 18.5 cm inside (g=0.672). The toe is inside on 12-13 of 64 phases.
- Same horse with neutral style: 3.7 cm (RF) and 5.8 cm (LF), on 3-4 phases.
- kneeAction 0.7: no penetration.
- A scratch side render of Tokai Teio at g=0.766 shows the near fore's white pastern rising into the girth, with the hoof hidden inside the barrel. Sheet 10's 'race g=3/4: high-headed, high knees' tile looks the same.
- At this phase the toe sits above the elbow (1.07 vs 0.99 m) and 26 cm behind it. A real hoof cannot get there: the elbow lies against the chest wall, and a hoof reaching even the elbow is the known interference fault called "elbow hitting".

**What differs from the finding.**

1. **The depth is overstated by about 5 cm.** I measure about 16-18 cm for Teio (finding: 23.4 cm) and about 4-6 cm at neutral (finding: 9.8 cm). My figure is measured at the limb's own z of ±0.165, where the trunk is shallower than at the midline.

2. **The cause is not the forward humerus limit.** The +2 deg bound (ARM_RANGE[1]) never binds in the swing: the humerus' largest swing angle is about -24 deg, at g=0.25 for RF.
   - **Where the toe is deepest:** the humerus is free (about -65 deg) and the forearm is still pointing back, 22-26 deg behind vertical. This is about 0.38 of the way through the swing, just after rise=0.25, when the fetlock target is already raised by the full lift × ka in the horse frame (index.html:1407) while swingX has barely brought the foot forward. So the raised target sits behind the forearm, and the cannon and hoof fold up under the girth.
   - **Where the elbow is most closed (16 deg):** this comes late in the swing, at RF g≈0.03-0.06. There the humerus is held at the other bound, ARM_RANGE[0] = -76 deg (about -78.7 in world after body pitch). That puts the elbow at y 1.07, only 7 cm below the shoulder joint at 1.14. The forearm then swings to 85 deg about this raised, parked elbow.

**What this means for the fix options.**
- **Option 1 (widen ARM_RANGE[1])** would not touch the phase where the toe goes inside, because that limit never binds in the swing.
- **Options 2 (clamp the swing target below the trunk) and 3 (stop scaling lift with ka)** do address it. So does tying the lift bump to forward progress, so the peak height comes when the foot is in front of the forearm.
- **The -76 deg retraction limit** is what lets the elbow close to 16 deg, so a fix for the elbow needs to address that bound as well.

**Real-horse reference.** The finding's expected behaviour holds. At speed, forelimb protraction comes from scapular rotation, shoulder extension and elbow extension, with the carpus flexed (Back & Clayton, Equine Locomotion). The equine elbow moves through only about 55-60 deg in total from about 140-150 deg standing (Sisson & Grossman / Getty), so an interior angle of 16-31 deg is not reachable.

The problem is real: the folded forefoot goes up into the barrel, and kneeAction makes it much worse. Penetration is about 4-6 cm at neutral and about 16.5-18.5 cm with the Tokai Teio preset, not 9.8 and 23.4 cm. The toe peaks above the elbow and 26 cm behind it.

The finding's cause is wrong. At the deepest phase (about 0.38 of the way through the swing) the humerus is free and the forearm still points back 22-26 deg, so the full ka-scaled lift in the horse frame raises the folded foot behind the forearm, before the foot has come forward. The forward limit ARM_RANGE[1] (+2 deg) never binds in the swing. The 16 deg elbow comes later in the swing from the retraction limit ARM_RANGE[0] (-76 deg), which parks the elbow only about 7 cm below the shoulder joint.

So fix option 1 (widen ARM_RANGE[1]) would not remove the penetration. Options 2 and 3 would, as would timing the lift peak to the foot's forward progress. The -76 deg bound needs work too.

findings.title: Stride slider changes airtime but not the bounce, so the airborne trunk falls at 0.87 g (stride runner) to 1.41 g (pitch runner)
findings.observed: tuneGait multiplies stride and T by st and divides duty by st, so stance stays at 86 ms over 1.40 m. Measured at Tokyo (16.3 m/s): st 0.88 gives 6.15 m at 2.64 Hz, aerial 148 ms, swing 292 ms; st 1.0 gives 7.02 m at 2.33 Hz, aerial 181 ms, swing 344 ms; st 1.12 gives 7.84 m at 2.08 Hz, aerial 211 ms, swing 396 ms. The withers path is identical in all three: 1.467-1.592 m (12.5 cm). BODY.race moves the spine by 0.05*cos(2pi(g-0.82)), so the downward acceleration at the crest of the flight is 0.05*(2pi/T)^2: 10.7 m/s^2 (1.09 g) at neutral, 8.5 (0.87 g) at 1.12 and 13.8 (1.41 g) at 0.88. The pitch runner is pulled down faster than gravity, and the stride runner floats.
findings.expected: In the aerial phase the centre of mass follows a parabola at exactly g, and the rise in flight is h = g*t^2/8: 2.7 cm for 148 ms, 4.0 cm for 181 ms, 5.5 cm for 211 ms. At the same speed, more airtime needs more vertical impulse in a shorter stance (lower duty), so a stride runner should bounce higher and load its fetlocks harder, and a pitch runner should run flatter. Peak limb force rises as duty falls (Witte et al. 2006 estimate it from duty factor: fore 24.7 N/kg at 17 m/s). Real spread: Schrurs et al. 2022 (421 TBs, hard gallop) peak stride 7.63 +/- 0.27 m, peak frequency 2.45 +/- 0.08 Hz; stayers 7.88 m / 2.34 Hz vs sprinters 7.61 m / 2.46 Hz, about a 5% difference. The slider's +/-12% is about +/-3.5 SD.

The physics at the centre of the finding holds for real horses, and so does the code reading. Some of the "expected" real-horse figures are wrong or overstated.

- tuneGait (index.html:256-264) sets T*st, stride*st and duty/st. The land[] phases do not change, so stance stays at 0.2*0.43 = 86 ms. That is 1.40 m at 16.3 m/s.
- BODY.race (index.html:1545) moves the spine by 0.05*cos(2pi(g-0.82)) whatever st is.
- The crest, g=0.82, falls inside the flight window. The leading fore lifts off at 0.37+0.2/st and the next touchdown is at g=1.0.
- Crest acceleration A*(2pi/T)^2 is 13.8, 10.7 and 8.5 m/s^2 for st 0.88, 1.0 and 1.12.
- measurements.json (race gait at 16.8 m/s) agrees: hooves on the ground from g=0 to about 0.59, then about 176 ms in the air. The spine moves 1.085-1.185 m and the withers 1.474-1.600 m.

WHAT REAL HORSES DO (supports the finding)
Pfau, Witte & Wilson 2006 put an inertial sensor on the withers of Thoroughbreds galloping at 7-17 m/s. The dorsoventral acceleration minimum was "independent of speed at about -10 m/s^2 (1 g) experienced during the aerial phase".
- The model's neutral crest (10.7 m/s^2) matches this.
- st 0.88 (1.41 g) is not physically possible.
- st 1.12 (0.87 g) floats.
So holding flight at about 1 g whatever the stride timing is correct, and the first fix option (vertical amplitude times st^2, so A*omega^2 stays constant) is the right idea.

Two figures are verified:
- Witte et al. 2006: peak forelimb force 24.7 N/kg at 17 m/s (range 22.6-26.0); hindlimb 15.3 N/kg.
- Schrurs et al. 2022: peak stride 7.63 +/- 0.27 m and peak frequency 2.45 +/- 0.08 Hz; sprinters 7.61 m / 2.46 Hz, stayers 7.88 m / 2.34 Hz.

CORRECTIONS
1. The flight-rise figures (2.7 / 4.0 / 5.5 cm) are the model's numbers, not a real horse's. Witte et al. 2006 report, at 17 m/s:
   - stance 77 ms (fore) and 94 ms (hind);
   - protraction 342 ms and 326 ms, so a stride of about 0.42 s;
   - overlap time "approached zero at maximum speed";
   - aerial phase "independent of speed".
   The time with no hoof down is therefore about 0.42 - (2x77 + 2x94 ms) = about 80 ms. That gives a real flight rise of g*t^2/8 = about 0.7 cm. The model's flight (176-185 ms) is roughly twice as long as a real one, and its footfall sequence (about 245 ms of contact) is much shorter than the real one (about 340 ms).
   Real vertical travel of the centre of mass at 17 m/s is 83 mm (range 75-91; Pfau 2006), and most of it happens during stance. Pfau notes the energy changes in the aerial phase are small.
2. "A stride runner should bounce higher, a pitch runner flatter" follows from the model's own choice to keep stance fixed and put the extra stride into airtime. It is not an observed fact about real horses.
   - Across speeds, real horses lengthen their stride while the aerial time stays constant (Witte) and the vertical travel falls from 185 to 83 mm (Pfau).
   - At the same speed, a horse with a longer stride could just as well have a longer stance (more limb sweep). No source here shows real stride runners get more airtime.
   The statement is right as physics inside the model, not as a claim about horses.
3. Range and spread figures:
   - Schrurs' values are peaks at about 66.8 km/h (18.6 m/s), not at one common speed.
   - Sprinters differ from stayers by about 3.5% in stride length and 5% in frequency, not 5% in both.
   - "+/-12% is about +/-3.5 SD" is correct arithmetic (12% against a 3.5% coefficient of variation).
   - A closer comparison at a fixed speed: Witte's 9 elite horses had peak forelimb forces of 22.6-26.0 N/kg at 17 m/s. That implies duty factor varies by about +/-7% between horses, while the slider spans +/-12% (duty 0.179-0.227).
4. Whether the pitch runner is "pulled down faster than gravity" depends on the measure. At the crest it is 1.41 g. Averaged over the whole flight, the cosine gives about 1.05 g (st 0.88), 0.77 g (neutral) and 0.58 g (st 1.12). So even the neutral setting is ballistic only at its crest, though the trend the finding describes holds either way.

SEVERITY
I lowered it to low. The amplitude stays 5 cm and only the rate changes by +/-12%. In a real Thoroughbred the effect of stride style on flight height is under 1 cm. The bigger realism problem is the model's suspension phase, which is about twice too long, and that belongs in its own finding.

Code
- tuneGait (index.html:256-264) returns stride*st, T*st and duty/st. It does not change the `land` phases. Its clamp is 0.85-1.15. The UI slider (index.html:3280) runs 0.88-1.12.
- BODY.race (index.html:1545) sets spine.position.y = rest - 0.085 + 0.05*cos(2pi(g-0.82)), which depends on gait phase g only.
- applyRun (index.html:1709-1720) adds no bounce term. bodyLow only shifts the mean height (0.05*k), and nothing else uses st.
- Every BODY motion is a function of g, so the vertical path in phase is identical for every st. Stretching T by st scales every vertical acceleration by 1/st^2.
- Speed stays the same: period = strides*T, and W/strides is about 7.0*st*s.

Measurements (measurements.json, race, studio, st=1, T=0.43)
- I took a Fourier fit of the spine y over the 32 samples. It is a pure first harmonic, mean 1.135 m and amplitude 0.0500 m, with crest at g=0.82. All four toes are off the ground from g of about 0.58 to 1.0, so the crest falls inside the flight.
- Crest downward acceleration of the spine: 10.61 m/s^2 (1.08 g) at st 1.0, 8.46 m/s^2 (0.86 g) at 1.12 and 13.70 m/s^2 (1.40 g) at 0.88. These match the finding's 1.09 / 0.87 / 1.41 g.
- Aerial time from the gait plan, (1 - 0.37 - 0.2/st)*0.43*st: 185, 217 and 152 ms. The finding's 181, 211 and 148 ms are about 4 ms shorter, probably because they used a toe-height threshold. This does not matter.
- Withers path in the studio: 1.474-1.600 m (12.6 cm), the same in phase for every st.

Points that refine the finding without overturning it
1. The quoted g-values are the peak at the crest of a cosine, not the acceleration through the whole flight.
   - Averaged over the aerial window (change in velocity / time), the spine falls at 0.77 g at neutral, 0.58 g at 1.12 and 1.05 g at 0.88.
   - Lift-off (g about 0.58) sits near the cosine's zero-acceleration point, so early flight is under-decelerated at every setting.
   - So the neutral race is already not ballistic, and on average the pitch runner is the closest to g. It is faster than g only around the crest and descent.
   - Within one flight the model rises 4.7 cm and falls 2.9 cm at neutral. At st 1.12 it rises 5.7 cm over 131 ms, where a ballistic flight would rise 8.4 cm, and falls 2.9 cm over 87 ms against 3.7 cm ballistic. At 0.88 it falls 2.9 cm over 68 ms against 2.3 cm ballistic. Qualitatively: the stride runner floats, and the pitch runner drops faster than g after the crest.
   - The st scaling multiplies an error that the cosine shape already has, so fix option 2 (a ballistic parabola in the aerial window) deals with the root cause. Option 1 (scale by st^2) only keeps the crest value constant.
2. Roster horses (data/quirks.js) only use run.stride from 0.95 to 1.10, which gives 0.89-1.20 g at the crest. Only the manual slider reaches the 0.88/1.12 extremes.

I lowered the severity to low.
- Over the roster's range, the error st adds is about the same size as the non-ballistic error the neutral gait already has.
- The bounce is 10 cm peak to peak at about 2.3 Hz, so the difference is hard to see.
- The part that matters to the user is the characterisation gap: stride runners described as bounding (e.g. "跳びの大きい走法" in quirks.js) get extra airtime but no higher bound.

I did not independently check the cited papers' figures. The physics (h = g t^2/8; vertical impulse per stride = mgT, so the same stance time over a longer T means higher stance forces) is standard.

truth.reasoning:
I checked the code first. The finding describes it correctly: tuneGait (index.html:255-262) scales stride and T by st and duty by 1/st, so stanceLen = stride*duty does not change, and xc and scapSwing are fixed per gait. Any stride gain therefore has to come from swing and air time. The real-horse reasoning behind the "expected" behaviour has several problems:

1. Witte et al. 2006 is quoted correctly. The PubMed abstract (PMID 17050854) gives fore protraction of 364 and 342 ms at 9 and 17 m/s, and hind protraction of 355 and 326 ms. But that is how the average changes with speed across 9 horses. It does not limit how much individual horses differ at the same speed. The same abstract gives a peak-force range of 22.6-26.0 N/kg at 17 m/s, which means duty factors differ by about ±7% between horses at one speed. It also says aerial time is independent of speed.

2. "Swing time is nearly fixed by limb pendulum mechanics, so ±15% would need a limb about 30% longer" is overstated. The arithmetic (T ∝ √L) is right, but swing in a horse is driven by muscle, not a free pendulum. The same limb swings for roughly 0.44 s at the walk, about 0.4 s at the trot and about 0.34 s at the gallop, a spread of about 25-30% with no change in limb length.

3. The direct evidence on how long-striding horses get their stride at a given speed partly contradicts the proposed fix:
   - Back et al. 1994 (Vet Q 16 S2:S91, warmbloods trotting on a treadmill at one speed): the variables that tracked gait quality were stride and swing duration of the fore and hind limbs, scapular rotation, maximal forelimb retraction, maximal hindlimb protraction and fetlock, stifle and hock flexion. Stance duration is not in that list.
   - Back et al. 1995 (Res Vet Sci 59:64) also names swing duration and total protraction-retraction range as markers of gait quality.
   - Barrey et al. 2001 (EVJ Suppl 33:99) tested Thoroughbreds at top speed. Winners of short races (<1400 m) had higher stride frequency and a larger share of the stride on the ground than winners of longer races. That fits stance time staying about the same while long-striders spend more of the stride in swing and flight.

   So the model's current pattern (stance kept, extra length in swing and air time) is broadly what real horses do. Capping swing time at ±5% and moving the gain into stance length is not supported.

4. What does hold up: long-striding horses also move the limb through a bigger range, with more scapular rotation, more forelimb retraction at lift-off and more hindlimb protraction late in swing (Back 1994). The model's fixed scapSwing and xc show none of that. The quirk notes for Oguri Cap ("reached the forelegs out to their full extent") and Almond Eye ("fling her forelegs out from the shoulder") describe exactly this kind of reach. That mismatch between the notes and the motion is a real gap.

5. Size of the effect: real differences are modest.
   - Schrurs et al. 2022 (PMC9741461): peak stride frequency was 2.43 Hz in sprinters and 2.31 Hz in stayers (about 5%), and stride length 7.45 m vs 7.62 m.
   - Takahashi et al. 2025 (PMID 41151162): 2.36 ± 0.12 Hz and 7.30 ± 0.39 m in Japanese races.
   - Oguri Cap's "20-30 cm per stride" is about 3-4% of a 7 m stride. His st of 1.04 gives a swing of about 361 ms, only +5%, which is inside the finding's own ±5% limit.
   - Roster values run from 0.95 to 1.10. At 1.10, swing is about +12% and stride frequency about 2.1 Hz, an outlier but not impossible for a famous long-strider.

Corrected claim: keeping stance length constant and putting most of the extra stride into a longer swing or flight fits what has been measured, and swing time is not pinned within ±5% between individual horses. What is missing is a modest extra limb range (scapular rotation, foreleg protraction and retraction, hindlimb protraction) tied to stride length or to a separate reach control. The finding's option 2 (a separate fore-reach control for Oguri Cap and Almond Eye) is consistent with the evidence. Option 1's ±5% cap on swing time is not.
truth.correction: Real long-striding horses at a given speed do lengthen swing duration, and the stride length gain does not have to come from a longer stance. Stance duration did not track gait quality in Back et al. 1994, and Barrey 2001 found that stayers have a smaller share of the stride on the ground than sprinters. Witte 2006's 6% change is how the average varies with speed, not a limit on differences between horses, and swing is not a passive pendulum: it varies about 25-30% across gaits with the same limb. The valid part is that long-striders also show more scapular rotation and more protraction and retraction (Back 1994), and the Oguri Cap and Almond Eye notes describe foreleg reach. So the model lacks a modest reach and limb-range component. It does not need its swing time held within ±5%. Real stride frequency differences between horses are about 5% (sprinters 2.43 Hz vs stayers 2.31 Hz).

The observed behaviour reproduces exactly from the code. tuneGait (index.html:260) sets stride*st, T*st and duty/st. Stance length is stride*duty = 7.0*0.2 = 1.400 m for every st, and stance time is T*duty = 86 ms for every st. Swing time is b.T*(st - b.duty): 292 ms at st 0.88, 344 ms at 1.00 and 396 ms at 1.12. Speed stays 16.28 m/s. tuneGait never touches fore/hind xc or scapSwing. toeDown (1384) depends only on xc, stanceLen and HOOF_TOE. The scapula angle at touchdown and lift-off is +/-scapSwing whatever the duty (the warp w at 1449-1450). So touchdown protraction is the same by construction. BODY.race (1542) depends only on g, so the small sweep differences between st values only reflect lift-off falling at a slightly different g. measurements.json holds only st = 1. There I measured RH sweep 64.4 deg (the critic's st=1 value exactly) and RF 59.7 deg, against the critic's 54.0. That gap comes from a different scenery width (stride 7.222 m, stance 1.444 m) and a different way of measuring, not a different conclusion. One small correction: peak late-swing protraction is not perfectly fixed. The swingX overshoot term scales with STRIDE*(1-DUTY): about 14.1 / 16.6 / 19.1 cm at st 0.88 / 1.00 / 1.12, so roughly +/-2.5 cm, about 1 deg. In practice, though, the critic is right that st adds no reach. The quirks.js notes are as quoted: Oguri Cap's 'reached the forelegs out' note is mapped to run.stride, and Almond Eye's 'fling from the shoulder' note has param null. The slider label (3280) promises 'long, reaching strides'. So the missing-reach gap is real.

What I refute is the 'expected' argument and the severity. Witte et al. 2006 checks out: fore protraction 364 to 342 ms and hind 355 to 326 ms over 9 to 17 m/s, with aerial time independent of speed. But that is how the population mean changes with speed. It does not say how individuals differ at one speed. At a fixed speed, a 12% longer stride means a 12% longer stride time (430 to 482 ms, +52 ms). Stance is only about 20% of the stride. If swing stayed within +/-5% (+17 ms), stance would have to grow about 35 ms, to roughly 121 ms and a 1.96 m stance (+40%). That is an implausible limb sweep. Most of the extra time therefore has to be swing or airtime in a real horse too. Schrurs et al. 2022 (Animals 12:3269) shows that stride-length and stride-frequency profiles differ between individuals: sprinters take shorter, higher-frequency strides than stayers. It gives no stance/flight breakdown, so it does not support the claim that real long-striders gain mainly per stance. The critic's own fix 1 (stanceLen x(1+0.5(st-1)), so +6% at 1.12) would still leave swing about +13%, which contradicts its own '+/-5% swing' goal. The +35% figure compares the two ends of the slider; against the default it is +/-15%. Roster values are mostly 0.95-1.10. Oguri Cap's 1.04 gives +5% swing and +0.28 m per stride, which matches his note's 20-30 cm.

What remains is a moderate cosmetic and customization gap: no visible reach (touchdown protraction, scapular swing) to go with the 'reaching' label and notes. It is not a kinematic error, so low severity. A separate small 'foreleg reach' control (critic's option 2) fits better than trying to cap swing time.

Most of the real-horse claim also holds:
- The horse walk is a pendular gait with no aerial phase and duty above 0.5, typically about 0.6-0.65 (Hildebrand 1965; Robilliard et al. 2007). Minetti et al. (1999) measured pendular walking mechanics in horses.

- A Thoroughbred walking freely does not undertrack by 16.6 cm. That is collected-walk territory.
- Holding swing near 0.4 s and duty near 0.6 while the stride changes is how real horses walk.

1. "Racing style doesn't predict how a horse walks" is too absolute. Movement traits are individual, and part of them carries across gaits.

The head-range and knee-lift changes (walk head range 8-15 cm, fore toe 15-20 cm) are within normal individual variation. The real defects are the timing ones: duty, swing duration and undertrack.

Severity stays medium. The mismatch with the RUN_SPEED comment is real, and the walk timing at stride 0.88-1.12 is visibly outside real walking.

The code observations hold. tuneGait (index.html:257-263) scales hind lift and flex by 0.85+0.15*hd, which is 0.97 to 1.03 over the 0.8-1.2 UI range at line 3282. hockPush is defined only in GAITS.race (line 217, 40 deg, so 32 to 48 deg). hindDrive appears nowhere else: hasRun at line 1721 excludes it from BODY motion, so duty, sweep, pitch and the lumbosacral motion do not change. The neutral hind-toe peaks in measurements.json match the finding (11.1 / 18.7 / 24.1 / 29.4 cm). The signed hock angle in race passes straight at push-off (about 192 deg at phase 6/32).

Real-horse claims that hold up:
(1) At the gallop the hind limbs give a net forward (accelerating) impulse and the forelimbs a net braking one. Self Davies, Spence and Wilson (2019), using force plates on ridden Thoroughbreds, report exactly this. Dutto et al. (2006) found the same at the trot: hind limb net work +0.34 J/kg, fore limb about 0.
(2) The hind stance is longer than the fore stance. Witte, Hirst and Wilson (2006) give mean stance of 77 ms fore vs 94 ms hind at 17 m/s, and 131 vs 143 ms at 9 m/s. The cited numbers are exact.
(3) Push-off comes mainly from hip extension and limb retraction, not from the hock. Dutto 2006: the hip does positive work throughout stance, the stifle passes it on and the distal joints act elastically. St George et al. (2023): the more propulsive trailing hind shows more gluteal activity, retraction and hip extension.
(4) The hock never reaches straight. Racehorses stand at a hock angle of about 160 +/- 4 deg (Ahmad et al. 2025, Morna racehorses).
(5) "Stepping under" means hind protraction at touchdown. That is the correct reading of the two quirk notes, "hind legs trailing out behind" and "hind legs did not step far under the body".

Overstated or wrong:
(a) "Stronger drive means a longer hind stance or duty" is not supported. Witte 2006 found no significant difference in any stride variable between lead and non-lead limbs, although they have different propulsive roles (Merkens 1993; St George 2023). Stance time is set by speed and limb sweep, not by how hard the leg pushes.
(b) "More lift into the flight" gets the horse gallop wrong. Its single suspension comes after the leading forelimb lifts off, with all four legs gathered under the body (Muybridge 1878/1887). The forelimbs launch the flight, not the hind push-off. Witte 2006 also found that aerial time does not depend on speed. The model's race footfalls (suspension after LF, phase 0.57-1.0) are already right.
(c) Williams et al. (2009) is about the limits on acceleration (pitch limits it at low speed, power at high speed). It does not show that horses with stronger drive pitch more at a steady speed. Larger pitch and lumbosacral amplitude with drive is plausible but not documented.
(d) The hock's limit comes mainly from the end of its own range of motion plus the stifle never straightening. The reciprocal apparatus links the two joints, but calling it the hard stop is an oversimplification. The conclusion is still right.

The core diagnosis stands: the slider is nearly invisible, it uses the wrong lever (opening the hock rather than hip retraction), and in the race it adds 7-8 deg of impossible hock hyperextension. The proposed fix should change. Express drive as more hip extension and retraction at lift-off, plus gather and pitch amplitude, while keeping hind duty about the same. Cap the hock at about 165-175 deg. Keep engagement (touchdown protraction) as a separate control. Medium severity is fair.
truth.correction:
The core real-horse claims hold:
- At the gallop the hind limbs give the net forward impulse and the forelimbs brake (Self Davies 2019).
- The hind stance is longer: 94 vs 77 ms at 17 m/s, and 143 vs 131 ms at 9 m/s (Witte 2006).
- Propulsion comes from hip extension and retraction. The distal hind joints, the hock included, mostly act as springs (Dutto 2006).
- The hock never reaches straight: racehorses stand at about 160 deg.
- "Stepping under" means protraction at touchdown.

Three parts should be dropped or softened:
1. That stronger drive means a longer hind stance or duty. Lead and non-lead limbs differ in propulsive role but have the same stance times (Witte 2006).
2. That drive adds "lift into the flight". The horse's only suspension follows lift-off of the leading forelimb, with the legs gathered under the body (Muybridge). The forelimbs, not the hinds, launch the flight.
3. Williams 2009 as support for "more trunk pitch". That paper is about the limits on acceleration, not about running style at a steady speed.

The hock limit is the joint's own end of range plus the coupling to the stifle, which never straightens. The reciprocal apparatus alone is not the stop.

Better fix: map hd to hip retraction and extension at lift-off, the hips gather and the pitch amplitude, with duty about the same. Clamp the hock at about 165-175 deg, and keep engagement (touchdown protraction) as a separate control.
