truth.reasoning:
The main complaint is right. The stated "expected" behaviour is partly wrong. I checked the real-horse side only and did not rerun the model.

What holds up:
- **No real limb can land twice that fast.** A limb has to finish its stance and its swing before it can land again. Swing alone takes about 0.34-0.43 s at trot, canter and racing gallop. The model's own GAITS table uses realistic values: trot T 0.72 s with duty 0.4 gives about 0.43 s of swing; canter T 0.6 s with duty 0.38 gives about 0.37 s; race T 0.43 s with duty 0.2 gives about 0.086 s of stance and 0.34 s of swing. The re-landings in the finding come 0.06 s, 0.11 s, 0.22 s and 0.29 s apart, which is impossible.
  - The 0.06-0.11 s cases are probably not real steps. They are more likely the hoof dipping in and out of the 4.5 mm contact band while index.html:1673-1690 blends, joint by joint, two IK poses with independent phases. That is still a visible defect, a scuff or double tap.
- **Pile-ups never happen in real gaits.** No horse gait has more than a diagonal or lateral pair landing together (FEI Art. 405; Hildebrand 1965, 1977). Three or four hooves landing within 60 ms is not physiological.
- **FEI Art. 405 is quoted correctly.** Canter to the right is left hind, left diagonal, right fore, then suspension. The model's left-lead table matches it (RH 0, LH+RF 0.27, LF 0.5).

What is wrong or overstated:
1. **"Within about one stride" is wrong for trot to canter.** Measured transitions take longer. Nauwelaerts, Aerts and Clayton (2013), Zoology 116:197-204, propose a series of kinematic events "that take about 2.5 strides to complete".
2. **"Outside hind first" is a convention, not what horses were measured doing.** The same study says "the transition is initiated by the fore limb". They saw "early and short placement of the fore limb... before the dissociation of the footfalls of one of the diagonal limb pairs", followed by changes in the hind limbs. A companion paper found the trailing hind's hip most variable at the transition stride (Vet J 2013;198 Suppl 1:e59-64).
   - Which forelimb steps early is my inference, not stated in the abstract. In a left-lead canter, LF lands about 0.25 of a stride earlier relative to the LH+RF pair than it does in the trot, and RH lands later. So the early, short step is most likely the leading fore, and the RH-LF diagonal is the pair that splits.
   - "Outside hind first" is the FEI stride-order definition and a riding-aid convention. It is not the measured transition sequence.
   - The 3-of-4 trials that started on the LH+RF pair are therefore not wrong in themselves.
   - One shortened step is normal, so "no limb steps twice" should read "no step shorter than is physically possible".
3. **The speed papers answer a different question.** Farley and Taylor (1991) found horses switch at a critical musculoskeletal force. Hoyt and Taylor (1981) is about energetics. Griffin et al. (2004) found walk-trot at Froude number about 0.35, or 1.6-2.3 m/s. All three explain when, or at what speed, a horse chooses to change gait. None describes footfall sequencing or the phase of a transition, and none supports "a specific phase within one stride". The model's transitions are user-commanded anyway.
4. **Canter to gallop and gallop to race are not gait switches in the same sense.** They keep the lead and the footfall order (RH, LH, RF, LF for a left lead). Real horses change them continuously over several strides, through diagonal dissociation and longer, faster strides. These need phase continuity, not a beat-matched entry.

**Severity.** I lowered it to medium. The defect is real and visible, but it lasts only the 0.6 s blend, and steady-state gaits are unaffected.
truth.correction:
Accurate version:
- During a gait change, no hoof should land again sooner than stance plus swing of the slower gait allows, roughly 0.3-0.4 s or more at trot, canter and gallop. One modestly shortened step is allowed.
- At most two hooves (a diagonal pair) may land together.
- The lead must be kept.
- A trot-to-canter transition spreads over about 2-3 strides (Nauwelaerts et al. 2013). The leading fore steps early and short, the RH-LF diagonal then splits, and the hind limbs change last.
- "Outside hind first" (FEI Art. 405) describes the canter stride order and riding aids. It is not a test for the first transition footfall.
- Canter-to-gallop and gallop-to-race keep the lead and footfall order. They should change continuously over several strides, with the phase carried through, rather than switching at a matched entry beat.
- Farley and Taylor (1991), Hoyt and Taylor (1981) and Griffin et al. (2004) set at what speed a transition happens (critical force; Froude number about 0.35 for walk-trot). They say nothing about footfall order during a transition and should not be cited for it.

Code check: the mechanism is as the critic describes. pose() (index.html:1675-1693) poses the old gait at wrap01(p*B.from.strides) and the new one at wrap01(p*rig.gait.strides), where p is the shared loop phase. It then slerps every node between the two over 0.6 s. setGait (3345-3362) switches straight away with no phase offset. The new gait's start phase is therefore set by the loop clock, not by the old gait's footfalls. Trot and gallop are a special case: both have 25 strides per loop, so g_new = g_old, but their land tables differ, so the beats still don't line up. The steady-state gaits are correct. GAITS canter for a left lead is RH 0, LH+RF 0.27, LF 0.5, which matches FEI Art. 405 mirrored. After about 0.7 s every recorded run settles into the right sequence.

Re-measurement: I re-ran the critic's an2/an3 on its 80 raw recordings and got the same counts (61/80 with a "stutter", 21/80 with a pile-up). The recordings were made at 14:33, after the last index.html commit at 12:51, and the worktree is clean. I also reproduced independently: I served this worktree on :8766 and ran 18 switches in headless Chromium (trot->canter, gallop->race and walk->trot, 6 offsets each). The irregular footfall order and the hoof sinking reproduce. Genuine re-steps appear too, e.g. gallop->race LH at 0.06 and 0.30 s with a 12.9 cm lift, and RF at 0.17 and 0.35 s with a 13.7 cm lift. Across all 132 such events, the hoof's highest point between the two touchdowns is: median 2.6 cm, first quartile 1.1 cm, minimum 0.4 cm. Often the hoof has first sunk 5 to 15 cm into the ground. Most events are a hoof bobbing at the ground surface, not a visible extra step. Runs whose worst event rises more than 5 cm: 27/80. More than 8 cm: 18/80.
(2) Several cited examples are at flicker level: trot->canter LH 0.16/0.45 rises 1.8 cm after sinking 7 cm; canter->gallop LH 0.14/0.20 rises 1.6 cm; walk->trot LH 0.09/0.31 rises 3.3 cm.

truth.reasoning:
This finding is a software determinism bug. It does not depend on any contested claim about real horses, and I found no real-horse grounds to refute it. What it expects is how real horses behave, with two small nuances that do not change the verdict.

1) Code check (read-only, index.html). pose() at 1675-1693 slerps every non-mesh node's quaternion between the old gait's pose and the new one. In three.js that rewrites all three Euler angles. Nothing resets the rig: poseGait (1722-1747) calls BODY[...] then solveLeg, and there is no identity/rest reset anywhere (grep finds no quaternion.identity or rotation.set(0,0,0) in the pose path). BODY.gallop/race write only spine.rotation.x, spine.rotation.z and spine.position. The tail segments get rotation.z and .y (1536-1537), so the tail's roll (.x) is never written. solveLeg writes scap/fem rotation.x (1444) and the chain's rotation.z (1497-1500), so scapula/femur yaw (.y) is never written. Any off-axis component the slerp leaves behind therefore persists. The next blend starts from the polluted pose, so the error builds up exactly as described. The method in residue.js is sound: steady 2 s windows, per-stance toe slip from contact detection, rotations dumped, and a non-blended reset tested.

2) Real-horse check of the "expected" behaviour.
(a) "A planted hoof does not skid." This is essentially right for the stance as a whole. Real hooves do slide briefly at impact, and some slip is functionally useful because it dissipates energy. Horan et al. 2024 (PLoS One, 389 hoof-ground contacts of galloping ex-racehorse Thoroughbreds filmed at 1000 fps) found that mean slip lasts only about 18-21 ms after impact (leading hind 18.3 ms; forelimbs and non-leading hind 20.4-21.5 ms). That is a small fraction of a racing-speed stance; after it the hoof is fixed until breakover. Slip distance rises with impact velocity (Parsons et al. 2011, EVJ, 338 footfalls at 11-19 m/s) and varies with surface and shoe (Crevier-Denoix 2013; Harvey 2012; Holden-Douilly 2013, where measurement differences were on the order of 1-2 cm at trot). Two consequences:
- A few cm of forward slip at touchdown would be realistic in itself.
- Real slip is (i) longitudinal, (ii) confined to the impact phase, and (iii) does not grow with the horse's history. The observed 6-15 cm sideways wander of the LH toe track, the 9-12 cm skids after 8 blends, and up to 1.26 m per stance in the sweep have no real-horse counterpart.
(b) "Limbs swing in their sagittal planes without accumulated hip or shoulder rotation." Strictly sagittal swing is a simplification. Real hind limbs show small out-of-plane motion: in Lanovaz et al. 2002 (EVJ Suppl, bone-pinned 3D tarsal kinematics) internal/external rotation and translations were mostly coupled to flexion, with some non-coupled internal/external rotation in stance. But that motion repeats with the stride phase and stays the same from stride to stride. It never accumulates into a constant 4-6 degree femur yaw that depends on earlier gait changes. The key word "accumulated" makes the claim correct.
(c) "The tail hangs straight at rest." This is broadly true. In gallop the tail swings with the stride, and a few individuals carry it habitually to one side, but a roll built up along the dock from blend history (about -32 degrees summed) is not real behaviour.
(d) "Same gait at the same phase gives the same pose." This is the intended property of a cyclic animation; real stride-to-stride variability is small and does not drift.

Corrections I would make only to the wording (they do not change the verdict): say "the hoof may slide forward a few cm in the first ~20 ms after impact but is then fixed, never sideways", and "limbs may show small, phase-coupled out-of-plane rotations, never history-dependent offsets".

Severity stays high. The error has no bound short of rebuilding the horse, it breaks the IK's planted-hoof guarantee, and normal UI use (repeated blended gait changes) triggers it. After only 2 blends the effect is about 4-5 cm, close in size to real impact slip but sideways and present throughout the stance, so it is subtle at first and grows from there.
truth.correction: The bug and its mechanism stand. Two small changes to the "expected" wording would make it more accurate. First, real Thoroughbred hooves do slide briefly at touchdown: about 18-21 ms of slip after impact at gallop (Horan et al. 2024), a few cm depending on surface, shoe and impact speed (Parsons et al. 2011; Crevier-Denoix et al. 2013). After that the hoof stays put until breakover, and it never slides sideways, so "no skid during stance" should read "no skid beyond a brief forward slip at impact". Second, real limbs are not strictly sagittal: the hock shows small internal/external rotations tied to flexion (Lanovaz et al. 2002). truth.reasoning:
I tried to refute the claims about real horses and could not. The cited code also checks out. makeGait gives period = strides*T (index.html 272-274). The change() handler sets dur: 0.6 for every gait pair (3351). The render loop uses rate = lerp(1/B.from.period, 1/rig.gait.period, smooth01(B.t/B.dur)), and the ground moves at W*rate (4092-4094). Walk to race in 0.6 s therefore averages 25.6 m/s2, and the smoothstep peak is 1.5 times that, about 38 m/s2.

Real-horse checks (Williams, Tan, Usherwood & Wilson 2009, Biol Lett 5:610, PMC2781967; read directly):
1. "maximal accelerations were 10 and 6 m s-2" for greyhounds and horses. Pitch limit: a_max = g*L_caud/L_leg, with L_caud 0.70 m and L_leg 1.32 m in the polo ponies (about 5.2 m/s2 predicted). Confirmed.
2. "At speeds above 5 m s-1, maximum accelerations are consistent with constant, constrained power". The limit is 30 W/kg of body mass. Confirmed. One caveat: the mass is horse plus rider. Polo ponies are largely Thoroughbred-type and carry a heavier rider than a jockey, so the figure transfers to a 475 kg Thoroughbred about one to one.
3. Ramp times (my script: C:/Users/Aaron/AppData/Local/Temp/skeptic404/env.js, with a = min(6, 30/v)):
   - walk to race: 4.9 s over 53 m
   - gallop to race: 4.1 s over 50 m
   - A generous Thoroughbred envelope (7 m/s2, 40 W/kg) still needs 3.7 s and 40 m.
   - So "roughly 5 s, 50-60 m" holds, and it is a lower bound. The 30/v envelope ignores drag and the power needed just to hold speed, so real acceleration falls toward zero near top speed.
4. Cadence: Witte, Hirst & Wilson 2006 (J Exp Biol 209:4389) measured Thoroughbreds at gallop from 9 to 17 m/s. Stance plus protraction gives strides of 495 ms (2.0 Hz) at 9 m/s and 419 ms (2.4 Hz) at 17 m/s. Real horses run from about 0.9 Hz at walk to about 2.4 Hz at full gallop. Leg cycles of 5.7 to 10.6 Hz, or 6.5 Hz in a gallop, are impossible. Confirmed.

Refinements (none overturns the finding):
(a) Slowing down is even more limited than speeding up. Williams 2009 gives a dissipative limit of about -23 W/kg and a forward-pitch limit of about g*L_cran/L_leg = 0.52/1.31 g, about 3.9 m/s2. Under that envelope, race to walk takes about 6.5 s and 70 m, and race to gallop about 5.3 s. The -38 m/s2 case is therefore even worse than stated. Any acceleration limit used in a fix should be lower for braking than for speeding up.
(b) Walk to trot is only marginal. The physical envelope allows it in about 0.36 s. The 0.6 s blend averages 3.6 m/s2 and only its smoothstep peak (8.2 m/s2) is above 6. Real walk-to-trot changes happen within about one stride, so 0.6 s is realistic there. The same holds for canter to gallop in this model, because its 'gallop' runs at only 6.19 m/s. The impossible cases are the transitions into and out of race speed.
(c) Fix option 1 chains walk to trot to canter to gallop to race. Real horses accelerating hard do not pass through trot. They strike off from walk or from a standstill straight into canter or gallop strides, as racehorses do leaving the stalls.
(d) "Smoothly" is slightly idealised. Stride frequency steps at each gait change (Heglund, Taylor & McMahon 1974), although each step is small.

Severity stays high. The race transitions break real-horse limits about 6 to 8 times over, and the legs visibly cycle at up to 10 Hz.

I tried to refute this on real-horse grounds and could not. The code reading is also right.

Code: in setGait (index.html ~3345-3352), switching again mid-blend sets B = { from: r.gait, frozen: true, q, v }. Here r.gait is the target of the first blend (race), not the speed actually being shown. The loop at 4092 then starts the rate at 1/B.from.period. In measurements.json, race is 16.8 m/s and gallop 6.19 m/s, so this explains a jump from about 5.7 m/s (part way through walk to race) up to 16.8 m/s, followed by an ease down to 6.2 m/s. The frozen q/v pose stops tracking the ground, which explains the skating.

Real horses:
(1) Speed continuity and acceleration limits. Williams, Tan, Usherwood & Wilson (2009, Biol Lett 5:610-613, PMC2781967) measured polo ponies, which are bred for acceleration, over 160 strides with differential GPS. Their maximum acceleration was about 6 m/s² at low speed. Above 5 m/s it is limited by muscle power of about 30 W/kg, so roughly 3 m/s² at 10 m/s. Deceleration is limited by a dissipative power of about -23 to -27 W/kg. Turning, where grip is the limit, reaches about 8 m/s² centripetal in ponies. The finding's 254 m/s² (26 g) spike is about 40 times what a real horse can do, and the trot to canter to trot spike of 58 m/s² is about 10 times. The 16.8 to 6.2 m/s drop in 0.6 s is about 18 m/s² of deceleration, about 3 times the real limit. No breed or normal Thoroughbred variation comes close.
(2) Planted hooves. The phrase "planted hooves do not move" is idealised. Real hooves do slip and sink at the start of stance, but only by centimetres. Holden-Douilly et al. (2013, Vet J 197:198-204) measured slip at a 7 m/s trot on sand and dirt in centimetres. Crevier-Denoix et al. (2013, Vet J 198 Suppl 1:e124-9) found larger but still small slip and sink on all-weather waxed tracks than on turf at the canter. Harvey, Williams & Singer (2012, Vet J 192:217-221) measured stud-dependent slip on grass at the canter. A 1.08 m or 4.2 m skid is two orders of magnitude beyond this. The penetration figures (5.7 cm, and 9-11 cm for 0.3 s) are about the size of real sink on soft dirt or sand. However, the model's ground is drawn rigid, so in the model this is still an artefact of the frozen pose, not realistic sink.

Nuance that does not weaken the finding: the expected behaviour (continuous speed) is necessary but not sufficient. Even an uninterrupted 0.6 s walk to race blend (1.44 to 16.8 m/s) averages about 26 m/s², roughly 4 times a real horse's limit. A real horse would need several seconds and many strides to make that change. Fix option 1 (carry the current rate and keep the old pose live) is the right minimum, and blend lengths scaled by the speed change would also help realism. Medium severity is reasonable: the glitch needs a quick second click and lasts about 0.6 s, but it is very visible (metre-scale skating, a hoof below the ground) and plainly unphysical.

truth.reasoning:
I could not refute this on real-horse grounds. The claim only says the legs should carry on from where they were, with no one-frame jump. Every study of horse gait transitions describes the limbs moving continuously through the change, and a hoof on the ground stays put until it lifts off. Muybridge's sequences show the same thing.
- Walk to trot (Griffin et al. 2004): the switch happens over about one stride, with the limbs moving continuously.
- Trot to gallop (Farley & Taylor 1991; Hoyt & Taylor 1981): the gait change happens within a stride cycle as the stride timing reorganises, not as a jump in limb position.

A real horse cannot move a limb 0.3 to 1.6 m in a single 16 ms frame. Nothing about Thoroughbreds or normal variation explains this away, so the stated expectation is correct.

I also checked the code claim, read-only:
- index.html:1680 poses the old gait at `wrap01(p * B.from.strides)`, with no per-horse offset.
- Parade and companion horses are posed at `wrap01(p*r.gait.strides + ex.phase)` (line 3782). `ex.phase` is a random value from `rnd()` (lines 3400 and 3420).
- Field horses are posed at `wrap01((scroll + x)/strideM + (number*0.61)%1)` (line 3662).
- On the first frame of a blend, `w = smooth01(B.t/B.dur)` is about 0. The blend timer starts at 0 and only goes up by one frame's dt (line 4095), so the pose shown is almost entirely the old gait at the wrong phase. The frame before showed the old gait at the right phase, so the legs jump by an amount set by each horse's offset. For the rest of the 0.6 s blend the old gait plays smoothly from that wrong phase, so the jump happens once, at the start.
- The hero is posed at `wrap01(p*rig.gait.strides)` with no offset (line 3754), so it is not affected, as the finding says.
- The scratch folder the finding cites exists (C:/Users/Aaron/AppData/Local/Temp/horse-transitions/).

Severity: medium holds. It only happens on a gait change. But then every background horse jumps at once, by up to about 1.6 m, which is several times their normal per-frame motion and easy to see.

The first fix option is sound: compute the old gait's phase as `gFrom = frac(g - frac(p*to.strides) + p*from.strides)`. For the parade and companion horses that works out to `p*from.strides + ex.phase`. For field horses it also works out to the old gait's x-based phase, because `(scroll + x)/strideM` scales with the stride count.

truth.reasoning:
The code defect is real. In pose(), index.html:1682 builds rig.nodes from root descendants with `!o.isMesh`. The ear meshes (rig.ears[].mesh, pushed at 1001) and the mane blades and locks (rig.mane[].mesh, 1098 and 1121) are Mesh objects that mergeRigid keeps as invisible nodes (1340-1343). So they never get a slot in B.q/B.v and are not slerped. They take the new gait's BODY values (race ears 0.32 rad at 1555, mane 0.42*amp at 1559, against walk's idleEars(-0.12) at 1580 and mane ~0.05*amp at 1582) in a single frame. The neck and head do ease over the 0.6 s blend. Racing ears 0.32 vs walking -0.12 is about 25 deg and mane lift 0.42 vs ~0.05 is about 21-34 deg, which matches the reported jump size.

The real-horse "expected" statement is half right.

1) Mane: confirmed. The mane is passive hair, so its lift comes from inertia and airflow and cannot change 30+ deg in 16 ms. It should build up and settle as speed changes. Muybridge's sequences show the mane lifting progressively with the stride, not jumping.

2) Ears: overstated. Real ear carriage is driven by attention and emotion, not by speed or gait, and it is not coupled to the head and neck. EquiFACS (Wathan et al. 2015) describes "an extremely complex and robust set of auricular muscles that allow a great range and specificity of movement" and says "the ears can, and often do, move independently" (left and right separately). Ears can flick forward or back in a fraction of a second at any gait, and racehorses do not reliably go from pricked to pinned as they speed up: they flick between forward, sideways (toward the jockey) and back. So "ear carriage changes gradually over the transition, together with the head and neck" is not a real-horse rule. A fast ear change is realistic. What is unrealistic is a zero-duration, perfectly symmetrical change locked to the gait switch frame.

The fix (put the ear and mane bones in the blend set, e.g. build rig.nodes from rig.skeleton.bones) is right for the mane. For the ears, sharing the 0.6 s neck ease is acceptable but not what a horse does. A shorter ease, or keeping the ears on the idleEars-style attention rhythm with small side-to-side offsets, would be more faithful. Severity stays medium: a 34 deg one-frame pop of every mane blade is clearly visible at each gait change, while the ear part is a smaller realism issue.

Ears are voluntary, attention-driven organs that move independently of each other and of the head and neck. They can flick within a fraction of a second at any gait and are not tied to speed (EquiFACS: "ears can, and often do, move independently"). So the expected behaviour for the ears is "no zero-duration, perfectly symmetrical jump", not "ease together with the head and neck over the transition". Ears can use a shorter, independent ease. Racehorses do not reliably go from pricked to pinned as speed rises.

truth.reasoning:
The main real-horse claims are correct. The finding overstates some details and misreads what the scene shows.

What holds up:
1. Racehorses run bends on the inside lead and are usually changed in the straight. The JRA glossary entry for 手前 (lead) says horses run right-handed courses on the right lead and left-handed courses on the left lead, otherwise they drift wide on the corners. It adds that in the final straight a horse switches to whichever lead is easier for it. That is a change to the easier lead, not always to the outside lead.
2. Horses do have individual lead preferences.
   - Deuel & Lawrence (1987, J Biomech 20:645) filmed 4 Quarter Horse fillies on a straight. They switched leads on their own and chose the left lead about twice as often as the right, even though riders asked for each lead equally.
   - Williams & Norris (2007, Anim Behav 74:941; doi 10.1016/j.anbehav.2007.01.014) found that racehorses prefer one lead and use it more in a 6-furlong workout.
   - Parkes et al. (2020, PLoS ONE e0244105) had riders let 7 Thoroughbreds choose their own lead on an anticlockwise UK oval. 359 of 1,931 strides (about 19%) were on the "incorrect" right lead, 195 of them on the curve. The authors put this down to a right-lead preference that many horses show.
3. Changing only the fore or only the hind leaves the horse disunited. A strongly one-sided horse may hold its lead. Symboli Rudolf held the right lead from the start to the final corner at Nakayama, which fits the quirk data.

What needs correcting:
(a) "Fore and hind change together during the suspension" is the dressage ideal (FEI Art. 405). Galloping racehorses often change in front first and behind one or more strides later, so a few disunited strides are a normal part of a racing lead change, not only an optional fault. A realistic routine would allow a hind lag of 0-2 strides.
(b) "Cross-firing" is the wrong term. It strictly means a hind hoof striking the diagonal fore, mostly in pacers. The gait problem is "disunited" or "cross-cantering", though racetrack slang sometimes uses cross-firing for it.
(c) "A field shows mixed leads" holds mainly on straights and around the change points. On a bend most of a field is on the inside lead: about 80% of strides even with no cue in Parkes et al.
(d) "Tired horses often change again late in the straight" is widely repeated racing lore. I found no study that puts a number on it, so it should be an optional, low-probability behaviour.
(e) Deuel & Lawrence studied 4 Quarter Horses, not Thoroughbreds. Williams & Norris and Parkes et al. are the Thoroughbred sources.

How this changes the finding: the race scene never shows a bend. Racecourses scroll on a straight strip; only one location (data/locations.js:795) uses a curved stadium path, and it is not a racecourse. turnIn at 28 s is only a story point where the field fans out. Tokyo is left-handed and its lead is set to 'R' (data/locations.js:42). That is the usual lead on the straights of a left-handed course, which are the only stretches the story shows. So the hero being on R for the whole race is not wrong for what is on screen. The real gaps are smaller:
- an 18-horse field in perfect unison, with no seeded per-horse leads or change timing;
- no left-lead stretch or change around the implied turn;
- no lead-preference parameter for the Oguri Cap, Symboli Rudolf and Silence Suzuka quirks.
The hoof jump when the lead is forced to change is a code bug I did not check. Against real horses the visible error is minor, so I lowered the severity to low. Option 3 (a seeded lead per horse plus preference from quirks), with an optional front-first change that has a hind lag, matches real racing best for the effort.
truth.correction: Real racehorses run bends on the inside lead and are usually changed in the straight, to the outside lead or whichever is easier for them (JRA glossary, 手前). They have individual lead preferences: Williams & Norris 2007 for Thoroughbreds, Deuel & Lawrence 1987 for 4 Quarter Horses, and Parkes et al. 2020, where about 19% of strides were on the outside lead when horses chose freely. In racing, lead changes are often made in front first, with the hind following 0-2 strides later. A clean change of fore and hind in one suspension is the dressage ideal, so a few disunited strides are normal. Use "disunited" or "cross-cantering", not "cross-firing". A field's leads are mixed mainly on straights; on a bend most horses are on the inside lead. Late changes from fatigue are anecdotal. In this scene the course is a straight scroll with no bend drawn, and 'R' on left-handed Tokyo is the conventional straight lead. So the realistic gaps are only the field moving in unison, the missing change timing around the implied turn, and the missing lead-preference quirks, not a wrong lead.

model.reasoning:
I re-checked the code. Two parts of the finding are wrong or overstated, and the rest is a feature gap rather than wrong behaviour on screen.

What the code confirms:
- setLocation sets state.lead = loc.lead ?? 'L' (index.html:3719). Tokyo has hand 'left', lead 'R' (data/locations.js:42).
- spawnField never sets a gait on the field rigs. setGait's change() gives the hero and every 'companion', 'parade' and 'field' rig makeGait(state.gait, …, state.lead, r.run) (3347, 3359). All 18 runners are therefore on the same lead for the whole 52 s story.
- There is no lead-change routine. look.run (1706-1719, tuneGait 256-264) has no lead or leadChange field, and the hash does not store lead (3901-3909).
- The quirks at data/quirks.js:106, 177 and 482 all have param:null.
- From the code, the teleport is real. When the key is unchanged, from.key === to.key, so r.blend = null (3350). makeGait only remaps land[] (270), so the hooves jump in one frame.

Where the finding is wrong or overstated:
1. The teleport is not a bug a user can hit. Nothing in the UI changes the lead while the horse moves. The gait buttons (3857) keep state.lead, and the lead changes only in setLocation, which rebuilds the whole world and sets the gait without a blend. The critic's flying.js reached it only through the debug hook window.__horse (4102), by setting state.lead and calling setGait by hand. It matters only as a limitation for anyone who later builds a lead change on top of setGait.
2. There is no visible bend in the race. The track builder is a straight strip that scrolls under the horse (section 7). The "home turn" between turnIn-6 and turnIn+5 is only a sideways fan-out, plus a small heading change from that drift (3647-3653). The HUD switches from "Back straight" to "Home straight" with no curve in between. For a left-handed course, real horses take the corners on the left (inside) lead and change to the right (outside) lead in the straights. On the left-handed course in Japan this is described as cornering on 左手前 and changing to 右手前. So a fixed 'R' at Tokyo, and 'L' on the right-handed courses, is the correct lead for everything the scene actually shows. "Inside lead on the bend" applies to nothing on screen.
3. The field is not in footfall unison. Each runner's phase is offset by its number (wrap01(... + (number*0.61)%1), 3662), and the phaseOffset values differ too. Only the lead side is the same for every horse.

What remains real is a variety and customisation gap:
- Every runner is on the same lead.
- No horse fails to change, or changes back late when tired (real horses do this in the straight).
- There is no per-horse lead parameter, even though three roster horses have documented lead quirks (Symboli Rudolf, Oguri Cap, Silence Suzuka).
- There is no flying-change routine for a future feature to use.

The fix options are still sensible (a per-horse lead parameter mapped from the quirks, a seeded lead for the field, and a flying change during the suspension phase). But since the scene shows no bend, this is a low-severity realism and customisation gap, not a medium motion error.

No horse changes lead, no horse varies from the others, and the look.run parameters have no lead preference, so the lead quirks for Symboli Rudolf, Oguri Cap and Silence Suzuka are not used (quirks.js:106, 177, 482: param:null). The race is shown entirely on a straight. The home turn is narrated (a sideways fan-out and the HUD text), not drawn as a bend. The fixed outside lead therefore matches what real racehorses do on straights; what is missing is variation: some horses not changing, late re-changes when tired, and per-horse preferences. The footfall phases already differ between runners, so the field is not in unison. The one-frame hoof jump happens only when state.lead is changed and setGait is called by hand from the debug console (window.__horse). No UI path changes the lead mid-stride. findings.title: On parade-ring bends the horse stays upright and straight: no lean, no lateral bend, no head to the inside, and any speed is allowed
findings.observed: Paddock ring (radius 11.4 m, ccw), sampled mid-bend for 1.2 s at each gait. Mean trunk roll: walk -0.08, trot -0.20, canter 0.00, gallop -0.05 deg; roll range is only the gait's own +/-1.0-1.4 deg. truth.reasoning:
I read the full texts of both cited papers and the Byström 2021 companion study. The direction and mechanism of the claim hold, but the magnitudes are taken from a much tighter circle than the paddock's and are presented as targets when they are not.

What checks out:
- Egenvall et al. 2023 does report pelvic roll near 0 at walk, 5-6 deg at trot and 16-17 deg at canter, an inside thoracolumbar bend of 5-6 deg (stride mean, all gaits), and a neck-to-trunk angle of 9, 12 and 14-15 deg to the inside. The quotes are accurate.
- Tan & Wilson 2011 fit the speed limit on turns tighter than 30 m with a friction model at mu = 0.6 (0.7 drawn as a bound), r = 0.99. On turns wider than 30 m, racehorses slowed in line with a limb-force limit.
- sqrt(0.6-0.7 g x 11.4 m) = 8.2-8.8 m/s. The 2.31 g needed by the 16.1 m/s race gait is physically impossible on that bend.

What is overstated:
1. **Lean is below the formula, not in line with it.** Real horses lean a few degrees less than atan(v^2/gR).
   - Egenvall's horses leaned 2.8 deg less than predicted at trot and 3.4 deg less at canter, and did not lean at all at walk.
   - Pfau et al. 2012 (cited by Egenvall) found 1.2 deg less on average, with individual horses ranging from -8.1 to +3.8 deg.
   - Greve & Dyson 2016: well-trained horses lean less than poorly trained ones.
   - Realistic targets at R = 11.4 m: trot about 4-6 deg, canter about 9-11 deg, gallop about 16 deg, walk about 0.
2. **The bend and head numbers come from a much tighter circle.** Egenvall used about 9 m diameter (R about 4.5 m), lunged, at 1.2 / 2.4 / 3.7 m/s. Byström 2021 used R about 5 m at 3.3 m/s trot and found the back bent 3.6-3.75 deg more to the inside than on the straight, and the neck about 5 deg more.
   - If the back simply follows the arc, the bend is about 0.95 m / (2R), which gives 6 deg at R = 4.5 m. That matches Egenvall's 5-6 deg.
   - At R = 11.4 m the same rule gives about 2.4 deg, not 5-6 deg.
   - The 9-15 deg head figures are a neck-to-trunk angle that was not corrected for lean. The authors flag possible projection error, and 52% of its variance was unexplained residual variation. The horses were also on a lunge line, so these figures are an upper bound for a horse led in hand on an 11.4 m bend.
3. **The real paddock scenario is walk, which the model already gets about right.** The paddock is the only path-mode location (data/locations.js:795). Its default gait is walk, and the horses there are led in hand round Tokyo's parade ring.
   - Real horses do not lean at walk (Egenvall), so the model's walk roll of -0.08 deg is correct.
   - At walk, the model only lacks a small inward bend of about 2-3 deg and a few degrees of head to the inside.
   - Trot to race round a parade ring is not something real racehorses do. The missing lean there is real physics, but only in a scenario the user has to force, which is why I lower the severity to low.
4. **The fix is calibrated too high.** Yawing chest and hips by ±k x 0.6 rad gives a total bend of 1.2/R: 6 deg at 11.4 m and 15 deg at 4.5 m. That is about 2.5 times the measured 5-6 deg at R about 4.5-5 m. A total thoracolumbar bend of about 0.5 m x k rad matches the data.

The remaining points stand: the code feeds no curvature into the body pose (placeOnPath 3741-3751 only turns the ring; makePath gives k = 1/R on the bends). Capping the speed on bends, or making the horse slow through them, and taking the canter lead from path.dir both stand as good fixes.
truth.correction: Real horses lean in proportion to v^2/(gR), but on average 1-3.4 deg less than the formula predicts (Pfau 2012: -1.2 deg, individuals -8.1 to +3.8; Egenvall 2023: -2.8 deg at trot, -3.4 deg at canter). They do not lean at walk. Egenvall's 5-6 deg back bend and 9-15 deg head-to-inside were measured on lunged horses on a ~9 m diameter circle (R about 4.5 m) at 1.2 / 2.4 / 3.7 m/s. The head angle was not corrected for lean, so treat it as an upper bound. Bend scales with curvature: about 0.95 m/(2R) rad, so roughly 2.4 deg at the paddock's 11.4 m radius. Realistic targets at R = 11.4 m: walk 0 deg lean, 2-3 deg back bend, a few degrees of head inside; trot lean about 4-6 deg; canter about 9-11 deg; gallop about 16 deg. The grip limit (Tan & Wilson: friction model with mu about 0.6 for radii under 30 m) is correct and gives v_max about 8.2-8.8 m/s on this bend; the 16.1 m/s race gait is impossible there. The paddock's real use is walk in hand, where the model's upright trunk is already correct; the large lean gaps appear only when the user picks faster gaits that real horses do not use in a parade ring. In the fix, chest and hip yaw of ±k x 0.6 rad gives a total bend of 1.2/R, about 2.5 times the measured values; use a total thoracolumbar bend of about 0.5 m x k rad.

fixOptions.label: Record real touchdowns
fixOptions.approach: When a hoof's sole reaches about SOLE with near-zero speed relative to the ground, push its ground-frame position into a per-hoof ring buffer; draw prints and spawn dust from that buffer.
fixOptions.risk: Prints must still wrap with the scenery period W (store strip x).

fixOptions.label: Freeze the old trail
fixOptions.approach: On a gait change, freeze the existing trail in ground coordinates and only lay new prints with the new gait.

references: Muybridge E (1887) Animal Locomotion (footprint spacing follows the footfalls actually made)

truth.reasoning:
I couldn't refute the real-horse part of this finding. A hoofprint is a fixed impression in the substrate. Once the hoof leaves, the mark stays where it is. Prints laid before a gait change therefore keep that gait's spacing, and nothing about a later change of gait can move them. This is plain physics, not a breed trait or a matter of normal variation.

Dust and sand thrown up at ground contact also start from where a hoof actually touched. In loose sand much of it is flicked backward during push-off and breakover, not only at impact.

The code matches the observation. buildPrints.update (index.html ~2997-3024) rebuilds every print position each frame from the current gait: for each print n it places it at x0 - d, where d = (since + n/G.strides)*W and since comes from G.land and G.strides. updateDust (~3079-3098) places each puff the same way, at x0 - G.stride*s*a with a computed from G.land. So when setGait swaps G, the whole trail and every puff are repositioned to the new gait's analytic spacing. The reported 6-20 m jumps follow directly from that.

Small refinements, none of which overturns the claim:
1) A real gait change is not a switch at one instant. It takes one or a few transition strides, and canter to walk usually passes through a few decelerating trot strides. So a real trail shows old-gait spacing, then one or more irregular transition prints, then new-gait spacing, not a clean split.
2) In sand the hoof slides forward a little at impact and rotates at breakover, so real prints are somewhat elongated or smeared. They are still fixed marks.
3) Muybridge is a weak citation for footprint spacing. Better ones are footfall and stride-length studies such as Hildebrand's gait analyses and the transition-energetics work of Hoyt and Taylor (1981), plus hoof-slip studies such as Pardoe et al. (2001).

The 'Record real touchdowns' fix matches what a real horse does. The 'Freeze the old trail' fix would still lay idealised new-gait prints during the blend, where real transition strides have irregular spacing.

Severity stays low: it is a visual artefact in the ground effects, not in the horse's anatomy or gait.

model.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and couldn't. The code does what the finding says.

Code check:
- buildPrints.update (index.html:2997-3024) does not store any touchdowns. Every frame it places all 14 prints per hoof with the formula xs = x0 - (since + n/G.strides)*W, where since = wrap01(p*G.strides - G.land[id])/G.strides and x0 = P.xc + G.stanceLen/2 + 0.4*HOOF_TOE.
- setGait (3345-3362) swaps r.gait to the new gait straight away. With blend:true it only adds r.blend, and only pose() (1675-1693) uses r.blend, to ease the joints.
- loopPhase p carries on across the switch (4092-4093), so the ground does not jump. But applyPhase (3753-3768) passes the new rig.gait to prints.update and updateDust. Every print, and every dust puff (a = wrap01(g - G.land) with g = frac(p*newStrides), x = x0 - stride*a), is therefore placed again from the new gait's strides, land and stanceLen.
- In steady play, d grows by dp*W while the ground moves by -dp*W, so prints stay fixed in the sand (0 drift), as the critic says.
- Only the beach location has prints (data/locations.js 'beach': W 120, prints true). The dust part applies wherever dust is on.

Re-measure: I copied GAITS, makeGait and the print formula into node (C:/Users/Aaron/AppData/Local/Temp/skeptic-prints-410/p.js) and swept 400 loop phases with W = 120.
- canter (40 strides of 3.000 m) to walk (75 of 1.600 m): the same print slot moves up to 19.50 m, which matches the critic's 19.6.
- canter to trot and canter to gallop (46 of 2.609 m): up to 7.5 m, which matches the critic's 5.7 and 6.5 at one phase.
- gallop to race: up to 26.7 m.

Nuance on size: the prints are identical instances, so how far a numbered slot moves overstates what a viewer sees. Measuring from each new print to the nearest old print of the same hoof gives a mean of 0.76-0.87 m and a maximum of 2.7-2.9 m (canter to walk, trot or gallop) and 5.9 m (gallop to race, trot to canter). The trail's length also changes: at p = 0.3 the LF trail on canter to walk goes in one frame from 13 prints 3 m apart reaching 36 m back, to 14 prints 1.6 m apart reaching only 20 m back. So the whole trail visibly re-lays: spacing changes, the far prints vanish, and the newest print can sit where no hoof has landed yet.

During the 0.6 s blend, pose() draws the hooves as a slerp between the old and new gait poses, while dust and prints use only the new gait's land spots. That mismatch is real too, though brief.

A real hoofprint stays where the hoof struck. Track spacing follows the footfalls actually made (Muybridge 1887). So the trail behind the horse should keep the old gait's spacing.

The finding is correct in substance and the severity of low fits: it is cosmetic and limited to the beach (prints) plus a brief dust re-phase.

findings.title: Right lead mirrors legs, roll and tail exactly, but not the mane sway or ear flicks
findings.observed: One stride each of canter, gallop and race on the left and right leads, compared as mirror images. Hoof positions, trunk roll and tail yaw mirror exactly (error 0). Mane sideways sway and ear flicks are identical on both leads instead of mirrored: the mismatch is twice their amplitude, mane 4.6-6.9 deg and ears 2.3-2.9 deg. There is no lateral head motion in any gait (head z = 0.000 m at every phase), so nothing there needs mirroring.

fixOptions.label: Apply the lead sign
fixOptions.approach: Multiply mane rotation.x by m, and for ears use side' = m * e.side in the phase and multiply rotation.x by m, in BODY.canter, BODY.gallop and BODY.race.

truth.reasoning:
The code matches what the finding observed. In BODY.gallop, BODY.race and BODY.canter, the lead sign m is applied only to spine.rotation.x (trunk roll) and to tail rotation.y. The ear rotation.x terms (0.04-0.05 * cyc(g,1,0.3+e.side*0.2)) and the mane rotation.x terms (0.08-0.12 * amp * cyc(...)) ignore the lead, so both leads produce the same motion.

The real-horse rule it rests on is overstated. The claim is that "every lateral motion should mirror; a right-lead stride is the left-lead stride reflected."

(1) Mirror symmetry is a reasonable idealisation for limbs and trunk, but real Thoroughbreds are not mirror images across leads. They show motor laterality and lead preferences (McGreevy & Rogers 2005; Williams & Norris 2007, racehorse stride-pattern laterality). FEI Art. 405 only defines the left and right canter as mirror-image footfall sequences.

(2) The mane does not reflect between leads. A real mane lies on one side of the neck, conventionally the off (right) side, and the model does the same: the mount rotation.x is about +0.95 rad, so the blades hang towards +Z. A strict reflection would move the mane to the near side, which no lead change does. In this rig, the blade's rotation.x mainly flaps it down and out around the crest. The tip moves along the blade's local Z, about (0, -0.81, +0.58) in the mount frame, so the motion is mostly vertical and only partly sideways. For a mane hanging on one side, that flap is driven mostly by vertical bounce and pitch, and those are the same on both leads in the model (spine y and pitch carry no m). In gallop and race the flap even runs twice per stride (k=2), so it is not coupled to the once-per-stride roll. Only a small roll-driven part (trunk roll is about ±1.2-1.4°) should change sign with the lead. The proposed fix would flip the whole mane flap and put it half a cycle out of phase with the bounce on the right lead. That is no more realistic than the current code.

(3) Real ear movements are voluntary and track attention (Wathan & McComb 2014). They are not locked to stride phase or to the lead, so nothing in real horses requires "ear flicks" to mirror. Only a passive ear wobble caused by head and trunk roll would mirror. Mirroring the model's stride-locked lateral ear wobble is a harmless consistency tweak, not a fix for something wrong in real-horse terms.

Severity stays low: the effect is a few degrees of secondary motion.
truth.correction: Footfalls, trunk roll and tail sway should mirror between leads, and they already do. Real horses are only roughly mirror-symmetric across leads, because laterality and lead preference exist. The mane is not reflected between leads: it lies on one side (here the off side, as is conventional). Its stride-locked down-and-out flap is driven mainly by vertical bounce, which is the same on both leads, so only a small part coupled to roll should change sign with m. Multiplying the whole mane rotation.x by m would be wrong; the better fix is a lead-independent bounce term plus a small m * roll term. Real ear movements are active and not tied to the lead, so mirroring the ear wobble is optional and only for consistency.

The code observation is right. makeGait swaps the footfalls for a right lead (index.html:250, 270), and the lead sign m is used only for spine.rotation.x and the tail's rotation.y (1510/1515/1537, 1543/1547/1565, 1594/1598/1616). Mane rotation.x (1531, 1560, 1611) and both ear rotations (1525-1526, 1555-1556, 1606-1607) do not use the lead, so their values are the same on both leads. The critic's lead.js compares these Euler values directly, so its "error = twice the amplitude" comes from that comparison by construction. The amplitudes it quotes are correct: mane rx 0.08 / 0.12 / 0.10 rad = 4.6 / 6.9 / 5.7 deg, ear rx 0.04-0.05 rad = 2.3-2.9 deg.

Where the finding goes wrong:

1. "Head z = 0.000 m at every phase / no lateral head motion" is wrong. measurements.json (left lead) shows the poll moving sideways by -0.018 to +0.014 m in gallop, ±0.014 m in canter, -0.012 to +0.010 m in race, and ±0.018-0.021 m in walk and trot. The eye and withers show similar values. The 0.000 in lead.js is the head's mirror error, not its z position. The head's sideways motion comes from the spine roll, which already flips with m.

2. Mane rotation.x is not mainly a sideways sway. Each blade sits on a mount with Euler XYZ = (0.95-1.15 rad, 0, θ) (1118). Mesh rotation.x therefore moves the blade tip along the mount's Z axis, which in the bone frame is (0, -sin a, cos a) ≈ (0, -0.87, 0.50). That motion is mostly vertical: a flop about the crest. Under a true z-mirror, M·Rx(a)Rz(θ)Rx(rx)Rz(rz)·M = Rx(-a)Rz(θ)Rx(-rx)Rz(rz). Negating rx mirrors the blade only if the mount tilt a is flipped too, which would mean rebuilding the mane on the other side. The mane is built leaning to one side, as real manes are, and they lie on the same side whichever lead the horse is on. I checked this in world space with node, over 16 blades and 64 phases. The blades are already 45-73 deg away from their own mirror image because of that one-sided mount and the larger rotation.z wave. The critic did not test the rotation.z wave, which is the mostly sideways one. The proposed fix (rx·m) moves the worst-case mirror error from 64.9 to 74.1 deg in gallop, 45.5 to 51.2 deg in canter, and 72.2 to 67.4 deg in race. So it does not make the right lead a mirror image, and in two of the three gaits it makes it worse. Physically, the main thing driving a galloping horse's mane is the up-and-down head and neck motion (pitch), which is the same on either lead. Only the small roll component (±1.2-1.4 deg here) depends on the lead. So keeping the flop the same on both leads is closer to a real horse than flipping it. The mane half of the finding is refuted.

3. What remains is the ears. Their phases depend on e.side, so the same ear flicks first on both leads. That ear is the left one for rotation.x (k=1 phases 0.1 vs 0.5) and the right one for rotation.z (k=2 phases 0.25 vs 0.05 in gallop). Also, +rotation.x tilts both ears toward +z, a sideways tilt of both ears together, and that does not flip with the lead. Computed against an exact mirror, the mismatch is about 1.8 deg in rx and 4-5.4 deg in rz. This is a cosmetic inconsistency, not an anatomy or motion error. A horse's ear movements depend on what it is paying attention to and each ear moves on its own; nothing ties them to the lead. The FEI reference covers footfall order only. The ear phases here are not in step with the roll either: the left ear's rx peaks 0.35 cycle away from the roll. The page sets one lead for every horse at once (state.lead / loc.lead, lines 3193 and 3719), so the two leads are never on screen side by side.

The accurate claim is in the correction field.

The mismatch is about 2-5 deg. This is a cosmetic consistency issue with no real-horse basis, because ear motion follows attention, not the lead. Mesh rotation.x is mostly a vertical flop (tip moves along about (0,-0.87,0.50)), not a sideways sway.
